﴿There is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah, and He knows its dwelling-place and its repository. All is in a clear Record.﴾: The word dābba here is general for every living being that needs provision. ﴿ʿalā Allāh﴾ is apparently obligatory, but it is actually a bounty; yet when He, exalted is He, guaranteed to bestow it upon them, He placed it within the scope of obligation. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿mustaqarrahā﴾ is where it takes refuge on the earth, and ﴿mustawdaʿahā﴾ is the place where it dies and is buried. He also related from him: mustaqarrahā is in the womb, and mustawdaʿahā is in the loins.

al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: mustaqarrahā is during the days of its life, and mustawdaʿahā is when it dies and when it is resurrected. It has also been said: mustaqarrahā is in Paradise or in the Fire, and mustawdaʿahā is in the grave. This is supported by ﴿How good a dwelling-place it is﴾ [al-Furqan 25:76] and ﴿How evil a dwelling-place it is﴾ [al-Furqan 25:66]. It has also been said: mustaqarr is where its deeds settle, and mustawdaʿ is where it will end up.

It has also been said: mustaqarr is what came into existence as a living being, and mustawdaʿ is what will come into existence after the mustaqarr. al-Zamakhshari said: mustaqarr is its place on the earth and its dwelling, and mustawdaʿ is where it existed before settling, whether from the loins, the womb, or the egg. End. Mustaqarr and mustawdaʿ may be verbal nouns, and they may be nouns of place. Mustawdaʿ may be a passive participle, since its verb is transitive, but mustaqarr cannot be, because its verb is intransitive. ﴿kullun﴾ means: each of the provision. The mustaqarr and mustawdaʿ are in the Preserved Tablet, meaning: its mention is written in it, clearly. It has also been said: the "Record" here is a metaphor for the knowledge of Allah, but taking it in its literal sense is better.

﴿He it is who created the heavens and the earth in six days, while His Throne was upon the water, in order to test you as to which of you is best in deed. And if you say, "Indeed you will be resurrected after death," those who disbelieve will surely say, "This is nothing but clear magic."﴾ ﴿And if We delay the punishment from them until a counted community, they will surely say, "What holds it back?" Unquestionably, on the day it comes to them, it will not be averted from them, and what they used to mock will surround them.﴾: When He, exalted is He, mentioned what indicates His being All-Knowing, He mentioned what indicates His being All-Powerful. The explanation of the first sentence was given in Surah Yunus. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿while His Throne was upon the water﴾ is: its estimated time is before the creation of the heavens and the earth, and in this is evidence that the water and the Throne were created before them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verses 5–11 (part 2 of 2):

Ka'b said: Allah created a green emerald (yaqutah khadra') and looked at it with awe (al-haybah), and it turned into water. Then He created the wind and placed the water on its back (matn), then He placed the Throne (al-'arsh) upon the water.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he was asked: "Upon what was the water?" He said: "It was upon the back of the wind."

The apparent reading is that the clause "li-yabluwakum" (so that He may test you) is connected to "khalaqa" (He created). Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, He created them for a profound wisdom, namely that He would make them dwellings for His servants, bestow upon them diverse kinds of blessings in them, and charge them with performing acts of obedience and avoiding acts of disobedience. Whoever gives thanks and obeys, He will reward; whoever disbelieves and disobeys, He will punish. Since this resembles the testing of one who tests, He said "li-yabluwakum," meaning: He will act toward you as one who tests does, to see how you act.

(If you say:) How is it permissible to make the act of testing dependent (ta'liq)? (I say:) Because testing contains the meaning of knowledge, since it is the way of Allah, so it is associated with it, as you say: "Look which of them is better in appearance (wajhan)," and "Listen which of them is better in voice (sawtan)," because looking and listening are among the means of knowledge. End of quote.

As for his words "and whoever disbelieves and disobeys, He punishes him," this is the subtle trace of Mu'tazilism (dasisat al-i'tizal). As for his saying "listen which of them is better in voice," I do not know of anyone who mentioned that "istama'" (listen) is subject to ta'liq; rather they mentioned, of non-mental verbs, only "sal" (ask) and "unzur" (look). The permissibility of ta'liq of the verb "ra'a" (to see, in the sense of visual perception) is a matter of disagreement among the Basrans.

It has also been said that "li-yabluwakum" is connected to a verb omitted in the text, the estimate being: "He informed of that so that He might test you," and the purpose of this interpretation is that these creatures were not created for the sake of humans.

It has been said: the estimated verb is: "And He created you so that He might test you." It has also been said: there are omitted clauses in the speech, the estimate being: "His creating them both was for benefits whose good returns to you in this world and not in the next, and He did that so that He might test you." The meaning of "Which of you is best in deed (ahsanu 'amalan)" is: Is this better or this?

Ibn Bahr said: It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Which of you is best in intellect, most scrupulous regarding the prohibitions of Allah, and quickest in obedience to Allah." And if this interpretation is indeed transmitted from the Messenger (ﷺ), one should not deviate from it.

Al-Hasan said: "most detached from Allah (azhad fi Allah)." Muqatil said: "most mindful of Allah (atqa li-Allah)." Al-Dahhak said: "most thankful (akthar shukran)."

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say:) How is it said "Which of you is best in deed," when the deeds of believers are what vary between good and better, whereas the deeds of believers and disbelievers vary between good and bad? (I say:) Those who are best in deed are the God-conscious (al-muttaqun), who are those who race to achieve what is Allah's aim from His servants. He singled them out for mention and disregarded those beyond them, honoring them and drawing attention to their rank, and so that this would be an alert for the listeners and an encouragement to attain their excellence. End of quote.

And if you say: it is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ). Isa al-Thaqafi read: "wa-la-in qultu" with a damma on the ta', as a report from Him, exalted is He, and the meaning is: "And if you (I) say," arguing for the resurrection after death, since in His saying, exalted is He, "And it is He who created," there is an indication of great power; so whenever He reports the occurrence of a possibility, it occurs without doubt, and He has reported the resurrection, so it is obligatory to accept it and be certain of its occurrence.

It was also read: "ayyukum" with a fatha on the hamza. Al-Zamakhshari said: Its aspect is that it may be from their saying: "Go to the market, for you may buy meat" (inna-ka tashtari lahman), in the sense of "la'alla-ka" (perhaps you), meaning: "If you say to them, 'Perhaps you will be resurrected,'" in the sense of: "Expect your resurrection and suppose it," they would affirm the statement by denying it, saying... And it is permissible that "qultu" be given the meaning of "dhakartu" (you mentioned), End of quote.

That is, with a fatha on the hamza, because it is in the position of the object of "dhakarta" (you mentioned). The apparent reference of "hadha" (this) is to the statement: that your statement "You will be resurrected" is nothing but magic (sihr), i.e., the falsity of this statement is like the falsity of magic. It may also be that it refers to what the sentence indicates of resurrection, i.e., that resurrection...

It has been said: they pointed with "hadha" to the Qur'an, which speaks of resurrection; so when they call it magic, the denial of what it contains of resurrection and other things is included under it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: They denied and said: "This is magic." This is a contradiction on their part: if it is acknowledged that the heavens and the earth were created by the Creator, the Originator of the heavens and the earth, then they are among those who acknowledge this, and yet they deny what is far easier than it, namely resurrection from the graves, since initiating creation is more difficult than restoring it, and since the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of people. End of quote.

al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah and a group of the Seven read: "sihrun" (magic). A group read: "sahir" (a magician), meaning: "and the magician is a liar, a falsifier."

"And if We delay" — Allah relates another kind of their falsehoods and mockery. The punishment here is the punishment of the Resurrection. It has also been said: the punishment of the Day of Badr. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: the killing of the mockers by Jibril. The apparent meaning is the promised punishment. The "ummah" here means a period of time, as Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid and the majority said, and its meaning is: "until a known time and appointed moment." "What holds it back?" is a question; they said it in the manner of denial and mockery. Al-Tabari said: the period was called "ummah" because within it a community (ummah) of people passes away and another arises; so it is, in this sense, a long period. Then he began the report by saying that it is a day which nothing can turn back or avert.

The apparent reading is that "yawma" is in the accusative, governed by "masrufan" (averted), so it is an operand of the predicate of "laysa" (not). This has been cited as evidence for permitting the fronting of the predicate of "laysa" over it; they said: because the fronting of the operand indicates the fronting of the operator. This doctrine is attributed to Sibawayh, and most Basrans hold it. But the Kufans and al-Mubarrad held that this is not permissible, and said: the permissibility of fronting the operand does not indicate the permissibility of fronting the operator.

Moreover, a prepositional adverbial phrase (zarf majrur) has more latitude in these two than in others, and they may occur where the operator cannot occur in them, such as: "Inna al-yawma Zayidan musafirun." I have examined a number of the diwans of the Arabs and did not find the fronting of the predicate of "laysa" over it, nor of its operand, except what the apparent meaning of this verse indicates, and the poet's saying: "He refuses, and his obstinacy only increases, and I was proud in secret; I do not advance." The explanation of the phrase "wa-haqa bihim" has already been given.

"And if We let man taste mercy from Us, then withdraw it from him, indeed he is despairing, ungrateful." "And if We let him taste bounty after adversity has touched him, he says: 'The evils have departed from me,' indeed he is exultant, boastful; except those who are patient and do righteous deeds—those, for them is forgiveness and a great reward."

When Allah mentioned the punishment of the disbelievers, and that however long delayed it must surely befall them, He mentioned what indicates their disbelief and that they deserve punishment, for they were created with ingratitude for Allah's blessings, and what follows from His kindness toward them of things unbecoming to them, namely their boasting over the servants of Allah. The apparent meaning is that "al-insan" here is a genus, the meaning being that this disposition is in the nature of people; then He excepted from them those whom the laws and faith guided to patience and righteous deeds, and therefore the exception is contiguous (muttasil) in His saying: "except those who are patient." It has been said: the intended "insan" here is the disbeliever.

It has been said: the intended one is a specific person. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, and it was concerning him that it was revealed. It has been said: 'Abd Allah ibn Umayyah al-Makhzumi, which al-Wahidi mentioned. On these two views the exception is disjunct (munqati'). The meaning of "mercy" (rahmah) is blessing, of health, security, and wealth.

"Then We withdrew it" means: We took it away from him.

"Laya'us" and "kafur" are intensive forms (sighat mubalaghah). The meaning: he is greatly despairing and abundantly so; he despairs that there will return to him the like of that blessing which was taken away, and he cuts off his hope in Allah's bounty without patience or submission to His decree. "Kafur": one who much denies the blessings Allah previously bestowed upon him. He mentioned the human condition when the blessing came first and was not preceded by harm, then mentioned his condition when blessing comes after harm.

The meaning of "the evils have departed" is: the calamities that distressed me. This statement implies both heedlessness and ignorance, for that is by Allah's favor, while he believes that it is mere coincidence or good fortune, and this is a corrupt belief.

"Indeed he is exultant": insolent, arrogant. This exultation is unrestricted, and therefore one characterized by it is blamed; and the Qur'an does not praise exultation except when restricted to what is good, as in His saying: "Rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty" (Al 'Imran: 170). The majority read "lafarihun" with a kasra on the ra', which is the analogical form of the active participle of the intransitive "fa'ila." A group read "lafaruhun" with a damma on the ra', as in your saying: "nadus" and "natus."

"Fakhr" (boasting) is his magnifying himself over people because of the blessing that befell him. Allah excepted the patient, meaning: in adversity, and those who do righteous deeds, among which is giving thanks for blessings. "Those, for them is forgiveness," for their sins, which entails the removal of punishment and deliverance from it; and "a great reward" is Paradise, which entails attaining the reward. He described the reward as "great" because of what it contains of everlasting bliss, the lifting of obligations, security from punishment, Allah's pleasure with them, and gazing upon His noble Face.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verses 5–11 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Surely they fold their breasts to hide from Him. Yet when they cover themselves with their garments, He knows what they conceal and what they reveal. Indeed, He is All-Knowing of what is within the breasts.﴾: It was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shuraygh, who would sit with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and swear that he loved him, while concealing the opposite of what he showed. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. He also related from him: it was revealed concerning people who were ashamed to relieve themselves in the open under the sky, and to have intercourse with their wives. It has also been said: it was revealed concerning some of the hypocrites who, when they passed by the Messenger (ﷺ), would bend their chest and back, lower their heads, and cover their faces so that they would not see the Messenger. This was said by 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad. It has also been said: it was revealed concerning a group who said, "If we close our doors, let down our curtains, cover ourselves with our garments and fold our chests, [in our enmity toward him], how will he know about us?" This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

It has also been said: they did this so that the voice of the Messenger (ﷺ) would not reach them and the Qur'an would not enter their ears. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. The word ﴿yathnūna﴾ is the imperfect of thana, and this is the reading of the majority. Sa'id ibn Jubayr read yuthnūna with a ḍamma on the yā', the imperfect of athna. As for ﴿ṣudūrahum﴾ with a fatḥa (naṣb), the author of al-Lawāmiḥ (a work on Qur'anic readings) said: "The meaning of ithnā' is not known in this context, unless it means: I found it folded (mathniyyah), like aḥmadtuhu and amjadtuhu. Perhaps he (the reader) opened the nūn, and this is something that was done to them. Thus the naṣb of ṣudūrahum would be by removing the preposition. It is also permissible that ṣudūruhum be in the nominative as a substitute, a badal al-ba'ḍ min al-kull (partial substitution: a part replacing the whole)." Abu al-Baqa' said: "Its past tense is athnā, and it is not known in the language, except that it is said that its meaning is: they presented them for folding, as one says, 'Have you sold the horse?' when you have offered it for sale."

Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn and his two sons Zayd and Muhammad, and his son Ja'far, Mujahid, Ibn Ya'mar, Nasr ibn 'Asim, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abza, al-Jahdari, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali, Abu Razin, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk read tathnūnī with a tā' (second person), the imperfect of athnawnī, on the pattern ifʿawʿala, like iʿshawshaba al-makān (the land became covered with grass). ﴿ṣudūruhum﴾ is in the nominative, meaning: "their breasts fold." Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Ya'mar and Ibn Abi Ishaq also read yathnūnī with a yā', and ﴿ṣudūruhum﴾ in the nominative, mentioned in the sense of the plural rather than the group. Ibn 'Abbas also read la-yathnūna with the emphatic lām in the predicate of inna, the yā' omitted for lightness, and ṣudūruhum was in the nominative. Ibn 'Abbas also, together with 'Urwa, Ibn Abi Abza, and al-A'sha, read yathabbanūna (or yaththannūna), whose pattern is yafʿawʿil from al-thann, from which ifʿawʿala is formed, and which is the dry, weak part of the pasture. Its root is yathnawnanu, meaning: the submission of their souls to something, as the dry plant bends. Or he meant the weakness of their faith and the sickness of their hearts. ﴿ṣudūruhum﴾ is in the nominative. 'Urwa and Mujahid also read in the same way, but with a hamza: yathnaʾinnu, like yaṭmaʾinnu, and ṣudūruhum in the nominative. This is a form in which the kasra was felt heavy on the waw, as it is said ashāḥa (he turned away).

It has also been said that yathnaʾinnu is yafʿaʾillu from the aforementioned thann, like taḥmārru and taṣfārru, so the alif was moved because of its meeting with the kasra, and it turned into a hamza. al-A'sha read yathnaʾūna, like yafʿalūna, with a hamzated lām, and ṣudūrahum in the accusative. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: "I do not know its basis, because it is said thaniytu, and I have not heard thana'tu." It is permissible that he changed the yā' into an alif according to the dialect of those who say aʿṭa'tu for aʿṭaytu, and then made it hamzated according to the dialect of those who say ﴿wa-lā al-ḍāllīn﴾ [al-Fatiha 1:7] (pronouncing the yā' as a hamza). Ibn 'Abbas read yathnawī with the thā' placed before the nūn, and without a nūn after the waw, on the pattern of tarʿawī. Abu Hatim said: "This reading is an error and does not hold up." He said this because he took the waw in this verb to be a root letter, and one does not say thanawtuhu fa-inthawā as one says ra'awtuhu, meaning I restrained him, so he turned away (fa-iṭ-ra'awā), and its pattern is if'alla.

Nasr ibn 'Asim, Ibn Ya'mar and Ibn Abi Ishaq read yanthūna, with the nūn placed before the thā'. These are ten readings for this word. The pronoun in ﴿innahum﴾ refers to some of the disbelievers present with the Messenger (ﷺ), meaning: they fold their chests against his enmity. al-Zamakhshari said: "(p-203) yathnūna ṣudūrahum means: they turn away from the truth and deviate from it, because whoever faces something presents his chest to it, and whoever turns away from it and deviates, folds his chest away from it and turns his side away from it. ﴿liyastakhfū minhu﴾ means: they wish to hide from Allah, so that they do not let His Messenger and the believers see their turning away. The parallel of the implied 'they wish' (yurīdūna), with the meaning returning to its implication, is the implication in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:63], meaning: he struck, and it parted. The meaning of ﴿alā ḥīna yastaghshūna thiyābahum﴾ is: and they wish to hide when they cover themselves with their garments, also out of aversion to hearing the words of Allah, like the saying of Nuh (peace be upon him): ﴿They put their fingers in their ears and covered themselves with their garments and persisted﴾ [Nuh 71:7]." End of quotation.

The pronoun in ﴿minhu﴾ refers to Allah. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is the most eloquent and most fitting in meaning." End.

It appears from some occasions of revelation that it refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), as Ibn 'Atiyya said. He said: "It is said that this verse was revealed concerning the disbelievers who, when they met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), would lower themselves, fold their chests like one hiding, turn their backs toward him, and cover their faces with their garments, out of distance from him and dislike of meeting him, while they thought that this would be hidden from him or from Allah, exalted is He. So the verse was revealed." End. On this basis, ﴿liyastakhfū﴾ is connected to the verb ﴿yathnūna﴾, and al-Hawfi said the same. It has also been said that it is a metaphor for the rancor and malice they concealed, as one says, "So-and-so folds his side over his enmity and folds his chest over it." The meaning of the verse is: surely they conceal enmity and hide it, thinking it will be hidden from Allah, mighty and majestic. He, exalted is He, knows what they conceal when they cover themselves and go to the extreme of concealment. Thus ﴿ḥīna﴾ is the object of the verb ﴿yaʿlamu﴾, as al-Hawfi said, and not of the implied verb proposed by al-Zamakhshari, which is: "and they wish to hide when they cover themselves with their garments." Abu al-Baqa' said: "﴿alā ḥīna﴾: the governing element of the adverbial phrase is omitted, meaning: alā ḥīna yastaghshūna thiyābahum yastakhfūna (when they cover themselves with their garments, they hide). It is also permissible that it be an adverbial of time for yaʿlamu."

It has also been said: some of them would bow to one another in whispers, slandering the Muslims, and their ignorance reached the point that they thought this would be hidden from Allah, exalted is He. Qatada said: "They are most hidden when they bend their backs and cover their garments, and conceal in their souls their resolve."

Mujahid said: "They fold them over disbelief." Ibn 'Abbas said: "They hide what is in their breasts of rancor." Qatada said: "They conceal so that they may hear the words of Allah." Ibn Zayd said: "They keep it secret when some of them confide in one another about the matter of the Messenger (ﷺ)."

It has also been said: they fold them out of shame before Allah, exalted is He. The meaning of yastaghshūna is: they make them into coverings. From this is the saying of al-Khansa':
"I graze the stars, though I was not charged with grazing them, and at times I cover myself with the surplus of my worn garments."

It has also been said: the intended meaning of "garments" is the night, and it is used figuratively for it because of the connection between them in covering, since the night covers as garments cover. From this is their saying: "The night is more concealing for the one who seeks secrecy (lil-wayl)." Ibn 'Abbas read: ('alā ḥīn yastaghshūna). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "From this usage is the saying of al-Nabigha:
"When I rebuked gray hair for my youth, and said: 'Would that I were sound,' while gray hair was restraining me."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "What they conceal in their hearts and what they declare with their mouths." It has also been said: what they conceal at night and what they declare by day. Ibn al-Anbari said: "Its meaning is that He knows their inner secrets as He knows their outward appearances."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "He means that there is no difference in His knowledge between their concealing and their declaring, so there is no way for them to reach what they wish of hiding, and Allah is aware of their folding of their chests and their covering themselves with their garments. Their hypocrisy is not hidden from Him." The author of al-Taḥrīr said: "What the context of the verse requires is that by what they conceal he means what their breasts harbor of polytheism, hypocrisy, rancor, envy, and hatred toward the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions, because all of that is among the deeds of the heart, and deeds of the heart are very hidden. By what they declare he means what they show of turning their backs on the Prophet (ﷺ), covering their garments, and stopping (p-204) their ears, and all of these are manifest actions that are not hidden."

﴿There is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah, and He knows its dwelling-place and its repository. All is in a clear Record.﴾: The word dābba here is general for every living being that needs provision. ﴿ʿalā Allāh﴾ is apparently obligatory, but it is actually a bounty; yet when He, exalted is He, guaranteed to bestow it upon them, He placed it within the scope of obligation. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿mustaqarrahā﴾ is where it takes refuge on the earth, and ﴿mustawdaʿahā﴾ is the place where it dies and is buried. He also related from him: mustaqarrahā is in the womb, and mustawdaʿahā is in the loins.

al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: mustaqarrahā is during the days of its life, and mustawdaʿahā is when it dies and when it is resurrected. It has also been said: mustaqarrahā is in Paradise or in the Fire, and mustawdaʿahā is in the grave. This is supported by ﴿How good a dwelling-place it is﴾ [al-Furqan 25:76] and ﴿How evil a dwelling-place it is﴾ [al-Furqan 25:66]. It has also been said: mustaqarr is where its deeds settle, and mustawdaʿ is where it will end up.

It has also been said: mustaqarr is what came into existence as a living being, and mustawdaʿ is what will come into existence after the mustaqarr. al-Zamakhshari said: mustaqarr is its place on the earth and its dwelling, and mustawdaʿ is where it existed before settling, whether from the loins, the womb, or the egg. End. Mustaqarr and mustawdaʿ may be verbal nouns, and they may be nouns of place. Mustawdaʿ may be a passive participle, since its verb is transitive, but mustaqarr cannot be, because its verb is intransitive. ﴿kullun﴾ means: each of the provision. The mustaqarr and mustawdaʿ are in the Preserved Tablet, meaning: its mention is written in it, clearly. It has also been said: the "Record" here is a metaphor for the knowledge of Allah, but taking it in its literal sense is better.

﴿He it is who created the heavens and the earth in six days, while His Throne was upon the water, in order to test you as to which of you is best in deed. And if you say, "Indeed you will be resurrected after death," those who disbelieve will surely say, "This is nothing but clear magic."﴾ ﴿And if We delay the punishment from them until a counted community, they will surely say, "What holds it back?" Unquestionably, on the day it comes to them, it will not be averted from them, and what they used to mock will surround them.﴾: When He, exalted is He, mentioned what indicates His being All-Knowing, He mentioned what indicates His being All-Powerful. The explanation of the first sentence was given in Surah Yunus. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿while His Throne was upon the water﴾ is: its estimated time is before the creation of the heavens and the earth, and in this is evidence that the water and the Throne were created before them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verses 5–11 (part 2 of 2):

Ka'b said: Allah created a green emerald (yaqutah khadra') and looked at it with awe (al-haybah), and it turned into water. Then He created the wind and placed the water on its back (matn), then He placed the Throne (al-'arsh) upon the water.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he was asked: "Upon what was the water?" He said: "It was upon the back of the wind."

The apparent reading is that the clause "li-yabluwakum" (so that He may test you) is connected to "khalaqa" (He created). Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, He created them for a profound wisdom, namely that He would make them dwellings for His servants, bestow upon them diverse kinds of blessings in them, and charge them with performing acts of obedience and avoiding acts of disobedience. Whoever gives thanks and obeys, He will reward; whoever disbelieves and disobeys, He will punish. Since this resembles the testing of one who tests, He said "li-yabluwakum," meaning: He will act toward you as one who tests does, to see how you act.

(If you say:) How is it permissible to make the act of testing dependent (ta'liq)? (I say:) Because testing contains the meaning of knowledge, since it is the way of Allah, so it is associated with it, as you say: "Look which of them is better in appearance (wajhan)," and "Listen which of them is better in voice (sawtan)," because looking and listening are among the means of knowledge. End of quote.

As for his words "and whoever disbelieves and disobeys, He punishes him," this is the subtle trace of Mu'tazilism (dasisat al-i'tizal). As for his saying "listen which of them is better in voice," I do not know of anyone who mentioned that "istama'" (listen) is subject to ta'liq; rather they mentioned, of non-mental verbs, only "sal" (ask) and "unzur" (look). The permissibility of ta'liq of the verb "ra'a" (to see, in the sense of visual perception) is a matter of disagreement among the Basrans.

It has also been said that "li-yabluwakum" is connected to a verb omitted in the text, the estimate being: "He informed of that so that He might test you," and the purpose of this interpretation is that these creatures were not created for the sake of humans.

It has been said: the estimated verb is: "And He created you so that He might test you." It has also been said: there are omitted clauses in the speech, the estimate being: "His creating them both was for benefits whose good returns to you in this world and not in the next, and He did that so that He might test you." The meaning of "Which of you is best in deed (ahsanu 'amalan)" is: Is this better or this?

Ibn Bahr said: It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Which of you is best in intellect, most scrupulous regarding the prohibitions of Allah, and quickest in obedience to Allah." And if this interpretation is indeed transmitted from the Messenger (ﷺ), one should not deviate from it.

Al-Hasan said: "most detached from Allah (azhad fi Allah)." Muqatil said: "most mindful of Allah (atqa li-Allah)." Al-Dahhak said: "most thankful (akthar shukran)."

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say:) How is it said "Which of you is best in deed," when the deeds of believers are what vary between good and better, whereas the deeds of believers and disbelievers vary between good and bad? (I say:) Those who are best in deed are the God-conscious (al-muttaqun), who are those who race to achieve what is Allah's aim from His servants. He singled them out for mention and disregarded those beyond them, honoring them and drawing attention to their rank, and so that this would be an alert for the listeners and an encouragement to attain their excellence. End of quote.

And if you say: it is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ). Isa al-Thaqafi read: "wa-la-in qultu" with a damma on the ta', as a report from Him, exalted is He, and the meaning is: "And if you (I) say," arguing for the resurrection after death, since in His saying, exalted is He, "And it is He who created," there is an indication of great power; so whenever He reports the occurrence of a possibility, it occurs without doubt, and He has reported the resurrection, so it is obligatory to accept it and be certain of its occurrence.

It was also read: "ayyukum" with a fatha on the hamza. Al-Zamakhshari said: Its aspect is that it may be from their saying: "Go to the market, for you may buy meat" (inna-ka tashtari lahman), in the sense of "la'alla-ka" (perhaps you), meaning: "If you say to them, 'Perhaps you will be resurrected,'" in the sense of: "Expect your resurrection and suppose it," they would affirm the statement by denying it, saying... And it is permissible that "qultu" be given the meaning of "dhakartu" (you mentioned), End of quote.

That is, with a fatha on the hamza, because it is in the position of the object of "dhakarta" (you mentioned). The apparent reference of "hadha" (this) is to the statement: that your statement "You will be resurrected" is nothing but magic (sihr), i.e., the falsity of this statement is like the falsity of magic. It may also be that it refers to what the sentence indicates of resurrection, i.e., that resurrection...

It has been said: they pointed with "hadha" to the Qur'an, which speaks of resurrection; so when they call it magic, the denial of what it contains of resurrection and other things is included under it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: They denied and said: "This is magic." This is a contradiction on their part: if it is acknowledged that the heavens and the earth were created by the Creator, the Originator of the heavens and the earth, then they are among those who acknowledge this, and yet they deny what is far easier than it, namely resurrection from the graves, since initiating creation is more difficult than restoring it, and since the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of people. End of quote.

al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah and a group of the Seven read: "sihrun" (magic). A group read: "sahir" (a magician), meaning: "and the magician is a liar, a falsifier."

"And if We delay" — Allah relates another kind of their falsehoods and mockery. The punishment here is the punishment of the Resurrection. It has also been said: the punishment of the Day of Badr. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: the killing of the mockers by Jibril. The apparent meaning is the promised punishment. The "ummah" here means a period of time, as Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid and the majority said, and its meaning is: "until a known time and appointed moment." "What holds it back?" is a question; they said it in the manner of denial and mockery. Al-Tabari said: the period was called "ummah" because within it a community (ummah) of people passes away and another arises; so it is, in this sense, a long period. Then he began the report by saying that it is a day which nothing can turn back or avert.

The apparent reading is that "yawma" is in the accusative, governed by "masrufan" (averted), so it is an operand of the predicate of "laysa" (not). This has been cited as evidence for permitting the fronting of the predicate of "laysa" over it; they said: because the fronting of the operand indicates the fronting of the operator. This doctrine is attributed to Sibawayh, and most Basrans hold it. But the Kufans and al-Mubarrad held that this is not permissible, and said: the permissibility of fronting the operand does not indicate the permissibility of fronting the operator.

Moreover, a prepositional adverbial phrase (zarf majrur) has more latitude in these two than in others, and they may occur where the operator cannot occur in them, such as: "Inna al-yawma Zayidan musafirun." I have examined a number of the diwans of the Arabs and did not find the fronting of the predicate of "laysa" over it, nor of its operand, except what the apparent meaning of this verse indicates, and the poet's saying: "He refuses, and his obstinacy only increases, and I was proud in secret; I do not advance." The explanation of the phrase "wa-haqa bihim" has already been given.

"And if We let man taste mercy from Us, then withdraw it from him, indeed he is despairing, ungrateful." "And if We let him taste bounty after adversity has touched him, he says: 'The evils have departed from me,' indeed he is exultant, boastful; except those who are patient and do righteous deeds—those, for them is forgiveness and a great reward."

When Allah mentioned the punishment of the disbelievers, and that however long delayed it must surely befall them, He mentioned what indicates their disbelief and that they deserve punishment, for they were created with ingratitude for Allah's blessings, and what follows from His kindness toward them of things unbecoming to them, namely their boasting over the servants of Allah. The apparent meaning is that "al-insan" here is a genus, the meaning being that this disposition is in the nature of people; then He excepted from them those whom the laws and faith guided to patience and righteous deeds, and therefore the exception is contiguous (muttasil) in His saying: "except those who are patient." It has been said: the intended "insan" here is the disbeliever.

It has been said: the intended one is a specific person. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, and it was concerning him that it was revealed. It has been said: 'Abd Allah ibn Umayyah al-Makhzumi, which al-Wahidi mentioned. On these two views the exception is disjunct (munqati'). The meaning of "mercy" (rahmah) is blessing, of health, security, and wealth.

"Then We withdrew it" means: We took it away from him.

"Laya'us" and "kafur" are intensive forms (sighat mubalaghah). The meaning: he is greatly despairing and abundantly so; he despairs that there will return to him the like of that blessing which was taken away, and he cuts off his hope in Allah's bounty without patience or submission to His decree. "Kafur": one who much denies the blessings Allah previously bestowed upon him. He mentioned the human condition when the blessing came first and was not preceded by harm, then mentioned his condition when blessing comes after harm.

The meaning of "the evils have departed" is: the calamities that distressed me. This statement implies both heedlessness and ignorance, for that is by Allah's favor, while he believes that it is mere coincidence or good fortune, and this is a corrupt belief.

"Indeed he is exultant": insolent, arrogant. This exultation is unrestricted, and therefore one characterized by it is blamed; and the Qur'an does not praise exultation except when restricted to what is good, as in His saying: "Rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty" (Al 'Imran: 170). The majority read "lafarihun" with a kasra on the ra', which is the analogical form of the active participle of the intransitive "fa'ila." A group read "lafaruhun" with a damma on the ra', as in your saying: "nadus" and "natus."

"Fakhr" (boasting) is his magnifying himself over people because of the blessing that befell him. Allah excepted the patient, meaning: in adversity, and those who do righteous deeds, among which is giving thanks for blessings. "Those, for them is forgiveness," for their sins, which entails the removal of punishment and deliverance from it; and "a great reward" is Paradise, which entails attaining the reward. He described the reward as "great" because of what it contains of everlasting bliss, the lifting of obligations, security from punishment, Allah's pleasure with them, and gazing upon His noble Face.

It is also permissible that ṣudūruhum be in the nominative as a substitute, a badal al-ba'ḍ min al-kull (partial substitution: a part replacing the whole)." Abu al-Baqa' said: "Its past tense is athnā, and it is not known in the language, except that it is said that its meaning is: they presented them for folding, as one says, 'Have you sold the horse?' when you have offered it for sale."

Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn and his two sons Zayd and Muhammad, and his son Ja'far, Mujahid, Ibn Ya'mar, Nasr ibn 'Asim, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abza, al-Jahdari, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali, Abu Razin, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk read tathnūnī with a tā' (second person), the imperfect of athnawnī, on the pattern ifʿawʿala, like iʿshawshaba al-makān (the land became covered with grass). ﴿ṣudūruhum﴾ is in the nominative, meaning: "their breasts fold." Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Ya'mar and Ibn Abi Ishaq also read yathnūnī with a yā', and ﴿ṣudūruhum﴾ in the nominative, mentioned in the sense of the plural rather than the group. Ibn 'Abbas also read la-yathnūna with the emphatic lām in the predicate of inna, the yā' omitted for lightness, and ṣudūruhum was in the nominative. Ibn 'Abbas also, together with 'Urwa, Ibn Abi Abza, and al-A'sha, read yathabbanūna (or yaththannūna), whose pattern is yafʿawʿil from al-thann, from which ifʿawʿala is formed, and which is the dry, weak part of the pasture. Its root is yathnawnanu, meaning: the submission of their souls to something, as the dry plant bends. Or he meant the weakness of their faith and the sickness of their hearts. ﴿ṣudūruhum﴾ is in the nominative. 'Urwa and Mujahid also read in the same way, but with a hamza: yathnaʾinnu, like yaṭmaʾinnu, and ṣudūruhum in the nominative. This is a form in which the kasra was felt heavy on the waw, as it is said ashāḥa (he turned away).

It has also been said that yathnaʾinnu is yafʿaʾillu from the aforementioned thann, like taḥmārru and taṣfārru, so the alif was moved because of its meeting with the kasra, and it turned into a hamza. al-A'sha read yathnaʾūna, like yafʿalūna, with a hamzated lām, and ṣudūrahum in the accusative. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: "I do not know its basis, because it is said thaniytu, and I have not heard thana'tu." It is permissible that he changed the yā' into an alif according to the dialect of those who say aʿṭa'tu for aʿṭaytu, and then made it hamzated according to the dialect of those who say ﴿wa-lā al-ḍāllīn﴾ [al-Fatiha 1:7] (pronouncing the yā' as a hamza). Ibn 'Abbas read yathnawī with the thā' placed before the nūn, and without a nūn after the waw, on the pattern of tarʿawī. Abu Hatim said: "This reading is an error and does not hold up." He said this because he took the waw in this verb to be a root letter, and one does not say thanawtuhu fa-inthawā as one says ra'awtuhu, meaning I restrained him, so he turned away (fa-iṭ-ra'awā), and its pattern is if'alla.

Nasr ibn 'Asim, Ibn Ya'mar and Ibn Abi Ishaq read yanthūna, with the nūn placed before the thā'. These are ten readings for this word. The pronoun in ﴿innahum﴾ refers to some of the disbelievers present with the Messenger (ﷺ), meaning: they fold their chests against his enmity. al-Zamakhshari said: "(p-203) yathnūna ṣudūrahum means: they turn away from the truth and deviate from it, because whoever faces something presents his chest to it, and whoever turns away from it and deviates, folds his chest away from it and turns his side away from it. ﴿liyastakhfū minhu﴾ means: they wish to hide from Allah, so that they do not let His Messenger and the believers see their turning away. The parallel of the implied 'they wish' (yurīdūna), with the meaning returning to its implication, is the implication in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:63], meaning: he struck, and it parted. The meaning of ﴿alā ḥīna yastaghshūna thiyābahum﴾ is: and they wish to hide when they cover themselves with their garments, also out of aversion to hearing the words of Allah, like the saying of Nuh (peace be upon him): ﴿They put their fingers in their ears and covered themselves with their garments and persisted﴾ [Nuh 71:7]." End of quotation.

The pronoun in ﴿minhu﴾ refers to Allah. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is the most eloquent and most fitting in meaning." End.

It appears from some occasions of revelation that it refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), as Ibn 'Atiyya said. He said: "It is said that this verse was revealed concerning the disbelievers who, when they met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), would lower themselves, fold their chests like one hiding, turn their backs toward him, and cover their faces with their garments, out of distance from him and dislike of meeting him, while they thought that this would be hidden from him or from Allah, exalted is He. So the verse was revealed." End. On this basis, ﴿liyastakhfū﴾ is connected to the verb ﴿yathnūna﴾, and al-Hawfi said the same. It has also been said that it is a metaphor for the rancor and malice they concealed, as one says, "So-and-so folds his side over his enmity and folds his chest over it." The meaning of the verse is: surely they conceal enmity and hide it, thinking it will be hidden from Allah, mighty and majestic. He, exalted is He, knows what they conceal when they cover themselves and go to the extreme of concealment. Thus ﴿ḥīna﴾ is the object of the verb ﴿yaʿlamu﴾, as al-Hawfi said, and not of the implied verb proposed by al-Zamakhshari, which is: "and they wish to hide when they cover themselves with their garments." Abu al-Baqa' said: "﴿alā ḥīna﴾: the governing element of the adverbial phrase is omitted, meaning: alā ḥīna yastaghshūna thiyābahum yastakhfūna (when they cover themselves with their garments, they hide). It is also permissible that it be an adverbial of time for yaʿlamu."

It has also been said: some of them would bow to one another in whispers, slandering the Muslims, and their ignorance reached the point that they thought this would be hidden from Allah, exalted is He. Qatada said: "They are most hidden when they bend their backs and cover their garments, and conceal in their souls their resolve."

Mujahid said: "They fold them over disbelief." Ibn 'Abbas said: "They hide what is in their breasts of rancor." Qatada said: "They conceal so that they may hear the words of Allah." Ibn Zayd said: "They keep it secret when some of them confide in one another about the matter of the Messenger (ﷺ)."

It has also been said: they fold them out of shame before Allah, exalted is He. The meaning of yastaghshūna is: they make them into coverings. From this is the saying of al-Khansa':
"I graze the stars, though I was not charged with grazing them, and at times I cover myself with the surplus of my worn garments."

It has also been said: the intended meaning of "garments" is the night, and it is used figuratively for it because of the connection between them in covering, since the night covers as garments cover. From this is their saying: "The night is more concealing for the one who seeks secrecy (lil-wayl)." Ibn 'Abbas read: ('alā ḥīn yastaghshūna). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "From this usage is the saying of al-Nabigha:
"When I rebuked gray hair for my youth, and said: 'Would that I were sound,' while gray hair was restraining me."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "What they conceal in their hearts and what they declare with their mouths." It has also been said: what they conceal at night and what they declare by day. Ibn al-Anbari said: "Its meaning is that He knows their inner secrets as He knows their outward appearances."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "He means that there is no difference in His knowledge between their concealing and their declaring, so there is no way for them to reach what they wish of hiding, and Allah is aware of their folding of their chests and their covering themselves with their garments. Their hypocrisy is not hidden from Him." The author of al-Taḥrīr said: "What the context of the verse requires is that by what they conceal he means what their breasts harbor of polytheism, hypocrisy, rancor, envy, and hatred toward the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions, because all of that is among the deeds of the heart, and deeds of the heart are very hidden. By what they declare he means what they show of turning their backs on the Prophet (ﷺ), covering their garments, and stopping (p-204) their ears, and all of these are manifest actions that are not hidden."

﴿There is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah, and He knows its dwelling-place and its repository. All is in a clear Record.﴾: The word dābba here is general for every living being that needs provision. ﴿ʿalā Allāh﴾ is apparently obligatory, but it is actually a bounty; yet when He, exalted is He, guaranteed to bestow it upon them, He placed it within the scope of obligation. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿mustaqarrahā﴾ is where it takes refuge on the earth, and ﴿mustawdaʿahā﴾ is the place where it dies and is buried. He also related from him: mustaqarrahā is in the womb, and mustawdaʿahā is in the loins.

al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: mustaqarrahā is during the days of its life, and mustawdaʿahā is when it dies and when it is resurrected. It has also been said: mustaqarrahā is in Paradise or in the Fire, and mustawdaʿahā is in the grave. This is supported by ﴿How good a dwelling-place it is﴾ [al-Furqan 25:76] and ﴿How evil a dwelling-place it is﴾ [al-Furqan 25:66]. It has also been said: mustaqarr is where its deeds settle, and mustawdaʿ is where it will end up.

It has also been said: mustaqarr is what came into existence as a living being, and mustawdaʿ is what will come into existence after the mustaqarr. al-Zamakhshari said: mustaqarr is its place on the earth and its dwelling, and mustawdaʿ is where it existed before settling, whether from the loins, the womb, or the egg. End. Mustaqarr and mustawdaʿ may be verbal nouns, and they may be nouns of place. Mustawdaʿ may be a passive participle, since its verb is transitive, but mustaqarr cannot be, because its verb is intransitive. ﴿kullun﴾ means: each of the provision. The mustaqarr and mustawdaʿ are in the Preserved Tablet, meaning: its mention is written in it, clearly. It has also been said: the "Record" here is a metaphor for the knowledge of Allah, but taking it in its literal sense is better.

﴿He it is who created the heavens and the earth in six days, while His Throne was upon the water, in order to test you as to which of you is best in deed. And if you say, "Indeed you will be resurrected after death," those who disbelieve will surely say, "This is nothing but clear magic."﴾ ﴿And if We delay the punishment from them until a counted community, they will surely say, "What holds it back?" Unquestionably, on the day it comes to them, it will not be averted from them, and what they used to mock will surround them.﴾: When He, exalted is He, mentioned what indicates His being All-Knowing, He mentioned what indicates His being All-Powerful. The explanation of the first sentence was given in Surah Yunus. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿while His Throne was upon the water﴾ is: its estimated time is before the creation of the heavens and the earth, and in this is evidence that the water and the Throne were created before them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verses 5–11 (part 2 of 2):

Ka'b said: Allah created a green emerald (yaqutah khadra') and looked at it with awe (al-haybah), and it turned into water. Then He created the wind and placed the water on its back (matn), then He placed the Throne (al-'arsh) upon the water.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he was asked: "Upon what was the water?" He said: "It was upon the back of the wind."

The apparent reading is that the clause "li-yabluwakum" (so that He may test you) is connected to "khalaqa" (He created). Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, He created them for a profound wisdom, namely that He would make them dwellings for His servants, bestow upon them diverse kinds of blessings in them, and charge them with performing acts of obedience and avoiding acts of disobedience. Whoever gives thanks and obeys, He will reward; whoever disbelieves and disobeys, He will punish. Since this resembles the testing of one who tests, He said "li-yabluwakum," meaning: He will act toward you as one who tests does, to see how you act.

(If you say:) How is it permissible to make the act of testing dependent (ta'liq)? (I say:) Because testing contains the meaning of knowledge, since it is the way of Allah, so it is associated with it, as you say: "Look which of them is better in appearance (wajhan)," and "Listen which of them is better in voice (sawtan)," because looking and listening are among the means of knowledge. End of quote.

As for his words "and whoever disbelieves and disobeys, He punishes him," this is the subtle trace of Mu'tazilism (dasisat al-i'tizal). As for his saying "listen which of them is better in voice," I do not know of anyone who mentioned that "istama'" (listen) is subject to ta'liq; rather they mentioned, of non-mental verbs, only "sal" (ask) and "unzur" (look). The permissibility of ta'liq of the verb "ra'a" (to see, in the sense of visual perception) is a matter of disagreement among the Basrans.

It has also been said that "li-yabluwakum" is connected to a verb omitted in the text, the estimate being: "He informed of that so that He might test you," and the purpose of this interpretation is that these creatures were not created for the sake of humans.

It has been said: the estimated verb is: "And He created you so that He might test you." It has also been said: there are omitted clauses in the speech, the estimate being: "His creating them both was for benefits whose good returns to you in this world and not in the next, and He did that so that He might test you." The meaning of "Which of you is best in deed (ahsanu 'amalan)" is: Is this better or this?

Ibn Bahr said: It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Which of you is best in intellect, most scrupulous regarding the prohibitions of Allah, and quickest in obedience to Allah." And if this interpretation is indeed transmitted from the Messenger (ﷺ), one should not deviate from it.

Al-Hasan said: "most detached from Allah (azhad fi Allah)." Muqatil said: "most mindful of Allah (atqa li-Allah)." Al-Dahhak said: "most thankful (akthar shukran)."

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say:) How is it said "Which of you is best in deed," when the deeds of believers are what vary between good and better, whereas the deeds of believers and disbelievers vary between good and bad? (I say:) Those who are best in deed are the God-conscious (al-muttaqun), who are those who race to achieve what is Allah's aim from His servants. He singled them out for mention and disregarded those beyond them, honoring them and drawing attention to their rank, and so that this would be an alert for the listeners and an encouragement to attain their excellence. End of quote.

And if you say: it is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ). Isa al-Thaqafi read: "wa-la-in qultu" with a damma on the ta', as a report from Him, exalted is He, and the meaning is: "And if you (I) say," arguing for the resurrection after death, since in His saying, exalted is He, "And it is He who created," there is an indication of great power; so whenever He reports the occurrence of a possibility, it occurs without doubt, and He has reported the resurrection, so it is obligatory to accept it and be certain of its occurrence.

It was also read: "ayyukum" with a fatha on the hamza. Al-Zamakhshari said: Its aspect is that it may be from their saying: "Go to the market, for you may buy meat" (inna-ka tashtari lahman), in the sense of "la'alla-ka" (perhaps you), meaning: "If you say to them, 'Perhaps you will be resurrected,'" in the sense of: "Expect your resurrection and suppose it," they would affirm the statement by denying it, saying... And it is permissible that "qultu" be given the meaning of "dhakartu" (you mentioned), End of quote.

That is, with a fatha on the hamza, because it is in the position of the object of "dhakarta" (you mentioned). The apparent reference of "hadha" (this) is to the statement: that your statement "You will be resurrected" is nothing but magic (sihr), i.e., the falsity of this statement is like the falsity of magic. It may also be that it refers to what the sentence indicates of resurrection, i.e., that resurrection...

It has been said: they pointed with "hadha" to the Qur'an, which speaks of resurrection; so when they call it magic, the denial of what it contains of resurrection and other things is included under it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: They denied and said: "This is magic." This is a contradiction on their part: if it is acknowledged that the heavens and the earth were created by the Creator, the Originator of the heavens and the earth, then they are among those who acknowledge this, and yet they deny what is far easier than it, namely resurrection from the graves, since initiating creation is more difficult than restoring it, and since the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of people. End of quote.

al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah and a group of the Seven read: "sihrun" (magic). A group read: "sahir" (a magician), meaning: "and the magician is a liar, a falsifier."

"And if We delay" — Allah relates another kind of their falsehoods and mockery. The punishment here is the punishment of the Resurrection. It has also been said: the punishment of the Day of Badr. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: the killing of the mockers by Jibril. The apparent meaning is the promised punishment. The "ummah" here means a period of time, as Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid and the majority said, and its meaning is: "until a known time and appointed moment." "What holds it back?" is a question; they said it in the manner of denial and mockery. Al-Tabari said: the period was called "ummah" because within it a community (ummah) of people passes away and another arises; so it is, in this sense, a long period. Then he began the report by saying that it is a day which nothing can turn back or avert.

The apparent reading is that "yawma" is in the accusative, governed by "masrufan" (averted), so it is an operand of the predicate of "laysa" (not). This has been cited as evidence for permitting the fronting of the predicate of "laysa" over it; they said: because the fronting of the operand indicates the fronting of the operator. This doctrine is attributed to Sibawayh, and most Basrans hold it. But the Kufans and al-Mubarrad held that this is not permissible, and said: the permissibility of fronting the operand does not indicate the permissibility of fronting the operator.

Moreover, a prepositional adverbial phrase (zarf majrur) has more latitude in these two than in others, and they may occur where the operator cannot occur in them, such as: "Inna al-yawma Zayidan musafirun." I have examined a number of the diwans of the Arabs and did not find the fronting of the predicate of "laysa" over it, nor of its operand, except what the apparent meaning of this verse indicates, and the poet's saying: "He refuses, and his obstinacy only increases, and I was proud in secret; I do not advance." The explanation of the phrase "wa-haqa bihim" has already been given.

"And if We let man taste mercy from Us, then withdraw it from him, indeed he is despairing, ungrateful." "And if We let him taste bounty after adversity has touched him, he says: 'The evils have departed from me,' indeed he is exultant, boastful; except those who are patient and do righteous deeds—those, for them is forgiveness and a great reward."

When Allah mentioned the punishment of the disbelievers, and that however long delayed it must surely befall them, He mentioned what indicates their disbelief and that they deserve punishment, for they were created with ingratitude for Allah's blessings, and what follows from His kindness toward them of things unbecoming to them, namely their boasting over the servants of Allah. The apparent meaning is that "al-insan" here is a genus, the meaning being that this disposition is in the nature of people; then He excepted from them those whom the laws and faith guided to patience and righteous deeds, and therefore the exception is contiguous (muttasil) in His saying: "except those who are patient." It has been said: the intended "insan" here is the disbeliever.

It has been said: the intended one is a specific person. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, and it was concerning him that it was revealed. It has been said: 'Abd Allah ibn Umayyah al-Makhzumi, which al-Wahidi mentioned. On these two views the exception is disjunct (munqati'). The meaning of "mercy" (rahmah) is blessing, of health, security, and wealth.

"Then We withdrew it" means: We took it away from him.

"Laya'us" and "kafur" are intensive forms (sighat mubalaghah). The meaning: he is greatly despairing and abundantly so; he despairs that there will return to him the like of that blessing which was taken away, and he cuts off his hope in Allah's bounty without patience or submission to His decree. "Kafur": one who much denies the blessings Allah previously bestowed upon him. He mentioned the human condition when the blessing came first and was not preceded by harm, then mentioned his condition when blessing comes after harm.

The meaning of "the evils have departed" is: the calamities that distressed me. This statement implies both heedlessness and ignorance, for that is by Allah's favor, while he believes that it is mere coincidence or good fortune, and this is a corrupt belief.

"Indeed he is exultant": insolent, arrogant. This exultation is unrestricted, and therefore one characterized by it is blamed; and the Qur'an does not praise exultation except when restricted to what is good, as in His saying: "Rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty" (Al 'Imran: 170). The majority read "lafarihun" with a kasra on the ra', which is the analogical form of the active participle of the intransitive "fa'ila." A group read "lafaruhun" with a damma on the ra', as in your saying: "nadus" and "natus."

"Fakhr" (boasting) is his magnifying himself over people because of the blessing that befell him. Allah excepted the patient, meaning: in adversity, and those who do righteous deeds, among which is giving thanks for blessings. "Those, for them is forgiveness," for their sins, which entails the removal of punishment and deliverance from it; and "a great reward" is Paradise, which entails attaining the reward. He described the reward as "great" because of what it contains of everlasting bliss, the lifting of obligations, security from punishment, Allah's pleasure with them, and gazing upon His noble Face.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verses 5–11 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Surely they fold their breasts to hide from Him. Yet when they cover themselves with their garments, He knows what they conceal and what they reveal. Indeed, He is All-Knowing of what is within the breasts.﴾: It was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shuraygh, who would sit with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and swear that he loved him, while concealing the opposite of what he showed. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. He also related from him: it was revealed concerning people who were ashamed to relieve themselves in the open under the sky, and to have intercourse with their wives. It has also been said: it was revealed concerning some of the hypocrites who, when they passed by the Messenger (ﷺ), would bend their chest and back, lower their heads, and cover their faces so that they would not see the Messenger. This was said by 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad. It has also been said: it was revealed concerning a group who said, "If we close our doors, let down our curtains, cover ourselves with our garments and fold our chests, [in our enmity toward him], how will he know about us?" This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

It has also been said: they did this so that the voice of the Messenger (ﷺ) would not reach them and the Qur'an would not enter their ears. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. The word ﴿yathnūna﴾ is the imperfect of thana, and this is the reading of the majority. Sa'id ibn Jubayr read yuthnūna with a ḍamma on the yā', the imperfect of athna. As for ﴿ṣudūrahum﴾ with a fatḥa (naṣb), the author of al-Lawāmiḥ (a work on Qur'anic readings) said: "The meaning of ithnā' is not known in this context, unless it means: I found it folded (mathniyyah), like aḥmadtuhu and amjadtuhu. Perhaps he (the reader) opened the nūn, and this is something that was done to them. Thus the naṣb of ṣudūrahum would be by removing the preposition. It is also permissible that ṣudūruhum be in the nominative as a substitute, a badal al-ba'ḍ min al-kull (partial substitution: a part replacing the whole)." Abu al-Baqa' said: "Its past tense is athnā, and it is not known in the language, except that it is said that its meaning is: they presented them for folding, as one says, 'Have you sold the horse?' when you have offered it for sale."

Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn and his two sons Zayd and Muhammad, and his son Ja'far, Mujahid, Ibn Ya'mar, Nasr ibn 'Asim, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abza, al-Jahdari, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali, Abu Razin, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk read tathnūnī with a tā' (second person), the imperfect of athnawnī, on the pattern ifʿawʿala, like iʿshawshaba al-makān (the land became covered with grass). ﴿ṣudūruhum﴾ is in the nominative, meaning: "their breasts fold." Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Ya'mar and Ibn Abi Ishaq also read yathnūnī with a yā', and ﴿ṣudūruhum﴾ in the nominative, mentioned in the sense of the plural rather than the group. Ibn 'Abbas also read la-yathnūna with the emphatic lām in the predicate of inna, the yā' omitted for lightness, and ṣudūruhum was in the nominative. Ibn 'Abbas also, together with 'Urwa, Ibn Abi Abza, and al-A'sha, read yathabbanūna (or yaththannūna), whose pattern is yafʿawʿil from al-thann, from which ifʿawʿala is formed, and which is the dry, weak part of the pasture. Its root is yathnawnanu, meaning: the submission of their souls to something, as the dry plant bends. Or he meant the weakness of their faith and the sickness of their hearts. ﴿ṣudūruhum﴾ is in the nominative. 'Urwa and Mujahid also read in the same way, but with a hamza: yathnaʾinnu, like yaṭmaʾinnu, and ṣudūruhum in the nominative. This is a form in which the kasra was felt heavy on the waw, as it is said ashāḥa (he turned away).

It has also been said that yathnaʾinnu is yafʿaʾillu from the aforementioned thann, like taḥmārru and taṣfārru, so the alif was moved because of its meeting with the kasra, and it turned into a hamza. al-A'sha read yathnaʾūna, like yafʿalūna, with a hamzated lām, and ṣudūrahum in the accusative. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: "I do not know its basis, because it is said thaniytu, and I have not heard thana'tu." It is permissible that he changed the yā' into an alif according to the dialect of those who say aʿṭa'tu for aʿṭaytu, and then made it hamzated according to the dialect of those who say ﴿wa-lā al-ḍāllīn﴾ [al-Fatiha 1:7] (pronouncing the yā' as a hamza). Ibn 'Abbas read yathnawī with the thā' placed before the nūn, and without a nūn after the waw, on the pattern of tarʿawī. Abu Hatim said: "This reading is an error and does not hold up." He said this because he took the waw in this verb to be a root letter, and one does not say thanawtuhu fa-inthawā as one says ra'awtuhu, meaning I restrained him, so he turned away (fa-iṭ-ra'awā), and its pattern is if'alla.

Nasr ibn 'Asim, Ibn Ya'mar and Ibn Abi Ishaq read yanthūna, with the nūn placed before the thā'. These are ten readings for this word. The pronoun in ﴿innahum﴾ refers to some of the disbelievers present with the Messenger (ﷺ), meaning: they fold their chests against his enmity. al-Zamakhshari said: "(p-203) yathnūna ṣudūrahum means: they turn away from the truth and deviate from it, because whoever faces something presents his chest to it, and whoever turns away from it and deviates, folds his chest away from it and turns his side away from it. ﴿liyastakhfū minhu﴾ means: they wish to hide from Allah, so that they do not let His Messenger and the believers see their turning away. The parallel of the implied 'they wish' (yurīdūna), with the meaning returning to its implication, is the implication in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:63], meaning: he struck, and it parted. The meaning of ﴿alā ḥīna yastaghshūna thiyābahum﴾ is: and they wish to hide when they cover themselves with their garments, also out of aversion to hearing the words of Allah, like the saying of Nuh (peace be upon him): ﴿They put their fingers in their ears and covered themselves with their garments and persisted﴾ [Nuh 71:7]." End of quotation.

The pronoun in ﴿minhu﴾ refers to Allah. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is the most eloquent and most fitting in meaning." End.

It appears from some occasions of revelation that it refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), as Ibn 'Atiyya said. He said: "It is said that this verse was revealed concerning the disbelievers who, when they met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), would lower themselves, fold their chests like one hiding, turn their backs toward him, and cover their faces with their garments, out of distance from him and dislike of meeting him, while they thought that this would be hidden from him or from Allah, exalted is He. So the verse was revealed." End. On this basis, ﴿liyastakhfū﴾ is connected to the verb ﴿yathnūna﴾, and al-Hawfi said the same. It has also been said that it is a metaphor for the rancor and malice they concealed, as one says, "So-and-so folds his side over his enmity and folds his chest over it." The meaning of the verse is: surely they conceal enmity and hide it, thinking it will be hidden from Allah, mighty and majestic. He, exalted is He, knows what they conceal when they cover themselves and go to the extreme of concealment. Thus ﴿ḥīna﴾ is the object of the verb ﴿yaʿlamu﴾, as al-Hawfi said, and not of the implied verb proposed by al-Zamakhshari, which is: "and they wish to hide when they cover themselves with their garments." Abu al-Baqa' said: "﴿alā ḥīna﴾: the governing element of the adverbial phrase is omitted, meaning: alā ḥīna yastaghshūna thiyābahum yastakhfūna (when they cover themselves with their garments, they hide). It is also permissible that it be an adverbial of time for yaʿlamu."

It has also been said: some of them would bow to one another in whispers, slandering the Muslims, and their ignorance reached the point that they thought this would be hidden from Allah, exalted is He. Qatada said: "They are most hidden when they bend their backs and cover their garments, and conceal in their souls their resolve."

Mujahid said: "They fold them over disbelief." Ibn 'Abbas said: "They hide what is in their breasts of rancor." Qatada said: "They conceal so that they may hear the words of Allah." Ibn Zayd said: "They keep it secret when some of them confide in one another about the matter of the Messenger (ﷺ)."

It has also been said: they fold them out of shame before Allah, exalted is He. The meaning of yastaghshūna is: they make them into coverings. From this is the saying of al-Khansa':
"I graze the stars, though I was not charged with grazing them, and at times I cover myself with the surplus of my worn garments."

It has also been said: the intended meaning of "garments" is the night, and it is used figuratively for it because of the connection between them in covering, since the night covers as garments cover. From this is their saying: "The night is more concealing for the one who seeks secrecy (lil-wayl)." Ibn 'Abbas read: ('alā ḥīn yastaghshūna). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "From this usage is the saying of al-Nabigha:
"When I rebuked gray hair for my youth, and said: 'Would that I were sound,' while gray hair was restraining me."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "What they conceal in their hearts and what they declare with their mouths." It has also been said: what they conceal at night and what they declare by day. Ibn al-Anbari said: "Its meaning is that He knows their inner secrets as He knows their outward appearances."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "He means that there is no difference in His knowledge between their concealing and their declaring, so there is no way for them to reach what they wish of hiding, and Allah is aware of their folding of their chests and their covering themselves with their garments. Their hypocrisy is not hidden from Him." The author of al-Taḥrīr said: "What the context of the verse requires is that by what they conceal he means what their breasts harbor of polytheism, hypocrisy, rancor, envy, and hatred toward the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions, because all of that is among the deeds of the heart, and deeds of the heart are very hidden. By what they declare he means what they show of turning their backs on the Prophet (ﷺ), covering their garments, and stopping (p-204) their ears, and all of these are manifest actions that are not hidden."

﴿There is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah, and He knows its dwelling-place and its repository. All is in a clear Record.﴾: The word dābba here is general for every living being that needs provision. ﴿ʿalā Allāh﴾ is apparently obligatory, but it is actually a bounty; yet when He, exalted is He, guaranteed to bestow it upon them, He placed it within the scope of obligation. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿mustaqarrahā﴾ is where it takes refuge on the earth, and ﴿mustawdaʿahā﴾ is the place where it dies and is buried. He also related from him: mustaqarrahā is in the womb, and mustawdaʿahā is in the loins.

al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: mustaqarrahā is during the days of its life, and mustawdaʿahā is when it dies and when it is resurrected. It has also been said: mustaqarrahā is in Paradise or in the Fire, and mustawdaʿahā is in the grave. This is supported by ﴿How good a dwelling-place it is﴾ [al-Furqan 25:76] and ﴿How evil a dwelling-place it is﴾ [al-Furqan 25:66]. It has also been said: mustaqarr is where its deeds settle, and mustawdaʿ is where it will end up.

It has also been said: mustaqarr is what came into existence as a living being, and mustawdaʿ is what will come into existence after the mustaqarr. al-Zamakhshari said: mustaqarr is its place on the earth and its dwelling, and mustawdaʿ is where it existed before settling, whether from the loins, the womb, or the egg. End. Mustaqarr and mustawdaʿ may be verbal nouns, and they may be nouns of place. Mustawdaʿ may be a passive participle, since its verb is transitive, but mustaqarr cannot be, because its verb is intransitive. ﴿kullun﴾ means: each of the provision. The mustaqarr and mustawdaʿ are in the Preserved Tablet, meaning: its mention is written in it, clearly. It has also been said: the "Record" here is a metaphor for the knowledge of Allah, but taking it in its literal sense is better.

﴿He it is who created the heavens and the earth in six days, while His Throne was upon the water, in order to test you as to which of you is best in deed. And if you say, "Indeed you will be resurrected after death," those who disbelieve will surely say, "This is nothing but clear magic."﴾ ﴿And if We delay the punishment from them until a counted community, they will surely say, "What holds it back?" Unquestionably, on the day it comes to them, it will not be averted from them, and what they used to mock will surround them.﴾: When He, exalted is He, mentioned what indicates His being All-Knowing, He mentioned what indicates His being All-Powerful. The explanation of the first sentence was given in Surah Yunus. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿while His Throne was upon the water﴾ is: its estimated time is before the creation of the heavens and the earth, and in this is evidence that the water and the Throne were created before them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verses 5–11 (part 2 of 2):

Ka'b said: Allah created a green emerald (yaqutah khadra') and looked at it with awe (al-haybah), and it turned into water. Then He created the wind and placed the water on its back (matn), then He placed the Throne (al-'arsh) upon the water.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he was asked: "Upon what was the water?" He said: "It was upon the back of the wind."

The apparent reading is that the clause "li-yabluwakum" (so that He may test you) is connected to "khalaqa" (He created). Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, He created them for a profound wisdom, namely that He would make them dwellings for His servants, bestow upon them diverse kinds of blessings in them, and charge them with performing acts of obedience and avoiding acts of disobedience. Whoever gives thanks and obeys, He will reward; whoever disbelieves and disobeys, He will punish. Since this resembles the testing of one who tests, He said "li-yabluwakum," meaning: He will act toward you as one who tests does, to see how you act.

(If you say:) How is it permissible to make the act of testing dependent (ta'liq)? (I say:) Because testing contains the meaning of knowledge, since it is the way of Allah, so it is associated with it, as you say: "Look which of them is better in appearance (wajhan)," and "Listen which of them is better in voice (sawtan)," because looking and listening are among the means of knowledge. End of quote.

As for his words "and whoever disbelieves and disobeys, He punishes him," this is the subtle trace of Mu'tazilism (dasisat al-i'tizal). As for his saying "listen which of them is better in voice," I do not know of anyone who mentioned that "istama'" (listen) is subject to ta'liq; rather they mentioned, of non-mental verbs, only "sal" (ask) and "unzur" (look). The permissibility of ta'liq of the verb "ra'a" (to see, in the sense of visual perception) is a matter of disagreement among the Basrans.

It has also been said that "li-yabluwakum" is connected to a verb omitted in the text, the estimate being: "He informed of that so that He might test you," and the purpose of this interpretation is that these creatures were not created for the sake of humans.

It has been said: the estimated verb is: "And He created you so that He might test you." It has also been said: there are omitted clauses in the speech, the estimate being: "His creating them both was for benefits whose good returns to you in this world and not in the next, and He did that so that He might test you." The meaning of "Which of you is best in deed (ahsanu 'amalan)" is: Is this better or this?

Ibn Bahr said: It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Which of you is best in intellect, most scrupulous regarding the prohibitions of Allah, and quickest in obedience to Allah." And if this interpretation is indeed transmitted from the Messenger (ﷺ), one should not deviate from it.

Al-Hasan said: "most detached from Allah (azhad fi Allah)." Muqatil said: "most mindful of Allah (atqa li-Allah)." Al-Dahhak said: "most thankful (akthar shukran)."

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say:) How is it said "Which of you is best in deed," when the deeds of believers are what vary between good and better, whereas the deeds of believers and disbelievers vary between good and bad? (I say:) Those who are best in deed are the God-conscious (al-muttaqun), who are those who race to achieve what is Allah's aim from His servants. He singled them out for mention and disregarded those beyond them, honoring them and drawing attention to their rank, and so that this would be an alert for the listeners and an encouragement to attain their excellence. End of quote.

And if you say: it is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ). Isa al-Thaqafi read: "wa-la-in qultu" with a damma on the ta', as a report from Him, exalted is He, and the meaning is: "And if you (I) say," arguing for the resurrection after death, since in His saying, exalted is He, "And it is He who created," there is an indication of great power; so whenever He reports the occurrence of a possibility, it occurs without doubt, and He has reported the resurrection, so it is obligatory to accept it and be certain of its occurrence.

It was also read: "ayyukum" with a fatha on the hamza. Al-Zamakhshari said: Its aspect is that it may be from their saying: "Go to the market, for you may buy meat" (inna-ka tashtari lahman), in the sense of "la'alla-ka" (perhaps you), meaning: "If you say to them, 'Perhaps you will be resurrected,'" in the sense of: "Expect your resurrection and suppose it," they would affirm the statement by denying it, saying...
