And it is permissible that "qultu" be given the meaning of "dhakartu" (you mentioned), End of quote.

That is, with a fatha on the hamza, because it is in the position of the object of "dhakarta" (you mentioned). The apparent reference of "hadha" (this) is to the statement: that your statement "You will be resurrected" is nothing but magic (sihr), i.e., the falsity of this statement is like the falsity of magic. It may also be that it refers to what the sentence indicates of resurrection, i.e., that resurrection...

It has been said: they pointed with "hadha" to the Qur'an, which speaks of resurrection; so when they call it magic, the denial of what it contains of resurrection and other things is included under it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: They denied and said: "This is magic." This is a contradiction on their part: if it is acknowledged that the heavens and the earth were created by the Creator, the Originator of the heavens and the earth, then they are among those who acknowledge this, and yet they deny what is far easier than it, namely resurrection from the graves, since initiating creation is more difficult than restoring it, and since the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of people. End of quote.

al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah and a group of the Seven read: "sihrun" (magic). A group read: "sahir" (a magician), meaning: "and the magician is a liar, a falsifier."

"And if We delay" — Allah relates another kind of their falsehoods and mockery. The punishment here is the punishment of the Resurrection. It has also been said: the punishment of the Day of Badr. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: the killing of the mockers by Jibril. The apparent meaning is the promised punishment. The "ummah" here means a period of time, as Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid and the majority said, and its meaning is: "until a known time and appointed moment." "What holds it back?" is a question; they said it in the manner of denial and mockery. Al-Tabari said: the period was called "ummah" because within it a community (ummah) of people passes away and another arises; so it is, in this sense, a long period. Then he began the report by saying that it is a day which nothing can turn back or avert.

The apparent reading is that "yawma" is in the accusative, governed by "masrufan" (averted), so it is an operand of the predicate of "laysa" (not). This has been cited as evidence for permitting the fronting of the predicate of "laysa" over it; they said: because the fronting of the operand indicates the fronting of the operator. This doctrine is attributed to Sibawayh, and most Basrans hold it. But the Kufans and al-Mubarrad held that this is not permissible, and said: the permissibility of fronting the operand does not indicate the permissibility of fronting the operator.

Moreover, a prepositional adverbial phrase (zarf majrur) has more latitude in these two than in others, and they may occur where the operator cannot occur in them, such as: "Inna al-yawma Zayidan musafirun." I have examined a number of the diwans of the Arabs and did not find the fronting of the predicate of "laysa" over it, nor of its operand, except what the apparent meaning of this verse indicates, and the poet's saying: "He refuses, and his obstinacy only increases, and I was proud in secret; I do not advance." The explanation of the phrase "wa-haqa bihim" has already been given.

"And if We let man taste mercy from Us, then withdraw it from him, indeed he is despairing, ungrateful." "And if We let him taste bounty after adversity has touched him, he says: 'The evils have departed from me,' indeed he is exultant, boastful; except those who are patient and do righteous deeds—those, for them is forgiveness and a great reward."

When Allah mentioned the punishment of the disbelievers, and that however long delayed it must surely befall them, He mentioned what indicates their disbelief and that they deserve punishment, for they were created with ingratitude for Allah's blessings, and what follows from His kindness toward them of things unbecoming to them, namely their boasting over the servants of Allah. The apparent meaning is that "al-insan" here is a genus, the meaning being that this disposition is in the nature of people; then He excepted from them those whom the laws and faith guided to patience and righteous deeds, and therefore the exception is contiguous (muttasil) in His saying: "except those who are patient." It has been said: the intended "insan" here is the disbeliever.

It has been said: the intended one is a specific person. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, and it was concerning him that it was revealed. It has been said: 'Abd Allah ibn Umayyah al-Makhzumi, which al-Wahidi mentioned. On these two views the exception is disjunct (munqati'). The meaning of "mercy" (rahmah) is blessing, of health, security, and wealth.

"Then We withdrew it" means: We took it away from him.

"Laya'us" and "kafur" are intensive forms (sighat mubalaghah). The meaning: he is greatly despairing and abundantly so; he despairs that there will return to him the like of that blessing which was taken away, and he cuts off his hope in Allah's bounty without patience or submission to His decree. "Kafur": one who much denies the blessings Allah previously bestowed upon him. He mentioned the human condition when the blessing came first and was not preceded by harm, then mentioned his condition when blessing comes after harm.

The meaning of "the evils have departed" is: the calamities that distressed me. This statement implies both heedlessness and ignorance, for that is by Allah's favor, while he believes that it is mere coincidence or good fortune, and this is a corrupt belief.

"Indeed he is exultant": insolent, arrogant. This exultation is unrestricted, and therefore one characterized by it is blamed; and the Qur'an does not praise exultation except when restricted to what is good, as in His saying: "Rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty" (Al 'Imran: 170). The majority read "lafarihun" with a kasra on the ra', which is the analogical form of the active participle of the intransitive "fa'ila." A group read "lafaruhun" with a damma on the ra', as in your saying: "nadus" and "natus."

"Fakhr" (boasting) is his magnifying himself over people because of the blessing that befell him. Allah excepted the patient, meaning: in adversity, and those who do righteous deeds, among which is giving thanks for blessings. "Those, for them is forgiveness," for their sins, which entails the removal of punishment and deliverance from it; and "a great reward" is Paradise, which entails attaining the reward. He described the reward as "great" because of what it contains of everlasting bliss, the lifting of obligations, security from punishment, Allah's pleasure with them, and gazing upon His noble Face.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verses 5–11 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Surely they fold their breasts to hide from Him. Yet when they cover themselves with their garments, He knows what they conceal and what they reveal. Indeed, He is All-Knowing of what is within the breasts.﴾: It was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shuraygh, who would sit with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and swear that he loved him, while concealing the opposite of what he showed. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. He also related from him: it was revealed concerning people who were ashamed to relieve themselves in the open under the sky, and to have intercourse with their wives. It has also been said: it was revealed concerning some of the hypocrites who, when they passed by the Messenger (ﷺ), would bend their chest and back, lower their heads, and cover their faces so that they would not see the Messenger. This was said by 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad. It has also been said: it was revealed concerning a group who said, "If we close our doors, let down our curtains, cover ourselves with our garments and fold our chests, [in our enmity toward him], how will he know about us?" This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

It has also been said: they did this so that the voice of the Messenger (ﷺ) would not reach them and the Qur'an would not enter their ears. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. The word ﴿yathnūna﴾ is the imperfect of thana, and this is the reading of the majority. Sa'id ibn Jubayr read yuthnūna with a ḍamma on the yā', the imperfect of athna. As for ﴿ṣudūrahum﴾ with a fatḥa (naṣb), the author of al-Lawāmiḥ (a work on Qur'anic readings) said: "The meaning of ithnā' is not known in this context, unless it means: I found it folded (mathniyyah), like aḥmadtuhu and amjadtuhu. Perhaps he (the reader) opened the nūn, and this is something that was done to them. Thus the naṣb of ṣudūrahum would be by removing the preposition. It is also permissible that ṣudūruhum be in the nominative as a substitute, a badal al-ba'ḍ min al-kull (partial substitution: a part replacing the whole)." Abu al-Baqa' said: "Its past tense is athnā, and it is not known in the language, except that it is said that its meaning is: they presented them for folding, as one says, 'Have you sold the horse?' when you have offered it for sale."

Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn and his two sons Zayd and Muhammad, and his son Ja'far, Mujahid, Ibn Ya'mar, Nasr ibn 'Asim, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abza, al-Jahdari, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali, Abu Razin, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk read tathnūnī with a tā' (second person), the imperfect of athnawnī, on the pattern ifʿawʿala, like iʿshawshaba al-makān (the land became covered with grass). ﴿ṣudūruhum﴾ is in the nominative, meaning: "their breasts fold." Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Ya'mar and Ibn Abi Ishaq also read yathnūnī with a yā', and ﴿ṣudūruhum﴾ in the nominative, mentioned in the sense of the plural rather than the group. Ibn 'Abbas also read la-yathnūna with the emphatic lām in the predicate of inna, the yā' omitted for lightness, and ṣudūruhum was in the nominative. Ibn 'Abbas also, together with 'Urwa, Ibn Abi Abza, and al-A'sha, read yathabbanūna (or yaththannūna), whose pattern is yafʿawʿil from al-thann, from which ifʿawʿala is formed, and which is the dry, weak part of the pasture. Its root is yathnawnanu, meaning: the submission of their souls to something, as the dry plant bends. Or he meant the weakness of their faith and the sickness of their hearts. ﴿ṣudūruhum﴾ is in the nominative. 'Urwa and Mujahid also read in the same way, but with a hamza: yathnaʾinnu, like yaṭmaʾinnu, and ṣudūruhum in the nominative. This is a form in which the kasra was felt heavy on the waw, as it is said ashāḥa (he turned away).

It has also been said that yathnaʾinnu is yafʿaʾillu from the aforementioned thann, like taḥmārru and taṣfārru, so the alif was moved because of its meeting with the kasra, and it turned into a hamza. al-A'sha read yathnaʾūna, like yafʿalūna, with a hamzated lām, and ṣudūrahum in the accusative. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: "I do not know its basis, because it is said thaniytu, and I have not heard thana'tu." It is permissible that he changed the yā' into an alif according to the dialect of those who say aʿṭa'tu for aʿṭaytu, and then made it hamzated according to the dialect of those who say ﴿wa-lā al-ḍāllīn﴾ [al-Fatiha 1:7] (pronouncing the yā' as a hamza). Ibn 'Abbas read yathnawī with the thā' placed before the nūn, and without a nūn after the waw, on the pattern of tarʿawī. Abu Hatim said: "This reading is an error and does not hold up." He said this because he took the waw in this verb to be a root letter, and one does not say thanawtuhu fa-inthawā as one says ra'awtuhu, meaning I restrained him, so he turned away (fa-iṭ-ra'awā), and its pattern is if'alla.

Nasr ibn 'Asim, Ibn Ya'mar and Ibn Abi Ishaq read yanthūna, with the nūn placed before the thā'. These are ten readings for this word. The pronoun in ﴿innahum﴾ refers to some of the disbelievers present with the Messenger (ﷺ), meaning: they fold their chests against his enmity. al-Zamakhshari said: "(p-203) yathnūna ṣudūrahum means: they turn away from the truth and deviate from it, because whoever faces something presents his chest to it, and whoever turns away from it and deviates, folds his chest away from it and turns his side away from it. ﴿liyastakhfū minhu﴾ means: they wish to hide from Allah, so that they do not let His Messenger and the believers see their turning away. The parallel of the implied 'they wish' (yurīdūna), with the meaning returning to its implication, is the implication in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:63], meaning: he struck, and it parted. The meaning of ﴿alā ḥīna yastaghshūna thiyābahum﴾ is: and they wish to hide when they cover themselves with their garments, also out of aversion to hearing the words of Allah, like the saying of Nuh (peace be upon him): ﴿They put their fingers in their ears and covered themselves with their garments and persisted﴾ [Nuh 71:7]." End of quotation.

The pronoun in ﴿minhu﴾ refers to Allah. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is the most eloquent and most fitting in meaning." End.

It appears from some occasions of revelation that it refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), as Ibn 'Atiyya said. He said: "It is said that this verse was revealed concerning the disbelievers who, when they met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), would lower themselves, fold their chests like one hiding, turn their backs toward him, and cover their faces with their garments, out of distance from him and dislike of meeting him, while they thought that this would be hidden from him or from Allah, exalted is He. So the verse was revealed." End. On this basis, ﴿liyastakhfū﴾ is connected to the verb ﴿yathnūna﴾, and al-Hawfi said the same. It has also been said that it is a metaphor for the rancor and malice they concealed, as one says, "So-and-so folds his side over his enmity and folds his chest over it." The meaning of the verse is: surely they conceal enmity and hide it, thinking it will be hidden from Allah, mighty and majestic. He, exalted is He, knows what they conceal when they cover themselves and go to the extreme of concealment. Thus ﴿ḥīna﴾ is the object of the verb ﴿yaʿlamu﴾, as al-Hawfi said, and not of the implied verb proposed by al-Zamakhshari, which is: "and they wish to hide when they cover themselves with their garments." Abu al-Baqa' said: "﴿alā ḥīna﴾: the governing element of the adverbial phrase is omitted, meaning: alā ḥīna yastaghshūna thiyābahum yastakhfūna (when they cover themselves with their garments, they hide). It is also permissible that it be an adverbial of time for yaʿlamu."

It has also been said: some of them would bow to one another in whispers, slandering the Muslims, and their ignorance reached the point that they thought this would be hidden from Allah, exalted is He. Qatada said: "They are most hidden when they bend their backs and cover their garments, and conceal in their souls their resolve."

Mujahid said: "They fold them over disbelief." Ibn 'Abbas said: "They hide what is in their breasts of rancor." Qatada said: "They conceal so that they may hear the words of Allah." Ibn Zayd said: "They keep it secret when some of them confide in one another about the matter of the Messenger (ﷺ)."

It has also been said: they fold them out of shame before Allah, exalted is He. The meaning of yastaghshūna is: they make them into coverings. From this is the saying of al-Khansa':
"I graze the stars, though I was not charged with grazing them, and at times I cover myself with the surplus of my worn garments."

It has also been said: the intended meaning of "garments" is the night, and it is used figuratively for it because of the connection between them in covering, since the night covers as garments cover. From this is their saying: "The night is more concealing for the one who seeks secrecy (lil-wayl)." Ibn 'Abbas read: ('alā ḥīn yastaghshūna). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "From this usage is the saying of al-Nabigha:
"When I rebuked gray hair for my youth, and said: 'Would that I were sound,' while gray hair was restraining me."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "What they conceal in their hearts and what they declare with their mouths." It has also been said: what they conceal at night and what they declare by day. Ibn al-Anbari said: "Its meaning is that He knows their inner secrets as He knows their outward appearances."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "He means that there is no difference in His knowledge between their concealing and their declaring, so there is no way for them to reach what they wish of hiding, and Allah is aware of their folding of their chests and their covering themselves with their garments. Their hypocrisy is not hidden from Him." The author of al-Taḥrīr said: "What the context of the verse requires is that by what they conceal he means what their breasts harbor of polytheism, hypocrisy, rancor, envy, and hatred toward the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions, because all of that is among the deeds of the heart, and deeds of the heart are very hidden. By what they declare he means what they show of turning their backs on the Prophet (ﷺ), covering their garments, and stopping (p-204) their ears, and all of these are manifest actions that are not hidden."

﴿There is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah, and He knows its dwelling-place and its repository. All is in a clear Record.﴾: The word dābba here is general for every living being that needs provision. ﴿ʿalā Allāh﴾ is apparently obligatory, but it is actually a bounty; yet when He, exalted is He, guaranteed to bestow it upon them, He placed it within the scope of obligation. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿mustaqarrahā﴾ is where it takes refuge on the earth, and ﴿mustawdaʿahā﴾ is the place where it dies and is buried. He also related from him: mustaqarrahā is in the womb, and mustawdaʿahā is in the loins.

al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: mustaqarrahā is during the days of its life, and mustawdaʿahā is when it dies and when it is resurrected. It has also been said: mustaqarrahā is in Paradise or in the Fire, and mustawdaʿahā is in the grave. This is supported by ﴿How good a dwelling-place it is﴾ [al-Furqan 25:76] and ﴿How evil a dwelling-place it is﴾ [al-Furqan 25:66]. It has also been said: mustaqarr is where its deeds settle, and mustawdaʿ is where it will end up.

It has also been said: mustaqarr is what came into existence as a living being, and mustawdaʿ is what will come into existence after the mustaqarr. al-Zamakhshari said: mustaqarr is its place on the earth and its dwelling, and mustawdaʿ is where it existed before settling, whether from the loins, the womb, or the egg. End. Mustaqarr and mustawdaʿ may be verbal nouns, and they may be nouns of place. Mustawdaʿ may be a passive participle, since its verb is transitive, but mustaqarr cannot be, because its verb is intransitive. ﴿kullun﴾ means: each of the provision. The mustaqarr and mustawdaʿ are in the Preserved Tablet, meaning: its mention is written in it, clearly. It has also been said: the "Record" here is a metaphor for the knowledge of Allah, but taking it in its literal sense is better.

﴿He it is who created the heavens and the earth in six days, while His Throne was upon the water, in order to test you as to which of you is best in deed. And if you say, "Indeed you will be resurrected after death," those who disbelieve will surely say, "This is nothing but clear magic."﴾ ﴿And if We delay the punishment from them until a counted community, they will surely say, "What holds it back?" Unquestionably, on the day it comes to them, it will not be averted from them, and what they used to mock will surround them.﴾: When He, exalted is He, mentioned what indicates His being All-Knowing, He mentioned what indicates His being All-Powerful. The explanation of the first sentence was given in Surah Yunus. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿while His Throne was upon the water﴾ is: its estimated time is before the creation of the heavens and the earth, and in this is evidence that the water and the Throne were created before them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verses 5–11 (part 2 of 2):

Ka'b said: Allah created a green emerald (yaqutah khadra') and looked at it with awe (al-haybah), and it turned into water. Then He created the wind and placed the water on its back (matn), then He placed the Throne (al-'arsh) upon the water.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he was asked: "Upon what was the water?" He said: "It was upon the back of the wind."

The apparent reading is that the clause "li-yabluwakum" (so that He may test you) is connected to "khalaqa" (He created). Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, He created them for a profound wisdom, namely that He would make them dwellings for His servants, bestow upon them diverse kinds of blessings in them, and charge them with performing acts of obedience and avoiding acts of disobedience. Whoever gives thanks and obeys, He will reward; whoever disbelieves and disobeys, He will punish. Since this resembles the testing of one who tests, He said "li-yabluwakum," meaning: He will act toward you as one who tests does, to see how you act.

(If you say:) How is it permissible to make the act of testing dependent (ta'liq)? (I say:) Because testing contains the meaning of knowledge, since it is the way of Allah, so it is associated with it, as you say: "Look which of them is better in appearance (wajhan)," and "Listen which of them is better in voice (sawtan)," because looking and listening are among the means of knowledge. End of quote.

As for his words "and whoever disbelieves and disobeys, He punishes him," this is the subtle trace of Mu'tazilism (dasisat al-i'tizal). As for his saying "listen which of them is better in voice," I do not know of anyone who mentioned that "istama'" (listen) is subject to ta'liq; rather they mentioned, of non-mental verbs, only "sal" (ask) and "unzur" (look). The permissibility of ta'liq of the verb "ra'a" (to see, in the sense of visual perception) is a matter of disagreement among the Basrans.

It has also been said that "li-yabluwakum" is connected to a verb omitted in the text, the estimate being: "He informed of that so that He might test you," and the purpose of this interpretation is that these creatures were not created for the sake of humans.

It has been said: the estimated verb is: "And He created you so that He might test you." It has also been said: there are omitted clauses in the speech, the estimate being: "His creating them both was for benefits whose good returns to you in this world and not in the next, and He did that so that He might test you." The meaning of "Which of you is best in deed (ahsanu 'amalan)" is: Is this better or this?

Ibn Bahr said: It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Which of you is best in intellect, most scrupulous regarding the prohibitions of Allah, and quickest in obedience to Allah." And if this interpretation is indeed transmitted from the Messenger (ﷺ), one should not deviate from it.

Al-Hasan said: "most detached from Allah (azhad fi Allah)." Muqatil said: "most mindful of Allah (atqa li-Allah)." Al-Dahhak said: "most thankful (akthar shukran)."

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say:) How is it said "Which of you is best in deed," when the deeds of believers are what vary between good and better, whereas the deeds of believers and disbelievers vary between good and bad? (I say:) Those who are best in deed are the God-conscious (al-muttaqun), who are those who race to achieve what is Allah's aim from His servants. He singled them out for mention and disregarded those beyond them, honoring them and drawing attention to their rank, and so that this would be an alert for the listeners and an encouragement to attain their excellence. End of quote.

And if you say: it is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ). Isa al-Thaqafi read: "wa-la-in qultu" with a damma on the ta', as a report from Him, exalted is He, and the meaning is: "And if you (I) say," arguing for the resurrection after death, since in His saying, exalted is He, "And it is He who created," there is an indication of great power; so whenever He reports the occurrence of a possibility, it occurs without doubt, and He has reported the resurrection, so it is obligatory to accept it and be certain of its occurrence.

It was also read: "ayyukum" with a fatha on the hamza. Al-Zamakhshari said: Its aspect is that it may be from their saying: "Go to the market, for you may buy meat" (inna-ka tashtari lahman), in the sense of "la'alla-ka" (perhaps you), meaning: "If you say to them, 'Perhaps you will be resurrected,'" in the sense of: "Expect your resurrection and suppose it," they would affirm the statement by denying it, saying... And it is permissible that "qultu" be given the meaning of "dhakartu" (you mentioned), End of quote.

That is, with a fatha on the hamza, because it is in the position of the object of "dhakarta" (you mentioned). The apparent reference of "hadha" (this) is to the statement: that your statement "You will be resurrected" is nothing but magic (sihr), i.e., the falsity of this statement is like the falsity of magic. It may also be that it refers to what the sentence indicates of resurrection, i.e., that resurrection...

It has been said: they pointed with "hadha" to the Qur'an, which speaks of resurrection; so when they call it magic, the denial of what it contains of resurrection and other things is included under it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: They denied and said: "This is magic." This is a contradiction on their part: if it is acknowledged that the heavens and the earth were created by the Creator, the Originator of the heavens and the earth, then they are among those who acknowledge this, and yet they deny what is far easier than it, namely resurrection from the graves, since initiating creation is more difficult than restoring it, and since the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of people. End of quote.

al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah and a group of the Seven read: "sihrun" (magic). A group read: "sahir" (a magician), meaning: "and the magician is a liar, a falsifier."

"And if We delay" — Allah relates another kind of their falsehoods and mockery. The punishment here is the punishment of the Resurrection. It has also been said: the punishment of the Day of Badr. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: the killing of the mockers by Jibril. The apparent meaning is the promised punishment. The "ummah" here means a period of time, as Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid and the majority said, and its meaning is: "until a known time and appointed moment." "What holds it back?" is a question; they said it in the manner of denial and mockery. Al-Tabari said: the period was called "ummah" because within it a community (ummah) of people passes away and another arises; so it is, in this sense, a long period. Then he began the report by saying that it is a day which nothing can turn back or avert.

The apparent reading is that "yawma" is in the accusative, governed by "masrufan" (averted), so it is an operand of the predicate of "laysa" (not). This has been cited as evidence for permitting the fronting of the predicate of "laysa" over it; they said: because the fronting of the operand indicates the fronting of the operator. This doctrine is attributed to Sibawayh, and most Basrans hold it. But the Kufans and al-Mubarrad held that this is not permissible, and said: the permissibility of fronting the operand does not indicate the permissibility of fronting the operator.

Moreover, a prepositional adverbial phrase (zarf majrur) has more latitude in these two than in others, and they may occur where the operator cannot occur in them, such as: "Inna al-yawma Zayidan musafirun." I have examined a number of the diwans of the Arabs and did not find the fronting of the predicate of "laysa" over it, nor of its operand, except what the apparent meaning of this verse indicates, and the poet's saying: "He refuses, and his obstinacy only increases, and I was proud in secret; I do not advance." The explanation of the phrase "wa-haqa bihim" has already been given.

"And if We let man taste mercy from Us, then withdraw it from him, indeed he is despairing, ungrateful." "And if We let him taste bounty after adversity has touched him, he says: 'The evils have departed from me,' indeed he is exultant, boastful; except those who are patient and do righteous deeds—those, for them is forgiveness and a great reward."

When Allah mentioned the punishment of the disbelievers, and that however long delayed it must surely befall them, He mentioned what indicates their disbelief and that they deserve punishment, for they were created with ingratitude for Allah's blessings, and what follows from His kindness toward them of things unbecoming to them, namely their boasting over the servants of Allah. The apparent meaning is that "al-insan" here is a genus, the meaning being that this disposition is in the nature of people; then He excepted from them those whom the laws and faith guided to patience and righteous deeds, and therefore the exception is contiguous (muttasil) in His saying: "except those who are patient." It has been said: the intended "insan" here is the disbeliever.

It has been said: the intended one is a specific person. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, and it was concerning him that it was revealed. It has been said: 'Abd Allah ibn Umayyah al-Makhzumi, which al-Wahidi mentioned. On these two views the exception is disjunct (munqati'). The meaning of "mercy" (rahmah) is blessing, of health, security, and wealth.

"Then We withdrew it" means: We took it away from him.

"Laya'us" and "kafur" are intensive forms (sighat mubalaghah). The meaning: he is greatly despairing and abundantly so; he despairs that there will return to him the like of that blessing which was taken away, and he cuts off his hope in Allah's bounty without patience or submission to His decree. "Kafur": one who much denies the blessings Allah previously bestowed upon him. He mentioned the human condition when the blessing came first and was not preceded by harm, then mentioned his condition when blessing comes after harm.

The meaning of "the evils have departed" is: the calamities that distressed me. This statement implies both heedlessness and ignorance, for that is by Allah's favor, while he believes that it is mere coincidence or good fortune, and this is a corrupt belief.

"Indeed he is exultant": insolent, arrogant. This exultation is unrestricted, and therefore one characterized by it is blamed; and the Qur'an does not praise exultation except when restricted to what is good, as in His saying: "Rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty" (Al 'Imran: 170). The majority read "lafarihun" with a kasra on the ra', which is the analogical form of the active participle of the intransitive "fa'ila." A group read "lafaruhun" with a damma on the ra', as in your saying: "nadus" and "natus."

"Fakhr" (boasting) is his magnifying himself over people because of the blessing that befell him. Allah excepted the patient, meaning: in adversity, and those who do righteous deeds, among which is giving thanks for blessings. "Those, for them is forgiveness," for their sins, which entails the removal of punishment and deliverance from it; and "a great reward" is Paradise, which entails attaining the reward. He described the reward as "great" because of what it contains of everlasting bliss, the lifting of obligations, security from punishment, Allah's pleasure with them, and gazing upon His noble Face.

﴿So perhaps you would leave out some of what is revealed to you, and your breast would be constricted by it, lest they say, "Why has no treasure been sent down to him, or why has no angel come with him?" You are only a warner, and God is Trustee over all things.﴾: Al-Zamakhshari said: They were proposing to him signs out of obstinacy, not out of a desire for guidance, because if they had been seeking guidance, one sign from what he brought would have been enough for their rightful guidance.

Among their proposals was: "Why has no treasure been sent down to him, or why has no angel come with him?" They did not give weight to the Qur'an, and they treated it and the other clear proofs he brought with contempt. So the breast of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would become constricted at having to convey to them what they would not accept and would laugh at. God therefore stirred him and roused him to fulfil the Message, and cast out concern for their rejection, their mockery and their proposals, by saying: ﴿So perhaps you would leave out some of what is revealed to you﴾, meaning: (p-207) perhaps you would refrain from conveying it to them and delivering it to them, out of fear of their rejection and their contempt for it. ﴿And your breast would be constricted by it﴾: by reciting it to them, lest they say, out of fear that they would say: "Why has no treasure been sent down to him? Why has not sent down to him what we propose, of treasure and angels?" He was not sent down anything that they did not desire or propose.

Then He said: ﴿You are only a warner﴾, meaning: it is not incumbent upon you except to warn them with what has been revealed to you and to convey to them what you have been commanded to convey. It is not upon you whether they reject, neglect or propose. ﴿And God is Trustee over all things﴾: He guards what they say, and He will do with them what He wishes to do. So put your trust in Him and entrust your affair to Him.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The occasion of revelation of this verse is that the disbelievers of Quraysh said: "O Muhammad, if you would only abandon reviling our gods and deriding our forefathers, we would sit with you and follow you," and they said: ﴿Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it﴾ [Yunus 10:15], and similar sayings. So God Most High addressed His Prophet (ﷺ) in this form of address, placing him in a position of questioning, responding to their sayings and nullifying them. The meaning is not that he (peace be upon him) intended something of that kind and then desisted from it, for he never at all wished to leave aside anything of what was revealed to him, nor did his breast become constricted by it. Rather, his breast used to be constricted by their sayings, their actions and their distance from faith.

Here ﴿la'alla﴾ (perhaps) carries the sense of reproach and confirmation. What is revealed to him is the Qur'an and the call to God, and in that is the reviling of their gods and the deriding of their forefathers, or other things. It is possible that the Prophet (ﷺ) felt great the hardship he suffered, so he inclined toward there being a permission from God to show the disbelievers some leniency, and similar beliefs that befit him (ﷺ), just as the verses of truce came.

He used the form ﴿ḍā'iq﴾ (constricted) rather than ﴿ḍayyiq﴾ for the sake of harmony in wording with ﴿tārik﴾ (leaving out). Although ﴿ḍayyiq﴾ is more commonly used, ﴿ḍā'iq﴾ is the one that describes a transient state, whereas ﴿ḍayyiq﴾ describes a constant attribute. Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say) why did he turn from ﴿ḍayyiq﴾ to ﴿ḍā'iq﴾? (I say) to show that ﴿ḍayyiq﴾ is accidental and not fixed, because the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was the most spacious of people in breast. The like of this is your saying: ﴿sayyid﴾ (lord) and ﴿jawād﴾ (generous), meaning the lordship and generosity that are fixed and established. When you wish to express occurrence, you say ﴿sā'id﴾ and ﴿jā'id﴾, end quote. This ruling is not restricted to these words; rather, every form derived from a triliteral root for permanence and stability, not in the pattern of ﴿fā'il﴾, is returned to that pattern when the sense of occurrence is intended. So we say: ﴿ḥāsin﴾ (becoming good) from ḥasuna (was good), ﴿thāqil﴾ (becoming heavy) from thaqula (was heavy), ﴿fāriḥ﴾ (becoming glad) from fariḥa (was glad), and ﴿sāmin﴾ (becoming fat) from samina (was fat). One of the thieves said, describing the prison and whoever is imprisoned in it:

"In a dwelling where the base man becomes fat, while the paleness of the noble people shows openly."

The apparent reference of the pronoun in ﴿bihi﴾ (by it) is to ﴿ba'ḍ﴾ (some). It was also said that it refers to ﴿mā﴾ (what), and it was said that it refers to the conveying, and it was said that it refers to the denial. It was said: ﴿la'alla﴾ here is in the sense of interrogation, meaning ﴿hal﴾ (is it that), and the meaning is: Are you leaving out what contains the foolishness of their intellects and the reviling of their gods, as they asked you to? They estimated his dislike for them saying, and that they might not say, and that they might say: three sayings. ﴿Kanz﴾ (treasure) means abundant wealth.

They said ﴿unzila﴾ (was sent down) and did not say ﴿u'ṭiya﴾ (was given), because their intent was to challenge, and that they asked for a treasure to be sent down to him from heaven contrary to custom, since treasures are usually in the earth.

Their request for a sign that compels faith is something God, Mighty and Majestic, did not send the prophets with: He sent them with signs for reflection and reasoning. He did not make a compulsive sign except for the nation whom He intended to punish for their disbelief after the sign of reasoning, like the she-camel for Thamud.

God put him at ease by saying: ﴿You are only a warner﴾, meaning: what has been entrusted to you is warning, not the attainment of their guidance, for that belongs only to God Most High. Muqatil said: It was also said: "He is the guarantor of the interests and capable of them." Ibn 'Atiyya said: He is the One who determines the faith of whomever He wills and the disbelief of whomever He wills. It was said: this verse is ﴿mansukh﴾ (abrogated), and it was said: it is ﴿muḥkam﴾ (not abrogated).

[p. 208] Apparently *am* here is disjunctive (*munqati'a*, "or rather"), and it is to be understood as *bal* plus a hamza, meaning: "Do they say he invented it?" Ibn al-Qushayri said: *am* is interrogative and occurs in the middle of the speech, meaning: "Are they content with what I have revealed to you of the Qur'an, or do they say that it is not from God? If they say that it is not from God, then let them produce something like it." Thus he made *am* connective (*muttasila*), whereas the apparent reading is disjunctive, as we have said. The pronoun in *aftarahu* ("he invented it") refers to ﴿what is revealed to you﴾ [Hud 11:12], which is the Qur'an.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that their desires were not attached to his leaving out some of what was revealed to him, except through their claim that it is not from God and that he himself invented it. He first challenged them with ten invented surahs before challenging them with a single surah, since this surah is Meccan, while al-Baqarah is Medinan, and Surah Yunus is also Meccan. The logic of challenging with ten is that it should come before the demand for a counter-challenge with one surah. When they attributed it to invention, he asked them to bring ten surahs like it, invented, in order to give them slack (*irkha'an li-'inanihim*). It is as if he were saying: "Suppose I fabricated it and it was not revealed to me. Then you bring speech like it, fabricated from yourselves. You are eloquent Arabs like me and you will not be unable to produce what I am able to produce of speech." The phrase "like it" (*mithlihi*) was specified with regard to the excellence of its composition and eloquence, even though it is invented. The manner of one who wants to show someone's inability is to first ask him to do many things like what he did, and then, when his inability is clear, to say to him: "Do one like it."

*Mithl* ("like") is applied to the singular, the dual and the plural, as God said: ﴿Shall we believe two humans like us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:47]. Agreement in the dual and plural is also permitted, as in His saying: ﴿then they will not be like you﴾ [Muhammad 47:38], ﴿and wide-eyed houris﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:22], ﴿like hidden pearls﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:23]. When it appears in the singular while being a modifier of a dual or plural, it is understood as dual or plural, that is, *mithlayn* and *amthal*.

The meaning here is: "ten surahs like it," with the reading that each surah among them is like it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The challenge in this verse was made with ten because He restricted it to fabrication, so He widened the quantity for them so that the proof would be established to the fullest. For He had already made them unable, in other verses, with a single surah like it without restriction. So it is a complete similarity in the unseen matters of the Qur'an, its composition, its promise and its threat. They were made unable in this verse by being told: "Counter an amount of it with ten like it in quantity, and the purpose is the same. Make it invented; then nothing remains for you except its composition. This is the greatest extent of latitude."

The meaning is not: "Counter ten surahs with ten," because that would come as countering one surah with one invented surah, and there is no concern about the sequence of the revelation of one before the other. What supports this view is that the obligation in the verse of al-Baqarah arises from doubt, and only knowledge that they cannot produce complete similarity removes doubt. In this verse, the obligation arises from their saying "he invented it," and they were charged with something like what they said. This does not hold for the verse of Yunus.

Some people said: This (challenge) comes before that one in revelation. It is not valid for a single surah to be anything other than invented. The verse of Surah Yunus is the obligation of a surah arranged upon their saying "he invented it." Likewise the verse of al-Baqarah only accused them of saying that the Qur'an was invented.

The speaker of this view did not notice the difference between the two obligations: in one, complete similarity is intended; in the other, it is confined to composition. End.

The apparent meaning is that His saying "like it" (*mithlihi*) does not mean likeness in the sense that the counter-challenger produces ten surahs. Rather, "like it" indicates similarity in some quantity of the Qur'an.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the surahs with which the counter-challenge was demanded are specific: al-Baqarah, Al 'Imran, al-Nisa', al-Ma'idah, al-An'am, al-A'raf, al-Anfal, al-Tawbah, Yunus and Hud.

So His saying "like it" means: like this, the ten surahs. Most of these surahs are Medinan, so how is the reference to Mecca valid for what had not yet been revealed? Perhaps this is not authentically from Ibn 'Abbas.

The pronoun in ﴿So if they do not respond to you﴾ refers to those from whom the counter-challenge was demanded. *Lakum* ("to you") is a plural pronoun that includes the Messenger and the believers.

It is permissible for it to be an address to the Messenger ﷺ as a form of honour, as came in ﴿if they do not respond to you﴾ [al-Qasas 28:50]. This was said by Mujahid. It was also said that the pronoun in *yastajibu* ("they respond") refers to those who are called upon, and *lakum* ("to you") is an address to those commanded to call upon whomever they could. This was said by al-Dahhak. That is: if the one you call to the counter-challenge does not respond, then submit at that point, and know that it is from God, and that it was sent down accompanied by what only God knows: composition that is inimitable for creation, and information about unseen matters to which they have no access. (p. 209) Know at that point that there is no god but Him, that His unity is obligatory, ﴿Will you then submit?﴾, meaning: will you adhere to Islam after the clarity of this decisive proof? If the address is to the believers, the meaning of *fa-'lamu* ("know") is: persist in knowledge, increase in certainty and firmness of foot that it is from God. The meaning of ﴿Will you then submit?﴾ is: will you be sincere in Islam? Muqatil said: *bi-'ilmi Allah* means "by God's permission." al-Kalbi said: "by His command." al-Qutabi said: "from God."

What appears to be the case is that the pronoun in ﴿So if they do not respond﴾ refers to ﴿whomever you can﴾, and the pronoun in *lakum* refers to the unbelievers, because the pronoun refers to the nearest previous mention, because the address is to one person, and because the answer is consequent upon the condition in a real sense, arising from the command to know. It is not right to say that He meant: "Persist in knowledge, and persist in knowing that there is no god but Him." And ﴿Will you then submit?﴾ is an exhortation to attain Islam, not something meant as sincerity.

When they were required to counter-challenge and commanded to call upon whoever might help them achieve the counter-challenge, and their idols and gods did not respond to them, they were commanded to know that it is from God and is not invented, so that it could be countered. He, exalted is He, is the one specially characterised by divinity; their gods and idols do not share with Him anything of it. Therefore they cannot respond, because their inability is clear, and because they neither benefit nor harm in any of the matters.

Zayd ibn 'Ali read *innama nazzala* with a fatha on the *nun* and *zay* and with the *shaddah*. It may be that *ma* is verbal (*masdariyyah*), meaning: "indeed the sending down," and it may be that it means "that which," meaning: "indeed He who sent it down." The object pronoun was omitted because the omission is permissible.

[p. 208] Apparently *am* here is disjunctive (*munqati'a*, "or rather"), and it is to be understood as *bal* plus a hamza, meaning: "Do they say he invented it?" Ibn al-Qushayri said: *am* is interrogative and occurs in the middle of the speech, meaning: "Are they content with what I have revealed to you of the Qur'an, or do they say that it is not from God? If they say that it is not from God, then let them produce something like it." Thus he made *am* connective (*muttasila*), whereas the apparent reading is disjunctive, as we have said. The pronoun in *aftarahu* ("he invented it") refers to ﴿what is revealed to you﴾ [Hud 11:12], which is the Qur'an.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that their desires were not attached to his leaving out some of what was revealed to him, except through their claim that it is not from God and that he himself invented it. He first challenged them with ten invented surahs before challenging them with a single surah, since this surah is Meccan, while al-Baqarah is Medinan, and Surah Yunus is also Meccan. The logic of challenging with ten is that it should come before the demand for a counter-challenge with one surah. When they attributed it to invention, he asked them to bring ten surahs like it, invented, in order to give them slack (*irkha'an li-'inanihim*). It is as if he were saying: "Suppose I fabricated it and it was not revealed to me. Then you bring speech like it, fabricated from yourselves. You are eloquent Arabs like me and you will not be unable to produce what I am able to produce of speech." The phrase "like it" (*mithlihi*) was specified with regard to the excellence of its composition and eloquence, even though it is invented. The manner of one who wants to show someone's inability is to first ask him to do many things like what he did, and then, when his inability is clear, to say to him: "Do one like it."

*Mithl* ("like") is applied to the singular, the dual and the plural, as God said: ﴿Shall we believe two humans like us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:47]. Agreement in the dual and plural is also permitted, as in His saying: ﴿then they will not be like you﴾ [Muhammad 47:38], ﴿and wide-eyed houris﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:22], ﴿like hidden pearls﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:23]. When it appears in the singular while being a modifier of a dual or plural, it is understood as dual or plural, that is, *mithlayn* and *amthal*.

The meaning here is: "ten surahs like it," with the reading that each surah among them is like it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The challenge in this verse was made with ten because He restricted it to fabrication, so He widened the quantity for them so that the proof would be established to the fullest. For He had already made them unable, in other verses, with a single surah like it without restriction. So it is a complete similarity in the unseen matters of the Qur'an, its composition, its promise and its threat. They were made unable in this verse by being told: "Counter an amount of it with ten like it in quantity, and the purpose is the same. Make it invented; then nothing remains for you except its composition. This is the greatest extent of latitude."

The meaning is not: "Counter ten surahs with ten," because that would come as countering one surah with one invented surah, and there is no concern about the sequence of the revelation of one before the other. What supports this view is that the obligation in the verse of al-Baqarah arises from doubt, and only knowledge that they cannot produce complete similarity removes doubt. In this verse, the obligation arises from their saying "he invented it," and they were charged with something like what they said. This does not hold for the verse of Yunus.

Some people said: This (challenge) comes before that one in revelation. It is not valid for a single surah to be anything other than invented. The verse of Surah Yunus is the obligation of a surah arranged upon their saying "he invented it." Likewise the verse of al-Baqarah only accused them of saying that the Qur'an was invented.

The speaker of this view did not notice the difference between the two obligations: in one, complete similarity is intended; in the other, it is confined to composition. End.

The apparent meaning is that His saying "like it" (*mithlihi*) does not mean likeness in the sense that the counter-challenger produces ten surahs. Rather, "like it" indicates similarity in some quantity of the Qur'an.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the surahs with which the counter-challenge was demanded are specific: al-Baqarah, Al 'Imran, al-Nisa', al-Ma'idah, al-An'am, al-A'raf, al-Anfal, al-Tawbah, Yunus and Hud.

So His saying "like it" means: like this, the ten surahs. Most of these surahs are Medinan, so how is the reference to Mecca valid for what had not yet been revealed? Perhaps this is not authentically from Ibn 'Abbas.

The pronoun in ﴿So if they do not respond to you﴾ refers to those from whom the counter-challenge was demanded. *Lakum* ("to you") is a plural pronoun that includes the Messenger and the believers.

It is permissible for it to be an address to the Messenger ﷺ as a form of honour, as came in ﴿if they do not respond to you﴾ [al-Qasas 28:50]. This was said by Mujahid. It was also said that the pronoun in *yastajibu* ("they respond") refers to those who are called upon, and *lakum* ("to you") is an address to those commanded to call upon whomever they could. This was said by al-Dahhak. That is: if the one you call to the counter-challenge does not respond, then submit at that point, and know that it is from God, and that it was sent down accompanied by what only God knows: composition that is inimitable for creation, and information about unseen matters to which they have no access. (p. 209) Know at that point that there is no god but Him, that His unity is obligatory, ﴿Will you then submit?﴾, meaning: will you adhere to Islam after the clarity of this decisive proof? If the address is to the believers, the meaning of *fa-'lamu* ("know") is: persist in knowledge, increase in certainty and firmness of foot that it is from God. The meaning of ﴿Will you then submit?﴾ is: will you be sincere in Islam? Muqatil said: *bi-'ilmi Allah* means "by God's permission." al-Kalbi said: "by His command." al-Qutabi said: "from God."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verse 15–16:

﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment – We will pay them in full for their deeds therein, and they will not be deprived therein.﴾ ﴿Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire; and what they did therein will be nullified, and what they used to do will be void.﴾: The connection (munasabah) of this verse to what precedes it is that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned some of the states of the disbelievers who oppose the Qur'an, He mentioned some of their worldly states and what they will come to in the Hereafter.

It is apparent from the generality of the words that it applies to everyone who desires the adornment of the life of this world, and the recompense is tied to His will, exalted is He, as He made clear in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever desires the hasty (life), We hasten for him therein whatever We will﴾ [al-Isra: 18], and so on. Mujahid said: it refers to the disbelievers and to those among the believers who show off (riya').

To this view also went Ma'un, when he was told the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning those who show off, and he recited this verse. Anas said: it refers to the Jews and the Christians. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the meaning of this is that they enter into this verse, not that it is exclusive of others.

It was also said: it refers to the hypocrites who fought alongside the Messenger and were given a share of the spoils. The meaning of ﴿desires the life of this world﴾ is that he intends by his deeds, which appear to be righteous, only the world, and does not believe in an Hereafter. Allah then recompenses him for his good deeds, as has been reported. As for the disbeliever, He feeds him in this world for his good deeds. And although the hypocrites from among the People of the Qibla fall under the generality, as you see one of them, when he leads prayer, chanting the words of the Qur'an, reciting it in the finest recitation, prolonging his bowing and prostration, and feigning weeping in his recitation; and when he prays alone he rushes through it hastily; and when he gives charity he displays his charity before those who will praise him, and gives it to one who does not deserve it until people praise him, and (gives it to) the people of the ribat to whom charity is given.

How far this is from a man who gives charity secretly and to one who does not know him, as has come in: the seven whom Allah shades under His shade on a day when there is no shade but His shade, and a man who gave charity and concealed it until his left hand does not know what his right hand has spent. This is an extreme exaggeration in concealing charity. And when he learns knowledge he shows off with it and boasts, and seeks with most of it a little trifle of the goods of this world.

Showing off has spread greatly in this verse, to the point that you can hardly see one who is sincere to Allah, neither in speech nor in action. These are among the first by whom the Fire will be kindled on the Day of Resurrection.

The majority read ﴿nuwaffi﴾ with the plural of majesty (nun of greatness); Talha ibn Maymun read ﴿yuwaffi﴾ with the ya' in the third person. Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿yuwfi﴾ with ya' and without the doubling, the present of awfa. It was also read ﴿tuwaff﴾ with ta' in the passive voice, and (a'malu-hum) with the nominative. On all these readings, the verb is jussive as the answer to the conditional, just as it is jussive in His saying: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We increase for him in his tilth﴾ [al-Shura: 20]. It is reported from al-Farra' that (kana) is superfluous, and for this reason the response is jussive. Perhaps this is not sound, for if it were superfluous the conditional verb would be (yurid) and would be jussive; and this construction, in which the conditional verb is past and the response is present, is not specific to kana but is permissible with other verbs as well.

Just as it is reported in the line of Zuhayr:

"Whoever fears the causes of death, they will overtake him, even if he tries to climb the sky with a ladder."

Al-Hasan read ﴿tuwfa﴾ with lightness and with the ya' retained. It may be that it is jussive by dropping the presumed vowel, according to the dialect of those who say: "alam ya'tika," which is a dialect of some Arabs; and it may be that it is nominative, as it is nominative in the saying of the poet: "He says, even if the gathering's vigor is destroyed out of fear: 'Woe to you, do not cause alarm!'"

The restriction in the Fire being theirs is clearly indicative that the verse concerns the disbelievers. If those who show off are included in it, then the meaning regarding them is: there is not due to them, or it is not right for them, anything but the Fire, like His saying: ﴿Then his recompense is Hell﴾ [al-Nisa: 93]. It is permissible that Allah cover them with His mercy, and this is the apparent view of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr.

The pronoun in His saying ﴿what they did therein﴾: the apparent view is that it refers to the Hereafter, and the prepositional phrase is connected to (habita), and the meaning is: the nullification of what they did in the Hereafter became manifest.

It is permissible for it to be connected to the saying (sana'u), in which case it refers to the life of this world, as it referred to it in (fiha) before. The (ma) in (ma sana'u) means "that which," or it is verbal (masdariyyah). And (batil) and what follows it are an emphasis for His saying: ﴿and what they did was nullified﴾. (Batil) is a fronted predicate if it is a coordination of sentences, and (ma kanu) is the subject; and if it is a predicate after a predicate, then the (ma) with (batil) is raised as the agent.

Zayd ibn 'Ali read (wa-batala), making it a past verb. Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read (wa-batilan) with the accusative, and the author of al-Lawami' explained it as an object of (ya'malun), so it is an operand of the predicate of (kana) which is fronted.

(Ma) is superfluous, meaning: "and they used to do falsehood." There is a difference among the grammarians regarding the permissibility of this construction, namely that the operand of the predicate precedes the whole sentence of kana, its subject and its predicate. The saying of the Exalted supports the permissibility: ﴿Was it you whom they used to worship?﴾ [Saba': 40]. Whoever prohibits it interprets it otherwise. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that (batilan) be in the accusative as a verbal noun, in the sense of (batala butlanan), "what they used to do," so (ma) would be the agent, and it would be the verbal noun which is a substitute for the verb in non-interrogative and non-imperative contexts. It was fitting that He nullify their deeds, because they were not done for a valid reason, and a void deed has no reward.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verse 17–27 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Is one who has a clear proof from his Lord, and a witness from Him recites it, and before it the Book of Moses as a guide and a mercy? Those believe in it. Whoever of the factions disbelieves in it, the Fire is his promised place. So do not be in doubt about it; indeed it is the truth from your Lord, but most people do not believe.﴾ When He mentioned the state of those who desire the life of this world, He mentioned the state of those who desire the Face of Allah, the Exalted, through their righteous deeds. The counterpart to which the interrogative hamza is attached has been omitted, and the estimated sense is: "Is he like one who desires the life of this world?"

Such omission occurs frequently in the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him, so that he sees it as good [equal to one who does not]?﴾ [Fatir: 8] and His saying: ﴿Or is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night﴾ [Az-Zumar: 9]. This interrogation carries the meaning of affirmation (taqrir). Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, you do not equal them in rank nor do you parallel them; he means that there is a vast disparity between the two groups and a clear difference. He intended by them those among the Jews who believed, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and others. "Upon a clear proof from his Lord" means upon a proof from Allah, the Exalted, and a demonstration that the religion of Islam is true, and this is the evidence of reason. "And a witness follows it": a witness that follows that proof, bearing witness to its soundness, and this is the Qur'an, "from Him," from Allah; or a witness from the Qur'an. "And before it": before the Qur'an, "the Book of Moses," which is the Torah; that is, the Book of Moses also follows it, coming before the Qur'an.

It is also read (Kitab Musa) in the accusative, and its meaning is: he is upon a clear proof from his Lord, which is the evidence that the Qur'an is true; and a witness from him recites (yatluhu) the Qur'an, a witness from among those who are upon a clear proof, like His saying: ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified to its like﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 10], and ﴿Say: Allah suffices as a witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 43].

﴿And before it the Book of Moses﴾: "recites it" and before the Torah; "as a guide" (imaman): a book that is followed in religion, a model in it. End of quote. It was said regarding ﴿Is one who was﴾: those who believe in the Messenger, and it was said: Muhammad ﷺ specifically. (p-211) Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: Muhammad and the believers all together. "The clear proof" is the Qur'an or the Messenger, and the ha' is for emphasis (intensiveness).

As for "the witness" (al-shahid): Ibn Abbas, al-Nakha'i, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Abu Salih and Ikrimah said: it is Gabriel. Al-Hasan ibn Ali said: it is the Messenger. Mujahid also said: it is an angel whom Allah appointed to guard the Qur'an.

Ibn Atiyyah said: It is possible that by these expressions he means Gabriel. It was also said: Ali ibn Abi Talib. Al-Minhal narrated from Ubadah ibn Abdullah, who said: Ali, may Allah honour his face, said: "There is no one in Quraysh except that a verse was revealed concerning him." It was asked: "What was revealed concerning you?" He said: ﴿And a witness from Him recites it﴾. Muhammad ibn Ali and Zayd ibn Ali also said this.

It was said: it is the Gospel, said by al-Farra'. It was said: it is the Qur'an. It was said: it is the inimitability of the Qur'an, said by al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl. It was said: it is the form of the Messenger ﷺ, his face and his features, because every intelligent person who looked at him knew that he was the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

It was said: and Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. The pronoun in "from Him" refers to the religion, or to the Messenger, or to the Qur'an. "Yatluhu" means "yatba'uhu" (follows it), or "yaqra'uhu" (recites it); the raised pronoun in yatluhu and the accusative and genitive pronouns in minhu are arranged according to what suits each opinion among these.

Muhammad ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kalbi and others read: ﴿Kitab Musa﴾ in the accusative, as a conjunction with the object of yatluhu, or by supposing a verb. And if the witness is not understood to be the Gospel, then he specifically mentioned the Torah because both religions agree that it is from Allah, whereas the Jews disagree regarding the Gospel; so citing that which establishes proof against both groups is more fitting.

This accords with the saying of the jinn: ﴿We have heard a Book revealed after Moses﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 30], and with the saying of al-Najashi: "Indeed this and what Moses brought come out of one niche." "Imaman" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). What appears in the interpretation of this verse is that when He mentioned the disbelievers and that for them there is only the Fire, He followed with their opposites, who are the believers, those who are upon a clear proof from their Lord. The witness is the Qur'an, and "from Him" refers back to "his Lord." What indicates that the witness is the Qur'an is the mention of His saying "and before it" — that is, before the Qur'an, the Book of Moses. So its meaning is that two things combined to guide him: that he is upon a clear matter from the proof of reason, and that this proof agrees with these two divine books, the Qur'an and the Torah, so that he has both reason and transmission.

The demonstrative "those" (ulaika) refers to "one who was upon a clear proof," observing the meaning of "one" (man) and so using the plural. The pronoun in "bihi" refers to the Torah, or the Qur'an, or the Messenger — three opinions. "Al-Ahzab" (the factions) means all the religious communities, said by Ibn Jubayr; or the Jews and Christians, said by Qatadah; or the Quraysh, said by al-Suddi; or the Banu Umayyah, the Banu al-Mughirah ibn Abdullah al-Makhzumi, and the family of Abu Talhah ibn Ubaydullah, said by Muqatil. Al-Zamakhshari said: he means the people of Makkah and those allied with them among the factions against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. End of quote.

﴿So the Fire is his promised place﴾: that is, the place of his promise to which they will go. Hassan said:
"You brought us to the watering-places of death in the open, so the Fire is its promised place, and death meets it."
The pronoun in "minhu" refers to the Qur'an; it was also said that it refers to the report that the disbelievers' promised place is the Fire. The majority read "fi miryah" with a kasrah on the mim, which is the dialect of the Hijaz. As-Sulami, Abu Raja', Abu al-Khattab al-Sadusi and al-Hasan read it with a dammah, which is the dialect of Asad and Tamim. "The people" (al-nas) means the people of Makkah, said by Ibn Abbas; or all the disbelievers, whether doubters, ignorant, or obstinate, said by the author of al-Iqyan.

﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah? Those will be presented before their Lord, and the witnesses will say: "These are the ones who lied against their Lord. Ah, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers, who bar from the way of Allah and seek to make it crooked, and they are, in the Hereafter, disbelievers." Those were not able to escape in the earth, and they had no protectors other than Allah; their punishment will be doubled. They could not hear, nor did they see. Those are the ones who have lost themselves, and what they used to fabricate has gone astray from them. Certainly, in the Hereafter they will be the greatest losers.﴾ When their saying "Has he fabricated it?" [Hud: 13] preceded, He mentioned that there is no one more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah. These are the fabricators who attributed a son to Allah, took others alongside Him, and declared lawful and unlawful without any law from Allah. Their being presented before Allah means exposing them to disgrace and indicating their lie; otherwise, both the obedient and the disobedient are presented before Allah: ﴿And they will be presented before your Lord in rows﴾ [Al-Kahf: 48]. "Al-ashhad" is the plural of shahid, like sahib and ashab, or the plural of shahid as in sharif and ashraf. "Al-ashhad" are the angels who guarded their deeds in the world, or the prophets, or both the believers, or their own limbs bearing witness against them, sayings. In His saying "these" (haʾulaʾ) there is an indication of belittling and humiliating them because of their evil deeds.

In His saying "before their Lord": that is, before One who does good to them and holds their forelocks, and they were worthy not to lie against Him. This is like when you see a criminal and say: "This is the one who did such and such." The sentence's explanation has been given previously. "Hum" is an emphasis for "wa hum." "Mu'jizin" means: they could not escape Allah in the world from punishing them, had He wished to punish them, and there was no one who could help them or prevent them from punishment; but He willed to delay them and postpone their punishment until this day.

Al-Zamakhshari said: This is the speech of the witnesses; that is, their speech is from "these" to the end of this sentence, which is "and they had no protectors other than Allah."

It may appear that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Ah, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾ is from the speech of Allah, not in the manner of narration. This supports al-Zamakhshari's view, and His saying: ﴿Then a caller calls out among them: the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾ [Al-A'raf: 44], etc. Just as that is the speech of created beings in that verse, so likewise here. "Yudaf lahum al-adhab": it is intensified and increased. This is a resumed statement about their state in the Hereafter, because they combined disbelief in resurrection with lying against Allah, barring His servants from the way of Allah, and seeking to make it crooked, though it is the straight path.

"They could not hear": a report about their state in the world, in the manner of exaggeration; that is, hearing the Qur'an and what the Messenger ﷺ brought.

"Nor did they see": that is, they did not look at it, out of their hatred for it. Do you not see how al-Tufayl ibn Amr stuffed his ears with cotton, and how Quraysh refused to hear what was conveyed to them of the Messenger's speech until their elders turned them away from it? Or it is a report about their state when the punishment is doubled for them: that is, Allah decreed this upon them, so they do not hear in a way that benefits them, nor do they see in that way. It was said: the pronoun in "kanu" refers to "their protectors," their gods; that is, in reality they had no protectors, though they believed them to be protectors. It means that one who cannot hear or see, how could he be fit for protection? And "yudaf lahum al-adhab" would then be a parenthetical clause, and "ma" in these opinions is negation. It was also said: "ma" is verbal (masdariyyah), meaning: the punishment is doubled for them for the duration of their ability to hear and see; and the meaning is that the punishment and its doubling is constant and continuous for them. Al-Farra' permitted "ma" to be verbal, with the preposition removed from it, as the preposition is removed with anna and in, its sisters; but this is remote in wording and in meaning.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He meant that because of their extreme deafness to following the truth and their aversion to it, it is as if they could not hear. Perhaps some of the Mujbira (determinists), when they stumble upon this, leap up and bark at the people of justice with it, as if he had not heard people saying in every language: "I cannot bear to hear this word; my hearing rejects it." End of quote.

That is: it can be used as evidence that the servant has no power, because Allah, exalted is He, has negated from him the ability to hear; and if ability is negated from him, his power is negated. Al-Zamakhshari, as is his habit, scoffs at the People of the Sunnah and their losing themselves, because they bought the worship of idols in exchange for the worship of Allah, the Exalted; so in their trade they suffered a loss than which none is greater.

This is with an elided modifier: that is, the comfort or happiness of their souls; otherwise their souls remain, tormented. What they had fabricated of worshipping idols went astray from them, and their belief that the idols would intercede faded when they saw that they neither interceded nor benefited.

"La jaram": the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh is that they were compounded from "la" and "jaram" and became one word, meaning "truly," and what follows is raised by it as the subject (fa'il). Al-Hawfi said: jaram, negated by la, means "truly"; it is built together with la in the place of a nominative as subject, and "annahum" is in the place of a nominative as the predicate of jaram. (p-213)

Some said: "jaram" is built with "la" on the fatha, as in your saying "la rajul" (no man), and its meaning is: "there is no doubt and no escape." Al-Kisa'i said: its meaning is: "no opposition and no prevention," so it is the subject of la, and it is built on fatha like the preceding saying; and "jaram" here is from the sense of cutting off, as we say: "jaramtu," meaning "I cut off." Al-Zajjaj said: there is no compounding between them and no refutation of them.

Because of all that preceded it, namely their claim that the idols would benefit them. "Jaram" is a past verb meaning "he earned," with an implied subject: "Does he earn it?" that is, their action; and "anna" and what follows it are in the place of an accusative as the object. "Jarama al-qawm" means: he earned for them. The poet said:
"We set his head upon a palm trunk, for what his hands had earned, and we did not transgress."
Another said: [the text breaks off here.]

The commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verses 17–27 (part 2 of 2):

﴿...[as for the one who is] a prostrate one on the top of a cliff, in whom you see, for the bones it has gathered, a cross.﴾ It is said: *la jirama* (no doubt, certainly) with *kasr* (a vowel marker on the letter *jim*), and *la jara*, with the letter *mim* omitted. Al-Nahhas (Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas, a grammarian) said: al-Kisa'i (a grammarian of Kufa) claimed that there are four dialects for it: *la jarama*, *la 'an dha jaramin*, *la an dha jaramin*. He said: "And some people of Fazara say *la jarama*." Al-Farra' (a Kufan grammarian) reported two other dialects for it. He said: "The Banu 'Amir say *la dha jaramin*, and some Arabs say *la juruma*, with the *jim* vowelled with *damma*." Al-Jubba'i said in his *Nawadir* (rare expressions): "It is reported from Fazara: *la jara wallahi la af'alu dhalika* (no, by God, I will not do that)." He said: "It is also said: *la dha jaramin*, *la dhu jaramin*, *la 'an dha jaramin*, *la an dha jaramin*, *la an jarama*, *la 'an jaramin*, *la dha jara wallahi*, without the *mim*, meaning: I will not do that." Some have reported without *la jarama*: *anna-ka anta fa'alta dhalika* (that you yourself did that). From Abu 'Amr: *la-ajrama anna lahumu al-nar* (surely it is certain that for them is the Fire), on the pattern of *la-akrama* (surely he honoured). *La jara*: they dropped it due to frequent use, just as they say *sawta tara* meaning *sawfa tara* (you will see).

When the loss of the self is the greatest loss, they were judged to be those who exceed all other losers among the sinners in loss, whose end is to rest and whose loss ends, unlike these, for their loss has no end.

﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds and humbled themselves before their Lord — those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.﴾ ﴿The likeness of the two groups is like the blind and the deaf, and the seeing and the hearing. Are they equal in likeness? Will you not remember?﴾

When He mentioned what the disbelievers would come to of the Fire, He mentioned what the believers would come to of Paradise. The "two groups" here are the disbeliever and the believer. Since the disbelievers had been mentioned first and the believers were mentioned after them, the comparison here begins with the disbeliever, so He said: ﴿like the blind and the deaf﴾.

It is possible that this is of the type of comparing two things with two things: the blind is matched with the seeing, which is an antithesis (*tibaq*, a rhetorical figure of contrast), and the deaf is matched with the hearing, which is also an antithesis. Blindness and deafness are two afflictions that prevent sight and hearing, and they are not opposites, because there is no alternation between them.

It may also be that it is a comparison of one thing with its two attributes to one thing with its two attributes, so that it is of the coordination of attributes, as the poet said:

*To the king, the peer, and the son of the lofty one, and the lion of the battle in the crowd.*

The construction did not come as "like the blind and the seeing and the deaf and the hearing", which would have been a contrast in the wording of the blind and its opposite and in the wording of the deaf and its opposite. This is because, when He mentioned the closing of the eye, He followed it with the closing of the hearing, and when He mentioned the opening of sight, He followed it with the opening of hearing. That is the method of contrast, and more complete in its inimitability. Insha'Allah, the parallel of this contrast will come in His saying in Ta-Ha: ﴿Indeed, for you there is that you will not hunger therein, nor be naked﴾ [Ta-Ha: 118] ﴿and that you will not thirst therein, nor be exposed to the sun﴾ [Ta-Ha: 119].

It is possible that the *ka* (like) itself is the predicate of the subject, so its meaning is the meaning of "likeness", as if it were said: "The likeness of the two groups is the likeness of the blind." It is also possible that *mathal* (likeness) is intended as the description, and *ka* as *mithl* (similar to), so it would be with an omitted noun: "like the likeness of the blind." This comparison is a comparison of the intelligible with the sensible: the blind of insight is deaf to it, is compared with the blind of sight who is deaf of hearing; that one is in the darkness of misguidance, wandering and confused, and this one is bewildered on the roads and does not find his way.

The words ﴿Will you not remember?﴾ came to alert that this blindness and this deafness of the intellect can be removed. It is therefore obligatory for the rational person to remember what he is in, and to strive to guide himself. *Mathalan* (as a likeness) is in the accusative as a *tamyiz* (specification, an accusative indicating the thing specified). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is permissible that it is a *hal* (circumstantial accusative)." End of quote. In that there is a remoteness, and the apparent view is the *tamyiz*, and that it is transferred from the subject; its original form is: "Are the two likenesses of them equal?"

﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people: "Indeed, I am to you a clear warner, that you worship none but God; indeed I fear for you the punishment of a painful day."﴾ ﴿The eminent ones of those of his people who disbelieved said: "We do not see you but as a human like ourselves, and we do not see that those who follow you are other than the lowest of us, in hasty opinion, and we do not see for you any superiority over us; rather, we think you are liars."﴾

This surah, in its narratives, resembles surah al-A'raf. It begins with Noah, then Hud, then Salih, then Lot, with Abraham placed before him because of the people of Lot, then Shu'ayb, then Musa and Harun, may God bless our Prophet and all of them.

They have mentioned aspects of wisdom and benefits of the repetition of these narratives in the Qur'an. The two grammarians and Ibn Kathir read *anni* with *fath* (the *hamza* vowelled with a fatha), i.e., *bi-anni* (that I...). The rest of the seven readers read it with *kasr* (*inni*), by implying the verb "to say". Abu 'Ali said regarding the reading with *fath*: "It is a shift from the third person to the second person." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "There is an issue with this; it is only a quotation of an address to his people. This is not truly a shift from absence to address. If the sentence had been 'warn them' or something similar, that would have been correct." End of quote.

﴿That you worship none but God﴾ [Hud: 2]: this clearly shows that they used to worship idols, as has been stated explicitly in other surahs. *An* is a *badal* (substitution) for *ay* (namely) in the reading of the one who reads with *fath*, and it is possible that it is an explanatory *an*.

As for the reading of the one who reads with *kasr*, it is possible that it is the explanatory *inna*, and what is considered before it is either *arsalna* (We sent) or *nadhir mubin* (clear warner).
