﴿...[as for the one who is] a prostrate one on the top of a cliff, in whom you see, for the bones it has gathered, a cross.﴾ It is said: *la jirama* (no doubt, certainly) with *kasr* (a vowel marker on the letter *jim*), and *la jara*, with the letter *mim* omitted. Al-Nahhas (Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas, a grammarian) said: al-Kisa'i (a grammarian of Kufa) claimed that there are four dialects for it: *la jarama*, *la 'an dha jaramin*, *la an dha jaramin*. He said: "And some people of Fazara say *la jarama*." Al-Farra' (a Kufan grammarian) reported two other dialects for it. He said: "The Banu 'Amir say *la dha jaramin*, and some Arabs say *la juruma*, with the *jim* vowelled with *damma*." Al-Jubba'i said in his *Nawadir* (rare expressions): "It is reported from Fazara: *la jara wallahi la af'alu dhalika* (no, by God, I will not do that)." He said: "It is also said: *la dha jaramin*, *la dhu jaramin*, *la 'an dha jaramin*, *la an dha jaramin*, *la an jarama*, *la 'an jaramin*, *la dha jara wallahi*, without the *mim*, meaning: I will not do that." Some have reported without *la jarama*: *anna-ka anta fa'alta dhalika* (that you yourself did that). From Abu 'Amr: *la-ajrama anna lahumu al-nar* (surely it is certain that for them is the Fire), on the pattern of *la-akrama* (surely he honoured). *La jara*: they dropped it due to frequent use, just as they say *sawta tara* meaning *sawfa tara* (you will see).

When the loss of the self is the greatest loss, they were judged to be those who exceed all other losers among the sinners in loss, whose end is to rest and whose loss ends, unlike these, for their loss has no end.

﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds and humbled themselves before their Lord — those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.﴾ ﴿The likeness of the two groups is like the blind and the deaf, and the seeing and the hearing. Are they equal in likeness? Will you not remember?﴾

When He mentioned what the disbelievers would come to of the Fire, He mentioned what the believers would come to of Paradise. The "two groups" here are the disbeliever and the believer. Since the disbelievers had been mentioned first and the believers were mentioned after them, the comparison here begins with the disbeliever, so He said: ﴿like the blind and the deaf﴾.

It is possible that this is of the type of comparing two things with two things: the blind is matched with the seeing, which is an antithesis (*tibaq*, a rhetorical figure of contrast), and the deaf is matched with the hearing, which is also an antithesis. Blindness and deafness are two afflictions that prevent sight and hearing, and they are not opposites, because there is no alternation between them.

It may also be that it is a comparison of one thing with its two attributes to one thing with its two attributes, so that it is of the coordination of attributes, as the poet said:

*To the king, the peer, and the son of the lofty one, and the lion of the battle in the crowd.*

The construction did not come as "like the blind and the seeing and the deaf and the hearing", which would have been a contrast in the wording of the blind and its opposite and in the wording of the deaf and its opposite. This is because, when He mentioned the closing of the eye, He followed it with the closing of the hearing, and when He mentioned the opening of sight, He followed it with the opening of hearing. That is the method of contrast, and more complete in its inimitability. Insha'Allah, the parallel of this contrast will come in His saying in Ta-Ha: ﴿Indeed, for you there is that you will not hunger therein, nor be naked﴾ [Ta-Ha: 118] ﴿and that you will not thirst therein, nor be exposed to the sun﴾ [Ta-Ha: 119].

It is possible that the *ka* (like) itself is the predicate of the subject, so its meaning is the meaning of "likeness", as if it were said: "The likeness of the two groups is the likeness of the blind." It is also possible that *mathal* (likeness) is intended as the description, and *ka* as *mithl* (similar to), so it would be with an omitted noun: "like the likeness of the blind." This comparison is a comparison of the intelligible with the sensible: the blind of insight is deaf to it, is compared with the blind of sight who is deaf of hearing; that one is in the darkness of misguidance, wandering and confused, and this one is bewildered on the roads and does not find his way.

The words ﴿Will you not remember?﴾ came to alert that this blindness and this deafness of the intellect can be removed. It is therefore obligatory for the rational person to remember what he is in, and to strive to guide himself. *Mathalan* (as a likeness) is in the accusative as a *tamyiz* (specification, an accusative indicating the thing specified). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is permissible that it is a *hal* (circumstantial accusative)." End of quote. In that there is a remoteness, and the apparent view is the *tamyiz*, and that it is transferred from the subject; its original form is: "Are the two likenesses of them equal?"

﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people: "Indeed, I am to you a clear warner, that you worship none but God; indeed I fear for you the punishment of a painful day."﴾ ﴿The eminent ones of those of his people who disbelieved said: "We do not see you but as a human like ourselves, and we do not see that those who follow you are other than the lowest of us, in hasty opinion, and we do not see for you any superiority over us; rather, we think you are liars."﴾

This surah, in its narratives, resembles surah al-A'raf. It begins with Noah, then Hud, then Salih, then Lot, with Abraham placed before him because of the people of Lot, then Shu'ayb, then Musa and Harun, may God bless our Prophet and all of them.

They have mentioned aspects of wisdom and benefits of the repetition of these narratives in the Qur'an. The two grammarians and Ibn Kathir read *anni* with *fath* (the *hamza* vowelled with a fatha), i.e., *bi-anni* (that I...). The rest of the seven readers read it with *kasr* (*inni*), by implying the verb "to say". Abu 'Ali said regarding the reading with *fath*: "It is a shift from the third person to the second person." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "There is an issue with this; it is only a quotation of an address to his people. This is not truly a shift from absence to address. If the sentence had been 'warn them' or something similar, that would have been correct." End of quote.

﴿That you worship none but God﴾ [Hud: 2]: this clearly shows that they used to worship idols, as has been stated explicitly in other surahs. *An* is a *badal* (substitution) for *ay* (namely) in the reading of the one who reads with *fath*, and it is possible that it is an explanatory *an*.

As for the reading of the one who reads with *kasr*, it is possible that it is the explanatory *inna*, and what is considered before it is either *arsalna* (We sent) or *nadhir mubin* (clear warner). It is also possible that it governs *arsalna*, i.e., "that you worship none but God." Attributing painfulness to the day is a metaphor (*majaz*), because the pain occurs in it, not by it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: then why is the punishment described by it [as painful]? I say: It is a metaphor like it, because the painful one in reality is the one who punishes. Their parallel is your saying: 'its day is fasting.'" End of quote.

This is on the basis that *alim* (painful) is an intensive adjective (*sifat mubalagha*) from *alima*, meaning one whose pain is great. If *alim* means *mu'lim* (causing pain), then its attribution to the day is a metaphor, and to the punishment it is literal.

When he warned them of God's punishment, commanded them to single Him out in worship, and informed them that he was a messenger from God, they mentioned that he was similar to them in humanity, and they found it unlikely that God would send a messenger from among humans. It seems they took the view of the Brahmins, who deny the prophethood of humans absolutely. Then they taunted him, saying that only the lowest people followed him; that is, "we do not equate ourselves with them." Then they denied that he had any superiority over them; that is, "you are equal to us in humanity and you have no superiority over us, so how are you distinguished by being the messenger of God?"

In His saying ﴿those who are the lowest of us﴾ there is an exaggeration in the report, and it seems to indicate an emphasis on restricting those who followed him, and that they were the lowest, with no nobleman sharing in that. In a hadith it is said that they were weavers and cuppers. Al-Nahhas said: "They were the poor and those without lineage, and those in base trades."

In the hadith of Heraclius: "Did the nobles of the people follow him, or his weak ones?" He said: "Rather, his weak ones." He said: "They are the followers of the messengers before him." This was so because leadership dominates the nobles, and it is hard to disengage from it, and they are proud to submit to others. The poor person is free of those obstacles, so he is quick to respond and submit.

(*Wa-naraka*, "and we see you"): it is possible that it is visual, and it is possible that it is cognitive. They said: *Arādhil* is a plural of a plural. It is said: it is the plural of *ardhal*, like *kalb* and *aklub* and *akalib*. It is also said: it is the plural of *aradhal*, and its analogical form would be *arādhīl*.

The apparent view is that it is the plural of *arədhal*, which is the comparative form (*af'al al-tafdil*), and it came as a plural, as *akabira mujrimiha* (its greatest criminals) and *ahasinukum akhlaqan* (the best of you in character) came.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Ma naraka illa basharan mithlana* (we do not see you but a human like ourselves)" is an allusion that they were more deserving of prophethood than him, and that if God wanted to place it in a human, He would have placed it among them. They said: "Suppose you are one of the eminent ones and equal to them in rank, what made you more deserving than them? Do you not see their saying: *wa ma nara lakum 'alaynā min fadl* (we do not see for you any superiority over us)?" Or they meant that he should have been an angel, not a human. What al-Zamakhshari said does not appear from the verse.

Abu 'Amr and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read *bādi'a al-ra'y* (initial opinion) from *bada'a yabda'u*, and its meaning is: the first opinion. The rest of the seven read *bādī* with *ya'* from *bada yabdu*, and its meaning is: the apparent opinion. It is also said: *bādī* with *ya'* means *bādi'* with *hamza*, and the *hamza* was made easier by replacing it with *ya'* because of the *kasra* before it.

They mentioned that it is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*zarf*), and the governing element is either *naraka* (we see you), or *ittaba'aka* (followed you), or *arādhiluna* (our lowest). That is: "and we do not see you, in what appears to us of opinion," or "in the first of our opinion," or "and we do not see that they followed you in the first of their opinion," or "in the apparent of their opinion." This possibility has two meanings. One is that he intends: "they followed you in the outward appearance of their affair, and perhaps their inner states are not with you." The second meaning is that he intends: "they followed you at first glance, and by the opinion that appears without reflection; had they reflected, they would not have followed you." In this view there is a condemnation of opinion that is not based on transmission.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "They followed you at first, or in apparent opinion. Its accusative status as an adverb is originally: at the time of the beginning of their affair, or at the time of the emergence of their apparent opinion. That was deleted, and the genitive noun was placed in its position. They meant: their following of you is merely something that came to them instantly, without deliberation or consideration." End of quote.

That it is in the accusative as an adverb is the view of Abu 'Ali in *al-Hujja*. He took it as an adverb though it is neither a time nor a place, because there is an implied *fi* (in) before it, meaning: "in the apparent matter," or "in the first matter."

According to these two estimates, namely that the governing element is *naraka* or *ittaba'aka*, it entails that this is not permissible, because what comes after *illa* (except) cannot be governed by what precedes it, unless it is an exception from something stated (*mustathna minhu*), as in: "the people stood except Zayd," or an exception as an exception (*mustathna*), as in: "the people came except Zayd," or a follower of the thing excepted from, as in: "no one came to me except Zayd; 'Amr informed me." *Bādi'a al-ra'y* is none of these three.

It has been answered that it is an adverb or like an adverb, like *juhda ra'yin innaka dhahib* (with utmost effort of opinion, you are going), meaning: "you are going with utmost effort of opinion." Adverbs are used with latitude. If the governing element is *arādhiluna*, then its meaning is: "those who are our lowest by the least consideration of them, and by the first opinion about them, it is known from them."

It is said: *bādiya al-ra'y* is an adjective of *basharan* (human). It is also said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial (*hal*) from the pronoun of Noah in *ittaba'aka*, meaning: "and you are exposed in opinion, with no sound judgment." It is also said: it is in the accusative as a vocative for Noah, meaning: "O one exposed in opinion," i.e., what is in your mind of opinion is manifest to everyone. They said this to belittle him.

It is also said: it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*), and an adverb and a verbal noun came on the pattern *fa'il*, which is not analogical. Then *ra'y* here is either from seeing with the eye or from thought.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "They only regarded the believers as base because of their poverty and their lateness in worldly means, because they were ignorant and did not know except the outward of the worldly life; so the most honourable among them was the one who had status and wealth." End of quote.

The apparent address in *lakum* (for you) includes Noah and those who followed him. The meaning is: "there is no excess for you over us in wealth, lineage, or religion." Ibn 'Abbas said: "in creation and character." It is also said: "in the abundance of rule and possession." It is also said: "by your following Noah and your opposition to us." It is also said: "from a nobility that qualifies you for prophethood." Al-Kalbi said: *nazunnukum* (we think you): "we are certain of you." Muqatil said: "we consider you," meaning in the claim of Noah and your affirmation of it. The author of *Sahib al-I'tiyan* said: "*bal nazunnukum kadhibin* (rather, we think you are liars)" in pursuit of leadership and fame.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verse 17–27 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Is one who has a clear proof from his Lord, and a witness from Him recites it, and before it the Book of Moses as a guide and a mercy? Those believe in it. Whoever of the factions disbelieves in it, the Fire is his promised place. So do not be in doubt about it; indeed it is the truth from your Lord, but most people do not believe.﴾ When He mentioned the state of those who desire the life of this world, He mentioned the state of those who desire the Face of Allah, the Exalted, through their righteous deeds. The counterpart to which the interrogative hamza is attached has been omitted, and the estimated sense is: "Is he like one who desires the life of this world?"

Such omission occurs frequently in the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him, so that he sees it as good [equal to one who does not]?﴾ [Fatir: 8] and His saying: ﴿Or is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night﴾ [Az-Zumar: 9]. This interrogation carries the meaning of affirmation (taqrir). Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, you do not equal them in rank nor do you parallel them; he means that there is a vast disparity between the two groups and a clear difference. He intended by them those among the Jews who believed, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and others. "Upon a clear proof from his Lord" means upon a proof from Allah, the Exalted, and a demonstration that the religion of Islam is true, and this is the evidence of reason. "And a witness follows it": a witness that follows that proof, bearing witness to its soundness, and this is the Qur'an, "from Him," from Allah; or a witness from the Qur'an. "And before it": before the Qur'an, "the Book of Moses," which is the Torah; that is, the Book of Moses also follows it, coming before the Qur'an.

It is also read (Kitab Musa) in the accusative, and its meaning is: he is upon a clear proof from his Lord, which is the evidence that the Qur'an is true; and a witness from him recites (yatluhu) the Qur'an, a witness from among those who are upon a clear proof, like His saying: ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified to its like﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 10], and ﴿Say: Allah suffices as a witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 43].

﴿And before it the Book of Moses﴾: "recites it" and before the Torah; "as a guide" (imaman): a book that is followed in religion, a model in it. End of quote. It was said regarding ﴿Is one who was﴾: those who believe in the Messenger, and it was said: Muhammad ﷺ specifically. (p-211) Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: Muhammad and the believers all together. "The clear proof" is the Qur'an or the Messenger, and the ha' is for emphasis (intensiveness).

As for "the witness" (al-shahid): Ibn Abbas, al-Nakha'i, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Abu Salih and Ikrimah said: it is Gabriel. Al-Hasan ibn Ali said: it is the Messenger. Mujahid also said: it is an angel whom Allah appointed to guard the Qur'an.

Ibn Atiyyah said: It is possible that by these expressions he means Gabriel. It was also said: Ali ibn Abi Talib. Al-Minhal narrated from Ubadah ibn Abdullah, who said: Ali, may Allah honour his face, said: "There is no one in Quraysh except that a verse was revealed concerning him." It was asked: "What was revealed concerning you?" He said: ﴿And a witness from Him recites it﴾. Muhammad ibn Ali and Zayd ibn Ali also said this.

It was said: it is the Gospel, said by al-Farra'. It was said: it is the Qur'an. It was said: it is the inimitability of the Qur'an, said by al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl. It was said: it is the form of the Messenger ﷺ, his face and his features, because every intelligent person who looked at him knew that he was the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

It was said: and Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. The pronoun in "from Him" refers to the religion, or to the Messenger, or to the Qur'an. "Yatluhu" means "yatba'uhu" (follows it), or "yaqra'uhu" (recites it); the raised pronoun in yatluhu and the accusative and genitive pronouns in minhu are arranged according to what suits each opinion among these.

Muhammad ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kalbi and others read: ﴿Kitab Musa﴾ in the accusative, as a conjunction with the object of yatluhu, or by supposing a verb. And if the witness is not understood to be the Gospel, then he specifically mentioned the Torah because both religions agree that it is from Allah, whereas the Jews disagree regarding the Gospel; so citing that which establishes proof against both groups is more fitting.

This accords with the saying of the jinn: ﴿We have heard a Book revealed after Moses﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 30], and with the saying of al-Najashi: "Indeed this and what Moses brought come out of one niche." "Imaman" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). What appears in the interpretation of this verse is that when He mentioned the disbelievers and that for them there is only the Fire, He followed with their opposites, who are the believers, those who are upon a clear proof from their Lord. The witness is the Qur'an, and "from Him" refers back to "his Lord." What indicates that the witness is the Qur'an is the mention of His saying "and before it" — that is, before the Qur'an, the Book of Moses. So its meaning is that two things combined to guide him: that he is upon a clear matter from the proof of reason, and that this proof agrees with these two divine books, the Qur'an and the Torah, so that he has both reason and transmission.

The demonstrative "those" (ulaika) refers to "one who was upon a clear proof," observing the meaning of "one" (man) and so using the plural. The pronoun in "bihi" refers to the Torah, or the Qur'an, or the Messenger — three opinions. "Al-Ahzab" (the factions) means all the religious communities, said by Ibn Jubayr; or the Jews and Christians, said by Qatadah; or the Quraysh, said by al-Suddi; or the Banu Umayyah, the Banu al-Mughirah ibn Abdullah al-Makhzumi, and the family of Abu Talhah ibn Ubaydullah, said by Muqatil. Al-Zamakhshari said: he means the people of Makkah and those allied with them among the factions against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. End of quote.

﴿So the Fire is his promised place﴾: that is, the place of his promise to which they will go. Hassan said:
"You brought us to the watering-places of death in the open, so the Fire is its promised place, and death meets it."
The pronoun in "minhu" refers to the Qur'an; it was also said that it refers to the report that the disbelievers' promised place is the Fire. The majority read "fi miryah" with a kasrah on the mim, which is the dialect of the Hijaz. As-Sulami, Abu Raja', Abu al-Khattab al-Sadusi and al-Hasan read it with a dammah, which is the dialect of Asad and Tamim. "The people" (al-nas) means the people of Makkah, said by Ibn Abbas; or all the disbelievers, whether doubters, ignorant, or obstinate, said by the author of al-Iqyan.

﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah? Those will be presented before their Lord, and the witnesses will say: "These are the ones who lied against their Lord. Ah, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers, who bar from the way of Allah and seek to make it crooked, and they are, in the Hereafter, disbelievers." Those were not able to escape in the earth, and they had no protectors other than Allah; their punishment will be doubled. They could not hear, nor did they see. Those are the ones who have lost themselves, and what they used to fabricate has gone astray from them. Certainly, in the Hereafter they will be the greatest losers.﴾ When their saying "Has he fabricated it?" [Hud: 13] preceded, He mentioned that there is no one more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah. These are the fabricators who attributed a son to Allah, took others alongside Him, and declared lawful and unlawful without any law from Allah. Their being presented before Allah means exposing them to disgrace and indicating their lie; otherwise, both the obedient and the disobedient are presented before Allah: ﴿And they will be presented before your Lord in rows﴾ [Al-Kahf: 48]. "Al-ashhad" is the plural of shahid, like sahib and ashab, or the plural of shahid as in sharif and ashraf. "Al-ashhad" are the angels who guarded their deeds in the world, or the prophets, or both the believers, or their own limbs bearing witness against them, sayings. In His saying "these" (haʾulaʾ) there is an indication of belittling and humiliating them because of their evil deeds.

In His saying "before their Lord": that is, before One who does good to them and holds their forelocks, and they were worthy not to lie against Him. This is like when you see a criminal and say: "This is the one who did such and such." The sentence's explanation has been given previously. "Hum" is an emphasis for "wa hum." "Mu'jizin" means: they could not escape Allah in the world from punishing them, had He wished to punish them, and there was no one who could help them or prevent them from punishment; but He willed to delay them and postpone their punishment until this day.

Al-Zamakhshari said: This is the speech of the witnesses; that is, their speech is from "these" to the end of this sentence, which is "and they had no protectors other than Allah."

It may appear that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Ah, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾ is from the speech of Allah, not in the manner of narration. This supports al-Zamakhshari's view, and His saying: ﴿Then a caller calls out among them: the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾ [Al-A'raf: 44], etc. Just as that is the speech of created beings in that verse, so likewise here. "Yudaf lahum al-adhab": it is intensified and increased. This is a resumed statement about their state in the Hereafter, because they combined disbelief in resurrection with lying against Allah, barring His servants from the way of Allah, and seeking to make it crooked, though it is the straight path.

"They could not hear": a report about their state in the world, in the manner of exaggeration; that is, hearing the Qur'an and what the Messenger ﷺ brought.

"Nor did they see": that is, they did not look at it, out of their hatred for it. Do you not see how al-Tufayl ibn Amr stuffed his ears with cotton, and how Quraysh refused to hear what was conveyed to them of the Messenger's speech until their elders turned them away from it? Or it is a report about their state when the punishment is doubled for them: that is, Allah decreed this upon them, so they do not hear in a way that benefits them, nor do they see in that way. It was said: the pronoun in "kanu" refers to "their protectors," their gods; that is, in reality they had no protectors, though they believed them to be protectors. It means that one who cannot hear or see, how could he be fit for protection? And "yudaf lahum al-adhab" would then be a parenthetical clause, and "ma" in these opinions is negation. It was also said: "ma" is verbal (masdariyyah), meaning: the punishment is doubled for them for the duration of their ability to hear and see; and the meaning is that the punishment and its doubling is constant and continuous for them. Al-Farra' permitted "ma" to be verbal, with the preposition removed from it, as the preposition is removed with anna and in, its sisters; but this is remote in wording and in meaning.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He meant that because of their extreme deafness to following the truth and their aversion to it, it is as if they could not hear. Perhaps some of the Mujbira (determinists), when they stumble upon this, leap up and bark at the people of justice with it, as if he had not heard people saying in every language: "I cannot bear to hear this word; my hearing rejects it." End of quote.

That is: it can be used as evidence that the servant has no power, because Allah, exalted is He, has negated from him the ability to hear; and if ability is negated from him, his power is negated. Al-Zamakhshari, as is his habit, scoffs at the People of the Sunnah and their losing themselves, because they bought the worship of idols in exchange for the worship of Allah, the Exalted; so in their trade they suffered a loss than which none is greater.

This is with an elided modifier: that is, the comfort or happiness of their souls; otherwise their souls remain, tormented. What they had fabricated of worshipping idols went astray from them, and their belief that the idols would intercede faded when they saw that they neither interceded nor benefited.

"La jaram": the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh is that they were compounded from "la" and "jaram" and became one word, meaning "truly," and what follows is raised by it as the subject (fa'il). Al-Hawfi said: jaram, negated by la, means "truly"; it is built together with la in the place of a nominative as subject, and "annahum" is in the place of a nominative as the predicate of jaram. (p-213)

Some said: "jaram" is built with "la" on the fatha, as in your saying "la rajul" (no man), and its meaning is: "there is no doubt and no escape." Al-Kisa'i said: its meaning is: "no opposition and no prevention," so it is the subject of la, and it is built on fatha like the preceding saying; and "jaram" here is from the sense of cutting off, as we say: "jaramtu," meaning "I cut off." Al-Zajjaj said: there is no compounding between them and no refutation of them.

Because of all that preceded it, namely their claim that the idols would benefit them. "Jaram" is a past verb meaning "he earned," with an implied subject: "Does he earn it?" that is, their action; and "anna" and what follows it are in the place of an accusative as the object. "Jarama al-qawm" means: he earned for them. The poet said:
"We set his head upon a palm trunk, for what his hands had earned, and we did not transgress."
Another said: [the text breaks off here.]

The commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verses 17–27 (part 2 of 2):

﴿...[as for the one who is] a prostrate one on the top of a cliff, in whom you see, for the bones it has gathered, a cross.﴾ It is said: *la jirama* (no doubt, certainly) with *kasr* (a vowel marker on the letter *jim*), and *la jara*, with the letter *mim* omitted. Al-Nahhas (Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas, a grammarian) said: al-Kisa'i (a grammarian of Kufa) claimed that there are four dialects for it: *la jarama*, *la 'an dha jaramin*, *la an dha jaramin*. He said: "And some people of Fazara say *la jarama*." Al-Farra' (a Kufan grammarian) reported two other dialects for it. He said: "The Banu 'Amir say *la dha jaramin*, and some Arabs say *la juruma*, with the *jim* vowelled with *damma*." Al-Jubba'i said in his *Nawadir* (rare expressions): "It is reported from Fazara: *la jara wallahi la af'alu dhalika* (no, by God, I will not do that)." He said: "It is also said: *la dha jaramin*, *la dhu jaramin*, *la 'an dha jaramin*, *la an dha jaramin*, *la an jarama*, *la 'an jaramin*, *la dha jara wallahi*, without the *mim*, meaning: I will not do that." Some have reported without *la jarama*: *anna-ka anta fa'alta dhalika* (that you yourself did that). From Abu 'Amr: *la-ajrama anna lahumu al-nar* (surely it is certain that for them is the Fire), on the pattern of *la-akrama* (surely he honoured). *La jara*: they dropped it due to frequent use, just as they say *sawta tara* meaning *sawfa tara* (you will see).

When the loss of the self is the greatest loss, they were judged to be those who exceed all other losers among the sinners in loss, whose end is to rest and whose loss ends, unlike these, for their loss has no end.

﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds and humbled themselves before their Lord — those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.﴾ ﴿The likeness of the two groups is like the blind and the deaf, and the seeing and the hearing. Are they equal in likeness? Will you not remember?﴾

When He mentioned what the disbelievers would come to of the Fire, He mentioned what the believers would come to of Paradise. The "two groups" here are the disbeliever and the believer. Since the disbelievers had been mentioned first and the believers were mentioned after them, the comparison here begins with the disbeliever, so He said: ﴿like the blind and the deaf﴾.

It is possible that this is of the type of comparing two things with two things: the blind is matched with the seeing, which is an antithesis (*tibaq*, a rhetorical figure of contrast), and the deaf is matched with the hearing, which is also an antithesis. Blindness and deafness are two afflictions that prevent sight and hearing, and they are not opposites, because there is no alternation between them.

It may also be that it is a comparison of one thing with its two attributes to one thing with its two attributes, so that it is of the coordination of attributes, as the poet said:

*To the king, the peer, and the son of the lofty one, and the lion of the battle in the crowd.*

The construction did not come as "like the blind and the seeing and the deaf and the hearing", which would have been a contrast in the wording of the blind and its opposite and in the wording of the deaf and its opposite. This is because, when He mentioned the closing of the eye, He followed it with the closing of the hearing, and when He mentioned the opening of sight, He followed it with the opening of hearing. That is the method of contrast, and more complete in its inimitability. Insha'Allah, the parallel of this contrast will come in His saying in Ta-Ha: ﴿Indeed, for you there is that you will not hunger therein, nor be naked﴾ [Ta-Ha: 118] ﴿and that you will not thirst therein, nor be exposed to the sun﴾ [Ta-Ha: 119].

It is possible that the *ka* (like) itself is the predicate of the subject, so its meaning is the meaning of "likeness", as if it were said: "The likeness of the two groups is the likeness of the blind." It is also possible that *mathal* (likeness) is intended as the description, and *ka* as *mithl* (similar to), so it would be with an omitted noun: "like the likeness of the blind." This comparison is a comparison of the intelligible with the sensible: the blind of insight is deaf to it, is compared with the blind of sight who is deaf of hearing; that one is in the darkness of misguidance, wandering and confused, and this one is bewildered on the roads and does not find his way.

The words ﴿Will you not remember?﴾ came to alert that this blindness and this deafness of the intellect can be removed. It is therefore obligatory for the rational person to remember what he is in, and to strive to guide himself. *Mathalan* (as a likeness) is in the accusative as a *tamyiz* (specification, an accusative indicating the thing specified). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is permissible that it is a *hal* (circumstantial accusative)." End of quote. In that there is a remoteness, and the apparent view is the *tamyiz*, and that it is transferred from the subject; its original form is: "Are the two likenesses of them equal?"

﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people: "Indeed, I am to you a clear warner, that you worship none but God; indeed I fear for you the punishment of a painful day."﴾ ﴿The eminent ones of those of his people who disbelieved said: "We do not see you but as a human like ourselves, and we do not see that those who follow you are other than the lowest of us, in hasty opinion, and we do not see for you any superiority over us; rather, we think you are liars."﴾

This surah, in its narratives, resembles surah al-A'raf. It begins with Noah, then Hud, then Salih, then Lot, with Abraham placed before him because of the people of Lot, then Shu'ayb, then Musa and Harun, may God bless our Prophet and all of them.

They have mentioned aspects of wisdom and benefits of the repetition of these narratives in the Qur'an. The two grammarians and Ibn Kathir read *anni* with *fath* (the *hamza* vowelled with a fatha), i.e., *bi-anni* (that I...). The rest of the seven readers read it with *kasr* (*inni*), by implying the verb "to say". Abu 'Ali said regarding the reading with *fath*: "It is a shift from the third person to the second person." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "There is an issue with this; it is only a quotation of an address to his people. This is not truly a shift from absence to address. If the sentence had been 'warn them' or something similar, that would have been correct." End of quote.

﴿That you worship none but God﴾ [Hud: 2]: this clearly shows that they used to worship idols, as has been stated explicitly in other surahs. *An* is a *badal* (substitution) for *ay* (namely) in the reading of the one who reads with *fath*, and it is possible that it is an explanatory *an*.

As for the reading of the one who reads with *kasr*, it is possible that it is the explanatory *inna*, and what is considered before it is either *arsalna* (We sent) or *nadhir mubin* (clear warner). It is also possible that it governs *arsalna*, i.e., "that you worship none but God." Attributing painfulness to the day is a metaphor (*majaz*), because the pain occurs in it, not by it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: then why is the punishment described by it [as painful]? I say: It is a metaphor like it, because the painful one in reality is the one who punishes. Their parallel is your saying: 'its day is fasting.'" End of quote.

This is on the basis that *alim* (painful) is an intensive adjective (*sifat mubalagha*) from *alima*, meaning one whose pain is great. If *alim* means *mu'lim* (causing pain), then its attribution to the day is a metaphor, and to the punishment it is literal.

When he warned them of God's punishment, commanded them to single Him out in worship, and informed them that he was a messenger from God, they mentioned that he was similar to them in humanity, and they found it unlikely that God would send a messenger from among humans. It seems they took the view of the Brahmins, who deny the prophethood of humans absolutely. Then they taunted him, saying that only the lowest people followed him; that is, "we do not equate ourselves with them." Then they denied that he had any superiority over them; that is, "you are equal to us in humanity and you have no superiority over us, so how are you distinguished by being the messenger of God?"

In His saying ﴿those who are the lowest of us﴾ there is an exaggeration in the report, and it seems to indicate an emphasis on restricting those who followed him, and that they were the lowest, with no nobleman sharing in that. In a hadith it is said that they were weavers and cuppers. Al-Nahhas said: "They were the poor and those without lineage, and those in base trades."

In the hadith of Heraclius: "Did the nobles of the people follow him, or his weak ones?" He said: "Rather, his weak ones." He said: "They are the followers of the messengers before him." This was so because leadership dominates the nobles, and it is hard to disengage from it, and they are proud to submit to others. The poor person is free of those obstacles, so he is quick to respond and submit.

(*Wa-naraka*, "and we see you"): it is possible that it is visual, and it is possible that it is cognitive. They said: *Arādhil* is a plural of a plural. It is said: it is the plural of *ardhal*, like *kalb* and *aklub* and *akalib*. It is also said: it is the plural of *aradhal*, and its analogical form would be *arādhīl*.

The apparent view is that it is the plural of *arədhal*, which is the comparative form (*af'al al-tafdil*), and it came as a plural, as *akabira mujrimiha* (its greatest criminals) and *ahasinukum akhlaqan* (the best of you in character) came.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Ma naraka illa basharan mithlana* (we do not see you but a human like ourselves)" is an allusion that they were more deserving of prophethood than him, and that if God wanted to place it in a human, He would have placed it among them. They said: "Suppose you are one of the eminent ones and equal to them in rank, what made you more deserving than them? Do you not see their saying: *wa ma nara lakum 'alaynā min fadl* (we do not see for you any superiority over us)?" Or they meant that he should have been an angel, not a human. What al-Zamakhshari said does not appear from the verse.

Abu 'Amr and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read *bādi'a al-ra'y* (initial opinion) from *bada'a yabda'u*, and its meaning is: the first opinion. The rest of the seven read *bādī* with *ya'* from *bada yabdu*, and its meaning is: the apparent opinion. It is also said: *bādī* with *ya'* means *bādi'* with *hamza*, and the *hamza* was made easier by replacing it with *ya'* because of the *kasra* before it.

They mentioned that it is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*zarf*), and the governing element is either *naraka* (we see you), or *ittaba'aka* (followed you), or *arādhiluna* (our lowest). That is: "and we do not see you, in what appears to us of opinion," or "in the first of our opinion," or "and we do not see that they followed you in the first of their opinion," or "in the apparent of their opinion." This possibility has two meanings. One is that he intends: "they followed you in the outward appearance of their affair, and perhaps their inner states are not with you." The second meaning is that he intends: "they followed you at first glance, and by the opinion that appears without reflection; had they reflected, they would not have followed you." In this view there is a condemnation of opinion that is not based on transmission.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "They followed you at first, or in apparent opinion. Its accusative status as an adverb is originally: at the time of the beginning of their affair, or at the time of the emergence of their apparent opinion. That was deleted, and the genitive noun was placed in its position. They meant: their following of you is merely something that came to them instantly, without deliberation or consideration." End of quote.

That it is in the accusative as an adverb is the view of Abu 'Ali in *al-Hujja*. He took it as an adverb though it is neither a time nor a place, because there is an implied *fi* (in) before it, meaning: "in the apparent matter," or "in the first matter."

According to these two estimates, namely that the governing element is *naraka* or *ittaba'aka*, it entails that this is not permissible, because what comes after *illa* (except) cannot be governed by what precedes it, unless it is an exception from something stated (*mustathna minhu*), as in: "the people stood except Zayd," or an exception as an exception (*mustathna*), as in: "the people came except Zayd," or a follower of the thing excepted from, as in: "no one came to me except Zayd; 'Amr informed me." *Bādi'a al-ra'y* is none of these three.

It has been answered that it is an adverb or like an adverb, like *juhda ra'yin innaka dhahib* (with utmost effort of opinion, you are going), meaning: "you are going with utmost effort of opinion." Adverbs are used with latitude. If the governing element is *arādhiluna*, then its meaning is: "those who are our lowest by the least consideration of them, and by the first opinion about them, it is known from them."

It is said: *bādiya al-ra'y* is an adjective of *basharan* (human). It is also said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial (*hal*) from the pronoun of Noah in *ittaba'aka*, meaning: "and you are exposed in opinion, with no sound judgment." It is also said: it is in the accusative as a vocative for Noah, meaning: "O one exposed in opinion," i.e., what is in your mind of opinion is manifest to everyone. They said this to belittle him.

It is also said: it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*), and an adverb and a verbal noun came on the pattern *fa'il*, which is not analogical. Then *ra'y* here is either from seeing with the eye or from thought.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "They only regarded the believers as base because of their poverty and their lateness in worldly means, because they were ignorant and did not know except the outward of the worldly life; so the most honourable among them was the one who had status and wealth." End of quote.

The apparent address in *lakum* (for you) includes Noah and those who followed him. The meaning is: "there is no excess for you over us in wealth, lineage, or religion." Ibn 'Abbas said: "in creation and character." It is also said: "in the abundance of rule and possession." It is also said: "by your following Noah and your opposition to us." It is also said: "from a nobility that qualifies you for prophethood." Al-Kalbi said: *nazunnukum* (we think you): "we are certain of you." Muqatil said: "we consider you," meaning in the claim of Noah and your affirmation of it. The author of *Sahib al-I'tiyan* said: "*bal nazunnukum kadhibin* (rather, we think you are liars)" in pursuit of leadership and fame.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verse 17–27 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Is one who has a clear proof from his Lord, and a witness from Him recites it, and before it the Book of Moses as a guide and a mercy? Those believe in it. Whoever of the factions disbelieves in it, the Fire is his promised place. So do not be in doubt about it; indeed it is the truth from your Lord, but most people do not believe.﴾ When He mentioned the state of those who desire the life of this world, He mentioned the state of those who desire the Face of Allah, the Exalted, through their righteous deeds. The counterpart to which the interrogative hamza is attached has been omitted, and the estimated sense is: "Is he like one who desires the life of this world?"

Such omission occurs frequently in the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him, so that he sees it as good [equal to one who does not]?﴾ [Fatir: 8] and His saying: ﴿Or is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night﴾ [Az-Zumar: 9]. This interrogation carries the meaning of affirmation (taqrir). Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, you do not equal them in rank nor do you parallel them; he means that there is a vast disparity between the two groups and a clear difference. He intended by them those among the Jews who believed, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and others. "Upon a clear proof from his Lord" means upon a proof from Allah, the Exalted, and a demonstration that the religion of Islam is true, and this is the evidence of reason. "And a witness follows it": a witness that follows that proof, bearing witness to its soundness, and this is the Qur'an, "from Him," from Allah; or a witness from the Qur'an. "And before it": before the Qur'an, "the Book of Moses," which is the Torah; that is, the Book of Moses also follows it, coming before the Qur'an.

It is also read (Kitab Musa) in the accusative, and its meaning is: he is upon a clear proof from his Lord, which is the evidence that the Qur'an is true; and a witness from him recites (yatluhu) the Qur'an, a witness from among those who are upon a clear proof, like His saying: ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified to its like﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 10], and ﴿Say: Allah suffices as a witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 43].

﴿And before it the Book of Moses﴾: "recites it" and before the Torah; "as a guide" (imaman): a book that is followed in religion, a model in it. End of quote. It was said regarding ﴿Is one who was﴾: those who believe in the Messenger, and it was said: Muhammad ﷺ specifically. (p-211) Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: Muhammad and the believers all together. "The clear proof" is the Qur'an or the Messenger, and the ha' is for emphasis (intensiveness).

As for "the witness" (al-shahid): Ibn Abbas, al-Nakha'i, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Abu Salih and Ikrimah said: it is Gabriel. Al-Hasan ibn Ali said: it is the Messenger. Mujahid also said: it is an angel whom Allah appointed to guard the Qur'an.

Ibn Atiyyah said: It is possible that by these expressions he means Gabriel. It was also said: Ali ibn Abi Talib. Al-Minhal narrated from Ubadah ibn Abdullah, who said: Ali, may Allah honour his face, said: "There is no one in Quraysh except that a verse was revealed concerning him." It was asked: "What was revealed concerning you?" He said: ﴿And a witness from Him recites it﴾. Muhammad ibn Ali and Zayd ibn Ali also said this.

It was said: it is the Gospel, said by al-Farra'. It was said: it is the Qur'an. It was said: it is the inimitability of the Qur'an, said by al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl. It was said: it is the form of the Messenger ﷺ, his face and his features, because every intelligent person who looked at him knew that he was the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

It was said: and Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. The pronoun in "from Him" refers to the religion, or to the Messenger, or to the Qur'an. "Yatluhu" means "yatba'uhu" (follows it), or "yaqra'uhu" (recites it); the raised pronoun in yatluhu and the accusative and genitive pronouns in minhu are arranged according to what suits each opinion among these.

Muhammad ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kalbi and others read: ﴿Kitab Musa﴾ in the accusative, as a conjunction with the object of yatluhu, or by supposing a verb. And if the witness is not understood to be the Gospel, then he specifically mentioned the Torah because both religions agree that it is from Allah, whereas the Jews disagree regarding the Gospel; so citing that which establishes proof against both groups is more fitting.

This accords with the saying of the jinn: ﴿We have heard a Book revealed after Moses﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 30], and with the saying of al-Najashi: "Indeed this and what Moses brought come out of one niche." "Imaman" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). What appears in the interpretation of this verse is that when He mentioned the disbelievers and that for them there is only the Fire, He followed with their opposites, who are the believers, those who are upon a clear proof from their Lord. The witness is the Qur'an, and "from Him" refers back to "his Lord." What indicates that the witness is the Qur'an is the mention of His saying "and before it" — that is, before the Qur'an, the Book of Moses. So its meaning is that two things combined to guide him: that he is upon a clear matter from the proof of reason, and that this proof agrees with these two divine books, the Qur'an and the Torah, so that he has both reason and transmission.

The demonstrative "those" (ulaika) refers to "one who was upon a clear proof," observing the meaning of "one" (man) and so using the plural. The pronoun in "bihi" refers to the Torah, or the Qur'an, or the Messenger — three opinions. "Al-Ahzab" (the factions) means all the religious communities, said by Ibn Jubayr; or the Jews and Christians, said by Qatadah; or the Quraysh, said by al-Suddi; or the Banu Umayyah, the Banu al-Mughirah ibn Abdullah al-Makhzumi, and the family of Abu Talhah ibn Ubaydullah, said by Muqatil. Al-Zamakhshari said: he means the people of Makkah and those allied with them among the factions against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. End of quote.

﴿So the Fire is his promised place﴾: that is, the place of his promise to which they will go. Hassan said:
"You brought us to the watering-places of death in the open, so the Fire is its promised place, and death meets it."
The pronoun in "minhu" refers to the Qur'an; it was also said that it refers to the report that the disbelievers' promised place is the Fire. The majority read "fi miryah" with a kasrah on the mim, which is the dialect of the Hijaz. As-Sulami, Abu Raja', Abu al-Khattab al-Sadusi and al-Hasan read it with a dammah, which is the dialect of Asad and Tamim. "The people" (al-nas) means the people of Makkah, said by Ibn Abbas; or all the disbelievers, whether doubters, ignorant, or obstinate, said by the author of al-Iqyan.

﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah? Those will be presented before their Lord, and the witnesses will say: "These are the ones who lied against their Lord. Ah, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers, who bar from the way of Allah and seek to make it crooked, and they are, in the Hereafter, disbelievers." Those were not able to escape in the earth, and they had no protectors other than Allah; their punishment will be doubled. They could not hear, nor did they see. Those are the ones who have lost themselves, and what they used to fabricate has gone astray from them. Certainly, in the Hereafter they will be the greatest losers.﴾ When their saying "Has he fabricated it?" [Hud: 13] preceded, He mentioned that there is no one more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah. These are the fabricators who attributed a son to Allah, took others alongside Him, and declared lawful and unlawful without any law from Allah. Their being presented before Allah means exposing them to disgrace and indicating their lie; otherwise, both the obedient and the disobedient are presented before Allah: ﴿And they will be presented before your Lord in rows﴾ [Al-Kahf: 48]. "Al-ashhad" is the plural of shahid, like sahib and ashab, or the plural of shahid as in sharif and ashraf. "Al-ashhad" are the angels who guarded their deeds in the world, or the prophets, or both the believers, or their own limbs bearing witness against them, sayings. In His saying "these" (haʾulaʾ) there is an indication of belittling and humiliating them because of their evil deeds.

In His saying "before their Lord": that is, before One who does good to them and holds their forelocks, and they were worthy not to lie against Him. This is like when you see a criminal and say: "This is the one who did such and such." The sentence's explanation has been given previously. "Hum" is an emphasis for "wa hum." "Mu'jizin" means: they could not escape Allah in the world from punishing them, had He wished to punish them, and there was no one who could help them or prevent them from punishment; but He willed to delay them and postpone their punishment until this day.

Al-Zamakhshari said: This is the speech of the witnesses; that is, their speech is from "these" to the end of this sentence, which is "and they had no protectors other than Allah."

It may appear that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Ah, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾ is from the speech of Allah, not in the manner of narration. This supports al-Zamakhshari's view, and His saying: ﴿Then a caller calls out among them: the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾ [Al-A'raf: 44], etc. Just as that is the speech of created beings in that verse, so likewise here. "Yudaf lahum al-adhab": it is intensified and increased. This is a resumed statement about their state in the Hereafter, because they combined disbelief in resurrection with lying against Allah, barring His servants from the way of Allah, and seeking to make it crooked, though it is the straight path.

"They could not hear": a report about their state in the world, in the manner of exaggeration; that is, hearing the Qur'an and what the Messenger ﷺ brought.

"Nor did they see": that is, they did not look at it, out of their hatred for it. Do you not see how al-Tufayl ibn Amr stuffed his ears with cotton, and how Quraysh refused to hear what was conveyed to them of the Messenger's speech until their elders turned them away from it? Or it is a report about their state when the punishment is doubled for them: that is, Allah decreed this upon them, so they do not hear in a way that benefits them, nor do they see in that way. It was said: the pronoun in "kanu" refers to "their protectors," their gods; that is, in reality they had no protectors, though they believed them to be protectors. It means that one who cannot hear or see, how could he be fit for protection? And "yudaf lahum al-adhab" would then be a parenthetical clause, and "ma" in these opinions is negation. It was also said: "ma" is verbal (masdariyyah), meaning: the punishment is doubled for them for the duration of their ability to hear and see; and the meaning is that the punishment and its doubling is constant and continuous for them. Al-Farra' permitted "ma" to be verbal, with the preposition removed from it, as the preposition is removed with anna and in, its sisters; but this is remote in wording and in meaning.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He meant that because of their extreme deafness to following the truth and their aversion to it, it is as if they could not hear. Perhaps some of the Mujbira (determinists), when they stumble upon this, leap up and bark at the people of justice with it, as if he had not heard people saying in every language: "I cannot bear to hear this word; my hearing rejects it." End of quote.

That is: it can be used as evidence that the servant has no power, because Allah, exalted is He, has negated from him the ability to hear; and if ability is negated from him, his power is negated. Al-Zamakhshari, as is his habit, scoffs at the People of the Sunnah and their losing themselves, because they bought the worship of idols in exchange for the worship of Allah, the Exalted; so in their trade they suffered a loss than which none is greater.

This is with an elided modifier: that is, the comfort or happiness of their souls; otherwise their souls remain, tormented. What they had fabricated of worshipping idols went astray from them, and their belief that the idols would intercede faded when they saw that they neither interceded nor benefited.

"La jaram": the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh is that they were compounded from "la" and "jaram" and became one word, meaning "truly," and what follows is raised by it as the subject (fa'il). Al-Hawfi said: jaram, negated by la, means "truly"; it is built together with la in the place of a nominative as subject, and "annahum" is in the place of a nominative as the predicate of jaram. (p-213)

Some said: "jaram" is built with "la" on the fatha, as in your saying "la rajul" (no man), and its meaning is: "there is no doubt and no escape." Al-Kisa'i said: its meaning is: "no opposition and no prevention," so it is the subject of la, and it is built on fatha like the preceding saying; and "jaram" here is from the sense of cutting off, as we say: "jaramtu," meaning "I cut off." Al-Zajjaj said: there is no compounding between them and no refutation of them.

Because of all that preceded it, namely their claim that the idols would benefit them. "Jaram" is a past verb meaning "he earned," with an implied subject: "Does he earn it?" that is, their action; and "anna" and what follows it are in the place of an accusative as the object. "Jarama al-qawm" means: he earned for them. The poet said:
"We set his head upon a palm trunk, for what his hands had earned, and we did not transgress."
Another said: [the text breaks off here.]

The commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verses 17–27 (part 2 of 2):

﴿...[as for the one who is] a prostrate one on the top of a cliff, in whom you see, for the bones it has gathered, a cross.﴾ It is said: *la jirama* (no doubt, certainly) with *kasr* (a vowel marker on the letter *jim*), and *la jara*, with the letter *mim* omitted. Al-Nahhas (Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas, a grammarian) said: al-Kisa'i (a grammarian of Kufa) claimed that there are four dialects for it: *la jarama*, *la 'an dha jaramin*, *la an dha jaramin*. He said: "And some people of Fazara say *la jarama*." Al-Farra' (a Kufan grammarian) reported two other dialects for it. He said: "The Banu 'Amir say *la dha jaramin*, and some Arabs say *la juruma*, with the *jim* vowelled with *damma*." Al-Jubba'i said in his *Nawadir* (rare expressions): "It is reported from Fazara: *la jara wallahi la af'alu dhalika* (no, by God, I will not do that)." He said: "It is also said: *la dha jaramin*, *la dhu jaramin*, *la 'an dha jaramin*, *la an dha jaramin*, *la an jarama*, *la 'an jaramin*, *la dha jara wallahi*, without the *mim*, meaning: I will not do that." Some have reported without *la jarama*: *anna-ka anta fa'alta dhalika* (that you yourself did that). From Abu 'Amr: *la-ajrama anna lahumu al-nar* (surely it is certain that for them is the Fire), on the pattern of *la-akrama* (surely he honoured). *La jara*: they dropped it due to frequent use, just as they say *sawta tara* meaning *sawfa tara* (you will see).

When the loss of the self is the greatest loss, they were judged to be those who exceed all other losers among the sinners in loss, whose end is to rest and whose loss ends, unlike these, for their loss has no end.

﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds and humbled themselves before their Lord — those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.﴾ ﴿The likeness of the two groups is like the blind and the deaf, and the seeing and the hearing. Are they equal in likeness? Will you not remember?﴾

When He mentioned what the disbelievers would come to of the Fire, He mentioned what the believers would come to of Paradise. The "two groups" here are the disbeliever and the believer. Since the disbelievers had been mentioned first and the believers were mentioned after them, the comparison here begins with the disbeliever, so He said: ﴿like the blind and the deaf﴾.

It is possible that this is of the type of comparing two things with two things: the blind is matched with the seeing, which is an antithesis (*tibaq*, a rhetorical figure of contrast), and the deaf is matched with the hearing, which is also an antithesis. Blindness and deafness are two afflictions that prevent sight and hearing, and they are not opposites, because there is no alternation between them.

It may also be that it is a comparison of one thing with its two attributes to one thing with its two attributes, so that it is of the coordination of attributes, as the poet said:

*To the king, the peer, and the son of the lofty one, and the lion of the battle in the crowd.*

The construction did not come as "like the blind and the seeing and the deaf and the hearing", which would have been a contrast in the wording of the blind and its opposite and in the wording of the deaf and its opposite. This is because, when He mentioned the closing of the eye, He followed it with the closing of the hearing, and when He mentioned the opening of sight, He followed it with the opening of hearing. That is the method of contrast, and more complete in its inimitability. Insha'Allah, the parallel of this contrast will come in His saying in Ta-Ha: ﴿Indeed, for you there is that you will not hunger therein, nor be naked﴾ [Ta-Ha: 118] ﴿and that you will not thirst therein, nor be exposed to the sun﴾ [Ta-Ha: 119].

It is possible that the *ka* (like) itself is the predicate of the subject, so its meaning is the meaning of "likeness", as if it were said: "The likeness of the two groups is the likeness of the blind." It is also possible that *mathal* (likeness) is intended as the description, and *ka* as *mithl* (similar to), so it would be with an omitted noun: "like the likeness of the blind." This comparison is a comparison of the intelligible with the sensible: the blind of insight is deaf to it, is compared with the blind of sight who is deaf of hearing; that one is in the darkness of misguidance, wandering and confused, and this one is bewildered on the roads and does not find his way.

The words ﴿Will you not remember?﴾ came to alert that this blindness and this deafness of the intellect can be removed. It is therefore obligatory for the rational person to remember what he is in, and to strive to guide himself. *Mathalan* (as a likeness) is in the accusative as a *tamyiz* (specification, an accusative indicating the thing specified). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is permissible that it is a *hal* (circumstantial accusative)." End of quote. In that there is a remoteness, and the apparent view is the *tamyiz*, and that it is transferred from the subject; its original form is: "Are the two likenesses of them equal?"

﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people: "Indeed, I am to you a clear warner, that you worship none but God; indeed I fear for you the punishment of a painful day."﴾ ﴿The eminent ones of those of his people who disbelieved said: "We do not see you but as a human like ourselves, and we do not see that those who follow you are other than the lowest of us, in hasty opinion, and we do not see for you any superiority over us; rather, we think you are liars."﴾

This surah, in its narratives, resembles surah al-A'raf. It begins with Noah, then Hud, then Salih, then Lot, with Abraham placed before him because of the people of Lot, then Shu'ayb, then Musa and Harun, may God bless our Prophet and all of them.

They have mentioned aspects of wisdom and benefits of the repetition of these narratives in the Qur'an. The two grammarians and Ibn Kathir read *anni* with *fath* (the *hamza* vowelled with a fatha), i.e., *bi-anni* (that I...). The rest of the seven readers read it with *kasr* (*inni*), by implying the verb "to say". Abu 'Ali said regarding the reading with *fath*: "It is a shift from the third person to the second person." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "There is an issue with this; it is only a quotation of an address to his people. This is not truly a shift from absence to address. If the sentence had been 'warn them' or something similar, that would have been correct." End of quote.

﴿That you worship none but God﴾ [Hud: 2]: this clearly shows that they used to worship idols, as has been stated explicitly in other surahs. *An* is a *badal* (substitution) for *ay* (namely) in the reading of the one who reads with *fath*, and it is possible that it is an explanatory *an*.

As for the reading of the one who reads with *kasr*, it is possible that it is the explanatory *inna*, and what is considered before it is either *arsalna* (We sent) or *nadhir mubin* (clear warner). It is also possible that it governs *arsalna*, i.e., "that you worship none but God." Attributing painfulness to the day is a metaphor (*majaz*), because the pain occurs in it, not by it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: then why is the punishment described by it [as painful]? I say: It is a metaphor like it, because the painful one in reality is the one who punishes. Their parallel is your saying: 'its day is fasting.'" End of quote.

This is on the basis that *alim* (painful) is an intensive adjective (*sifat mubalagha*) from *alima*, meaning one whose pain is great. If *alim* means *mu'lim* (causing pain), then its attribution to the day is a metaphor, and to the punishment it is literal.

When he warned them of God's punishment, commanded them to single Him out in worship, and informed them that he was a messenger from God, they mentioned that he was similar to them in humanity, and they found it unlikely that God would send a messenger from among humans. It seems they took the view of the Brahmins, who deny the prophethood of humans absolutely. Then they taunted him, saying that only the lowest people followed him; that is, "we do not equate ourselves with them." Then they denied that he had any superiority over them; that is, "you are equal to us in humanity and you have no superiority over us, so how are you distinguished by being the messenger of God?"

In His saying ﴿those who are the lowest of us﴾ there is an exaggeration in the report, and it seems to indicate an emphasis on restricting those who followed him, and that they were the lowest, with no nobleman sharing in that. In a hadith it is said that they were weavers and cuppers. Al-Nahhas said: "They were the poor and those without lineage, and those in base trades."

In the hadith of Heraclius: "Did the nobles of the people follow him, or his weak ones?" He said: "Rather, his weak ones." He said: "They are the followers of the messengers before him." This was so because leadership dominates the nobles, and it is hard to disengage from it, and they are proud to submit to others. The poor person is free of those obstacles, so he is quick to respond and submit.

(*Wa-naraka*, "and we see you"): it is possible that it is visual, and it is possible that it is cognitive. They said: *Arādhil* is a plural of a plural. It is said: it is the plural of *ardhal*, like *kalb* and *aklub* and *akalib*. It is also said: it is the plural of *aradhal*, and its analogical form would be *arādhīl*.

The apparent view is that it is the plural of *arədhal*, which is the comparative form (*af'al al-tafdil*), and it came as a plural, as *akabira mujrimiha* (its greatest criminals) and *ahasinukum akhlaqan* (the best of you in character) came.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Ma naraka illa basharan mithlana* (we do not see you but a human like ourselves)" is an allusion that they were more deserving of prophethood than him, and that if God wanted to place it in a human, He would have placed it among them. They said: "Suppose you are one of the eminent ones and equal to them in rank, what made you more deserving than them? Do you not see their saying: *wa ma nara lakum 'alaynā min fadl* (we do not see for you any superiority over us)?" Or they meant that he should have been an angel, not a human. What al-Zamakhshari said does not appear from the verse.

Abu 'Amr and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read *bādi'a al-ra'y* (initial opinion) from *bada'a yabda'u*, and its meaning is: the first opinion. The rest of the seven read *bādī* with *ya'* from *bada yabdu*, and its meaning is: the apparent opinion. It is also said: *bādī* with *ya'* means *bādi'* with *hamza*, and the *hamza* was made easier by replacing it with *ya'* because of the *kasra* before it.

They mentioned that it is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*zarf*), and the governing element is either *naraka* (we see you), or *ittaba'aka* (followed you), or *arādhiluna* (our lowest). That is: "and we do not see you, in what appears to us of opinion," or "in the first of our opinion," or "and we do not see that they followed you in the first of their opinion," or "in the apparent of their opinion." This possibility has two meanings. One is that he intends: "they followed you in the outward appearance of their affair, and perhaps their inner states are not with you." The second meaning is that he intends: "they followed you at first glance, and by the opinion that appears without reflection; had they reflected, they would not have followed you." In this view there is a condemnation of opinion that is not based on transmission.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "They followed you at first, or in apparent opinion. Its accusative status as an adverb is originally: at the time of the beginning of their affair, or at the time of the emergence of their apparent opinion. That was deleted, and the genitive noun was placed in its position. They meant: their following of you is merely something that came to them instantly, without deliberation or consideration." End of quote.

That it is in the accusative as an adverb is the view of Abu 'Ali in *al-Hujja*. He took it as an adverb though it is neither a time nor a place, because there is an implied *fi* (in) before it, meaning: "in the apparent matter," or "in the first matter."

According to these two estimates, namely that the governing element is *naraka* or *ittaba'aka*, it entails that this is not permissible, because what comes after *illa* (except) cannot be governed by what precedes it, unless it is an exception from something stated (*mustathna minhu*), as in: "the people stood except Zayd," or an exception as an exception (*mustathna*), as in: "the people came except Zayd," or a follower of the thing excepted from, as in: "no one came to me except Zayd; 'Amr informed me." *Bādi'a al-ra'y* is none of these three.

It has been answered that it is an adverb or like an adverb, like *juhda ra'yin innaka dhahib* (with utmost effort of opinion, you are going), meaning: "you are going with utmost effort of opinion." Adverbs are used with latitude. If the governing element is *arādhiluna*, then its meaning is: "those who are our lowest by the least consideration of them, and by the first opinion about them, it is known from them."

It is said: *bādiya al-ra'y* is an adjective of *basharan* (human). It is also said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial (*hal*) from the pronoun of Noah in *ittaba'aka*, meaning: "and you are exposed in opinion, with no sound judgment." It is also said: it is in the accusative as a vocative for Noah, meaning: "O one exposed in opinion," i.e., what is in your mind of opinion is manifest to everyone. They said this to belittle him.

It is also said: it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*), and an adverb and a verbal noun came on the pattern *fa'il*, which is not analogical. Then *ra'y* here is either from seeing with the eye or from thought.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "They only regarded the believers as base because of their poverty and their lateness in worldly means, because they were ignorant and did not know except the outward of the worldly life; so the most honourable among them was the one who had status and wealth." End of quote.

The apparent address in *lakum* (for you) includes Noah and those who followed him. The meaning is: "there is no excess for you over us in wealth, lineage, or religion." Ibn 'Abbas said: "in creation and character." It is also said: "in the abundance of rule and possession." It is also said: "by your following Noah and your opposition to us." It is also said: "from a nobility that qualifies you for prophethood." Al-Kalbi said: *nazunnukum* (we think you): "we are certain of you." Muqatil said: "we consider you," meaning in the claim of Noah and your affirmation of it. The author of *Sahib al-I'tiyan* said: "*bal nazunnukum kadhibin* (rather, we think you are liars)" in pursuit of leadership and fame.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verse 17–27 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Is one who has a clear proof from his Lord, and a witness from Him recites it, and before it the Book of Moses as a guide and a mercy? Those believe in it. Whoever of the factions disbelieves in it, the Fire is his promised place. So do not be in doubt about it; indeed it is the truth from your Lord, but most people do not believe.﴾ When He mentioned the state of those who desire the life of this world, He mentioned the state of those who desire the Face of Allah, the Exalted, through their righteous deeds. The counterpart to which the interrogative hamza is attached has been omitted, and the estimated sense is: "Is he like one who desires the life of this world?"

Such omission occurs frequently in the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him, so that he sees it as good [equal to one who does not]?﴾ [Fatir: 8] and His saying: ﴿Or is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night﴾ [Az-Zumar: 9]. This interrogation carries the meaning of affirmation (taqrir). Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, you do not equal them in rank nor do you parallel them; he means that there is a vast disparity between the two groups and a clear difference. He intended by them those among the Jews who believed, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and others. "Upon a clear proof from his Lord" means upon a proof from Allah, the Exalted, and a demonstration that the religion of Islam is true, and this is the evidence of reason. "And a witness follows it": a witness that follows that proof, bearing witness to its soundness, and this is the Qur'an, "from Him," from Allah; or a witness from the Qur'an. "And before it": before the Qur'an, "the Book of Moses," which is the Torah; that is, the Book of Moses also follows it, coming before the Qur'an.

It is also read (Kitab Musa) in the accusative, and its meaning is: he is upon a clear proof from his Lord, which is the evidence that the Qur'an is true; and a witness from him recites (yatluhu) the Qur'an, a witness from among those who are upon a clear proof, like His saying: ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified to its like﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 10], and ﴿Say: Allah suffices as a witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 43].

﴿And before it the Book of Moses﴾: "recites it" and before the Torah; "as a guide" (imaman): a book that is followed in religion, a model in it. End of quote. It was said regarding ﴿Is one who was﴾: those who believe in the Messenger, and it was said: Muhammad ﷺ specifically. (p-211) Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: Muhammad and the believers all together. "The clear proof" is the Qur'an or the Messenger, and the ha' is for emphasis (intensiveness).

As for "the witness" (al-shahid): Ibn Abbas, al-Nakha'i, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Abu Salih and Ikrimah said: it is Gabriel. Al-Hasan ibn Ali said: it is the Messenger. Mujahid also said: it is an angel whom Allah appointed to guard the Qur'an.

Ibn Atiyyah said: It is possible that by these expressions he means Gabriel. It was also said: Ali ibn Abi Talib. Al-Minhal narrated from Ubadah ibn Abdullah, who said: Ali, may Allah honour his face, said: "There is no one in Quraysh except that a verse was revealed concerning him." It was asked: "What was revealed concerning you?" He said: ﴿And a witness from Him recites it﴾. Muhammad ibn Ali and Zayd ibn Ali also said this.

It was said: it is the Gospel, said by al-Farra'. It was said: it is the Qur'an. It was said: it is the inimitability of the Qur'an, said by al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl. It was said: it is the form of the Messenger ﷺ, his face and his features, because every intelligent person who looked at him knew that he was the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

It was said: and Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. The pronoun in "from Him" refers to the religion, or to the Messenger, or to the Qur'an. "Yatluhu" means "yatba'uhu" (follows it), or "yaqra'uhu" (recites it); the raised pronoun in yatluhu and the accusative and genitive pronouns in minhu are arranged according to what suits each opinion among these.

Muhammad ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kalbi and others read: ﴿Kitab Musa﴾ in the accusative, as a conjunction with the object of yatluhu, or by supposing a verb. And if the witness is not understood to be the Gospel, then he specifically mentioned the Torah because both religions agree that it is from Allah, whereas the Jews disagree regarding the Gospel; so citing that which establishes proof against both groups is more fitting.

This accords with the saying of the jinn: ﴿We have heard a Book revealed after Moses﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 30], and with the saying of al-Najashi: "Indeed this and what Moses brought come out of one niche." "Imaman" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). What appears in the interpretation of this verse is that when He mentioned the disbelievers and that for them there is only the Fire, He followed with their opposites, who are the believers, those who are upon a clear proof from their Lord. The witness is the Qur'an, and "from Him" refers back to "his Lord." What indicates that the witness is the Qur'an is the mention of His saying "and before it" — that is, before the Qur'an, the Book of Moses. So its meaning is that two things combined to guide him: that he is upon a clear matter from the proof of reason, and that this proof agrees with these two divine books, the Qur'an and the Torah, so that he has both reason and transmission.

The demonstrative "those" (ulaika) refers to "one who was upon a clear proof," observing the meaning of "one" (man) and so using the plural. The pronoun in "bihi" refers to the Torah, or the Qur'an, or the Messenger — three opinions. "Al-Ahzab" (the factions) means all the religious communities, said by Ibn Jubayr; or the Jews and Christians, said by Qatadah; or the Quraysh, said by al-Suddi; or the Banu Umayyah, the Banu al-Mughirah ibn Abdullah al-Makhzumi, and the family of Abu Talhah ibn Ubaydullah, said by Muqatil. Al-Zamakhshari said: he means the people of Makkah and those allied with them among the factions against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. End of quote.

﴿So the Fire is his promised place﴾: that is, the place of his promise to which they will go. Hassan said:
"You brought us to the watering-places of death in the open, so the Fire is its promised place, and death meets it."
The pronoun in "minhu" refers to the Qur'an; it was also said that it refers to the report that the disbelievers' promised place is the Fire. The majority read "fi miryah" with a kasrah on the mim, which is the dialect of the Hijaz. As-Sulami, Abu Raja', Abu al-Khattab al-Sadusi and al-Hasan read it with a dammah, which is the dialect of Asad and Tamim. "The people" (al-nas) means the people of Makkah, said by Ibn Abbas; or all the disbelievers, whether doubters, ignorant, or obstinate, said by the author of al-Iqyan.

﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah? Those will be presented before their Lord, and the witnesses will say: "These are the ones who lied against their Lord.
