Or: the spring in the island, the spring of al-Warda, reported by Ikrima. Or: from the farthest part of Noah's house, as stated by Muqatil. Or: the place where water gathers in the ship, reported from al-Hasan. Or: the rising of the sun, reported from Ali. Or: the light of dawn, from their saying "نَوَّرَ الفَجْرُ تنويرًا" (the dawn brightened), as stated by Ali and Mujahid. Or: it is a metaphor, and what is meant is the overwhelming of water and the manifestation of the punishment, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said at the intensity of battle: "The oven has grown hot" (حمي الوطيس). Al-Watis also means the place where fire is kindled, so there is no difference between (حمي) and (فار), since both are used for fire. God the Exalted said: ﴿they will hear its roaring while it boils﴾ [al-Mulk: 7]. There is no difference between (الوطيس) and (التنور). The apparent meaning of these statements is to understand it as the oven, which is the place where fire is kindled. It is possible that (ال) in it is for a specific known oven, and it is possible that it is generic, so that the fire erupted from the ovens, and that was among the most wondrous things, that water should boil from the place where fires are kindled.

There is no contradiction between this and His saying ﴿and We caused the earth to burst forth with springs﴾ [al-Qamar: 12], since it is possible that by "the earth" is meant the places of the ovens. The gushing (التفجير) is different from the boiling (الفوران), so the boiling was for the oven and the gushing was for the earth.

The pronoun in (فيها) refers to the ark, which is masculine but was made feminine according to the meaning of ship (السفينة), and likewise His saying ﴿and he said: "Board it"﴾ [Hud: 41].

Hafs recited ﴿of every kind two pairs﴾ with tanwin on (كل), meaning: of every animal; (زوجين) is the object, and (اثنين) is an emphatic adjective. The rest of the seven readers recited it with the genitive construction, and (اثنين) is the object of (احمل). (زوجين) is in the general sense, meaning: of everything that has a mate. This is the meaning of "of every kind two pairs," as stated by Abu Ali and others.

Ibn Atiyya said: if the meaning were: "load in it two of every pair, each of which is two loaders," it would be obligatory that he carry four of every kind. The word (زوج) in the well-known usage of the Arabs means one of a pair that has a mate, so it is said: "this is the mate of this," and "they are two mates," and this is the established usage in the Qur'an in His saying ﴿eight pairs﴾ [al-An'am: 143], then He explained them, and in His saying ﴿and that He created the pairs, the male and the female﴾ [al-Najm: 45]. Al-Akhfash said: it is sometimes said in Arabic usage for two: "zawj" (a pair). Thus the arithmetic scholars take it.

Also in Arabic usage, (زوج) means "kind," as in His saying: [p. 223] ﴿and We caused to grow in it every beautiful kind﴾ [Qaf: 7], and His saying: ﴿Glory be to He who created all the kinds﴾ [Ya-Sin: 36], end of quote.

When the rain began to fall like the mouths of waterskins, the wild animals began seeking the middle of the earth fleeing from the water, until they gathered near the ark. God commanded him to carry two of each pair, meaning a male and a female, so that the root of the offspring would remain after the Flood. It is reported that the animal kinds would come to him, and he would place his right hand on the male and his left on the female. The ark had three levels: the lowest for the wild animals, the middle for food and drink, and the upper for him and those who believed.

(وأهلك) is coordinated with (زوجين) if (كل) is with tanwin, and with (اثنين) if it is in the genitive construction. He excepted from his family whoever the word of destruction had preceded regarding, and that he was among the people of the Fire.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "The word preceded regarding him that he would choose disbelief, not because of God's decree upon him and His will to other than that," end of quote.

This is on the path of the Mu'tazila (i'tizal). The one against whom the word preceded was his wife Wa'ila, with an unpointed ʿayn, and his son Kan'an.

﴿And those who believed﴾: coordinated with (وأهلك). It has been said that they were eighty men and eighty women. It has been said that they were seventy-three.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Eighty men believed with him." And from him: "Eighty people": three of his sons, Sam, Ham and Yafith, and three of his daughters-in-law (kanāʾin).

When they came out of the ship, they built a town called today "the Town of the Eighty" in the region of Mosul.

It was also said: they were seventy-eight, half of them men and half of them women.

Ibn Ishaq said: they were ten, besides their wives: Nuh, and his sons Sam, Ham and Yafith, and six men from among those who had believed in him, and their wives, all of them. And from Ibn Ishaq: they were ten: five men and five women.

It was said: they were nine: Nuh and eight sons of his, and his wife. It was also said: they were eight, and Nuh and his wife, other than the one who was punished, and his three sons and their wives. This is the saying of Qatadah, al-Hakam, Ibn ʿUyaynah, Ibn Jurayj and Muhammad ibn Kaʿb.

Al-Aʿmash said: they were seven: Nuh, three daughters-in-law (kanāʾin), and three sons. These are conflicting sayings. What Allah, exalted is He, has informed us of is that only a few believed with him, and the number of this small group, whose number Allah has left unspecified, cannot be determined with certainty except by an explicit text from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verses 41–43 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And he said, "Embark therein; in the name of God is its course and its mooring. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving, Merciful."﴾ ﴿And it sailed with them through waves like mountains. And Noah called to his son, who was apart, "O my son, embark with us and do not be with the disbelievers."﴾ ﴿He said, "I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water." [Noah] said, "There is no protector today from the command of God, except for whom He has mercy." And the wave came between them, and he was among the drowned.﴾ ﴿And it was said, "O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold," and the water subsided and the matter was decided, and it came to rest on al-Judi. And it was said, "Away with the wrongdoing people."﴾ [Hud: 44] ﴿And Noah called to his Lord and said, "My Lord, indeed my son is of my family, and indeed Your promise is true, and You are the most just of judges."﴾ [Hud: 45] ﴿He said, "O Noah, indeed he is not of your family; indeed, he is of unrighteous conduct. So do not ask Me for that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant."﴾ [Hud: 46] ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge. And unless You forgive me and have mercy on me, I will be among the losers."﴾ [Hud: 47] ﴿It was said, "O Noah, descend with peace from Us and blessings upon you and upon nations [descended] from those with you. And there are nations whom We will grant enjoyment; then a painful punishment from Us will touch them."﴾ [Hud: 48] ﴿That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you. Neither you nor your people knew it before this. So be patient; indeed, the good outcome is for the righteous.﴾ [Hud: 49] ﴿And to 'Ad [We sent] their brother Hud. He said, "O my people, worship God; you have no deity other than Him. You are but fabricators."﴾ [Hud: 50] ﴿"O my people, I do not ask you for any reward for it. My reward is only from He who originated me. Then will you not reason?"﴾ [Hud: 51] ﴿"And O my people, seek forgiveness from your Lord and then repent to Him; He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain and increase you in strength upon your strength. And do not turn away as criminals."﴾ [Hud: 52] ﴿They said, "O Hud, you have not brought us any clear proof, and we will not leave our gods on your word, and we are not believers in you."﴾ [Hud: 53] ﴿"We say only that some of our gods have struck you with evil." He said, "Indeed, I call God to witness, and bear witness yourselves that I am free from what you associate."﴾ [Hud: 54] ﴿"Other than Him. So scheme against me all together, then give me no respite."﴾ [Hud: 55] ﴿"Indeed, I have relied upon God, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path."﴾ [Hud: 56] ﴿"And if you turn away, I have already conveyed to you that with which I was sent to you. And my Lord will replace you with another people, and you will not harm Him at all. Indeed, my Lord is Guardian over all things."﴾ [Hud: 57] ﴿And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and We saved them from a severe punishment.﴾ [Hud: 58] ﴿And those were 'Ad; they denied the signs of their Lord, disobeyed His messengers, and followed the command of every obstinate tyrant.﴾ [Hud: 59] ﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, 'Ad disbelieved in their Lord. Unquestionably, away with 'Ad, the people of Hud.﴾ [Hud: 60]

(p. 224) *Rasa* (ـرسا) al-shay'u yarsu: it became firm and settled. He said:
"So I patiently [stood] with a free soul at that moment, firm, while the soul of the coward rises up in alarm."

*Al-balʿ* (swallowing) is well known. Its verb is *balaʿa*, with the vowel of the lam being either *kasra* or *fatḥa*; these are two dialects related by al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', who say *yabla'u balʿan*. *Al-bālūʿa* is the place that absorbs water.

*Al-iqlāʿ* means withholding. It is said: *aqla'a al-maṭar* (the rain stopped) and *aqla'at al-ḥummā* (the fever subsided), meaning that it withheld from the one with fever. It is also said that *aqla'a ʿan al-shay'* means he abandoned it, which is close to withholding. *Ghāḍa al-māʾ* means the water decreased in itself; *ghaḍtuhu* means I diminished it. It comes both intransitive and transitive. *Al-Judi* is the proper name of a mountain near Mosul. As for those who say it is in al-Jazira or Amid, these two are near Mosul. It is also said that *al-Judi* is the name of any mountain, and from this is the saying of Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl:
"Glory be to Him, then glory; we seek refuge in Him, and before us al-Judi and the rocks glorified [Him]."

*Iʿtarāhu bi-kadhā* means it afflicted him with it. It is also said that it is *iftaʿala* from *ʿarāhu yaʿrūhu*. *Al-nāṣiya* is the place of hair growth at the front of the head, and the hair growing there is called *nāṣiya* after its place of growth. *Naṣawtu al-rajul anṣūhu naṣwan* means I pulled his forelock. *Al-jabbār* is the arrogant one. *Al-ʿanīd* is the rebellious tyrant who does not accept the truth nor listen to it, from *ʿanada yaʿnudu*, meaning he swerved from the truth to one side. It is said that from this comes *ʿindī kadhā*, meaning "at my side." Abu ʿUbayda said: *al-ʿanīd*, *al-ʿanūd*, *al-muʿānid* and *al-ʿānid* mean one who opposes with contrariness. From this the vein that bursts with blood is called *ʿāniḍ*.

﴿And he said, "Embark therein; in the name of God is its course and its mooring. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving, Merciful."﴾ ﴿And it sailed with them through waves like mountains. And Noah called to his son, who was apart, "O my son, embark with us and do not be with the disbelievers."﴾ ﴿He said, "I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water." [Noah] said, "There is no protector today from the command of God, except for whom He has mercy." And the wave came between them, and he was among the drowned.﴾: The pronoun in *wa-qāla* refers to Noah, meaning: Noah said, when he was commanded to carry in the ship those who believed with him and whoever was commanded to be carried: "Embark therein." It is also said that the pronoun refers to God, and the meaning is: God said to Noah and those with him. This is weakened by His saying: "Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving, Merciful." It is said that the masculine rational form was given precedence in His saying "Embark" (*ārkabū*), even though those who were carried in it, who are not rational, were more numerous. The apparent meaning is that it is an address only to rational beings, because it is not fitting for non-rational beings.

*Irkabū* is made transitive with *fī* by implying the meaning of *ṣayyirū* (make it [a place]) therein, or the meaning of *udkhulū* (enter) therein. It is also said that the sense is *irkabū al-māʾ fīhā* (ride the water in it). It is also said that *fī* is extra, for emphasis, meaning "ride it." The *bāʾ* in *bi-smi Allāh* is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), or (p. 225) [meaning] "seeking blessing by the name of God." *Majrāhā wa-mursāhā* are in the accusative, either as adverbs of time or place, since they come for that purpose; or as adverbs of time by way of ellipsis, as in *ji'tuka maqdam al-ḥājj*, meaning "the time of the arrival of the pilgrim." Then *majrāhā wa-mursāhā* would be verbal nouns originally, with the genitive element omitted, and they are in the accusative by what is in *bi-smi Allāh* of the meaning of the verb. It is permissible that *bi-smi Allāh* be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *fīhā*, and *majrāhā wa-mursāhā* are verbal nouns in the nominative as subjects, meaning: "Embark therein, bound to the name of God, [with] its running and its stopping," that is, "by the blessing of the name of God."

Or *majrāhā wa-mursāhā* are in the nominative as subject of a nominal sentence (*mubtadaʾ*), with *bi-smi Allāh* as predicate, and the sentence is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *fīhā*. Under these three interpretations the speech is one sentence, and the circumstantial clause is anticipated. With the nominative *majrāhā wa-mursāhā* as subject or topic, it is not permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *irkabū*, because there is no returning pronoun to it in what functions as a circumstantial clause. It is also permissible that *bi-smi Allāh majrāhā wa-mursāhā* be a second sentence consisting of subject and predicate, with no grammatical connection to the first sentence. He first commanded them to embark, then informed them that its running and its stopping are by the mention of God, or by His command and power. The two sentences are then two reported statements. It is said: just as the second sentence is also reported by *qāla* (he said).

Al-Dahhak said: when [Noah] wanted the ship to run he said, "In the name of God is its running," and it ran; and when he wanted it to stop he said, "In the name of God is its stopping," and it stopped.

Mujahid, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', al-A'raj, Shayba and the majority of the seven readers — the two Haramis (Ibn Kathir and Nafi'), the two Iraqis (Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr?) and Abu Bakr — read *majrāhā* with *ḍamma* on the *mīm*. Al-Akhawan (Hamza and al-Kisa'i) and Hafs read it with *fatḥa*. All of them read the *mīm* of *mursāhā* with *ḍamma*. Ibn Mas'ud, 'Isa al-Thaqafi, Zayd ibn 'Ali and al-A'mash read *majrāhā wa-mursāhā* with *fatḥa* on both *mīms*, as adverbs of time or place, or as verbal nouns according to the previous interpretations.

Al-Dahhak, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Thabit, Abu Raja', Mujahid, Ibn Jundab, al-Kalbi and al-Jahdari read *mujrīhā wa-mursīhā*, as active participles from *ajrā* and *arsā*, in apposition to the name of God. They are then in the position of a predicate, and they cannot be adjectives because they are indefinite.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: in this reading they are two adjectives referring back to the name [of God] in their saying *bi-smi Allāh*. End of quotation.

They cannot be adjectives except on the assumption that they are definite. Al-Khalil held that whatever has a non-pure (*ghayr maḥḍa*) annexation may sometimes be made pure, and thus become definite, except for the attributive adjective (*ṣifa mushabbaha*), whose annexation is never made pure, so it does not become definite.

﴿Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving﴾: *Sattūr* (Concealer) of your sins for you, through your repentance and faith. *(Raḥīm)*: Merciful to you when He saves you from drowning. It is related in a hadith: "Noah boarded the ship on the first day of Rajab and fasted the whole month." And from ʿIkrima: on the tenth [day] of Rajab.

﴿And it sailed with them﴾: an informing by God Exalted of what happened to the ship. *Bihim* is a circumstantial clause, meaning "in connection with them," i.e., with them in it. The meaning is: it runs while they are in it. ﴿Through waves like mountains﴾: that is, through the waves of the deluge. He likened each wave of it to a mountain in its piling up and height. It is related that the sky poured down all of its water, so that there was no direction in the air but that it rained, and the whole earth gushed forth with springs; this is the meaning of the meeting of the waters.

It is related that the water rose above the mountains and the high parts of the earth by forty cubits, and it is said fifteen. That the ship ran through waves indicates that there were waves in the water, that the water did not cover all between the sky and the earth, and that the ship did not run inside the water with the water above and below it; rather it swam in the water as a fish swims, as al-Zajjaj, al-Zamakhshari and others indicated.

Ibn 'Atiyya found this improbable. He said: "Where were the waves like mountains on this view? And how did the life of those in the ship remain sound?" Al-Zamakhshari answered: the running in the waves was before the covering, and before the water overspread the mountains. Do you not see the saying of his son: ﴿I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water﴾?

﴿And Noah called to his son﴾: the *wāw* does not indicate order. This calling was before the ship ran in His saying ﴿and it sailed with them through waves﴾. In the attribution of the son to him here, and in His saying ﴿indeed, my son is of my family﴾ [Hud: 45] and in his calling to him, there is evidence that he was his son by his loins. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, al-Dahhak, Ibn Jubayr, Maymun ibn Mihran (p. 226) and the majority. His name was Kan'an. It is said he was Yam. It is also said he was a close relative whom he called "son" out of tenderness and gentleness.

The majority read the *tanwīn* of *Nūḥ* with *kasra*. Wakī' ibn al-Jarrāḥ read it with *ḍamma*, making its vowel follow the case-ending vowel on the *ḥāʾ*. Abu Hatim said: this is a bad dialect, unknown.

The majority read the pronoun *hāʾ* joined with a *wāw*. Ibn 'Abbas read *innah* with the *hāʾ* vowel-less. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: this is according to the dialect of al-Azd al-Shurat, who make the pronominal *hāʾ* of the masculine vowel-less. From this is the poet's saying:
"And my two thighs are both longing for him, both sleepless."
Others mentioned that it is a dialect of Banu Kilab and ʿUqayl. Some grammarians restrict this vowel-lessness to poetic necessity, and they recite:
"And I drink water though I have no thirst for it, except because its springs are the flood of its valley."

Al-Suddi read *ibnāh* with an *alif* and the *hāʾ al-sakt*. Abu al-Fath said: this is in the form of a vocative. A group held that it is in the form of lamentation and elegy. ʿAli, ʿUrwa, ʿAli ibn al-Husayn and his son Abu Ja'far and his son Ja'far read *ibnah* with *fatḥa* on the *hāʾ* without an *alif*, meaning *ibnahā* (her son), attached to the pronoun of his wife, so the vowel *fatḥa* sufficed in place of the *alif*. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is a dialect. From it is the poet's saying:
"If you lead with her a sheep and eat it, or sell it in some of the markets."
Ibn al-A'rabi cited the following for this:
"You will not catch up with what has passed from me by lamenting, nor by 'if only,' nor by 'had I'."
End of quotation.

He means *talahhufan* (lamentation). Al-Nahhas criticized Abu Hatim for deleting this *alif*. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is not as he said." End of quotation.

This, I mean the like of تَلَهَّفَ (tala-hhafa) with the alif elided, is by the consensus of our companions (the Basran grammarians) a poetic necessity (ḍarūratan). For this reason they do not permit يا غُلامُ (yā ghulāmu) with the alif elided, and they dispense with the alif by the vowel fatḥa, just as they dispensed with the kasra in يا غُلامِ (yā ghulāmi) in place of the yā'. Al-Akhfash permitted this.

ʿAlī and ʿUrwa also read ابْنَها (ibnahā) with a fatḥa on the hā' and an alif, meaning ابْنَ امْرَأتِهِ (ibna imra'atihi), the son of his wife. That he was not his son by his loins, but the son of his wife, is the view of ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Sīrīn and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr. Al-Ḥasan used to swear that he was not his son by his loins. Qatāda said: I said to him, "God has related of him: ﴿Indeed, my son is of my family﴾ [Hūd: 45], and you say he was not his son, while the People of the Book do not differ that he was his son." He said: "And who takes his religion from the People of the Book?" He cited in support His saying ﴿of my family﴾ [Hūd: 45] and not "of me," so on this view he would be a stepson (rabīb).

ʿIkrima and al-Ḍaḥḥāk used to swear that he was his son. It is not to be supposed that he was of illegitimate birth (li-ghayri rishda), because that is a disgrace from which the prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, are protected. This is related from al-Ḥasan and Ibn Jurayj, though it is perhaps not authentically transmitted from them. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "The wife of a prophet never committed adultery at all." What the apparent sense of the verse indicates is that he was his son. As for the reading of whoever read ابْنَهُ or ابْنَها, it is irregular (shādhdha). It is possible that he was attributed to his mother and was made to belong to her, and was not attributed to his father because he was an unbeliever like her; this meaning is observed in him, and he was not attributed to him out of disapproval of him, and out of caution that an unbeliever not be attributed to a prophet. He called him only out of his assumption that he was a believer, and had it not been for that he would not have loved his deliverance. Or [he called him] out of his assumption that he would believe if he was an unbeliever, because of the great terrors he witnessed, and that he would accept faith. His saying ﴿Board with us﴾ would be like an indication that he requested of him faith, and it was reinforced by His saying ﴿and do not be with the unbelievers﴾, that is: board with the believers, since none boards with them except a believer, by His saying ﴿and whoever believed﴾ [Hūd: 40].

﴿In a place apart﴾ (fī maʿzil), that is: in a place where he isolated himself from his father and from the vessel of the believers. It was said: in a place apart from his father's religion.

His calling him with the diminutive is an address of tenderness and compassion. The meaning: board with us in the ship so that you may be saved, and do not be with the unbelievers so that you perish. ʿĀṣim read يا بَنِيَ (yā baniya) with a fatḥa on the bā'. It is explained as having dispensed with the alif by the fatḥa, and its origin is يا بُنَيًّا (yā bunayyan), like your saying يا غُلامًا (yā ghulāman). The rest of the seven [readers] dispensed with the yā' by the kasra in their reading يا بَنِي (yā bani) with a kasra on the yā'. Or the alif was elided because it met the rāʾ of ارْكَبْ (irkab).

Ibn Nūḥ assumed that that rain and the bursting forth [of waters] were according to the usual custom, and therefore he said: ﴿I will betake myself to a mountain that will protect me from the water﴾, that is: from the water reaching me so that I do not drown. This indicates his habit in unbelief and his lack of trust in his father regarding what he reported.

It was said: the mountain he meant was Ṭūr Zaytā, but it did not protect him. The apparent sense is to keep ʿāṣim (protector) on its literal meaning, and that he negated every protector from the command of God at that time, and that whoever He has mercy upon falls within [the scope of] مَن (man) referring to the one protected. The subject pronoun returns to God, the Exalted, the relative pronoun is omitted, and the exception is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ), meaning: but whomever God has mercy upon is protected. They also permitted that it be from God, the Exalted, meaning: there is no protector except the Merciful; and that ʿāṣim be in the sense of "one possessing protection," as they say لابِنٌ (labin), meaning: one possessing milk; and "one possessing protection" (dhū ʿiṣma) is applied both to a protector and to one protected, and what is meant here is the protected one. Or it is an active form in the sense of a passive, so ʿāṣim means maʿṣūm (protected), like māʾun dāfiq in the sense of madfūq (poured forth). The poet said:

*Slow to rise, gentle of speech*
*my heart has become enamored of him*

meaning: enchanted (maftūnan). And مَن (man) is for the protected one, meaning: there is no one possessing protection, or: no one is protected except the one shown mercy. On these two permissible readings, the exception is contiguous (muttaṣil). Al-Zamakhsharī made it contiguous by another way, namely by omitting a modifier, and estimated it as: no protector today from a mountain or the like protects you, except one protector, which is the place of those whom God has shown mercy to and saved, meaning in the ship. End.

The apparent view is that the predicate of ﴿there is no protector﴾ is omitted, because when it is known, as in this position, the Banū Tamīm are bound to omit it, and its omission is frequent among the people of the Ḥijāz. For when he said ﴿I will betake myself to a mountain that will protect me from the water﴾, Nūḥ said to him: ﴿There is no protector﴾, that is: there is no existing protector.

اليَوْمَ (al-yawma, "today") would be in the accusative by an implied verb indicated by عاصِمَ (ʿāṣima), that is: no protector protects today from the command of God; and مِن أمْرِ اللَّهِ (min amri llāh, "from the command of God") is connected to that omitted verb. It is not permissible for اليَوْمَ to be in the accusative by ﴿there is no protector﴾, nor for مِن أمْرِ اللَّهِ to be connected to it, because the noun after لا (lā) would then be extended (muṭawwal), and if it were extended it would require tanwīn and i'rāb, while it is built (mabnī) [on the fatḥa], so that is invalid.

Al-Ḥawfī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya permitted that اليَوْمَ be the predicate of ﴿there is no protector﴾. Al-Ḥawfī said: "It is permissible that اليَوْمَ be the predicate and be connected with the sense of 'being established,' and مِن (min) be connected to what اليَوْمَ is connected to." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "اليَوْمَ is an adverb of time, and it is connected to ﴿from the command of God﴾, or to the predicate whose estimate is: 'existing today'." End.

Abū al-Baqāʾ rejected this, saying: "As for the predicate of لا (lā), it is not permissible that it be اليَوْمَ, because an adverb of time cannot be a predicate about the essence (al-jathth, the bodies); rather the predicate is مِن أمْرِ اللَّهِ, and اليَوْمُ is an object of مِن أمْرِ اللَّهِ." Al-Ḥawfī said: "It is permissible that اليَوْمَ be an attribute of عاصِمَ, and مِن be the predicate." End.

This is refuted by what Abū al-Baqāʾ refuted with, namely that an adverb of time cannot be an attribute of bodies, just as it cannot be a predicate. It was read: إلّا مَن رُحِمَ (illā man ruḥima), with a ḍamma on the rāʾ, in the passive voice, and this indicates that what is meant by مَن (man) in the reading of the majority, who read the rāʾ with a fatḥa, is the one shown mercy and not the merciful.

﴿And a wave came between them﴾, that is: between Nūḥ and his son. It was said: they were exchanging words, and before the exchange was complete a huge wave came, and he was riding a horse that had become arrogant and self-admiring, so it swallowed him and his horse, and he was prevented from [reaching] Nūḥ, and so he drowned. Al-Farrāʾ said: "بَيْنَهُما (baynahumā), that is: between the son of Nūḥ and the mountain that he thought would protect him."

[p-227]

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verses 41–43 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And he said, "Embark therein; in the name of God is its course and its mooring. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving, Merciful."﴾ ﴿And it sailed with them through waves like mountains. And Noah called to his son, who was apart, "O my son, embark with us and do not be with the disbelievers."﴾ ﴿He said, "I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water." [Noah] said, "There is no protector today from the command of God, except for whom He has mercy." And the wave came between them, and he was among the drowned.﴾ ﴿And it was said, "O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold," and the water subsided and the matter was decided, and it came to rest on al-Judi. And it was said, "Away with the wrongdoing people."﴾ [Hud: 44] ﴿And Noah called to his Lord and said, "My Lord, indeed my son is of my family, and indeed Your promise is true, and You are the most just of judges."﴾ [Hud: 45] ﴿He said, "O Noah, indeed he is not of your family; indeed, he is of unrighteous conduct. So do not ask Me for that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant."﴾ [Hud: 46] ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge. And unless You forgive me and have mercy on me, I will be among the losers."﴾ [Hud: 47] ﴿It was said, "O Noah, descend with peace from Us and blessings upon you and upon nations [descended] from those with you. And there are nations whom We will grant enjoyment; then a painful punishment from Us will touch them."﴾ [Hud: 48] ﴿That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you. Neither you nor your people knew it before this. So be patient; indeed, the good outcome is for the righteous.﴾ [Hud: 49] ﴿And to 'Ad [We sent] their brother Hud. He said, "O my people, worship God; you have no deity other than Him. You are but fabricators."﴾ [Hud: 50] ﴿"O my people, I do not ask you for any reward for it. My reward is only from He who originated me. Then will you not reason?"﴾ [Hud: 51] ﴿"And O my people, seek forgiveness from your Lord and then repent to Him; He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain and increase you in strength upon your strength. And do not turn away as criminals."﴾ [Hud: 52] ﴿They said, "O Hud, you have not brought us any clear proof, and we will not leave our gods on your word, and we are not believers in you."﴾ [Hud: 53] ﴿"We say only that some of our gods have struck you with evil." He said, "Indeed, I call God to witness, and bear witness yourselves that I am free from what you associate."﴾ [Hud: 54] ﴿"Other than Him. So scheme against me all together, then give me no respite."﴾ [Hud: 55] ﴿"Indeed, I have relied upon God, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path."﴾ [Hud: 56] ﴿"And if you turn away, I have already conveyed to you that with which I was sent to you. And my Lord will replace you with another people, and you will not harm Him at all. Indeed, my Lord is Guardian over all things."﴾ [Hud: 57] ﴿And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and We saved them from a severe punishment.﴾ [Hud: 58] ﴿And those were 'Ad; they denied the signs of their Lord, disobeyed His messengers, and followed the command of every obstinate tyrant.﴾ [Hud: 59] ﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, 'Ad disbelieved in their Lord. Unquestionably, away with 'Ad, the people of Hud.﴾ [Hud: 60]

(p. 224) *Rasa* (ـرسا) al-shay'u yarsu: it became firm and settled. He said:
"So I patiently [stood] with a free soul at that moment, firm, while the soul of the coward rises up in alarm."

*Al-balʿ* (swallowing) is well known. Its verb is *balaʿa*, with the vowel of the lam being either *kasra* or *fatḥa*; these are two dialects related by al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', who say *yabla'u balʿan*. *Al-bālūʿa* is the place that absorbs water.

*Al-iqlāʿ* means withholding. It is said: *aqla'a al-maṭar* (the rain stopped) and *aqla'at al-ḥummā* (the fever subsided), meaning that it withheld from the one with fever. It is also said that *aqla'a ʿan al-shay'* means he abandoned it, which is close to withholding. *Ghāḍa al-māʾ* means the water decreased in itself; *ghaḍtuhu* means I diminished it. It comes both intransitive and transitive. *Al-Judi* is the proper name of a mountain near Mosul. As for those who say it is in al-Jazira or Amid, these two are near Mosul. It is also said that *al-Judi* is the name of any mountain, and from this is the saying of Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl:
"Glory be to Him, then glory; we seek refuge in Him, and before us al-Judi and the rocks glorified [Him]."

*Iʿtarāhu bi-kadhā* means it afflicted him with it. It is also said that it is *iftaʿala* from *ʿarāhu yaʿrūhu*. *Al-nāṣiya* is the place of hair growth at the front of the head, and the hair growing there is called *nāṣiya* after its place of growth. *Naṣawtu al-rajul anṣūhu naṣwan* means I pulled his forelock. *Al-jabbār* is the arrogant one. *Al-ʿanīd* is the rebellious tyrant who does not accept the truth nor listen to it, from *ʿanada yaʿnudu*, meaning he swerved from the truth to one side. It is said that from this comes *ʿindī kadhā*, meaning "at my side." Abu ʿUbayda said: *al-ʿanīd*, *al-ʿanūd*, *al-muʿānid* and *al-ʿānid* mean one who opposes with contrariness. From this the vein that bursts with blood is called *ʿāniḍ*.

﴿And he said, "Embark therein; in the name of God is its course and its mooring. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving, Merciful."﴾ ﴿And it sailed with them through waves like mountains. And Noah called to his son, who was apart, "O my son, embark with us and do not be with the disbelievers."﴾ ﴿He said, "I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water." [Noah] said, "There is no protector today from the command of God, except for whom He has mercy." And the wave came between them, and he was among the drowned.﴾: The pronoun in *wa-qāla* refers to Noah, meaning: Noah said, when he was commanded to carry in the ship those who believed with him and whoever was commanded to be carried: "Embark therein." It is also said that the pronoun refers to God, and the meaning is: God said to Noah and those with him. This is weakened by His saying: "Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving, Merciful." It is said that the masculine rational form was given precedence in His saying "Embark" (*ārkabū*), even though those who were carried in it, who are not rational, were more numerous. The apparent meaning is that it is an address only to rational beings, because it is not fitting for non-rational beings.

*Irkabū* is made transitive with *fī* by implying the meaning of *ṣayyirū* (make it [a place]) therein, or the meaning of *udkhulū* (enter) therein. It is also said that the sense is *irkabū al-māʾ fīhā* (ride the water in it). It is also said that *fī* is extra, for emphasis, meaning "ride it." The *bāʾ* in *bi-smi Allāh* is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), or (p. 225) [meaning] "seeking blessing by the name of God." *Majrāhā wa-mursāhā* are in the accusative, either as adverbs of time or place, since they come for that purpose; or as adverbs of time by way of ellipsis, as in *ji'tuka maqdam al-ḥājj*, meaning "the time of the arrival of the pilgrim." Then *majrāhā wa-mursāhā* would be verbal nouns originally, with the genitive element omitted, and they are in the accusative by what is in *bi-smi Allāh* of the meaning of the verb. It is permissible that *bi-smi Allāh* be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *fīhā*, and *majrāhā wa-mursāhā* are verbal nouns in the nominative as subjects, meaning: "Embark therein, bound to the name of God, [with] its running and its stopping," that is, "by the blessing of the name of God."

Or *majrāhā wa-mursāhā* are in the nominative as subject of a nominal sentence (*mubtadaʾ*), with *bi-smi Allāh* as predicate, and the sentence is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *fīhā*. Under these three interpretations the speech is one sentence, and the circumstantial clause is anticipated. With the nominative *majrāhā wa-mursāhā* as subject or topic, it is not permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *irkabū*, because there is no returning pronoun to it in what functions as a circumstantial clause. It is also permissible that *bi-smi Allāh majrāhā wa-mursāhā* be a second sentence consisting of subject and predicate, with no grammatical connection to the first sentence. He first commanded them to embark, then informed them that its running and its stopping are by the mention of God, or by His command and power. The two sentences are then two reported statements. It is said: just as the second sentence is also reported by *qāla* (he said).

Al-Dahhak said: when [Noah] wanted the ship to run he said, "In the name of God is its running," and it ran; and when he wanted it to stop he said, "In the name of God is its stopping," and it stopped.

Mujahid, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', al-A'raj, Shayba and the majority of the seven readers — the two Haramis (Ibn Kathir and Nafi'), the two Iraqis (Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr?) and Abu Bakr — read *majrāhā* with *ḍamma* on the *mīm*. Al-Akhawan (Hamza and al-Kisa'i) and Hafs read it with *fatḥa*. All of them read the *mīm* of *mursāhā* with *ḍamma*. Ibn Mas'ud, 'Isa al-Thaqafi, Zayd ibn 'Ali and al-A'mash read *majrāhā wa-mursāhā* with *fatḥa* on both *mīms*, as adverbs of time or place, or as verbal nouns according to the previous interpretations.

Al-Dahhak, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Thabit, Abu Raja', Mujahid, Ibn Jundab, al-Kalbi and al-Jahdari read *mujrīhā wa-mursīhā*, as active participles from *ajrā* and *arsā*, in apposition to the name of God. They are then in the position of a predicate, and they cannot be adjectives because they are indefinite.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: in this reading they are two adjectives referring back to the name [of God] in their saying *bi-smi Allāh*. End of quotation.

They cannot be adjectives except on the assumption that they are definite. Al-Khalil held that whatever has a non-pure (*ghayr maḥḍa*) annexation may sometimes be made pure, and thus become definite, except for the attributive adjective (*ṣifa mushabbaha*), whose annexation is never made pure, so it does not become definite.

﴿Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving﴾: *Sattūr* (Concealer) of your sins for you, through your repentance and faith. *(Raḥīm)*: Merciful to you when He saves you from drowning. It is related in a hadith: "Noah boarded the ship on the first day of Rajab and fasted the whole month." And from ʿIkrima: on the tenth [day] of Rajab.

﴿And it sailed with them﴾: an informing by God Exalted of what happened to the ship. *Bihim* is a circumstantial clause, meaning "in connection with them," i.e., with them in it. The meaning is: it runs while they are in it. ﴿Through waves like mountains﴾: that is, through the waves of the deluge. He likened each wave of it to a mountain in its piling up and height. It is related that the sky poured down all of its water, so that there was no direction in the air but that it rained, and the whole earth gushed forth with springs; this is the meaning of the meeting of the waters.

It is related that the water rose above the mountains and the high parts of the earth by forty cubits, and it is said fifteen. That the ship ran through waves indicates that there were waves in the water, that the water did not cover all between the sky and the earth, and that the ship did not run inside the water with the water above and below it; rather it swam in the water as a fish swims, as al-Zajjaj, al-Zamakhshari and others indicated.

Ibn 'Atiyya found this improbable. He said: "Where were the waves like mountains on this view? And how did the life of those in the ship remain sound?" Al-Zamakhshari answered: the running in the waves was before the covering, and before the water overspread the mountains. Do you not see the saying of his son: ﴿I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water﴾?

﴿And Noah called to his son﴾: the *wāw* does not indicate order. This calling was before the ship ran in His saying ﴿and it sailed with them through waves﴾. In the attribution of the son to him here, and in His saying ﴿indeed, my son is of my family﴾ [Hud: 45] and in his calling to him, there is evidence that he was his son by his loins. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, al-Dahhak, Ibn Jubayr, Maymun ibn Mihran (p. 226) and the majority. His name was Kan'an. It is said he was Yam. It is also said he was a close relative whom he called "son" out of tenderness and gentleness.

The majority read the *tanwīn* of *Nūḥ* with *kasra*. Wakī' ibn al-Jarrāḥ read it with *ḍamma*, making its vowel follow the case-ending vowel on the *ḥāʾ*. Abu Hatim said: this is a bad dialect, unknown.

The majority read the pronoun *hāʾ* joined with a *wāw*. Ibn 'Abbas read *innah* with the *hāʾ* vowel-less. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: this is according to the dialect of al-Azd al-Shurat, who make the pronominal *hāʾ* of the masculine vowel-less. From this is the poet's saying:
"And my two thighs are both longing for him, both sleepless."
Others mentioned that it is a dialect of Banu Kilab and ʿUqayl. Some grammarians restrict this vowel-lessness to poetic necessity, and they recite:
"And I drink water though I have no thirst for it, except because its springs are the flood of its valley."

Al-Suddi read *ibnāh* with an *alif* and the *hāʾ al-sakt*. Abu al-Fath said: this is in the form of a vocative. A group held that it is in the form of lamentation and elegy. ʿAli, ʿUrwa, ʿAli ibn al-Husayn and his son Abu Ja'far and his son Ja'far read *ibnah* with *fatḥa* on the *hāʾ* without an *alif*, meaning *ibnahā* (her son), attached to the pronoun of his wife, so the vowel *fatḥa* sufficed in place of the *alif*. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is a dialect. From it is the poet's saying:
"If you lead with her a sheep and eat it, or sell it in some of the markets."
Ibn al-A'rabi cited the following for this:
"You will not catch up with what has passed from me by lamenting, nor by 'if only,' nor by 'had I'."
End of quotation.

He means *talahhufan* (lamentation). Al-Nahhas criticized Abu Hatim for deleting this *alif*. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is not as he said." End of quotation.

This, I mean the like of تَلَهَّفَ (tala-hhafa) with the alif elided, is by the consensus of our companions (the Basran grammarians) a poetic necessity (ḍarūratan). For this reason they do not permit يا غُلامُ (yā ghulāmu) with the alif elided, and they dispense with the alif by the vowel fatḥa, just as they dispensed with the kasra in يا غُلامِ (yā ghulāmi) in place of the yā'. Al-Akhfash permitted this.

ʿAlī and ʿUrwa also read ابْنَها (ibnahā) with a fatḥa on the hā' and an alif, meaning ابْنَ امْرَأتِهِ (ibna imra'atihi), the son of his wife. That he was not his son by his loins, but the son of his wife, is the view of ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Sīrīn and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr. Al-Ḥasan used to swear that he was not his son by his loins. Qatāda said: I said to him, "God has related of him: ﴿Indeed, my son is of my family﴾ [Hūd: 45], and you say he was not his son, while the People of the Book do not differ that he was his son." He said: "And who takes his religion from the People of the Book?" He cited in support His saying ﴿of my family﴾ [Hūd: 45] and not "of me," so on this view he would be a stepson (rabīb).

ʿIkrima and al-Ḍaḥḥāk used to swear that he was his son. It is not to be supposed that he was of illegitimate birth (li-ghayri rishda), because that is a disgrace from which the prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, are protected. This is related from al-Ḥasan and Ibn Jurayj, though it is perhaps not authentically transmitted from them. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "The wife of a prophet never committed adultery at all." What the apparent sense of the verse indicates is that he was his son. As for the reading of whoever read ابْنَهُ or ابْنَها, it is irregular (shādhdha). It is possible that he was attributed to his mother and was made to belong to her, and was not attributed to his father because he was an unbeliever like her; this meaning is observed in him, and he was not attributed to him out of disapproval of him, and out of caution that an unbeliever not be attributed to a prophet. He called him only out of his assumption that he was a believer, and had it not been for that he would not have loved his deliverance. Or [he called him] out of his assumption that he would believe if he was an unbeliever, because of the great terrors he witnessed, and that he would accept faith. His saying ﴿Board with us﴾ would be like an indication that he requested of him faith, and it was reinforced by His saying ﴿and do not be with the unbelievers﴾, that is: board with the believers, since none boards with them except a believer, by His saying ﴿and whoever believed﴾ [Hūd: 40].

﴿In a place apart﴾ (fī maʿzil), that is: in a place where he isolated himself from his father and from the vessel of the believers. It was said: in a place apart from his father's religion.

His calling him with the diminutive is an address of tenderness and compassion. The meaning: board with us in the ship so that you may be saved, and do not be with the unbelievers so that you perish. ʿĀṣim read يا بَنِيَ (yā baniya) with a fatḥa on the bā'. It is explained as having dispensed with the alif by the fatḥa, and its origin is يا بُنَيًّا (yā bunayyan), like your saying يا غُلامًا (yā ghulāman). The rest of the seven [readers] dispensed with the yā' by the kasra in their reading يا بَنِي (yā bani) with a kasra on the yā'. Or the alif was elided because it met the rāʾ of ارْكَبْ (irkab).

Ibn Nūḥ assumed that that rain and the bursting forth [of waters] were according to the usual custom, and therefore he said: ﴿I will betake myself to a mountain that will protect me from the water﴾, that is: from the water reaching me so that I do not drown. This indicates his habit in unbelief and his lack of trust in his father regarding what he reported.

It was said: the mountain he meant was Ṭūr Zaytā, but it did not protect him. The apparent sense is to keep ʿāṣim (protector) on its literal meaning, and that he negated every protector from the command of God at that time, and that whoever He has mercy upon falls within [the scope of] مَن (man) referring to the one protected. The subject pronoun returns to God, the Exalted, the relative pronoun is omitted, and the exception is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ), meaning: but whomever God has mercy upon is protected. They also permitted that it be from God, the Exalted, meaning: there is no protector except the Merciful; and that ʿāṣim be in the sense of "one possessing protection," as they say لابِنٌ (labin), meaning: one possessing milk; and "one possessing protection" (dhū ʿiṣma) is applied both to a protector and to one protected, and what is meant here is the protected one. Or it is an active form in the sense of a passive, so ʿāṣim means maʿṣūm (protected), like māʾun dāfiq in the sense of madfūq (poured forth). The poet said:

*Slow to rise, gentle of speech*
*my heart has become enamored of him*

meaning: enchanted (maftūnan). And مَن (man) is for the protected one, meaning: there is no one possessing protection, or: no one is protected except the one shown mercy. On these two permissible readings, the exception is contiguous (muttaṣil). Al-Zamakhsharī made it contiguous by another way, namely by omitting a modifier, and estimated it as: no protector today from a mountain or the like protects you, except one protector, which is the place of those whom God has shown mercy to and saved, meaning in the ship. End.

The apparent view is that the predicate of ﴿there is no protector﴾ is omitted, because when it is known, as in this position, the Banū Tamīm are bound to omit it, and its omission is frequent among the people of the Ḥijāz. For when he said ﴿I will betake myself to a mountain that will protect me from the water﴾, Nūḥ said to him: ﴿There is no protector﴾, that is: there is no existing protector.

اليَوْمَ (al-yawma, "today") would be in the accusative by an implied verb indicated by عاصِمَ (ʿāṣima), that is: no protector protects today from the command of God; and مِن أمْرِ اللَّهِ (min amri llāh, "from the command of God") is connected to that omitted verb. It is not permissible for اليَوْمَ to be in the accusative by ﴿there is no protector﴾, nor for مِن أمْرِ اللَّهِ to be connected to it, because the noun after لا (lā) would then be extended (muṭawwal), and if it were extended it would require tanwīn and i'rāb, while it is built (mabnī) [on the fatḥa], so that is invalid.

Al-Ḥawfī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya permitted that اليَوْمَ be the predicate of ﴿there is no protector﴾. Al-Ḥawfī said: "It is permissible that اليَوْمَ be the predicate and be connected with the sense of 'being established,' and مِن (min) be connected to what اليَوْمَ is connected to." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "اليَوْمَ is an adverb of time, and it is connected to ﴿from the command of God﴾, or to the predicate whose estimate is: 'existing today'." End.

Abū al-Baqāʾ rejected this, saying: "As for the predicate of لا (lā), it is not permissible that it be اليَوْمَ, because an adverb of time cannot be a predicate about the essence (al-jathth, the bodies); rather the predicate is مِن أمْرِ اللَّهِ, and اليَوْمُ is an object of مِن أمْرِ اللَّهِ." Al-Ḥawfī said: "It is permissible that اليَوْمَ be an attribute of عاصِمَ, and مِن be the predicate." End.

This is refuted by what Abū al-Baqāʾ refuted with, namely that an adverb of time cannot be an attribute of bodies, just as it cannot be a predicate. It was read: إلّا مَن رُحِمَ (illā man ruḥima), with a ḍamma on the rāʾ, in the passive voice, and this indicates that what is meant by مَن (man) in the reading of the majority, who read the rāʾ with a fatḥa, is the one shown mercy and not the merciful.

﴿And a wave came between them﴾, that is: between Nūḥ and his son. It was said: they were exchanging words, and before the exchange was complete a huge wave came, and he was riding a horse that had become arrogant and self-admiring, so it swallowed him and his horse, and he was prevented from [reaching] Nūḥ, and so he drowned. Al-Farrāʾ said: "بَيْنَهُما (baynahumā), that is: between the son of Nūḥ and the mountain that he thought would protect him."

[p-227]

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verses 41–43 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And he said, "Embark therein; in the name of God is its course and its mooring. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving, Merciful."﴾ ﴿And it sailed with them through waves like mountains. And Noah called to his son, who was apart, "O my son, embark with us and do not be with the disbelievers."﴾ ﴿He said, "I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water." [Noah] said, "There is no protector today from the command of God, except for whom He has mercy." And the wave came between them, and he was among the drowned.﴾ ﴿And it was said, "O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold," and the water subsided and the matter was decided, and it came to rest on al-Judi. And it was said, "Away with the wrongdoing people."﴾ [Hud: 44] ﴿And Noah called to his Lord and said, "My Lord, indeed my son is of my family, and indeed Your promise is true, and You are the most just of judges."﴾ [Hud: 45] ﴿He said, "O Noah, indeed he is not of your family; indeed, he is of unrighteous conduct. So do not ask Me for that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant."﴾ [Hud: 46] ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge. And unless You forgive me and have mercy on me, I will be among the losers."﴾ [Hud: 47] ﴿It was said, "O Noah, descend with peace from Us and blessings upon you and upon nations [descended] from those with you. And there are nations whom We will grant enjoyment; then a painful punishment from Us will touch them."﴾ [Hud: 48] ﴿That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you. Neither you nor your people knew it before this. So be patient; indeed, the good outcome is for the righteous.﴾ [Hud: 49] ﴿And to 'Ad [We sent] their brother Hud. He said, "O my people, worship God; you have no deity other than Him. You are but fabricators."﴾ [Hud: 50] ﴿"O my people, I do not ask you for any reward for it. My reward is only from He who originated me. Then will you not reason?"﴾ [Hud: 51] ﴿"And O my people, seek forgiveness from your Lord and then repent to Him; He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain and increase you in strength upon your strength. And do not turn away as criminals."﴾ [Hud: 52] ﴿They said, "O Hud, you have not brought us any clear proof, and we will not leave our gods on your word, and we are not believers in you."﴾ [Hud: 53] ﴿"We say only that some of our gods have struck you with evil." He said, "Indeed, I call God to witness, and bear witness yourselves that I am free from what you associate."﴾ [Hud: 54] ﴿"Other than Him. So scheme against me all together, then give me no respite."﴾ [Hud: 55] ﴿"Indeed, I have relied upon God, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path."﴾ [Hud: 56] ﴿"And if you turn away, I have already conveyed to you that with which I was sent to you. And my Lord will replace you with another people, and you will not harm Him at all. Indeed, my Lord is Guardian over all things."﴾ [Hud: 57] ﴿And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and We saved them from a severe punishment.﴾ [Hud: 58] ﴿And those were 'Ad; they denied the signs of their Lord, disobeyed His messengers, and followed the command of every obstinate tyrant.﴾ [Hud: 59] ﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, 'Ad disbelieved in their Lord. Unquestionably, away with 'Ad, the people of Hud.﴾ [Hud: 60]

(p. 224) *Rasa* (ـرسا) al-shay'u yarsu: it became firm and settled. He said:
"So I patiently [stood] with a free soul at that moment, firm, while the soul of the coward rises up in alarm."

*Al-balʿ* (swallowing) is well known. Its verb is *balaʿa*, with the vowel of the lam being either *kasra* or *fatḥa*; these are two dialects related by al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', who say *yabla'u balʿan*. *Al-bālūʿa* is the place that absorbs water.

*Al-iqlāʿ* means withholding. It is said: *aqla'a al-maṭar* (the rain stopped) and *aqla'at al-ḥummā* (the fever subsided), meaning that it withheld from the one with fever. It is also said that *aqla'a ʿan al-shay'* means he abandoned it, which is close to withholding. *Ghāḍa al-māʾ* means the water decreased in itself; *ghaḍtuhu* means I diminished it. It comes both intransitive and transitive. *Al-Judi* is the proper name of a mountain near Mosul. As for those who say it is in al-Jazira or Amid, these two are near Mosul. It is also said that *al-Judi* is the name of any mountain, and from this is the saying of Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl:
"Glory be to Him, then glory; we seek refuge in Him, and before us al-Judi and the rocks glorified [Him]."

*Iʿtarāhu bi-kadhā* means it afflicted him with it. It is also said that it is *iftaʿala* from *ʿarāhu yaʿrūhu*. *Al-nāṣiya* is the place of hair growth at the front of the head, and the hair growing there is called *nāṣiya* after its place of growth. *Naṣawtu al-rajul anṣūhu naṣwan* means I pulled his forelock. *Al-jabbār* is the arrogant one. *Al-ʿanīd* is the rebellious tyrant who does not accept the truth nor listen to it, from *ʿanada yaʿnudu*, meaning he swerved from the truth to one side. It is said that from this comes *ʿindī kadhā*, meaning "at my side." Abu ʿUbayda said: *al-ʿanīd*, *al-ʿanūd*, *al-muʿānid* and *al-ʿānid* mean one who opposes with contrariness. From this the vein that bursts with blood is called *ʿāniḍ*.

﴿And he said, "Embark therein; in the name of God is its course and its mooring. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving, Merciful."﴾ ﴿And it sailed with them through waves like mountains. And Noah called to his son, who was apart, "O my son, embark with us and do not be with the disbelievers."﴾ ﴿He said, "I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water." [Noah] said, "There is no protector today from the command of God, except for whom He has mercy." And the wave came between them, and he was among the drowned.﴾: The pronoun in *wa-qāla* refers to Noah, meaning: Noah said, when he was commanded to carry in the ship those who believed with him and whoever was commanded to be carried: "Embark therein." It is also said that the pronoun refers to God, and the meaning is: God said to Noah and those with him. This is weakened by His saying: "Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving, Merciful." It is said that the masculine rational form was given precedence in His saying "Embark" (*ārkabū*), even though those who were carried in it, who are not rational, were more numerous. The apparent meaning is that it is an address only to rational beings, because it is not fitting for non-rational beings.

*Irkabū* is made transitive with *fī* by implying the meaning of *ṣayyirū* (make it [a place]) therein, or the meaning of *udkhulū* (enter) therein. It is also said that the sense is *irkabū al-māʾ fīhā* (ride the water in it). It is also said that *fī* is extra, for emphasis, meaning "ride it." The *bāʾ* in *bi-smi Allāh* is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), or (p. 225) [meaning] "seeking blessing by the name of God." *Majrāhā wa-mursāhā* are in the accusative, either as adverbs of time or place, since they come for that purpose; or as adverbs of time by way of ellipsis, as in *ji'tuka maqdam al-ḥājj*, meaning "the time of the arrival of the pilgrim." Then *majrāhā wa-mursāhā* would be verbal nouns originally, with the genitive element omitted, and they are in the accusative by what is in *bi-smi Allāh* of the meaning of the verb. It is permissible that *bi-smi Allāh* be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *fīhā*, and *majrāhā wa-mursāhā* are verbal nouns in the nominative as subjects, meaning: "Embark therein, bound to the name of God, [with] its running and its stopping," that is, "by the blessing of the name of God."

Or *majrāhā wa-mursāhā* are in the nominative as subject of a nominal sentence (*mubtadaʾ*), with *bi-smi Allāh* as predicate, and the sentence is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *fīhā*. Under these three interpretations the speech is one sentence, and the circumstantial clause is anticipated. With the nominative *majrāhā wa-mursāhā* as subject or topic, it is not permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *irkabū*, because there is no returning pronoun to it in what functions as a circumstantial clause. It is also permissible that *bi-smi Allāh majrāhā wa-mursāhā* be a second sentence consisting of subject and predicate, with no grammatical connection to the first sentence. He first commanded them to embark, then informed them that its running and its stopping are by the mention of God, or by His command and power. The two sentences are then two reported statements. It is said: just as the second sentence is also reported by *qāla* (he said).

Al-Dahhak said: when [Noah] wanted the ship to run he said, "In the name of God is its running," and it ran; and when he wanted it to stop he said, "In the name of God is its stopping," and it stopped.

Mujahid, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', al-A'raj, Shayba and the majority of the seven readers — the two Haramis (Ibn Kathir and Nafi'), the two Iraqis (Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr?) and Abu Bakr — read *majrāhā* with *ḍamma* on the *mīm*. Al-Akhawan (Hamza and al-Kisa'i) and Hafs read it with *fatḥa*. All of them read the *mīm* of *mursāhā* with *ḍamma*. Ibn Mas'ud, 'Isa al-Thaqafi, Zayd ibn 'Ali and al-A'mash read *majrāhā wa-mursāhā* with *fatḥa* on both *mīms*, as adverbs of time or place, or as verbal nouns according to the previous interpretations.

Al-Dahhak, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Thabit, Abu Raja', Mujahid, Ibn Jundab, al-Kalbi and al-Jahdari read *mujrīhā wa-mursīhā*, as active participles from *ajrā* and *arsā*, in apposition to the name of God. They are then in the position of a predicate, and they cannot be adjectives because they are indefinite.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: in this reading they are two adjectives referring back to the name [of God] in their saying *bi-smi Allāh*. End of quotation.

They cannot be adjectives except on the assumption that they are definite. Al-Khalil held that whatever has a non-pure (*ghayr maḥḍa*) annexation may sometimes be made pure, and thus become definite, except for the attributive adjective (*ṣifa mushabbaha*), whose annexation is never made pure, so it does not become definite.

﴿Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving﴾: *Sattūr* (Concealer) of your sins for you, through your repentance and faith. *(Raḥīm)*: Merciful to you when He saves you from drowning. It is related in a hadith: "Noah boarded the ship on the first day of Rajab and fasted the whole month." And from ʿIkrima: on the tenth [day] of Rajab.

﴿And it sailed with them﴾: an informing by God Exalted of what happened to the ship. *Bihim* is a circumstantial clause, meaning "in connection with them," i.e., with them in it. The meaning is: it runs while they are in it. ﴿Through waves like mountains﴾: that is, through the waves of the deluge. He likened each wave of it to a mountain in its piling up and height. It is related that the sky poured down all of its water, so that there was no direction in the air but that it rained, and the whole earth gushed forth with springs; this is the meaning of the meeting of the waters.

It is related that the water rose above the mountains and the high parts of the earth by forty cubits, and it is said fifteen. That the ship ran through waves indicates that there were waves in the water, that the water did not cover all between the sky and the earth, and that the ship did not run inside the water with the water above and below it; rather it swam in the water as a fish swims, as al-Zajjaj, al-Zamakhshari and others indicated.

Ibn 'Atiyya found this improbable. He said: "Where were the waves like mountains on this view? And how did the life of those in the ship remain sound?" Al-Zamakhshari answered: the running in the waves was before the covering, and before the water overspread the mountains. Do you not see the saying of his son: ﴿I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water﴾?

﴿And Noah called to his son﴾: the *wāw* does not indicate order. This calling was before the ship ran in His saying ﴿and it sailed with them through waves﴾. In the attribution of the son to him here, and in His saying ﴿indeed, my son is of my family﴾ [Hud: 45] and in his calling to him, there is evidence that he was his son by his loins. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, al-Dahhak, Ibn Jubayr, Maymun ibn Mihran (p. 226) and the majority. His name was Kan'an. It is said he was Yam. It is also said he was a close relative whom he called "son" out of tenderness and gentleness.

The majority read the *tanwīn* of *Nūḥ* with *kasra*. Wakī' ibn al-Jarrāḥ read it with *ḍamma*, making its vowel follow the case-ending vowel on the *ḥāʾ*. Abu Hatim said: this is a bad dialect, unknown.

The majority read the pronoun *hāʾ* joined with a *wāw*. Ibn 'Abbas read *innah* with the *hāʾ* vowel-less. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: this is according to the dialect of al-Azd al-Shurat, who make the pronominal *hāʾ* of the masculine vowel-less. From this is the poet's saying:
"And my two thighs are both longing for him, both sleepless."
Others mentioned that it is a dialect of Banu Kilab and ʿUqayl. Some grammarians restrict this vowel-lessness to poetic necessity, and they recite:
"And I drink water though I have no thirst for it, except because its springs are the flood of its valley."

Al-Suddi read *ibnāh* with an *alif* and the *hāʾ al-sakt*. Abu al-Fath said: this is in the form of a vocative. A group held that it is in the form of lamentation and elegy. ʿAli, ʿUrwa, ʿAli ibn al-Husayn and his son Abu Ja'far and his son Ja'far read *ibnah* with *fatḥa* on the *hāʾ* without an *alif*, meaning *ibnahā* (her son), attached to the pronoun of his wife, so the vowel *fatḥa* sufficed in place of the *alif*. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is a dialect. From it is the poet's saying:
"If you lead with her a sheep and eat it, or sell it in some of the markets."
Ibn al-A'rabi cited the following for this:
"You will not catch up with what has passed from me by lamenting, nor by 'if only,' nor by 'had I'."
End of quotation.

He means *talahhufan* (lamentation). Al-Nahhas criticized Abu Hatim for deleting this *alif*. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is not as he said." End of quotation.

This, I mean the like of تَلَهَّفَ (tala-hhafa) with the alif elided, is by the consensus of our companions (the Basran grammarians) a poetic necessity (ḍarūratan). For this reason they do not permit يا غُلامُ (yā ghulāmu) with the alif elided, and they dispense with the alif by the vowel fatḥa, just as they dispensed with the kasra in يا غُلامِ (yā ghulāmi) in place of the yā'. Al-Akhfash permitted this.

ʿAlī and ʿUrwa also read ابْنَها (ibnahā) with a fatḥa on the hā' and an alif, meaning ابْنَ امْرَأتِهِ (ibna imra'atihi), the son of his wife. That he was not his son by his loins, but the son of his wife, is the view of ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Sīrīn and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr. Al-Ḥasan used to swear that he was not his son by his loins. Qatāda said: I said to him, "God has related of him: ﴿Indeed, my son is of my family﴾ [Hūd: 45], and you say he was not his son, while the People of the Book do not differ that he was his son." He said: "And who takes his religion from the People of the Book?" He cited in support His saying ﴿of my family﴾ [Hūd: 45] and not "of me," so on this view he would be a stepson (rabīb).

ʿIkrima and al-Ḍaḥḥāk used to swear that he was his son. It is not to be supposed that he was of illegitimate birth (li-ghayri rishda), because that is a disgrace from which the prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, are protected. This is related from al-Ḥasan and Ibn Jurayj, though it is perhaps not authentically transmitted from them. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "The wife of a prophet never committed adultery at all." What the apparent sense of the verse indicates is that he was his son. As for the reading of whoever read ابْنَهُ or ابْنَها, it is irregular (shādhdha). It is possible that he was attributed to his mother and was made to belong to her, and was not attributed to his father because he was an unbeliever like her; this meaning is observed in him, and he was not attributed to him out of disapproval of him, and out of caution that an unbeliever not be attributed to a prophet. He called him only out of his assumption that he was a believer, and had it not been for that he would not have loved his deliverance. Or [he called him] out of his assumption that he would believe if he was an unbeliever, because of the great terrors he witnessed, and that he would accept faith. His saying ﴿Board with us﴾ would be like an indication that he requested of him faith, and it was reinforced by His saying ﴿and do not be with the unbelievers﴾, that is: board with the believers, since none boards with them except a believer, by His saying ﴿and whoever believed﴾ [Hūd: 40].

﴿In a place apart﴾ (fī maʿzil), that is: in a place where he isolated himself from his father and from the vessel of the believers. It was said: in a place apart from his father's religion.

His calling him with the diminutive is an address of tenderness and compassion. The meaning: board with us in the ship so that you may be saved, and do not be with the unbelievers so that you perish. ʿĀṣim read يا بَنِيَ (yā baniya) with a fatḥa on the bā'. It is explained as having dispensed with the alif by the fatḥa, and its origin is يا بُنَيًّا (yā bunayyan), like your saying يا غُلامًا (yā ghulāman). The rest of the seven [readers] dispensed with the yā' by the kasra in their reading يا بَنِي (yā bani) with a kasra on the yā'. Or the alif was elided because it met the rāʾ of ارْكَبْ (irkab).

Ibn Nūḥ assumed that that rain and the bursting forth [of waters] were according to the usual custom, and therefore he said: ﴿I will betake myself to a mountain that will protect me from the water﴾, that is: from the water reaching me so that I do not drown. This indicates his habit in unbelief and his lack of trust in his father regarding what he reported.

It was said: the mountain he meant was Ṭūr Zaytā, but it did not protect him. The apparent sense is to keep ʿāṣim (protector) on its literal meaning, and that he negated every protector from the command of God at that time, and that whoever He has mercy upon falls within [the scope of] مَن (man) referring to the one protected. The subject pronoun returns to God, the Exalted, the relative pronoun is omitted, and the exception is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ), meaning: but whomever God has mercy upon is protected. They also permitted that it be from God, the Exalted, meaning: there is no protector except the Merciful; and that ʿāṣim be in the sense of "one possessing protection," as they say لابِنٌ (labin), meaning: one possessing milk; and "one possessing protection" (dhū ʿiṣma) is applied both to a protector and to one protected, and what is meant here is the protected one. Or it is an active form in the sense of a passive, so ʿāṣim means maʿṣūm (protected), like māʾun dāfiq in the sense of madfūq (poured forth). The poet said:

*Slow to rise, gentle of speech*
*my heart has become enamored of him*

meaning: enchanted (maftūnan). And مَن (man) is for the protected one, meaning: there is no one possessing protection, or: no one is protected except the one shown mercy. On these two permissible readings, the exception is contiguous (muttaṣil). Al-Zamakhsharī made it contiguous by another way, namely by omitting a modifier, and estimated it as: no protector today from a mountain or the like protects you, except one protector, which is the place of those whom God has shown mercy to and saved, meaning in the ship. End.

The apparent view is that the predicate of ﴿there is no protector﴾ is omitted, because when it is known, as in this position, the Banū Tamīm are bound to omit it, and its omission is frequent among the people of the Ḥijāz. For when he said ﴿I will betake myself to a mountain that will protect me from the water﴾, Nūḥ said to him: ﴿There is no protector﴾, that is: there is no existing protector.

اليَوْمَ (al-yawma, "today") would be in the accusative by an implied verb indicated by عاصِمَ (ʿāṣima), that is: no protector protects today from the command of God; and مِن أمْرِ اللَّهِ (min amri llāh, "from the command of God") is connected to that omitted verb. It is not permissible for اليَوْمَ to be in the accusative by ﴿there is no protector﴾, nor for مِن أمْرِ اللَّهِ to be connected to it, because the noun after لا (lā) would then be extended (muṭawwal), and if it were extended it would require tanwīn and i'rāb, while it is built (mabnī) [on the fatḥa], so that is invalid.

Al-Ḥawfī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya permitted that اليَوْمَ be the predicate of ﴿there is no protector﴾. Al-Ḥawfī said: "It is permissible that اليَوْمَ be the predicate and be connected with the sense of 'being established,' and مِن (min) be connected to what اليَوْمَ is connected to." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "اليَوْمَ is an adverb of time, and it is connected to ﴿from the command of God﴾, or to the predicate whose estimate is: 'existing today'." End.

Abū al-Baqāʾ rejected this, saying: "As for the predicate of لا (lā), it is not permissible that it be اليَوْمَ, because an adverb of time cannot be a predicate about the essence (al-jathth, the bodies); rather the predicate is مِن أمْرِ اللَّهِ, and اليَوْمُ is an object of مِن أمْرِ اللَّهِ." Al-Ḥawfī said: "It is permissible that اليَوْمَ be an attribute of عاصِمَ, and مِن be the predicate." End.

This is refuted by what Abū al-Baqāʾ refuted with, namely that an adverb of time cannot be an attribute of bodies, just as it cannot be a predicate. It was read: إلّا مَن رُحِمَ (illā man ruḥima), with a ḍamma on the rāʾ, in the passive voice, and this indicates that what is meant by مَن (man) in the reading of the majority, who read the rāʾ with a fatḥa, is the one shown mercy and not the merciful.

﴿And a wave came between them﴾, that is: between Nūḥ and his son. It was said: they were exchanging words, and before the exchange was complete a huge wave came, and he was riding a horse that had become arrogant and self-admiring, so it swallowed him and his horse, and he was prevented from [reaching] Nūḥ, and so he drowned. Al-Farrāʾ said: "بَيْنَهُما (baynahumā), that is: between the son of Nūḥ and the mountain that he thought would protect him."

[p-227]

(p-٢٢٨)﴿And it was said: "O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold!" And the water subsided, the matter was decided, and it came to rest upon al-Judi. And it was said: "Away with the wrongdoing people!"﴾ ﴿And Noah called out to his Lord and said: "My Lord, indeed my son is of my family, and indeed Your promise is the truth, and You are the most just of judges."﴾ ﴿He said: "O Noah, indeed he is not of your family; indeed, he is one whose conduct is not righteous. So do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge. I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant."﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge. And unless You forgive me and have mercy on me, I will be among the losers."﴾

al-Zamakhshari said: He addressed the earth and the sky with the address used for a discerning human being, using the particle of specification and turning to them with direct address from among all other created things, namely His words: ﴿O earth﴾ and (O sky). Then He commanded them with what is commanded to people who discern and possess reason, namely His words: ﴿swallow your water﴾ and ﴿withhold﴾. This indicates immense power, and that the heavens, the earth, and these great bodies are subject to His bringing into being within them whatever He wills, not resisting Him, as if they were intelligent and discerning beings who have known His greatness, majesty, reward, punishment, and power over every possible thing, and who have understood the necessity of obeying Him and submitting to Him, fearing Him and dreading to hesitate in complying with Him or to delay in carrying out His will immediately, without doubt.

Thus, as His command reaches them, the thing commanded occurs without any delay or slowness. al-Zamakhshari expanded upon and elaborated this fine statement. al-Hasan said: It indicates the greatness of these bodies, while the Exalted Truth has dominion over them, disposing of them as He wills and desires, and this becomes a cause for the rational faculty to stand before the perfection of Allah's majesty, the exaltedness of His power, and His awe-inspiring might. End of quotation.

The use of the passive verb in (It was said) and what follows it is more emphatic in magnifying and in conveying majesty, and it is more concise. al-Zamakhshari said: The reporting of this in the passive verb serves to indicate majesty and grandeur, and that such great affairs cannot occur except by the act of a capable doer and the creation of an overpowering creator. Also, the doer of these actions is one doer, who has no partner in His actions. So let not the mind imagine that anyone other than Him could say ﴿O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold!﴾, nor that anyone other than Him could decree that tremendous matter, nor that the ship could come to rest upon al-Judi and settle upon it, except by His leveling and establishing it. This is also due to the meanings and subtleties we have mentioned.

The scholars of rhetoric (ʿulamaʾ al-bayan) regarded this verse as eloquent to an extreme, and they shook their heads in admiration of it. This is not because of the similarity (tajanus) of the two words, namely His words ﴿ibla'i﴾ and ﴿aqli'i﴾, although the statement is not devoid of beauty. Compared to those beauties that are the core, such features are like something not worth noticing, while everything else is mere husk. End of quotation.
