Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verses 48–49:

﴿It was said: "O Noah, descend with peace from Us and blessings upon you and upon nations from those with you. And there are nations whom We will provide for, then a painful punishment from Us will touch them."﴾ ﴿That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you. Neither you nor your people knew it before this. So be patient; indeed the final outcome is for the righteous.﴾

The verb is in the passive form (buniya li-l-maf'ul), so it was said. Some say the speaker is God Most High, and others say it was the angels, conveying (tabligh) from God Most High. The first view is the apparent one, because of His words "from Us" (minna) and "We will provide for them" (sanumatti'uhum). When Noah disembarked, he was commanded to descend from the ship and from the mountain with his companions in order to spread out over the earth. The ba' (bi) is for the state (hal), meaning accompanied by safety (salama), security (amn) and blessings (barakat), which are the goods that grow in every direction.

It is also possible that the lam (in li-salam, "for peace") carries the sense of greeting (taslim), meaning: descend, greeted and honored. It was also recited as "ihbut" with a damma on the ba' (ihbuṭ). 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Yahya narrated, from al-Kisa'i, the reading "wa-barakatin" in the singular (tawhid). He was given the good news of safety as an announcement (idhan) to him of his Lord's forgiveness and His mercy towards him, and of his settling on the earth secure from worldly calamities. The earth had been emptied of whatever benefits people, of plants and animals, so this was good news to him of the earth's return to its best condition. For this reason He said: "and blessings upon you," meaning lasting and enduring blessings upon you. The apparent meaning is that min (from) indicates the starting point (ibtida' al-ghaya), meaning: arising from those who are with you, and they are the believing nations until the end of time. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is possible that min is explanatory (lil-bayan), so the nations intended are those who were with him in the ship, because they were groups (jama'at). They were called nations because the nations branched out from them." End of quotation.

This has a degree of remoteness and artificiality, since the sense would become: "and upon nations who are those with you." Even if this meaning were intended, it would not be necessary. It would have been more concise, closer to understanding, and further from ambiguity to say "and upon nations with you" or "upon those with you."

The word "nations" (umam) is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'). Al-Zamakhshari said: "'We will provide for them' (sanumatti'uhum) is a qualifier (sifa), and the predicate is omitted, its estimate being: 'and from those with you are nations whom We will provide for.' It was omitted because His words 'from those with you' (mimman ma'aka) indicate it. The meaning is: the peace from Us and the blessings upon you and upon nations of believers who arise from those with you, and nations enjoying worldly provision who will return to the Fire." End of quotation.

It is also possible that "nations" is the subject, with the qualifier omitted, and this omitted qualifier is what permits beginning with an indefinite noun (nakira). The estimate is: "and nations from them," meaning from those with you, that is, arising from those with you. "We will provide for them" is the predicate, as the Arabs said: "Samn manawan bi-dirham" (ghee is two manas for a dirham), meaning two manas of it. "Min-hu" (of it) is omitted, and it is the qualifier of "manawan," and for this reason the beginning with "manawan," which is indefinite, is permitted. It is also possible to estimate a subject without estimating a qualifier for the predicate "We will provide for them," and the justification for beginning with the indefinite is that the position is one of detailing (tafsil), so it is like the words of the poet:

*When she weeps from behind her, she turns to him with one side, and the other side with us is not turned.*

Al-Qurtubi said: "'Nations' is raised with the meaning: and there will be nations." End of quotation. If he intended an explanation of meaning, then it is good; if he intended grammatical analysis (i'rab), then it is not good, because this is not one of the positions where "yakun" (there will be) is omitted. Al-Akhfash said: "This is like your saying: 'I spoke to Zayd, and 'Amr is seated.'" End of quotation. It is therefore possible that it is of the type of conjoining sentences ('atf al-jumal), and it is possible that the waw is for the state (hal), and it would be a presumed state (hal muqaddara), because at the time of the command to descend those nations did not yet exist.

Abu al-Baqa' said: "'Umam' is conjoined to the pronoun in 'ihbut' (descend), its estimate being: descend you and nations, and the separation between them makes emphasis unnecessary. 'Sanumatti'uhum' is a description of 'umam.'" End of quotation. This estimate and this meaning are not suitable, because those who were with Noah in the ship were only believers, as His words indicate: "and none believed except a few" (Hud 40). They were not two categories, unbelievers and believers, so the unbelievers would be commanded to descend with Noah. This would only be possible if it were supposed that some of those believers would disbelieve after the descent, and the verse informed about them by the state they would come to. This is possible but remote. What ought to be understood from the verse is that among those with him there would arise believers and unbelievers. He alerted to faith by the fact that those characterized by it have peace and blessings from God, and to disbelief by the fact that those characterized by it will be provided for in this world and then punished in the Hereafter. This is of the type of metonymy (kinaya), as in the saying: "So-and-so has a long cloak-strap and much ash," meaning he is generous. The apparent sense of His words "from those with you" indicates that both believers and unbelievers arose from those with him. If those who were with him in the ship were only his three sons, or with them their wives, then the view of the exegetes is consistent that Noah, peace be upon him, is the father of all creation, and for this reason he was called "the Lesser Adam." If they were his sons and others, according to the disagreement over the number, then if the others other than his sons died without producing offspring, it is correct that he is the father of mankind after Adam, but it is not correct that there arose from those with him a believer and an unbeliever, unless by "those with him" is meant his sons, in which case it is the general term used for the specific. If they had produced offspring, as most exegetes hold, then it is not consistent that he is the father of mankind after Adam; rather, creation after the Flood is from him and from those who were with him in the ship.

The nations who are provided for are not specified; rather, they are an expression for the unbelievers. It was said: they are the people of Hud, Salih, Lot and Shu'ayb, upon them be prayers and peace.

﴿That﴾ is a reference to the story of Noah. Grammatical analyses were already presented for a similar construction in His words: "That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you" (Al 'Imran 44), in Al 'Imran. "Tilka" (that) is used for the distant, because between this story and the Messenger there are immeasurable periods of time. It was also said: the reference of "that" is to the verses of the Qur'an, and "from the news of the unseen" is what has long been past and whose knowledge remains only with God. "We reveal it to you" so that it may be guidance and an example for you in what other prophets encountered, and its knowledge was not with you or with your people. We informed them of it so that it might be an example for them and a warning that what befell those people may befall them if they deny you. It is for the sake of noticing this meaning that the eloquence of His words becomes evident: "So be patient" over their harm, striving in conveying from God, for the final outcome is yours just as it was for Noah in this story. The meaning of "you did not know it" is: in such detail as We have related to you. The knowledge of the Flood was known to the world in general terms.

The Magians now deny it. The clause "you did not know" is in the position of a state (hal) from the object of "We reveal it," or from the object of "to you." Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as a meaning, saying: "that is, unknown to you and to your people." It is also possible that it is a predicate after a predicate. The reference in "before this" is to the time, or to the revelation, or to the knowledge acquired through revelation, these are all possibilities. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud it reads: "before this Qur'an." Al-Zamakhshari said: "'Nor your people' means: your people, of whom you are one, despite their numbers and abundance, if this was not their situation and they had neither heard it nor known it, then how about a man from among them? Just as you say: 'Abd Allah did not know this, nor did the people of his town?'" End of quotation.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 11, verses 50–60 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿To the 'Ad [We sent] their brother Hud. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. You are only inventors of falsehood."﴾ ﴿"O my people, I do not ask you for any wage for it. My wage is only from the One who created me. Will you not then reason?"﴾ ﴿"And O my people, seek forgiveness from your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance. He will send down the sky upon you in abundant rain and increase you in strength upon your strength. And do not turn away as criminals."﴾

﴿وإلى عادٍ أخاهم﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf, conjoined) with His saying ﴿We sent Noah to his people﴾ (Hud: 25). The conjunction particle (al-waw) has joined a genitive-marked element to a genitive-marked element and an accusative to an accusative, just as a nominative and accusative may be conjoined to a nominative and accusative, as in: "Zayd struck 'Amr, and Bakr [struck] Khalid." It is not a case of separating the conjunction particle from the conjoined element by a prepositional phrase, as in: "I struck Zayd, and in the house, 'Amr." From this arises the disagreement among the grammarians: is this permissible in ordinary speech, or is it restricted to poetry? The intended meaning of the sentence is: "[We sent] to Hud, and to 'Ad and their brother [Hud], among them [the Prophets mentioned] in al-A'raf." The reading of al-Kisa'i is (ghayrihi) with the genitive (kasra) ending. It has also been said that there is an omitted verb here, meaning "And We sent to 'Ad their brother," in which case it is conjunction of clauses ('atf al-jumal), while the first is conjunction of single words (mufradat). This second view is closer to the truth, because of the long separation by many clauses between the two conjoined elements.

(Hudan): this is either an apposition (badal) or a clarifying apposition ('atf bayan). Muhaysin read (ya qawmu) with a damma on the mim, like the reading of Hafs for: ﴿He said: "My Lord, judge with truth"﴾ (al-Anbiya: 112) with a damma. This is a dialect form for the vocative with a possessive attachment, which Sibawayh and others have transmitted. Their "inventing falsehood," according to al-Hasan, lies in their assigning divinity to other than Allah, the Exalted. Al-Zamakhshari said: it lies in their taking idols as partners to Him.

The pronoun in ﴿عليه﴾ ("for it") refers to the call to Allah. By His saying ﴿the One who created me﴾ he alerts them to refute their worship of idols and their belief that these idols act. That He, the Exalted, is the Originator of all existing things makes Him deserving of being singled out for worship.

﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ is a rebuke establishing the impossibility of divinity for other than the Originator. It is also possible that ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ refers to the fact that, since I do not seek any worldly gain from you, but only desire your benefit, you must submit to what contains your salvation. It is as if it were said: "Will you not reason the advice of one who seeks no reward for it except from Allah, the Exalted, which is the reward of the Hereafter? Nothing is more effective in dispelling accusation than this." The discussion of ﴿Seek forgiveness from your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance﴾ (Hud: 3) has already been covered at the beginning of this surah.

Hud intended to win them over to faith and encourage them toward it by [promising] abundant rain (p-233) and increased strength, because they were people of crops, gardens and buildings, zealously eager for them to the utmost degree. So they were most in need of water, and they were proud of the strength, violence and might they had been given, being fully equipped in every region.

It has been said: he meant strength in wealth. It has also been said: strength in procreation. It has been said that rain was withheld from them for three years and the wombs of their women became barren. Al-Hasan ibn 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) drew from this, and from His saying ﴿and He will supply you with wealth and children﴾ (Nuh: 12), that abundant seeking of forgiveness may cause Allah to make it a cause of abundant offspring. He answered one who asked him, and informed him that he had wealth but no children were born to him: "Seek forgiveness," so he sought it abundantly and ten sons were born to him.

Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿and increase you in strength upon your strength﴾ that it means offspring and the offspring of offspring. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: [it means] in body and might. Al-Dahhak said: fertility upon your fertility. It has been said: blessing upon His earlier blessing upon you. It has been said: strength in your faith upon strength in your bodies.

﴿They said: "O Hud, you have brought us no clear proof, and we will not abandon our gods on your word, nor are we going to believe you."﴾ ﴿"We only say that some of our gods have struck you with evil." He said: "I call Allah to witness, and bear witness yourselves that I am free of what you associate"﴾ ﴿"other than Him. So scheme against me, all of you, and give me no respite."﴾ ﴿"I have put my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is upon a straight path."﴾ ﴿"But if you turn away, I have already conveyed to you what I was sent with. My Lord will bring another people in your place, and you will not harm Him at all. Indeed, my Lord is Guardian over all things."﴾

"A clear proof" (bayyinah): a clear evidence or manifest argument that indicates the truth of what you say. They lied in this and slandered him, just as Quraysh lied when they said: ﴿Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ (Yunus: 20), though he had brought them many signs. Or, because of their blindness to the truth and their failure to reflect upon the signs, they considered what was indeed a sign to be no sign, and so they said: "You have brought us no proof that compels us to faith." Otherwise, Hud and the other prophets have miracles, even if he did not specify some of them for us.

Do you not see the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "There is no prophet except that he was given signs of the kind by which mankind believed"?

The particle (ʿan) in ﴿on your word﴾ is a circumstantial element (hal) referring to the pronoun in ﴿abandoning our gods﴾. It is as if it were said: "departing from your word." This is the view of al-Zamakhshari. It has also been said: "ʿan" expresses causation, as in His saying: ﴿except for a promise he had made to him﴾ (al-Tawbah: 114), so it is connected to "abandoning," as if it were said: "because of your word." Ibn 'Atiyyah has indicated the causal meaning and its basis, saying: that is, your word would not be a cause for our abandoning [our gods], since it is bare of any sign. The sentence after it is an emphasis and a despairing of them ever entering his religion. Then they attributed what came from him, namely his calling them to Allah and his singling Him out for divinity, to insanity and madness, and that this was something some of their gods had inflicted upon him, because he had reviled them, urged the abandonment of them, and called to the abandonment of their worship. So they made him speak in the manner of madmen, in requital, just as Quraysh said: ﴿A taught, possessed man﴾ (al-Dukhan: 14), and ﴿Or do they say: "He has a madness"?﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 70).

﴿i'tarak﴾ ("has struck you") is a reported clause following (naqulu, "we say"), so it occupies the position of the object. It indicates extreme foolishness and excessive ignorance, in that they believed that stones could give victory and take vengeance.

Hud's reply to them: ﴿I call Allah to witness﴾ to the end, in which he disassociates himself from their gods and urges them all, despite his being alone, to scheme against him with whatever they wish. His not being delayed is among the greatest signs of his truthfulness and his confidence in his Lord's promise of support for him, of assistance, and of protection from their reaching him with any harm. Yet they were eager to kill him, shooting at him from one bow. Similar is Noah's saying to his people: ﴿Then decide your affair against me, and give me no respite﴾ (Yunus: 71). He also confirmed his disavowal of their gods and their polytheism, and he strengthened this by what people customarily do in confirming matters: by calling upon the witness of Allah and the witness of the servants.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): Why was it not said: "I call Allah to witness and I call you to witness"? (I answer): Because calling Allah to witness regarding disavowal of polytheism is a valid and established testimony, in the sense of establishing monotheism. As for calling them to witness, it is nothing but a showing of contempt for their religion and an indication of indifference toward them, and nothing more. Therefore, it was turned away from the wording of the first, due to the difference between the two, and was expressed in the imperative form of the command to bear witness. End of quotation.

(Inni bari'un, "I am free"): the verb (ushhidu, "I call to witness") and (ishhadu, "bear witness") both govern it, and two verbs may compete for the same noun when that noun is suitable to be governed by both. You say: "I gave Zayd and gave 'Amr a dinar," just as an intransitive and a transitive verb may compete, as in: "Stood, and I struck Zayd."

(Ma) in (ma tushrikun, "what you associate") is a relative pronoun, either verbal-source (masdariyyah) or meaning "that which": that is, "free of your associating other gods beside Him," or "free of those whom you associate."

(Jamiʿan, "all of you") is a circumstantial element (hal) from the subject pronoun in (kidūni, "scheme against me"), and the address is directed only to his people. Al-Zamakhshari said: "you and your gods." End of quotation.

It has been said: Hud's open declaration to them of his freedom from their religions, and his urging them to scheme against him together with their idols, is itself a miracle for Hud. Or, he urged their whole community against him despite his being alone and their being strong and numerous, yet they were unable to reach him with any harm. Then he mentioned his reliance upon Allah, informing them that He is his Lord and their Lord, alerting them that because He is their Lord it is obligatory for them not to worship any but Him, and entrusting his affair to Him, the Exalted, in confidence in His protection and in the fulfilment of His promise. Then he described the power of Allah, the Exalted, and the magnitude of His dominion: that every creature is in His grip, His possession, and under His subjugation and sovereignty. So you are among those subjugated.

His saying ﴿holds its forelock﴾ is a figure of speech (tamthil), since the capable owner leads the one over whom he has power by its forelock, just as a captive or a horse is led by its forelock. The grasping of the forelock came to be a convention for power over an animal. The Arabs used to cut the forelock of a captive who had been spared, as a sign that he had been overpowered and that his forelock was in another's grasp. Ibn Jurayj said: He singled out the forelock because when the Arabs describe a person as humbled and submissive, they say: "The forelock of so-and-so is only in the hand of so-and-so," meaning that he obeys him and he directs him as he wishes. Then He informed that His actions, the Exalted, are in the utmost perfection, and in the path of truth and justice in His dominion: no wrongdoer escapes Him, and no one who relies upon Him is lost in His sight. His word is true and His promise is real.

The majority read ﴿فَإنْ تَوَلَّوْا﴾ (fa-in tawallaw) as (tatawallaw), the present tense of (tawalla). Al-A'raj and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read (tuwallu) with damma on the ta' and lam, the present tense of (walla). It has also been said that (tawallaw) is a past tense verb, and that the answer to the condition requires an implied verb of speech, meaning: "Then say to them: 'I have already conveyed to you.'" There is no need to make it a past tense verb and to supply an implied speech verb.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is possible that (tawallaw) is a past tense verb, and that there is a shift in the speech from the third person to the second person, meaning: "Then I have conveyed to you." End of quotation. This requires no implied element. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (tawallaw) refers to the people of Hud, and the address to them is part of the speech that was said earlier. Al-Tabrizi said: it refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh, and this is a shift of address (talwin al-khitab), in which the speech moves from addressing the people of Hud to reporting about those present with the Messenger (ﷺ). As if it were said: "Inform them about the story of the people of Hud, and call them to faith in Allah, lest what befell the people of Hud befall them. If they turn away, then say to them: 'I have already conveyed to you.'"

The answer to the condition is His saying ﴿I have already conveyed to you﴾, and it is correct that this should be the answer, because in his conveying his message to them is included what will befall them of the total punishment. It is as if it were said: "If you turn away, you will be utterly destroyed by punishment." This is indicated by the declarative clause: ﴿My Lord will bring another people in your place﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): The conveying was before the turning away, so how did it become the answer to the condition? (I answer): Its meaning is: "If you turn away, I will not be punished for any negligence in conveying, since what I was sent with has reached you, but you refused anything except rejecting the message and hostility toward the Messenger." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The meaning is that I bear no great concern on your account if you turn away; my conscience is clear through the conveying, and you are the ones at fault in turning away from faith.

The majority read ﴿و يَسْتَخْلِفُ﴾ (wa yastakhlifu) with a damma on the fa', as a new declarative sentence: that is, He will destroy you and bring other people who will succeed you in your dwellings and your wealth. Hafs, in the transmission of Hubayra, read it with a jussive ending (wa yastakhlif), in coordination with the position of the condition's answer. 'Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud] also read it like this, and read ﴿وَلَا تَضُرُّوهُ﴾ (wa la tadurruhu, al-Tawbah: 39) with a jussive ending. The majority read ﴿وَلَا تَضُرُّونَهُ﴾ (wa la tadurrunahu), meaning: not any harm at all by your turning away, because He, the Exalted, is not subject to harm or benefit. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The meaning may bear two interpretations. One: "You will not harm Him by your going away and your destruction at all," meaning His dominion does not diminish and His affair is not disturbed. According to this meaning, 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud read ﴿وَلَا تَنْقُصُونَهُ شَيْئًا﴾ (wa la tanqusunahu shay'an, "nor will you diminish Him at all"). The other meaning: "You will not harm Him," that is, when He destroys you, you will be unable to harm Him in any way, nor to retaliate against Him, nor will you oppose His action with anything that could harm Him. End of quotation.

This is a negated verb whose implied object is indefinite, so all forms of harm are negated and none is specified. (Hafiz, "Guardian") means: a watcher encompassing things in knowledge, to whom your deeds are not hidden, and who does not neglect to call you to account. He guards me from what you plot against me.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 11, verses 50–60 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿When Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and We saved them from a severe punishment.﴾ ﴿And that was 'Ad, who denied the signs of their Lord, disobeyed His messengers, and followed the command of every obstinate tyrant.﴾ ﴿They were pursued by a curse in this world and on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, 'Ad disbelieved in their Lord. Away with 'Ad, the people of Hud!﴾: *al-Amr* (the command) is the singular of *al-umur* (affairs). It may therefore be a metonymy (*kinaya*) for the punishment, or for the decree of their destruction. Or it may be a verbal noun (*masdar*) of *amara*, meaning: Our command to the wind, or to its guardians (*khazanatuha*).

﴿Those who believed with him﴾: It was said they were four thousand, and it was said they were three thousand.

The apparent connection of *bi-rahmatin minna* (by a mercy from Us) is to *najjayna* (We saved), meaning: We saved them solely by a mercy from Allah that reached them, not by their righteous deeds. Or the mercy is a metonymy for their righteous deeds, since their being granted success in them is only due to the mercy of the Exalted toward them. It is also possible that it is connected to *amanu* (believed), meaning: their faith in Allah and their affirmation of His messenger is only by the mercy of Allah toward them, since He granted them success in that. The saving is repeated for emphasis (*ta'kid*), and out of concern lest someone think that the second saving is connected to *minna* (from). Or this result is the punishment of the Hereafter, and there is no punishment more severe than it, so it is repeated because its objects differ. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, what is the meaning of repeating the saving? I say: He mentioned first that when He destroyed their enemy, He saved them. Then He said: ﴿And We saved them from a severe punishment﴾, meaning: and the saving was from a severe punishment." He said: "That is because Allah, Mighty and Exalted, sent upon them the *samum* (scorching wind), which entered their noses and exited their anuses, and cut them apart limb by limb." This is what al-Zajjaj said. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is possible that he means: the earlier salvation was from a severe punishment, meaning the wind. In that case, the intended purpose is to enumerate the blessing. What is well known about their punishment by the wind is that it used to carry them, demolish their dwellings and uproot them, and carry the howdah as it was, and similar things."

*Tilka 'Adun* (That was 'Ad): This is a reference to their graves and their remains, as if He said: ﴿Travel through the land﴾ [al-Tawba: 2], meaning: look at them and take heed. Then He resumed the report about them, saying: ﴿They denied the signs of their Lord﴾, meaning: they rejected them. He attributed the signs to "their Lord" to draw attention to the fact that He is their Owner and Sustainer, so they rejected His signs, while the obligation was to acknowledge them. The root *jahada* is originally transitive by itself, but it was treated as *kafara* (to disbelieve) and so was followed by a preposition (*bi*), just as *kafara* was followed directly by its object in His saying: ﴿Indeed, 'Ad disbelieved in their Lord﴾, treating it as *jahada*.

It was also said: *kafara* like *shakara* (to be grateful) is sometimes transitive by itself and sometimes by a preposition.

*Wa 'asaw rusulahu* (and they disobeyed His messengers): It was said that they disobeyed Hud and the messengers who came before him. It was also said: the denial of one messenger is treated as the denial of all the messengers, because they all agree on faith in Allah and the acknowledgment of His lordship, as in His saying: ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [al-Baqara: 285].

*Wa-ttaba'u* (and they followed): That is, their lowly followers followed the command of their leaders and great ones, meaning: they obeyed them in what they commanded them.

Al-Kalbi said: *al-jabbar* is the one who kills in anger and punishes for disobedience. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the one who compels people to what he wants. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned that it is the one who is great in himself, arrogant toward the servants.

The apparent meaning is that His saying *wa-ttaba'u* is general, covering all of 'Ad. Al-Zamakhshari said: since they followed him rather than the messengers, the curse was made to follow them in both abodes, casting them on their faces into the punishment of Allah. End of quote.

The apparent meaning of his words indicates that the curse is specific to those who followed the leaders. He noted the reason the curse follows them in both abodes: that they disbelieved in their Lord. So disbelief is what necessitates the curse. Then he repeated the alert with His saying *ala* (Indeed/Behold), in the supplication against them, to magnify their affair, to make it terrible, and to urge reflection upon them and caution against a state like theirs.

The purpose of His saying *qawmi Hud* (the people of Hud) is to add further emphasis for the sake of thorough specification, or to identify this 'Ad as the 'Ad of Iram, since there were two 'Ads, and for this reason the Exalted said: ﴿And that He destroyed the first 'Ad﴾ [al-Najm: 50]. Thus it is established that the supplication is against this 'Ad, and it has not been confused with another.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 11, verses 50–60 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿To the 'Ad [We sent] their brother Hud. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. You are only inventors of falsehood."﴾ ﴿"O my people, I do not ask you for any wage for it. My wage is only from the One who created me. Will you not then reason?"﴾ ﴿"And O my people, seek forgiveness from your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance. He will send down the sky upon you in abundant rain and increase you in strength upon your strength. And do not turn away as criminals."﴾

﴿وإلى عادٍ أخاهم﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf, conjoined) with His saying ﴿We sent Noah to his people﴾ (Hud: 25). The conjunction particle (al-waw) has joined a genitive-marked element to a genitive-marked element and an accusative to an accusative, just as a nominative and accusative may be conjoined to a nominative and accusative, as in: "Zayd struck 'Amr, and Bakr [struck] Khalid." It is not a case of separating the conjunction particle from the conjoined element by a prepositional phrase, as in: "I struck Zayd, and in the house, 'Amr." From this arises the disagreement among the grammarians: is this permissible in ordinary speech, or is it restricted to poetry? The intended meaning of the sentence is: "[We sent] to Hud, and to 'Ad and their brother [Hud], among them [the Prophets mentioned] in al-A'raf." The reading of al-Kisa'i is (ghayrihi) with the genitive (kasra) ending. It has also been said that there is an omitted verb here, meaning "And We sent to 'Ad their brother," in which case it is conjunction of clauses ('atf al-jumal), while the first is conjunction of single words (mufradat). This second view is closer to the truth, because of the long separation by many clauses between the two conjoined elements.

(Hudan): this is either an apposition (badal) or a clarifying apposition ('atf bayan). Muhaysin read (ya qawmu) with a damma on the mim, like the reading of Hafs for: ﴿He said: "My Lord, judge with truth"﴾ (al-Anbiya: 112) with a damma. This is a dialect form for the vocative with a possessive attachment, which Sibawayh and others have transmitted. Their "inventing falsehood," according to al-Hasan, lies in their assigning divinity to other than Allah, the Exalted. Al-Zamakhshari said: it lies in their taking idols as partners to Him.

The pronoun in ﴿عليه﴾ ("for it") refers to the call to Allah. By His saying ﴿the One who created me﴾ he alerts them to refute their worship of idols and their belief that these idols act. That He, the Exalted, is the Originator of all existing things makes Him deserving of being singled out for worship.

﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ is a rebuke establishing the impossibility of divinity for other than the Originator. It is also possible that ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ refers to the fact that, since I do not seek any worldly gain from you, but only desire your benefit, you must submit to what contains your salvation. It is as if it were said: "Will you not reason the advice of one who seeks no reward for it except from Allah, the Exalted, which is the reward of the Hereafter? Nothing is more effective in dispelling accusation than this." The discussion of ﴿Seek forgiveness from your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance﴾ (Hud: 3) has already been covered at the beginning of this surah.

Hud intended to win them over to faith and encourage them toward it by [promising] abundant rain (p-233) and increased strength, because they were people of crops, gardens and buildings, zealously eager for them to the utmost degree. So they were most in need of water, and they were proud of the strength, violence and might they had been given, being fully equipped in every region.

It has been said: he meant strength in wealth. It has also been said: strength in procreation. It has been said that rain was withheld from them for three years and the wombs of their women became barren. Al-Hasan ibn 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) drew from this, and from His saying ﴿and He will supply you with wealth and children﴾ (Nuh: 12), that abundant seeking of forgiveness may cause Allah to make it a cause of abundant offspring. He answered one who asked him, and informed him that he had wealth but no children were born to him: "Seek forgiveness," so he sought it abundantly and ten sons were born to him.

Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿and increase you in strength upon your strength﴾ that it means offspring and the offspring of offspring. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: [it means] in body and might. Al-Dahhak said: fertility upon your fertility. It has been said: blessing upon His earlier blessing upon you. It has been said: strength in your faith upon strength in your bodies.

﴿They said: "O Hud, you have brought us no clear proof, and we will not abandon our gods on your word, nor are we going to believe you."﴾ ﴿"We only say that some of our gods have struck you with evil." He said: "I call Allah to witness, and bear witness yourselves that I am free of what you associate"﴾ ﴿"other than Him. So scheme against me, all of you, and give me no respite."﴾ ﴿"I have put my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is upon a straight path."﴾ ﴿"But if you turn away, I have already conveyed to you what I was sent with. My Lord will bring another people in your place, and you will not harm Him at all. Indeed, my Lord is Guardian over all things."﴾

"A clear proof" (bayyinah): a clear evidence or manifest argument that indicates the truth of what you say. They lied in this and slandered him, just as Quraysh lied when they said: ﴿Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ (Yunus: 20), though he had brought them many signs. Or, because of their blindness to the truth and their failure to reflect upon the signs, they considered what was indeed a sign to be no sign, and so they said: "You have brought us no proof that compels us to faith." Otherwise, Hud and the other prophets have miracles, even if he did not specify some of them for us.

Do you not see the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "There is no prophet except that he was given signs of the kind by which mankind believed"?

The particle (ʿan) in ﴿on your word﴾ is a circumstantial element (hal) referring to the pronoun in ﴿abandoning our gods﴾. It is as if it were said: "departing from your word." This is the view of al-Zamakhshari. It has also been said: "ʿan" expresses causation, as in His saying: ﴿except for a promise he had made to him﴾ (al-Tawbah: 114), so it is connected to "abandoning," as if it were said: "because of your word." Ibn 'Atiyyah has indicated the causal meaning and its basis, saying: that is, your word would not be a cause for our abandoning [our gods], since it is bare of any sign. The sentence after it is an emphasis and a despairing of them ever entering his religion. Then they attributed what came from him, namely his calling them to Allah and his singling Him out for divinity, to insanity and madness, and that this was something some of their gods had inflicted upon him, because he had reviled them, urged the abandonment of them, and called to the abandonment of their worship. So they made him speak in the manner of madmen, in requital, just as Quraysh said: ﴿A taught, possessed man﴾ (al-Dukhan: 14), and ﴿Or do they say: "He has a madness"?﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 70).

﴿i'tarak﴾ ("has struck you") is a reported clause following (naqulu, "we say"), so it occupies the position of the object. It indicates extreme foolishness and excessive ignorance, in that they believed that stones could give victory and take vengeance.

Hud's reply to them: ﴿I call Allah to witness﴾ to the end, in which he disassociates himself from their gods and urges them all, despite his being alone, to scheme against him with whatever they wish. His not being delayed is among the greatest signs of his truthfulness and his confidence in his Lord's promise of support for him, of assistance, and of protection from their reaching him with any harm. Yet they were eager to kill him, shooting at him from one bow. Similar is Noah's saying to his people: ﴿Then decide your affair against me, and give me no respite﴾ (Yunus: 71). He also confirmed his disavowal of their gods and their polytheism, and he strengthened this by what people customarily do in confirming matters: by calling upon the witness of Allah and the witness of the servants.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): Why was it not said: "I call Allah to witness and I call you to witness"? (I answer): Because calling Allah to witness regarding disavowal of polytheism is a valid and established testimony, in the sense of establishing monotheism. As for calling them to witness, it is nothing but a showing of contempt for their religion and an indication of indifference toward them, and nothing more. Therefore, it was turned away from the wording of the first, due to the difference between the two, and was expressed in the imperative form of the command to bear witness. End of quotation.

(Inni bari'un, "I am free"): the verb (ushhidu, "I call to witness") and (ishhadu, "bear witness") both govern it, and two verbs may compete for the same noun when that noun is suitable to be governed by both. You say: "I gave Zayd and gave 'Amr a dinar," just as an intransitive and a transitive verb may compete, as in: "Stood, and I struck Zayd."

(Ma) in (ma tushrikun, "what you associate") is a relative pronoun, either verbal-source (masdariyyah) or meaning "that which": that is, "free of your associating other gods beside Him," or "free of those whom you associate."

(Jamiʿan, "all of you") is a circumstantial element (hal) from the subject pronoun in (kidūni, "scheme against me"), and the address is directed only to his people. Al-Zamakhshari said: "you and your gods." End of quotation.

It has been said: Hud's open declaration to them of his freedom from their religions, and his urging them to scheme against him together with their idols, is itself a miracle for Hud. Or, he urged their whole community against him despite his being alone and their being strong and numerous, yet they were unable to reach him with any harm. Then he mentioned his reliance upon Allah, informing them that He is his Lord and their Lord, alerting them that because He is their Lord it is obligatory for them not to worship any but Him, and entrusting his affair to Him, the Exalted, in confidence in His protection and in the fulfilment of His promise. Then he described the power of Allah, the Exalted, and the magnitude of His dominion: that every creature is in His grip, His possession, and under His subjugation and sovereignty. So you are among those subjugated.

His saying ﴿holds its forelock﴾ is a figure of speech (tamthil), since the capable owner leads the one over whom he has power by its forelock, just as a captive or a horse is led by its forelock. The grasping of the forelock came to be a convention for power over an animal. The Arabs used to cut the forelock of a captive who had been spared, as a sign that he had been overpowered and that his forelock was in another's grasp. Ibn Jurayj said: He singled out the forelock because when the Arabs describe a person as humbled and submissive, they say: "The forelock of so-and-so is only in the hand of so-and-so," meaning that he obeys him and he directs him as he wishes. Then He informed that His actions, the Exalted, are in the utmost perfection, and in the path of truth and justice in His dominion: no wrongdoer escapes Him, and no one who relies upon Him is lost in His sight. His word is true and His promise is real.

The majority read ﴿فَإنْ تَوَلَّوْا﴾ (fa-in tawallaw) as (tatawallaw), the present tense of (tawalla). Al-A'raj and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read (tuwallu) with damma on the ta' and lam, the present tense of (walla). It has also been said that (tawallaw) is a past tense verb, and that the answer to the condition requires an implied verb of speech, meaning: "Then say to them: 'I have already conveyed to you.'" There is no need to make it a past tense verb and to supply an implied speech verb.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is possible that (tawallaw) is a past tense verb, and that there is a shift in the speech from the third person to the second person, meaning: "Then I have conveyed to you." End of quotation. This requires no implied element. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (tawallaw) refers to the people of Hud, and the address to them is part of the speech that was said earlier. Al-Tabrizi said: it refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh, and this is a shift of address (talwin al-khitab), in which the speech moves from addressing the people of Hud to reporting about those present with the Messenger (ﷺ). As if it were said: "Inform them about the story of the people of Hud, and call them to faith in Allah, lest what befell the people of Hud befall them. If they turn away, then say to them: 'I have already conveyed to you.'"

The answer to the condition is His saying ﴿I have already conveyed to you﴾, and it is correct that this should be the answer, because in his conveying his message to them is included what will befall them of the total punishment. It is as if it were said: "If you turn away, you will be utterly destroyed by punishment." This is indicated by the declarative clause: ﴿My Lord will bring another people in your place﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): The conveying was before the turning away, so how did it become the answer to the condition? (I answer): Its meaning is: "If you turn away, I will not be punished for any negligence in conveying, since what I was sent with has reached you, but you refused anything except rejecting the message and hostility toward the Messenger." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The meaning is that I bear no great concern on your account if you turn away; my conscience is clear through the conveying, and you are the ones at fault in turning away from faith.

The majority read ﴿و يَسْتَخْلِفُ﴾ (wa yastakhlifu) with a damma on the fa', as a new declarative sentence: that is, He will destroy you and bring other people who will succeed you in your dwellings and your wealth. Hafs, in the transmission of Hubayra, read it with a jussive ending (wa yastakhlif), in coordination with the position of the condition's answer. 'Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud] also read it like this, and read ﴿وَلَا تَضُرُّوهُ﴾ (wa la tadurruhu, al-Tawbah: 39) with a jussive ending. The majority read ﴿وَلَا تَضُرُّونَهُ﴾ (wa la tadurrunahu), meaning: not any harm at all by your turning away, because He, the Exalted, is not subject to harm or benefit. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The meaning may bear two interpretations. One: "You will not harm Him by your going away and your destruction at all," meaning His dominion does not diminish and His affair is not disturbed. According to this meaning, 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud read ﴿وَلَا تَنْقُصُونَهُ شَيْئًا﴾ (wa la tanqusunahu shay'an, "nor will you diminish Him at all"). The other meaning: "You will not harm Him," that is, when He destroys you, you will be unable to harm Him in any way, nor to retaliate against Him, nor will you oppose His action with anything that could harm Him. End of quotation.

This is a negated verb whose implied object is indefinite, so all forms of harm are negated and none is specified. (Hafiz, "Guardian") means: a watcher encompassing things in knowledge, to whom your deeds are not hidden, and who does not neglect to call you to account. He guards me from what you plot against me.

Thus it is established that the supplication is against this 'Ad, and it has not been confused with another.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 11, verses 50–60 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿To the 'Ad [We sent] their brother Hud. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. You are only inventors of falsehood."﴾ ﴿"O my people, I do not ask you for any wage for it. My wage is only from the One who created me. Will you not then reason?"﴾ ﴿"And O my people, seek forgiveness from your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance. He will send down the sky upon you in abundant rain and increase you in strength upon your strength. And do not turn away as criminals."﴾

﴿وإلى عادٍ أخاهم﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf, conjoined) with His saying ﴿We sent Noah to his people﴾ (Hud: 25). The conjunction particle (al-waw) has joined a genitive-marked element to a genitive-marked element and an accusative to an accusative, just as a nominative and accusative may be conjoined to a nominative and accusative, as in: "Zayd struck 'Amr, and Bakr [struck] Khalid." It is not a case of separating the conjunction particle from the conjoined element by a prepositional phrase, as in: "I struck Zayd, and in the house, 'Amr." From this arises the disagreement among the grammarians: is this permissible in ordinary speech, or is it restricted to poetry? The intended meaning of the sentence is: "[We sent] to Hud, and to 'Ad and their brother [Hud], among them [the Prophets mentioned] in al-A'raf." The reading of al-Kisa'i is (ghayrihi) with the genitive (kasra) ending. It has also been said that there is an omitted verb here, meaning "And We sent to 'Ad their brother," in which case it is conjunction of clauses ('atf al-jumal), while the first is conjunction of single words (mufradat). This second view is closer to the truth, because of the long separation by many clauses between the two conjoined elements.

(Hudan): this is either an apposition (badal) or a clarifying apposition ('atf bayan). Muhaysin read (ya qawmu) with a damma on the mim, like the reading of Hafs for: ﴿He said: "My Lord, judge with truth"﴾ (al-Anbiya: 112) with a damma. This is a dialect form for the vocative with a possessive attachment, which Sibawayh and others have transmitted. Their "inventing falsehood," according to al-Hasan, lies in their assigning divinity to other than Allah, the Exalted. Al-Zamakhshari said: it lies in their taking idols as partners to Him.

The pronoun in ﴿عليه﴾ ("for it") refers to the call to Allah. By His saying ﴿the One who created me﴾ he alerts them to refute their worship of idols and their belief that these idols act. That He, the Exalted, is the Originator of all existing things makes Him deserving of being singled out for worship.

﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ is a rebuke establishing the impossibility of divinity for other than the Originator. It is also possible that ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ refers to the fact that, since I do not seek any worldly gain from you, but only desire your benefit, you must submit to what contains your salvation. It is as if it were said: "Will you not reason the advice of one who seeks no reward for it except from Allah, the Exalted, which is the reward of the Hereafter? Nothing is more effective in dispelling accusation than this." The discussion of ﴿Seek forgiveness from your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance﴾ (Hud: 3) has already been covered at the beginning of this surah.

Hud intended to win them over to faith and encourage them toward it by [promising] abundant rain (p-233) and increased strength, because they were people of crops, gardens and buildings, zealously eager for them to the utmost degree. So they were most in need of water, and they were proud of the strength, violence and might they had been given, being fully equipped in every region.

It has been said: he meant strength in wealth. It has also been said: strength in procreation. It has been said that rain was withheld from them for three years and the wombs of their women became barren. Al-Hasan ibn 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) drew from this, and from His saying ﴿and He will supply you with wealth and children﴾ (Nuh: 12), that abundant seeking of forgiveness may cause Allah to make it a cause of abundant offspring. He answered one who asked him, and informed him that he had wealth but no children were born to him: "Seek forgiveness," so he sought it abundantly and ten sons were born to him.

Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿and increase you in strength upon your strength﴾ that it means offspring and the offspring of offspring. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: [it means] in body and might. Al-Dahhak said: fertility upon your fertility. It has been said: blessing upon His earlier blessing upon you. It has been said: strength in your faith upon strength in your bodies.

﴿They said: "O Hud, you have brought us no clear proof, and we will not abandon our gods on your word, nor are we going to believe you."﴾ ﴿"We only say that some of our gods have struck you with evil." He said: "I call Allah to witness, and bear witness yourselves that I am free of what you associate"﴾ ﴿"other than Him. So scheme against me, all of you, and give me no respite."﴾ ﴿"I have put my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is upon a straight path."﴾ ﴿"But if you turn away, I have already conveyed to you what I was sent with. My Lord will bring another people in your place, and you will not harm Him at all. Indeed, my Lord is Guardian over all things."﴾

"A clear proof" (bayyinah): a clear evidence or manifest argument that indicates the truth of what you say. They lied in this and slandered him, just as Quraysh lied when they said: ﴿Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ (Yunus: 20), though he had brought them many signs. Or, because of their blindness to the truth and their failure to reflect upon the signs, they considered what was indeed a sign to be no sign, and so they said: "You have brought us no proof that compels us to faith." Otherwise, Hud and the other prophets have miracles, even if he did not specify some of them for us.

Do you not see the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "There is no prophet except that he was given signs of the kind by which mankind believed"?

The particle (ʿan) in ﴿on your word﴾ is a circumstantial element (hal) referring to the pronoun in ﴿abandoning our gods﴾. It is as if it were said: "departing from your word." This is the view of al-Zamakhshari. It has also been said: "ʿan" expresses causation, as in His saying: ﴿except for a promise he had made to him﴾ (al-Tawbah: 114), so it is connected to "abandoning," as if it were said: "because of your word." Ibn 'Atiyyah has indicated the causal meaning and its basis, saying: that is, your word would not be a cause for our abandoning [our gods], since it is bare of any sign. The sentence after it is an emphasis and a despairing of them ever entering his religion. Then they attributed what came from him, namely his calling them to Allah and his singling Him out for divinity, to insanity and madness, and that this was something some of their gods had inflicted upon him, because he had reviled them, urged the abandonment of them, and called to the abandonment of their worship. So they made him speak in the manner of madmen, in requital, just as Quraysh said: ﴿A taught, possessed man﴾ (al-Dukhan: 14), and ﴿Or do they say: "He has a madness"?﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 70).

﴿i'tarak﴾ ("has struck you") is a reported clause following (naqulu, "we say"), so it occupies the position of the object. It indicates extreme foolishness and excessive ignorance, in that they believed that stones could give victory and take vengeance.

Hud's reply to them: ﴿I call Allah to witness﴾ to the end, in which he disassociates himself from their gods and urges them all, despite his being alone, to scheme against him with whatever they wish. His not being delayed is among the greatest signs of his truthfulness and his confidence in his Lord's promise of support for him, of assistance, and of protection from their reaching him with any harm. Yet they were eager to kill him, shooting at him from one bow. Similar is Noah's saying to his people: ﴿Then decide your affair against me, and give me no respite﴾ (Yunus: 71). He also confirmed his disavowal of their gods and their polytheism, and he strengthened this by what people customarily do in confirming matters: by calling upon the witness of Allah and the witness of the servants.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): Why was it not said: "I call Allah to witness and I call you to witness"? (I answer): Because calling Allah to witness regarding disavowal of polytheism is a valid and established testimony, in the sense of establishing monotheism. As for calling them to witness, it is nothing but a showing of contempt for their religion and an indication of indifference toward them, and nothing more. Therefore, it was turned away from the wording of the first, due to the difference between the two, and was expressed in the imperative form of the command to bear witness. End of quotation.

(Inni bari'un, "I am free"): the verb (ushhidu, "I call to witness") and (ishhadu, "bear witness") both govern it, and two verbs may compete for the same noun when that noun is suitable to be governed by both. You say: "I gave Zayd and gave 'Amr a dinar," just as an intransitive and a transitive verb may compete, as in: "Stood, and I struck Zayd."

(Ma) in (ma tushrikun, "what you associate") is a relative pronoun, either verbal-source (masdariyyah) or meaning "that which": that is, "free of your associating other gods beside Him," or "free of those whom you associate."

(Jamiʿan, "all of you") is a circumstantial element (hal) from the subject pronoun in (kidūni, "scheme against me"), and the address is directed only to his people. Al-Zamakhshari said: "you and your gods." End of quotation.

It has been said: Hud's open declaration to them of his freedom from their religions, and his urging them to scheme against him together with their idols, is itself a miracle for Hud. Or, he urged their whole community against him despite his being alone and their being strong and numerous, yet they were unable to reach him with any harm. Then he mentioned his reliance upon Allah, informing them that He is his Lord and their Lord, alerting them that because He is their Lord it is obligatory for them not to worship any but Him, and entrusting his affair to Him, the Exalted, in confidence in His protection and in the fulfilment of His promise. Then he described the power of Allah, the Exalted, and the magnitude of His dominion: that every creature is in His grip, His possession, and under His subjugation and sovereignty. So you are among those subjugated.

His saying ﴿holds its forelock﴾ is a figure of speech (tamthil), since the capable owner leads the one over whom he has power by its forelock, just as a captive or a horse is led by its forelock. The grasping of the forelock came to be a convention for power over an animal. The Arabs used to cut the forelock of a captive who had been spared, as a sign that he had been overpowered and that his forelock was in another's grasp. Ibn Jurayj said: He singled out the forelock because when the Arabs describe a person as humbled and submissive, they say: "The forelock of so-and-so is only in the hand of so-and-so," meaning that he obeys him and he directs him as he wishes. Then He informed that His actions, the Exalted, are in the utmost perfection, and in the path of truth and justice in His dominion: no wrongdoer escapes Him, and no one who relies upon Him is lost in His sight. His word is true and His promise is real.

The majority read ﴿فَإنْ تَوَلَّوْا﴾ (fa-in tawallaw) as (tatawallaw), the present tense of (tawalla). Al-A'raj and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read (tuwallu) with damma on the ta' and lam, the present tense of (walla). It has also been said that (tawallaw) is a past tense verb, and that the answer to the condition requires an implied verb of speech, meaning: "Then say to them: 'I have already conveyed to you.'" There is no need to make it a past tense verb and to supply an implied speech verb.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is possible that (tawallaw) is a past tense verb, and that there is a shift in the speech from the third person to the second person, meaning: "Then I have conveyed to you." End of quotation. This requires no implied element. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (tawallaw) refers to the people of Hud, and the address to them is part of the speech that was said earlier. Al-Tabrizi said: it refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh, and this is a shift of address (talwin al-khitab), in which the speech moves from addressing the people of Hud to reporting about those present with the Messenger (ﷺ). As if it were said: "Inform them about the story of the people of Hud, and call them to faith in Allah, lest what befell the people of Hud befall them. If they turn away, then say to them: 'I have already conveyed to you.'"

The answer to the condition is His saying ﴿I have already conveyed to you﴾, and it is correct that this should be the answer, because in his conveying his message to them is included what will befall them of the total punishment. It is as if it were said: "If you turn away, you will be utterly destroyed by punishment." This is indicated by the declarative clause: ﴿My Lord will bring another people in your place﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): The conveying was before the turning away, so how did it become the answer to the condition? (I answer): Its meaning is: "If you turn away, I will not be punished for any negligence in conveying, since what I was sent with has reached you, but you refused anything except rejecting the message and hostility toward the Messenger." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The meaning is that I bear no great concern on your account if you turn away; my conscience is clear through the conveying, and you are the ones at fault in turning away from faith.

The majority read ﴿و يَسْتَخْلِفُ﴾ (wa yastakhlifu) with a damma on the fa', as a new declarative sentence: that is, He will destroy you and bring other people who will succeed you in your dwellings and your wealth. Hafs, in the transmission of Hubayra, read it with a jussive ending (wa yastakhlif), in coordination with the position of the condition's answer. 'Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud] also read it like this, and read ﴿وَلَا تَضُرُّوهُ﴾ (wa la tadurruhu, al-Tawbah: 39) with a jussive ending. The majority read ﴿وَلَا تَضُرُّونَهُ﴾ (wa la tadurrunahu), meaning: not any harm at all by your turning away, because He, the Exalted, is not subject to harm or benefit. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The meaning may bear two interpretations. One: "You will not harm Him by your going away and your destruction at all," meaning His dominion does not diminish and His affair is not disturbed. According to this meaning, 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud read ﴿وَلَا تَنْقُصُونَهُ شَيْئًا﴾ (wa la tanqusunahu shay'an, "nor will you diminish Him at all"). The other meaning: "You will not harm Him," that is, when He destroys you, you will be unable to harm Him in any way, nor to retaliate against Him, nor will you oppose His action with anything that could harm Him. End of quotation.

This is a negated verb whose implied object is indefinite, so all forms of harm are negated and none is specified. (Hafiz, "Guardian") means: a watcher encompassing things in knowledge, to whom your deeds are not hidden, and who does not neglect to call you to account. He guards me from what you plot against me.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 11, verses 50–60 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿When Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and We saved them from a severe punishment.﴾ ﴿And that was 'Ad, who denied the signs of their Lord, disobeyed His messengers, and followed the command of every obstinate tyrant.﴾ ﴿They were pursued by a curse in this world and on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, 'Ad disbelieved in their Lord. Away with 'Ad, the people of Hud!﴾: *al-Amr* (the command) is the singular of *al-umur* (affairs). It may therefore be a metonymy (*kinaya*) for the punishment, or for the decree of their destruction. Or it may be a verbal noun (*masdar*) of *amara*, meaning: Our command to the wind, or to its guardians (*khazanatuha*).

﴿Those who believed with him﴾: It was said they were four thousand, and it was said they were three thousand.

The apparent connection of *bi-rahmatin minna* (by a mercy from Us) is to *najjayna* (We saved), meaning: We saved them solely by a mercy from Allah that reached them, not by their righteous deeds. Or the mercy is a metonymy for their righteous deeds, since their being granted success in them is only due to the mercy of the Exalted toward them. It is also possible that it is connected to *amanu* (believed), meaning: their faith in Allah and their affirmation of His messenger is only by the mercy of Allah toward them, since He granted them success in that. The saving is repeated for emphasis (*ta'kid*), and out of concern lest someone think that the second saving is connected to *minna* (from). Or this result is the punishment of the Hereafter, and there is no punishment more severe than it, so it is repeated because its objects differ. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, what is the meaning of repeating the saving? I say: He mentioned first that when He destroyed their enemy, He saved them. Then He said: ﴿And We saved them from a severe punishment﴾, meaning: and the saving was from a severe punishment." He said: "That is because Allah, Mighty and Exalted, sent upon them the *samum* (scorching wind), which entered their noses and exited their anuses, and cut them apart limb by limb." This is what al-Zajjaj said. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is possible that he means: the earlier salvation was from a severe punishment, meaning the wind. In that case, the intended purpose is to enumerate the blessing. What is well known about their punishment by the wind is that it used to carry them, demolish their dwellings and uproot them, and carry the howdah as it was, and similar things."

*Tilka 'Adun* (That was 'Ad): This is a reference to their graves and their remains, as if He said: ﴿Travel through the land﴾ [al-Tawba: 2], meaning: look at them and take heed. Then He resumed the report about them, saying: ﴿They denied the signs of their Lord﴾, meaning: they rejected them. He attributed the signs to "their Lord" to draw attention to the fact that He is their Owner and Sustainer, so they rejected His signs, while the obligation was to acknowledge them. The root *jahada* is originally transitive by itself, but it was treated as *kafara* (to disbelieve) and so was followed by a preposition (*bi*), just as *kafara* was followed directly by its object in His saying: ﴿Indeed, 'Ad disbelieved in their Lord﴾, treating it as *jahada*.

It was also said: *kafara* like *shakara* (to be grateful) is sometimes transitive by itself and sometimes by a preposition.

*Wa 'asaw rusulahu* (and they disobeyed His messengers): It was said that they disobeyed Hud and the messengers who came before him. It was also said: the denial of one messenger is treated as the denial of all the messengers, because they all agree on faith in Allah and the acknowledgment of His lordship, as in His saying: ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [al-Baqara: 285].

*Wa-ttaba'u* (and they followed): That is, their lowly followers followed the command of their leaders and great ones, meaning: they obeyed them in what they commanded them.

Al-Kalbi said: *al-jabbar* is the one who kills in anger and punishes for disobedience. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the one who compels people to what he wants. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned that it is the one who is great in himself, arrogant toward the servants.

The apparent meaning is that His saying *wa-ttaba'u* is general, covering all of 'Ad. Al-Zamakhshari said: since they followed him rather than the messengers, the curse was made to follow them in both abodes, casting them on their faces into the punishment of Allah. End of quote.

The apparent meaning of his words indicates that the curse is specific to those who followed the leaders. He noted the reason the curse follows them in both abodes: that they disbelieved in their Lord. So disbelief is what necessitates the curse. Then he repeated the alert with His saying *ala* (Indeed/Behold), in the supplication against them, to magnify their affair, to make it terrible, and to urge reflection upon them and caution against a state like theirs.

The purpose of His saying *qawmi Hud* (the people of Hud) is to add further emphasis for the sake of thorough specification, or to identify this 'Ad as the 'Ad of Iram, since there were two 'Ads, and for this reason the Exalted said: ﴿And that He destroyed the first 'Ad﴾ [al-Najm: 50]. Thus it is established that the supplication is against this 'Ad, and it has not been confused with another.
