The angels' address to her with ﴿people of the house﴾ is evidence that the wife is included among the people of the house. This is also indicated in Surat al-Ahzab. This is contrary to the Shi'a, who do not count the wife as among the household of her husband. "House" (bayt) here refers to the house of dwelling.

﴿Indeed He is Praiseworthy﴾ [11:73]: Abu al-Haytham said: "His actions are praised," and it has the meaning of "praised" (mahmud). al-Zamakhshari said: "He is the doer of what is deserved from His servants, Glorious, Generous, abundant in beneficence toward them."

(p. 241) It has been mentioned that the order of the stories in this surah is like the order of the stories in al-A'raf. He included some accounts of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) between the story of Salih and the story of Lut, because Ibrahim has a connection to the story of Lut, and Ibrahim was the maternal cousin of Lut.

The "messengers" here are the angels. They brought Ibrahim three good tidings: of a son, of friendship (with Allah), and of the deliverance of Lut and those who believed with him.

It is said that they were twelve angels, narrated from Ibn Abbas. Al-Suddi said eleven. The author of al-Ghunyan related ten, of whom Jibril was one. Al-Dahhak said nine, Muhammad ibn Ka'b said eight, and al-Mawardi related four. Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said three: Jibril, Mika'il and Israfil. Muqatil said: Jibril, Mika'il and the Angel of Death.

It is related that Jibril (peace be upon him) was specifically assigned to destroy the people of Lut, Mika'il to bring the good tiding of Ishaq to Ibrahim, and Israfil to deliver Lut and those who believed with him (peace be upon them both).

It is said: the angels were beardless youths, of the utmost beauty, grace and radiance, and for this reason they are used as a proverbial example of beauty, as Allah the Exalted said, relating what was said about Yusuf: ﴿This is not a human; this is nothing but a noble angel﴾ [Yusuf: 31]. And al-Ghazzi said:

*A people who, when faced, were angels in beauty, and when fought, were demons.*

The word (salaman) is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning: "We greet you with a greeting." So (salaman) is a cognate object of the implied verb, which is reported by (qalu). Ibn Atiyya said: "It is also possible that (salaman) is a report of the meaning of what they said, not a report of their exact words; this is the view of Mujahid and al-Suddi."

For this reason the verb "said" governs it, just as you would say to a man who said "There is no god but Allah": "You said: truly and sincerely." If you reported their exact words, the verb "said" could not govern it. End of quotation. He means: the verb "said" could not govern their utterance itself, that is, the wording, even though what they uttered is in the position of the object of "said."

And (salamun) is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "My affair, or your affair, is peace"; or it is the subject with an omitted predicate, meaning: "Upon you is peace." The sentence is protected (in its meaning) even though one of its two parts has been omitted, as the poet said:

*When you taste her mouth, you say: "The taste is that of wine,"*

meaning: "Its taste is the taste of wine."

The two brothers (Hamzah and al-Kisa'i) read: *qala silmun*. And (al-silm) means (al-salam), like (hirm) and (haram). From this is the poet's saying:

*We passed by, and we said: "Greetings," and she greeted back, as the shining clouds crown themselves with lightning.*

(iktalla) means: took a crown. Ibn Atiyya said: "It is possible that by (al-silm) he means the opposite of war; one says: 'We are at peace with you'." End of quotation.

The accusative (salaman) indicates renewal, while the nominative (salamun) indicates permanence and stability. As for the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of ﴿fa-ma labitha﴾, the most likely view is that (ma) is negative, and (labitha) means: delayed and was slow. And ﴿an ja'a﴾ is the subject of (labitha). The estimate is: "so his coming was not delayed," as said by al-Farra'.

They allowed that the pronoun in (labitha) refers to Ibrahim, so he is the subject, and ﴿an ja'a﴾ is with the preposition dropped, so it is estimated with (an), (ba'd) or (fi). Some of them made (an) mean (hatta) (until), as related by Ibn al-Arabi. And (ma) may be verbal (masdariyya), so that verbal noun is in the nominative position as a subject, and its predicate is ﴿an ja'a﴾ with an omitted (qadr, the amount), meaning: "the amount of his coming." Or (ma) may mean (alladhi), that is: "his delay," or "what he delayed," and the predicate is ﴿an ja'a﴾. This is from the etiquette of hospitality, which is hastening the provision of food. Ibrahim's wealth was cattle, so he presented the best of it, which is the calf (p. 242).

Mujahid said: (haniadh) means roasted. Al-Hasan said: ripe, roasted, fat, dripping with fat. Al-Suddi said: fat. It is also said: (samit), that is, skinned and roasted, which they do not touch, meaning: they do not reach the calf.

The meaning is: they did not extend their hands to eat it. He did not negate the reaching that results from extending; rather, the non-reaching was used metaphorically for their refusal to eat. ﴿nakiraham﴾ means: he disapproved of them. The poet said:

*She disapproved of me, and what she disapproved of was none of the events except the grey hair and the baldness.*

It is also said: (nakira) is used for what is seen, and (ankara) for what is not seen of meanings. So it is as if the poet said: "She disowned my love, then she came with the strange sight of grey hair and baldness, which are seen with the eye." And from this is Abu Dhu'ayb's saying:

*They disliked him and fled, and a wild one with a loud bray seized him, and a strong, hairy-necked donkey.*

It was related that they used to shake (or draw) lots with arrows that were in their hands over the meat, while their hands could not reach it. It is necessary that the guest should be watched to see whether he eats or not, and this should be done with a glance and haste, not by fixing the gaze, because that would make the guest reluctant to eat. It is said: Ibrahim (peace be upon him) used to stay at the edge of the land, for fear that they might intend him some harm.

It is also said: their custom was that if the one who came to them touched their food, they felt secure; otherwise they feared him. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It appears that he sensed they were angels and disapproved of them, because he feared that their coming was for a matter Allah disapproved of, or for punishing his people."

Do you not see their saying: ﴿Do not fear; we have been sent to the people of Lut﴾? This is said only to someone who recognized them but did not know for what purpose they had been sent. Muqatil said: (fa-awjasa): it came into his heart. Al-Hasan said: he spoke it to himself. It is said: the origin of (wujus) is entering, as if fear entered upon him.

It is apparent that he did not know they were angels, because they came in the form of humans, and he was devoted to honouring guests; therefore they came in their forms, and because of his haste in bringing food to them, and because the angels' refusal to eat does not indicate that evil is present. He only knew they were angels from their saying: ﴿Do not fear; we have been sent to the people of Lut﴾, so they forbade him from something that had occurred in his mind, and they knew his fear because Allah had given them knowledge beyond that given to others, as in His saying: ﴿They know what you do﴾ [al-Infitar: 12]. And in the authentic hadith: "The angels said: 'My Lord, Your servant wants to commit an evil deed'," the hadith continues; or they knew it from what appears on the features of the face of one who is afraid.

﴿And his wife was standing﴾ is a nominal sentence. Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' said it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). Abu al-Baqa' said: it is from the implied subject of (arsalna), meaning the passive object whose agent is not named. Al-Zamakhshari calls it the subject, because it takes the place of the subject. Al-Hawfi said: the estimate is: "We were sent to the people of Lut while his wife was standing," meaning the wife of Ibrahim. It is apparent that it is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "they said": "They said to Ibrahim: Do not fear, while his wife was standing," and she was Sarah, daughter of Haran ibn Nahur, and she was his paternal cousin. (Standing) means: to serve the guests. Their women did not veil, as was the custom of the Bedouins and the people of the open desert, and displaying oneself was not disliked. She was an elderly woman. Serving guests is among the noble qualities of character, as said by Mujahid.

Something similar is found in our sharia, from the hadith of Abu Usayd al-Sa'idi: his wife was a newlywed bride, and she served the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and those present with him of his companions.

Wahb said: she was standing behind the curtain, listening to their conversation. Ibn Ishaq said: standing means praying. Al-Mubarrad said: standing from child-bearing. Al-Zamakhshari said: in the codex of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud): "His wife was standing while he was sitting." Ibn Atiyya said: in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "She was standing while he was sitting." The wife of Ibrahim was not mentioned before, so the pronoun would be implied, but the context of the speech explains it.

Mujahid and Ikrimah said: ﴿fa-dahikat﴾ means she menstruated. The majority said it is the well-known laughter. It is said it is a metaphor expressing the brightness of her face and her joy at the deliverance of her brother and the destruction of his people. It is said: "I came upon a meadow that laughs," meaning: bright. It is also said it is literal. Muqatil said, and it is related from Ibn Abbas: she laughed out of the intensity of Ibrahim's fear (p. 243) while he was among his family and servants. Those who came to him were three, while she was watching him, and he surpassed forty, and it is said a hundred. Qatada said: she laughed at the heedlessness of the people of Lut and the nearness of the punishment to them.

Al-Suddi said: she laughed at the guests' refraining from eating, and she said: "How strange! We serve our guests with our own hands, and they do not eat our food." Wahb ibn Munabbih said: it is related from Ibn Abbas: she laughed at the good tiding of Ishaq; and he said: this is an advance meaning a delay. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned that her laughter was joy at the truth of her expectation, because she used to say to Ibrahim: "Take in your brother's son Lut," and he was her brother, for the punishment would descend upon his people. It is also said: she laughed at the miraculous sign she saw, which is that the angels touched the roasted calf and it stood up alive, leaping. What appears to be the case, and Allah knows best, is that when they did not eat, and fear settled in his soul after he disapproved of their condition, the woman was affected more by that than the man.

When they said: "Do not fear," and mentioned the reason for their coming, the fear left him and he was glad, so joy overcame her too, and she laughed, for women are more prone to rejoicing and gladness than men, and that quality predominates in them. Al-Zamakhshari pointed to part of this, saying: she laughed out of joy at the removal of fear.

Muhammad ibn Qays mentioned a reason for her laughter that we have left unmentioned because of its enormity; it can be found in the commentary of Ibn Atiyya. Muhammad ibn Ziyad al-A'rabi, a reciter of Makkah, read ﴿fa-dahikat﴾ with a fatha on the ha (fa-dahakat). Al-Mahdawi said: fatha on the ha is not well known.

﴿fa-bashsharnaha﴾ agrees with His saying: ﴿And indeed Our messengers came to Ibrahim with good tidings﴾. The meaning is: "So We gave her good tidings through Our messengers," the angels gave her the good tiding of Ishaq, and that Ishaq would beget Ya'qub.

Ibn Atiyya said: He attributed the action of the angels to the pronoun of Allah's name, since it was by His command and revelation. Others said: when Isma'il was born to Ibrahim from Hajar, Sarah wished that she might have a son, but she despaired because of her old age, so she was given the good tiding of a son who would be a prophet and would beget a prophet. This was a good tiding to her that she would see the son of her son. They gave her the good tiding apart from Ibrahim because a woman is quicker to rejoice at a child, and because they had already given Ibrahim the good tiding and reassured him from his fear, so they followed his good tiding with hers. It is also said that she was specially given the good tiding because she had no son, whereas Ibrahim had his son Isma'il.

The apparent meaning is that (wara') here is an adverb used as a noun, by the entrance of (min) upon it, as if it were said: "and after Ishaq," or "from behind Ishaq," and it means "after." This is related from Ibn Abbas and was chosen by Muqatil and Ibn Qutayba. It is also related from Ibn Abbas that (al-wara') is the son's son, and this was said by al-Sha'bi and chosen by Abu Ubayda. Calling him (wara') is close to the meaning of (wara') as an adverb, since it is what is behind and after a thing.

If it is said: how can Ya'qub be "after" Ishaq when he is his son by his loins, and "after" means only a son's son? Ibn al-Anbari answered this, saying: the meaning is "and from the after attributed to Ishaq is Ya'qub," because the "after" belonged to Ibrahim through Ishaq. If he had said "and from the after Ya'qub," it would not be known whether this "after" is attributed to Ishaq or to Isma'il. So it was attributed to Ishaq to make the meaning clear and remove the ambiguity. End of quotation.

She was given the good tiding of Ya'qub from among the children of Ishaq because she saw him and did not see anyone else. This good tiding to Sarah was when she was ninety-nine years old, and Ibrahim was a hundred years old. It is also said that the difference between them was other than that, and these are contradictory statements.

This verse indicates that Ishmael is the one who was sacrificed (al-dhabih), because when the tyrant king gave Hagar to Sarah as a servant, Hagar, the mother of Ishmael, was a young and beautiful woman. Abraham took Hagar as a concubine (surriyyah, a slave-woman who bore a master's child), so Sarah became jealous of her. He then set out with her and her son Ishmael from al-Sham (Greater Syria) on al-Buraq (the winged steed), came to Mecca the same day, and returned to al-Sham the same day. After that came the good news of Isaac, when Sarah was an old, barren woman. The proof of this will also come later from Surat al-Saffat, ﴿By those who range in ranks﴾ [37:1].

It is possible that God named her at the time of the good news with these two names. It is also possible that the two names were given to her at the time of birth, and that the good news was of a male child, after which a male child was born. The narration of the good news, with mention of the male child by her name, is like the speaker who says: if one is given good news in a dream of a male child, and a male child is then born to him, and he names him, for example, ʿAbd Allah, then he says: "I was given good news of ʿAbd Allah." (p. 244)

The two Harams (Meccan and Medinan readers), the two Kufan grammarians (al-Kisa'i and Hamzah, the two al-Nahwiyyan), and Abu Bakr Yaʿqub read Yaʿqub in the nominative (raf'), as the subject (mubtada'), with ﴿from behind﴾ [33:53] as the predicate. It is as if it were said: "and from behind Isaac there is Yaʿqub existing." al-Zamakhshari estimated the predicate as "born" (mawlud) or "existing" (mawjud). al-Nahhas said: "The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) included within the good news, i.e., 'We gave her good news of Isaac, with Yaʿqub connected to him.'"

Abu ʿAli (al-Farisi) permitted that it be in the nominative as a predicate of the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa'l-majrur), as al-Akhfash also permitted. That is, "there settled for her, from behind Isaac, Yaʿqub." Another group said the nominative is by way of resumption (al-qat'), meaning: "and from behind Isaac, Yaʿqub will come into being." al-Nahhas said: "It is also permissible for it to be the subject of an implied verb, whose estimate is: 'and from behind Isaac, Yaʿqub will come into being.'"

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "According to this, the good news does not include him." There is no need to strain with the notion of a break in the sentence (al-qat') and turning away from the apparent meaning, which requires that he be included in the good news.

Ibn ʿAmir, Hamzah, Hafs, and Zayd ibn ʿAli read Yaʿqub in the accusative (nasb). al-Zamakhshari said: "It is as if it were said: 'and We granted her Isaac, and from behind Isaac, Yaʿqub,' following the manner of his saying: 'They are not reformers of a clan, nor a crier of the dead [crow].'" He ended. He means that it was conjoined upon an assumed (tawahhum) construction. Conjoining upon an assumed construction is not analogical (la yanqas). The more apparent reading is that Yaʿqub is in the accusative by an implied verb whose estimate is: "and from behind Isaac, We granted Yaʿqub," and what indicates it is His saying: "So We gave her good news," because the good news is in the meaning of a gift. Abu ʿAli preferred this view. As for those who held that it is in the genitive, conjoined upon the wording of "bi-Ishaq," or upon its place, their view is weak, because it is not permissible to separate, with an adverbial or a prepositional phrase, between the conjunctive particle and its genitive conjunct. One may not say: "I passed by Zayd today and Amr yesterday," and if it occurs, it is in poetry.

If the conjunct is in the accusative or nominative, there is disagreement about the permissibility of this, as in: "Zayd stood and today ʿAmr," and "I struck Zayd and today ʿAmr." The apparent view is that the alif in ﴿Woe is me!﴾ [5:31] is a substitute for the first-person possessive ya' (ya' al-idafah), as in: "Ya lahfa" and "Ya ʿajaba." ʿAsim, Abu ʿAmr, and al-A'sha made the alif in ﴿Woe is me!﴾ [5:31] into an imala (vowel-inclination), since it is a substitute for the ya'. al-Hasan read "Ya wayltī" with the ya' according to the original form.

It is also said that the alif is the alif of lamentation (alif al-nudbah), and it is pausal with a ha'. Its origin is calling upon "woe" and the like in lamentation because of a severe calamity that overwhelms the soul. Then it was subsequently used for a wonder that overwhelms the soul. "Ya waylata" is a phrase that is light on the lips of women when something befalls them that causes them to wonder. She questioned with her saying: ﴿Shall I bear a child?﴾ [11:72], as a question of denial and wonder. "I am an old woman" and what follows are two circumstantial clauses (jumlatay hal). "Shaykhan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state according to the Basran grammarians, and as the predicate of "approximation" (khabar al-taqrib) according to the Kufan grammarians. This circumstantial state cannot be dispensed with when the predicate is known to the addressee, because the benefit is achieved only through this circumstantial state. But if it is unknown to him, and you wish to inform the addressee of what he did not know, then the circumstantial state takes its ordinary place and can be dispensed with.

Ibn Masʿud, in his codex, and al-Aʿmash read ﴿shaykh﴾ [28:23] in the nominative. They permitted, with respect to it and to "baʿli" (my husband), that both be predicates, like the saying: "this is sweet, sour," and that "baʿli" be the predicate, with ﴿shaykh﴾ [28:23] an implied predicate, or an apposition to "baʿli," and that "baʿli" be an apposition or a clarifying apposition (ʿatf bayan), with ﴿shaykh﴾ [28:23] the predicate.

The reference with "this" to the birth or to the good news of it: she wondered at the occurrence of a child between two aged, decrepit elders, and found this strange from the standpoint of custom, not as a denial of God's power. They said, that is, the angels: ﴿Do you wonder?﴾ [11:73] is a question of denial of her wonder. al-Zamakhshari said: "Because she was in the house of the signs, the place of descent of miracles and matters that break custom, it was incumbent upon her to be composed, and not to be elated by what elates other women outside the house of prophethood, and to glorify and praise God in place of wonder."

To this the angels alluded in their saying: ﴿The mercy of God and His blessings be upon you, people of the house﴾ [11:73]. They meant: "These and similar things, which the Lord of Might honors you with and singles you out with bounty, O people of the House of Prophethood, are not a strange matter." And ﴿the command of God﴾ [2:27] means His power and wisdom. His saying: ﴿The mercy of God and His blessings be upon you﴾ is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), by which the denial of wonder is justified, as if it were said: "Beware of wonder, for the likes of this mercy and blessing from God upon you are abundant."

It is also said: the mercy (rahmah) is prophethood, and the blessings (barakat) are the tribes (asbat) of the Children of Israel, since the prophets were from them, and all of them are descendants of Abraham. He ended.

It is also said: His mercy is His greeting, and His blessings are the abundance of His goodness through friendship (khullah) and leadership (imamah). It is narrated (ruwiya) that Sarah said to Gabriel, peace be upon him: "What is the sign of this?" So he took a dry stick and twisted it between his fingers, and it swayed green, so her alarm subsided and her wonder ceased.

This resumed clause may be a statement of fact, and this is the more apparent, because it implies that mercy and blessing are attained by them. It may also be a supplication, but this is less preferred, because supplication implies a matter hoped for that has not yet been realized. ﴿People of﴾ (ahla) is in the accusative by way of vocative or by way of specification (ikhtisas). There is a difference between the accusative of praise (madh) and the accusative of specification, and for this reason Sibawayh placed them in separate sections. The accusative of praise is a term which by its form includes praise, just as the accusative of blame includes blame by its form. The accusative of specification is used only for praise or blame, but its wording does not by its form include praise or blame, as in his saying: "Through us Tamim is uncovered from the murk," and his saying: "Nor al-Hajjaj, the eye of mine, daughter of water."

The angels' address to her with ﴿people of the house﴾ is evidence that the wife is included among the people of the house. This is also indicated in Surat al-Ahzab. This is contrary to the Shi'a, who do not count the wife as among the household of her husband. "House" (bayt) here refers to the house of dwelling.

﴿Indeed He is Praiseworthy﴾ [11:73]: Abu al-Haytham said: "His actions are praised," and it has the meaning of "praised" (mahmud). al-Zamakhshari said: "He is the doer of what is deserved from His servants, Glorious, Generous, abundant in beneficence toward them."

And al-Ghazzi said:

*A people who, when faced, were angels in beauty, and when fought, were demons.*

It was related that they used to shake (or draw) lots with arrows that were in their hands over the meat, while their hands could not reach it. It is necessary that the guest should be watched to see whether he eats or not, and this should be done with a glance and haste, not by fixing the gaze, because that would make the guest reluctant to eat. It is said: Ibrahim (peace be upon him) used to stay at the edge of the land, for fear that they might intend him some harm.

It is also said: their custom was that if the one who came to them touched their food, they felt secure; otherwise they feared him. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It appears that he sensed they were angels and disapproved of them, because he feared that their coming was for a matter Allah disapproved of, or for punishing his people."

Do you not see their saying: ﴿Do not fear; we have been sent to the people of Lut﴾? This is said only to someone who recognized them but did not know for what purpose they had been sent. Muqatil said: (fa-awjasa): it came into his heart. Al-Hasan said: he spoke it to himself. It is said: the origin of (wujus) is entering, as if fear entered upon him.

It is apparent that he did not know they were angels, because they came in the form of humans, and he was devoted to honouring guests; therefore they came in their forms, and because of his haste in bringing food to them, and because the angels' refusal to eat does not indicate that evil is present. He only knew they were angels from their saying: ﴿Do not fear; we have been sent to the people of Lut﴾, so they forbade him from something that had occurred in his mind, and they knew his fear because Allah had given them knowledge beyond that given to others, as in His saying: ﴿They know what you do﴾ [al-Infitar: 12]. And in the authentic hadith: "The angels said: 'My Lord, Your servant wants to commit an evil deed'," the hadith continues; or they knew it from what appears on the features of the face of one who is afraid.

﴿And his wife was standing﴾ is a nominal sentence. Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' said it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). Abu al-Baqa' said: it is from the implied subject of (arsalna), meaning the passive object whose agent is not named. Al-Zamakhshari calls it the subject, because it takes the place of the subject. Al-Hawfi said: the estimate is: "We were sent to the people of Lut while his wife was standing," meaning the wife of Ibrahim. It is apparent that it is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "they said": "They said to Ibrahim: Do not fear, while his wife was standing," and she was Sarah, daughter of Haran ibn Nahur, and she was his paternal cousin. (Standing) means: to serve the guests. Their women did not veil, as was the custom of the Bedouins and the people of the open desert, and displaying oneself was not disliked. She was an elderly woman. Serving guests is among the noble qualities of character, as said by Mujahid.

Something similar is found in our sharia, from the hadith of Abu Usayd al-Sa'idi: his wife was a newlywed bride, and she served the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and those present with him of his companions.

Wahb said: she was standing behind the curtain, listening to their conversation. Ibn Ishaq said: standing means praying. Al-Mubarrad said: standing from child-bearing. Al-Zamakhshari said: in the codex of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud): "His wife was standing while he was sitting." Ibn Atiyya said: in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "She was standing while he was sitting." The wife of Ibrahim was not mentioned before, so the pronoun would be implied, but the context of the speech explains it.

Mujahid and Ikrimah said: ﴿fa-dahikat﴾ means she menstruated. The majority said it is the well-known laughter. It is said it is a metaphor expressing the brightness of her face and her joy at the deliverance of her brother and the destruction of his people. It is said: "I came upon a meadow that laughs," meaning: bright. It is also said it is literal. Muqatil said, and it is related from Ibn Abbas: she laughed out of the intensity of Ibrahim's fear (p. 243) while he was among his family and servants. Those who came to him were three, while she was watching him, and he surpassed forty, and it is said a hundred. Qatada said: she laughed at the heedlessness of the people of Lut and the nearness of the punishment to them.

Al-Suddi said: she laughed at the guests' refraining from eating, and she said: "How strange! We serve our guests with our own hands, and they do not eat our food." Wahb ibn Munabbih said: it is related from Ibn Abbas: she laughed at the good tiding of Ishaq; and he said: this is an advance meaning a delay. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned that her laughter was joy at the truth of her expectation, because she used to say to Ibrahim: "Take in your brother's son Lut," and he was her brother, for the punishment would descend upon his people. It is also said: she laughed at the miraculous sign she saw, which is that the angels touched the roasted calf and it stood up alive, leaping. What appears to be the case, and Allah knows best, is that when they did not eat, and fear settled in his soul after he disapproved of their condition, the woman was affected more by that than the man.

When they said: "Do not fear," and mentioned the reason for their coming, the fear left him and he was glad, so joy overcame her too, and she laughed, for women are more prone to rejoicing and gladness than men, and that quality predominates in them. Al-Zamakhshari pointed to part of this, saying: she laughed out of joy at the removal of fear.

Muhammad ibn Qays mentioned a reason for her laughter that we have left unmentioned because of its enormity; it can be found in the commentary of Ibn Atiyya. Muhammad ibn Ziyad al-A'rabi, a reciter of Makkah, read ﴿fa-dahikat﴾ with a fatha on the ha (fa-dahakat). Al-Mahdawi said: fatha on the ha is not well known.

﴿fa-bashsharnaha﴾ agrees with His saying: ﴿And indeed Our messengers came to Ibrahim with good tidings﴾. The meaning is: "So We gave her good tidings through Our messengers," the angels gave her the good tiding of Ishaq, and that Ishaq would beget Ya'qub.

Ibn Atiyya said: He attributed the action of the angels to the pronoun of Allah's name, since it was by His command and revelation. Others said: when Isma'il was born to Ibrahim from Hajar, Sarah wished that she might have a son, but she despaired because of her old age, so she was given the good tiding of a son who would be a prophet and would beget a prophet. This was a good tiding to her that she would see the son of her son. They gave her the good tiding apart from Ibrahim because a woman is quicker to rejoice at a child, and because they had already given Ibrahim the good tiding and reassured him from his fear, so they followed his good tiding with hers. It is also said that she was specially given the good tiding because she had no son, whereas Ibrahim had his son Isma'il.

The apparent meaning is that (wara') here is an adverb used as a noun, by the entrance of (min) upon it, as if it were said: "and after Ishaq," or "from behind Ishaq," and it means "after." This is related from Ibn Abbas and was chosen by Muqatil and Ibn Qutayba. It is also related from Ibn Abbas that (al-wara') is the son's son, and this was said by al-Sha'bi and chosen by Abu Ubayda. Calling him (wara') is close to the meaning of (wara') as an adverb, since it is what is behind and after a thing.

If it is said: how can Ya'qub be "after" Ishaq when he is his son by his loins, and "after" means only a son's son? Ibn al-Anbari answered this, saying: the meaning is "and from the after attributed to Ishaq is Ya'qub," because the "after" belonged to Ibrahim through Ishaq. If he had said "and from the after Ya'qub," it would not be known whether this "after" is attributed to Ishaq or to Isma'il. So it was attributed to Ishaq to make the meaning clear and remove the ambiguity. End of quotation.

She was given the good tiding of Ya'qub from among the children of Ishaq because she saw him and did not see anyone else. This good tiding to Sarah was when she was ninety-nine years old, and Ibrahim was a hundred years old. It is also said that the difference between them was other than that, and these are contradictory statements.

This verse indicates that Ishmael is the one who was sacrificed (al-dhabih), because when the tyrant king gave Hagar to Sarah as a servant, Hagar, the mother of Ishmael, was a young and beautiful woman. Abraham took Hagar as a concubine (surriyyah, a slave-woman who bore a master's child), so Sarah became jealous of her. He then set out with her and her son Ishmael from al-Sham (Greater Syria) on al-Buraq (the winged steed), came to Mecca the same day, and returned to al-Sham the same day. After that came the good news of Isaac, when Sarah was an old, barren woman. The proof of this will also come later from Surat al-Saffat, ﴿By those who range in ranks﴾ [37:1].

It is possible that God named her at the time of the good news with these two names. It is also possible that the two names were given to her at the time of birth, and that the good news was of a male child, after which a male child was born. The narration of the good news, with mention of the male child by her name, is like the speaker who says: if one is given good news in a dream of a male child, and a male child is then born to him, and he names him, for example, ʿAbd Allah, then he says: "I was given good news of ʿAbd Allah." (p. 244)

The two Harams (Meccan and Medinan readers), the two Kufan grammarians (al-Kisa'i and Hamzah, the two al-Nahwiyyan), and Abu Bakr Yaʿqub read Yaʿqub in the nominative (raf'), as the subject (mubtada'), with ﴿from behind﴾ [33:53] as the predicate. It is as if it were said: "and from behind Isaac there is Yaʿqub existing." al-Zamakhshari estimated the predicate as "born" (mawlud) or "existing" (mawjud). al-Nahhas said: "The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) included within the good news, i.e., 'We gave her good news of Isaac, with Yaʿqub connected to him.'"

Abu ʿAli (al-Farisi) permitted that it be in the nominative as a predicate of the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa'l-majrur), as al-Akhfash also permitted. That is, "there settled for her, from behind Isaac, Yaʿqub." Another group said the nominative is by way of resumption (al-qat'), meaning: "and from behind Isaac, Yaʿqub will come into being." al-Nahhas said: "It is also permissible for it to be the subject of an implied verb, whose estimate is: 'and from behind Isaac, Yaʿqub will come into being.'"

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "According to this, the good news does not include him." There is no need to strain with the notion of a break in the sentence (al-qat') and turning away from the apparent meaning, which requires that he be included in the good news.

Ibn ʿAmir, Hamzah, Hafs, and Zayd ibn ʿAli read Yaʿqub in the accusative (nasb). al-Zamakhshari said: "It is as if it were said: 'and We granted her Isaac, and from behind Isaac, Yaʿqub,' following the manner of his saying: 'They are not reformers of a clan, nor a crier of the dead [crow].'" He ended. He means that it was conjoined upon an assumed (tawahhum) construction. Conjoining upon an assumed construction is not analogical (la yanqas). The more apparent reading is that Yaʿqub is in the accusative by an implied verb whose estimate is: "and from behind Isaac, We granted Yaʿqub," and what indicates it is His saying: "So We gave her good news," because the good news is in the meaning of a gift. Abu ʿAli preferred this view. As for those who held that it is in the genitive, conjoined upon the wording of "bi-Ishaq," or upon its place, their view is weak, because it is not permissible to separate, with an adverbial or a prepositional phrase, between the conjunctive particle and its genitive conjunct. One may not say: "I passed by Zayd today and Amr yesterday," and if it occurs, it is in poetry.

If the conjunct is in the accusative or nominative, there is disagreement about the permissibility of this, as in: "Zayd stood and today ʿAmr," and "I struck Zayd and today ʿAmr." The apparent view is that the alif in ﴿Woe is me!﴾ [5:31] is a substitute for the first-person possessive ya' (ya' al-idafah), as in: "Ya lahfa" and "Ya ʿajaba." ʿAsim, Abu ʿAmr, and al-A'sha made the alif in ﴿Woe is me!﴾ [5:31] into an imala (vowel-inclination), since it is a substitute for the ya'. al-Hasan read "Ya wayltī" with the ya' according to the original form.

It is also said that the alif is the alif of lamentation (alif al-nudbah), and it is pausal with a ha'. Its origin is calling upon "woe" and the like in lamentation because of a severe calamity that overwhelms the soul. Then it was subsequently used for a wonder that overwhelms the soul. "Ya waylata" is a phrase that is light on the lips of women when something befalls them that causes them to wonder. She questioned with her saying: ﴿Shall I bear a child?﴾ [11:72], as a question of denial and wonder. "I am an old woman" and what follows are two circumstantial clauses (jumlatay hal). "Shaykhan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state according to the Basran grammarians, and as the predicate of "approximation" (khabar al-taqrib) according to the Kufan grammarians. This circumstantial state cannot be dispensed with when the predicate is known to the addressee, because the benefit is achieved only through this circumstantial state. But if it is unknown to him, and you wish to inform the addressee of what he did not know, then the circumstantial state takes its ordinary place and can be dispensed with.

Ibn Masʿud, in his codex, and al-Aʿmash read ﴿shaykh﴾ [28:23] in the nominative. They permitted, with respect to it and to "baʿli" (my husband), that both be predicates, like the saying: "this is sweet, sour," and that "baʿli" be the predicate, with ﴿shaykh﴾ [28:23] an implied predicate, or an apposition to "baʿli," and that "baʿli" be an apposition or a clarifying apposition (ʿatf bayan), with ﴿shaykh﴾ [28:23] the predicate.

The reference with "this" to the birth or to the good news of it: she wondered at the occurrence of a child between two aged, decrepit elders, and found this strange from the standpoint of custom, not as a denial of God's power. They said, that is, the angels: ﴿Do you wonder?﴾ [11:73] is a question of denial of her wonder. al-Zamakhshari said: "Because she was in the house of the signs, the place of descent of miracles and matters that break custom, it was incumbent upon her to be composed, and not to be elated by what elates other women outside the house of prophethood, and to glorify and praise God in place of wonder."

To this the angels alluded in their saying: ﴿The mercy of God and His blessings be upon you, people of the house﴾ [11:73]. They meant: "These and similar things, which the Lord of Might honors you with and singles you out with bounty, O people of the House of Prophethood, are not a strange matter." And ﴿the command of God﴾ [2:27] means His power and wisdom. His saying: ﴿The mercy of God and His blessings be upon you﴾ is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), by which the denial of wonder is justified, as if it were said: "Beware of wonder, for the likes of this mercy and blessing from God upon you are abundant."

It is also said: the mercy (rahmah) is prophethood, and the blessings (barakat) are the tribes (asbat) of the Children of Israel, since the prophets were from them, and all of them are descendants of Abraham. He ended.

It is also said: His mercy is His greeting, and His blessings are the abundance of His goodness through friendship (khullah) and leadership (imamah). It is narrated (ruwiya) that Sarah said to Gabriel, peace be upon him: "What is the sign of this?" So he took a dry stick and twisted it between his fingers, and it swayed green, so her alarm subsided and her wonder ceased.

This resumed clause may be a statement of fact, and this is the more apparent, because it implies that mercy and blessing are attained by them. It may also be a supplication, but this is less preferred, because supplication implies a matter hoped for that has not yet been realized. ﴿People of﴾ (ahla) is in the accusative by way of vocative or by way of specification (ikhtisas). There is a difference between the accusative of praise (madh) and the accusative of specification, and for this reason Sibawayh placed them in separate sections. The accusative of praise is a term which by its form includes praise, just as the accusative of blame includes blame by its form. The accusative of specification is used only for praise or blame, but its wording does not by its form include praise or blame, as in his saying: "Through us Tamim is uncovered from the murk," and his saying: "Nor al-Hajjaj, the eye of mine, daughter of water."

The angels' address to her with ﴿people of the house﴾ is evidence that the wife is included among the people of the house. This is also indicated in Surat al-Ahzab. This is contrary to the Shi'a, who do not count the wife as among the household of her husband. "House" (bayt) here refers to the house of dwelling.

﴿Indeed He is Praiseworthy﴾ [11:73]: Abu al-Haytham said: "His actions are praised," and it has the meaning of "praised" (mahmud). al-Zamakhshari said: "He is the doer of what is deserved from His servants, Glorious, Generous, abundant in beneficence toward them."

**Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah Hud (11), verses 74–76:**

﴿So when the fear had left Abraham and the good tidings had reached him, he began to plead with Us concerning the people of Lot.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Abraham was forbearing, tender-hearted and repentant.﴾ ﴿"O Abraham, turn away from this. Indeed, the command of your Lord has come, and a punishment that cannot be averted is coming upon them."﴾

*Al-ruʿb* (the fear): the dread that he had sensed within himself when he did not recognize his guests. The meaning is that his heart became reassured by knowing that they were angels.

*Al-bushra* (the good tidings): his being given tidings of a son, or that what was meant by their coming was something other than that.

The answer to *lammā* (when) is omitted, as it is omitted in His saying: ﴿So when they took him away﴾ [Yusuf: 15]. Its implied sense is: he became bold in address when he perceived the matter of disputation, or he said: such and such. The resumptive clause, which is ﴿he began to plead with Us﴾, indicates this, as al-Zamakhshari said with this meaning.

It has been said: the answer is ﴿he began to plead with Us﴾, and the present tense has been placed in the position of the past tense, meaning: he pleaded with Us. This is permissible because the meaning is clear, and this is the closest of the opinions.

It has been said: ﴿he began to plead with Us﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring to Abraham, and ﴿had reached him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 211] is also a circumstantial clause, or refers to the pronoun in *jāʾathu*. The answer to *lammā* is omitted, its implied sense being: We said, "O Abraham, turn away from this." Abu ʿAli chose this interpretation.

It has been said: the answer is omitted, its implied sense being: he continued or began to plead with Us. It is omitted for brevity, since the apparent wording points to it. As for the pleading, it has been said that it was his question: "Is the punishment certain to befall them, or is it by way of frightening them so that they return to obedience?" It has also been said that they both spoke by way of intercession, and the meaning is: Our messengers disputed.

It is reported from Hudhayfah that when they said to him, ﴿Indeed, We are going to destroy the people of this town﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 31], he said: "Tell me, if there are fifty Muslims in it, will you destroy it?" They said, "No." He said, "Forty?" They said, "No." He said, "Thirty?" They said, "No." He said, "Twenty?" They said, "No." He said, "If there are ten, or five—the narrator is doubtful—?" They said, "No." He said, "Tell me, if there is one man among them who is a Muslim, will you destroy it?" They said, "No." At that he said: ﴿Indeed, Lot is in it﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 32]. They said: ﴿We know best who is in it﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 32], "We shall surely save him and his family." This was from Abraham out of his eagerness for the faith and salvation of the people of Lot. In the town there were four thousand thousand people.

The explanation of *ḥalīm*, *awwāh* and *munīb* has already been given earlier.

﴿O Abraham﴾: that is, the angels said. The reference of "this" is to the disputation and argument over a matter that has already been decided. The "command" is what He decreed and ruled concerning their punishment, which is certain to befall them, and it cannot be averted by disputation, supplication, or anything else.

ʿAmr ibn Harim recited *wa-innahum atāhum* with the past tense, and *ʿadhāb* is the agent of it. He expressed the imperfect by the past tense because its occurrence is certain, as in His saying: ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1].

(p-246)﴿When Our messengers came to Lot, he was troubled on their account and felt powerless to protect them, and he said, "This is a distressing day."﴾ ﴿His people came rushing toward him, and before this they had been doing evil deeds. He said, "O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear God and do not disgrace me concerning my guests. Is there not among you one right-minded man?"﴾ ﴿They said, "You know that we have no claim on your daughters, and you know well what we want."﴾ ﴿He said, "If only I had strength against you, or could take refuge in a mighty support."﴾ The angels set out from the town of Abraham toward the town of Lot. The distance between them is said to be eight miles, and it is said to be four farsakh. They came to it at night, and it is said that they came at midday, and they found Lot in his field. It is said that they found his daughter drawing water in the river of Sodom, which was the largest of the cities of the people of Lot. They asked her for directions to someone who would host them, and she saw their appearance and feared for them from the people of Lot. She told them, "Wait here," and went to her father and informed him. He went out to them, and they said, "We want you to host us tonight." He said to them, "Have you not heard of the deeds of these people?" They said, "And what are their deeds?" He said, "I testify before God that they are the most evil people on earth." God had told the angels, "Do not punish them until Lot has given four testimonies against them." When he said this, Gabriel said, "This is one." The matter was repeated among them until Lot had repeated the testimony four times. Then Lot entered the city, and at that point he was troubled by them, that is, harm came upon him because of them, and his capacity was strained by them, and he said, "This is a distressing day," that is, a severe one, because of what he feared from his people's aggression against his guests.

﴿His people came rushing toward him﴾: When Lot brought his guests, no one knew of it except the members of his household. His wife went out until she reached the gatherings of her people and said, "Lot has hosted tonight young men whose beauty has never been seen, and so-and-so." Then they came rushing, that is, hastening, as they push forward, like one who is greedy and fearful lest he miss what he seeks. The majority of readers recited (yuhra'ūna), in the passive form from aharra, meaning that desire drives them. A group recited (yahra'ūna) with a fatḥa on the yā' from hara'a. Muhalhil said:

"They came rushing, while they were captives, led by them in spite of their noses."

﴿Before this they had been doing evil deeds﴾: That is, this was their habit and custom. They persisted in it and became accustomed to it, so this was not the first time they had committed this sin. They came rushing, with no shame restraining them, because of their eagerness for it. The implied sense of (before this) is: before their coming to these guests and seeking them out.

It is also said: before Lot was sent as a messenger to them. The word "evil deeds" is in the plural, although what is meant is the sin of approaching males, either with regard to its doers or with regard to its repetition. It is also said that they were many evil deeds, differing in kind. Among them were approaching males, approaching women in other than the proper place, throwing pebbles and shouting in gatherings and markets, whistling and clapping, playing with pigeons, gambling, mocking people in the streets, placing a dirham on the ground while standing far from it, so that whoever took it they would shout at and shame, and if a boy took it they would follow him and solicit him.

﴿These are my daughters﴾: The better view is that the idafa here is figurative, meaning "the daughters of my people," that is, the daughters are purer for you, since the prophet takes the position of a father to his people. In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves, and his wives are their mothers, and he is a father to them." What supports this is that it is said he had only two daughters, while this is expressed in the plural. Also, it is not possible that he would marry his two daughters to all his people. It is also said that he pointed to the daughters of his own household and urged them toward marriage, since it was their custom to marry a believing woman to an unbeliever. Or it is that his words contain an implication that they should believe. It is also said that they had two leaders who were obeyed, and he wanted to marry his two daughters to them, Zaghura and Zayta. It is also said that they were three.

The meaning of "purer" (aṭhar) is cleaner in deed. It is also said: more lawful and purer in household, and it is not the comparative form, since there is no purity in approaching males. The majority recited (aṭhar) with a ḍamma, and the better grammatical analysis is that there are two sentences, each of which is a subject and predicate. For (banātī) it is permitted that it be a substitute or an appositive, with (hunna) as a separator pronoun (faṣl) and (aṭhar) as the predicate. Al-Hasan, Zayd ibn 'Ali, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Muhammad ibn Marwan al-Suddi recited (aṭhara) with a fatḥa.

Sibawayh said: it is a grammatical error (laḥn). Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala said: Ibn Marwan sat cross-legged in his error, meaning he sat in the quarter position (tarabbu'). This reading is related from Marwan ibn al-Hakam, and it has been explained as the fatḥa on aṭhar being a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). It was said: (hā'ulā'): is a subject, and "my daughters, they" is a subject and predicate in the position of the predicate of (hā'ulā'). This is related from al-Mubarrad. It was also said: "These are my daughters" is a subject and predicate, and (hunna) is a subject, and (lakum) is its predicate, and the governing element is said to be the implied one. It was also said: (lakum) with what it contains of the sense of settledness. It was also said: "These are my daughters" is a subject and predicate, (hunna) is a separator, and (aṭhara) is a circumstantial accusative. This was rejected on the ground that a separator occurs only between the two parts of a sentence, and does not occur between a circumstantial accusative and the element it qualifies. Some have permitted this and claimed that it is heard from the Arabs, but it is rare.

Then he commanded them to fear God in regard to preferring the daughters over the guests. (Do not disgrace me): It may be from disgrace (khizy), which is scandal, or from shame (khazāya), which is embarrassment, because when a man's guest or neighbor is disgraced, he himself is disgraced, and that comes from the nobility of generosity and the root of manliness. (Is there not among you a man): one who is guided to the path of truth, and to doing good, and to refraining from evil? In this is a great rebuke to them, since not one of them was rightly guided at all.

Ibn 'Abbas said: rashīd means a believer. Abu Malik said: one who forbids wrongdoing. Rashīd means one possessed of right guidance, or one who guides, like "hakīm" in the sense of "muḥkam." The apparent meaning of (min ḥaqq) is "of any share," neither of purpose nor of desire, and they said this to him in a manner of wantonness. It was also said: "of any right," because you do not see from us our kinsmen, since they had proposed for his daughters and he had refused them, and their custom was that whoever was refused in proposing to a woman would never be lawful to him again.

It was also said: when they adopted approaching males as a doctrine, it was their belief that this was the truth, and that marrying females was falsehood. It was also said: because their custom was that a man would marry only one wife, yet all of them were married.

﴿And you know what we want﴾: that is, approaching males, and what desire they had for it. He said: ﴿If only I had strength against you﴾: He said this in the manner of grief. The answer to "law" (if) is omitted, as it is omitted in: ﴿And if a Qur'an by which the mountains were moved﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:31], and its implied meaning is: "I would have done to you and acted." The sense of ﴿to a mighty support﴾ is someone to whom he would lean and by whom he would be protected from his tribe. He likened the one by whom he would be protected to the pillar of a mountain in its strength and its defense. It is as if he were prevented from being able to defend himself, or to protect himself by himself or by others, of whatever could serve as a support for him.

Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' said: (aw ā'ī) is coordinated with the meaning, the implied sense being: "or that I take refuge." The apparent view is that "or" coordinates a verbal sentence with a verbal sentence, if you assume that "that I" is in the position of the nominative as agent, according to the view of al-Mubarrad, meaning: "if it were established that I had strength against you, or [that] I took refuge." The implied present verb, and this (āwī), stand in the place of the past tense, and "law" which is a particle for what would have happened because of the occurrence of something else, shifts the present to the past. If you assume that "that" and what follows it form a nominal sentence, according to the view of Sibawayh, then it is coordinated with it, insofar as "law" is followed by an implied nominal sentence when what is constructed from "that" and its operand is the subject.

Abu al-Baqa' said: it may also be that (aw ā'ī) is a new independent sentence. It is also permitted, according to the view of the Kufans, that "or" has the meaning of "bal" (rather), and he has turned away from the previous sentence and said: "Rather I take refuge in my state with you at a mighty support," and by it he referred to the presence of God, exalted is He.

Shayba and Abu Ja'far recited (aw ā'ī) with a fatḥa on the yā', by implying "an" (that) after "aw," so that it is interpreted as a verbal noun coordinated with his saying (quwwatan, strength). A parallel of the accusative by implying "an" after "aw" is the words of the poet:

"Had it not been for men of Rizam, honored, and the family of Subay', or [that] your displeasure would make you taste bitterness."

That is: "or [that] your displeasure would be bitterness."
