It is also permitted, according to the view of the Kufans, that "or" has the meaning of "bal" (rather), and he has turned away from the previous sentence and said: "Rather I take refuge in my state with you at a mighty support," and by it he referred to the presence of God, exalted is He.

Shayba and Abu Ja'far recited (aw ā'ī) with a fatḥa on the yā', by implying "an" (that) after "aw," so that it is interpreted as a verbal noun coordinated with his saying (quwwatan, strength). A parallel of the accusative by implying "an" after "aw" is the words of the poet:

"Had it not been for men of Rizam, honored, and the family of Subay', or [that] your displeasure would make you taste bitterness."

That is: "or [that] your displeasure would be bitterness."

(p-246)﴿When Our messengers came to Lot, he was troubled on their account and felt powerless to protect them, and he said, "This is a distressing day."﴾ ﴿His people came rushing toward him, and before this they had been doing evil deeds. He said, "O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear God and do not disgrace me concerning my guests. Is there not among you one right-minded man?"﴾ ﴿They said, "You know that we have no claim on your daughters, and you know well what we want."﴾ ﴿He said, "If only I had strength against you, or could take refuge in a mighty support."﴾ The angels set out from the town of Abraham toward the town of Lot. The distance between them is said to be eight miles, and it is said to be four farsakh. They came to it at night, and it is said that they came at midday, and they found Lot in his field. It is said that they found his daughter drawing water in the river of Sodom, which was the largest of the cities of the people of Lot. They asked her for directions to someone who would host them, and she saw their appearance and feared for them from the people of Lot. She told them, "Wait here," and went to her father and informed him. He went out to them, and they said, "We want you to host us tonight." He said to them, "Have you not heard of the deeds of these people?" They said, "And what are their deeds?" He said, "I testify before God that they are the most evil people on earth." God had told the angels, "Do not punish them until Lot has given four testimonies against them." When he said this, Gabriel said, "This is one." The matter was repeated among them until Lot had repeated the testimony four times. Then Lot entered the city, and at that point he was troubled by them, that is, harm came upon him because of them, and his capacity was strained by them, and he said, "This is a distressing day," that is, a severe one, because of what he feared from his people's aggression against his guests.

﴿His people came rushing toward him﴾: When Lot brought his guests, no one knew of it except the members of his household. His wife went out until she reached the gatherings of her people and said, "Lot has hosted tonight young men whose beauty has never been seen, and so-and-so." Then they came rushing, that is, hastening, as they push forward, like one who is greedy and fearful lest he miss what he seeks. The majority of readers recited (yuhra'ūna), in the passive form from aharra, meaning that desire drives them. A group recited (yahra'ūna) with a fatḥa on the yā' from hara'a. Muhalhil said:

"They came rushing, while they were captives, led by them in spite of their noses."

﴿Before this they had been doing evil deeds﴾: That is, this was their habit and custom. They persisted in it and became accustomed to it, so this was not the first time they had committed this sin. They came rushing, with no shame restraining them, because of their eagerness for it. The implied sense of (before this) is: before their coming to these guests and seeking them out.

It is also said: before Lot was sent as a messenger to them. The word "evil deeds" is in the plural, although what is meant is the sin of approaching males, either with regard to its doers or with regard to its repetition. It is also said that they were many evil deeds, differing in kind. Among them were approaching males, approaching women in other than the proper place, throwing pebbles and shouting in gatherings and markets, whistling and clapping, playing with pigeons, gambling, mocking people in the streets, placing a dirham on the ground while standing far from it, so that whoever took it they would shout at and shame, and if a boy took it they would follow him and solicit him.

﴿These are my daughters﴾: The better view is that the idafa here is figurative, meaning "the daughters of my people," that is, the daughters are purer for you, since the prophet takes the position of a father to his people. In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves, and his wives are their mothers, and he is a father to them." What supports this is that it is said he had only two daughters, while this is expressed in the plural. Also, it is not possible that he would marry his two daughters to all his people. It is also said that he pointed to the daughters of his own household and urged them toward marriage, since it was their custom to marry a believing woman to an unbeliever. Or it is that his words contain an implication that they should believe. It is also said that they had two leaders who were obeyed, and he wanted to marry his two daughters to them, Zaghura and Zayta. It is also said that they were three.

The meaning of "purer" (aṭhar) is cleaner in deed. It is also said: more lawful and purer in household, and it is not the comparative form, since there is no purity in approaching males. The majority recited (aṭhar) with a ḍamma, and the better grammatical analysis is that there are two sentences, each of which is a subject and predicate. For (banātī) it is permitted that it be a substitute or an appositive, with (hunna) as a separator pronoun (faṣl) and (aṭhar) as the predicate. Al-Hasan, Zayd ibn 'Ali, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Muhammad ibn Marwan al-Suddi recited (aṭhara) with a fatḥa.

Sibawayh said: it is a grammatical error (laḥn). Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala said: Ibn Marwan sat cross-legged in his error, meaning he sat in the quarter position (tarabbu'). This reading is related from Marwan ibn al-Hakam, and it has been explained as the fatḥa on aṭhar being a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). It was said: (hā'ulā'): is a subject, and "my daughters, they" is a subject and predicate in the position of the predicate of (hā'ulā'). This is related from al-Mubarrad. It was also said: "These are my daughters" is a subject and predicate, and (hunna) is a subject, and (lakum) is its predicate, and the governing element is said to be the implied one. It was also said: (lakum) with what it contains of the sense of settledness. It was also said: "These are my daughters" is a subject and predicate, (hunna) is a separator, and (aṭhara) is a circumstantial accusative. This was rejected on the ground that a separator occurs only between the two parts of a sentence, and does not occur between a circumstantial accusative and the element it qualifies. Some have permitted this and claimed that it is heard from the Arabs, but it is rare.

Then he commanded them to fear God in regard to preferring the daughters over the guests. (Do not disgrace me): It may be from disgrace (khizy), which is scandal, or from shame (khazāya), which is embarrassment, because when a man's guest or neighbor is disgraced, he himself is disgraced, and that comes from the nobility of generosity and the root of manliness. (Is there not among you a man): one who is guided to the path of truth, and to doing good, and to refraining from evil? In this is a great rebuke to them, since not one of them was rightly guided at all.

Ibn 'Abbas said: rashīd means a believer. Abu Malik said: one who forbids wrongdoing. Rashīd means one possessed of right guidance, or one who guides, like "hakīm" in the sense of "muḥkam." The apparent meaning of (min ḥaqq) is "of any share," neither of purpose nor of desire, and they said this to him in a manner of wantonness. It was also said: "of any right," because you do not see from us our kinsmen, since they had proposed for his daughters and he had refused them, and their custom was that whoever was refused in proposing to a woman would never be lawful to him again.

It was also said: when they adopted approaching males as a doctrine, it was their belief that this was the truth, and that marrying females was falsehood. It was also said: because their custom was that a man would marry only one wife, yet all of them were married.

﴿And you know what we want﴾: that is, approaching males, and what desire they had for it. He said: ﴿If only I had strength against you﴾: He said this in the manner of grief. The answer to "law" (if) is omitted, as it is omitted in: ﴿And if a Qur'an by which the mountains were moved﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:31], and its implied meaning is: "I would have done to you and acted." The sense of ﴿to a mighty support﴾ is someone to whom he would lean and by whom he would be protected from his tribe. He likened the one by whom he would be protected to the pillar of a mountain in its strength and its defense. It is as if he were prevented from being able to defend himself, or to protect himself by himself or by others, of whatever could serve as a support for him.

Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' said: (aw ā'ī) is coordinated with the meaning, the implied sense being: "or that I take refuge." The apparent view is that "or" coordinates a verbal sentence with a verbal sentence, if you assume that "that I" is in the position of the nominative as agent, according to the view of al-Mubarrad, meaning: "if it were established that I had strength against you, or [that] I took refuge." The implied present verb, and this (āwī), stand in the place of the past tense, and "law" which is a particle for what would have happened because of the occurrence of something else, shifts the present to the past. If you assume that "that" and what follows it form a nominal sentence, according to the view of Sibawayh, then it is coordinated with it, insofar as "law" is followed by an implied nominal sentence when what is constructed from "that" and its operand is the subject.

Abu al-Baqa' said: it may also be that (aw ā'ī) is a new independent sentence. It is also permitted, according to the view of the Kufans, that "or" has the meaning of "bal" (rather), and he has turned away from the previous sentence and said: "Rather I take refuge in my state with you at a mighty support," and by it he referred to the presence of God, exalted is He.

Shayba and Abu Ja'far recited (aw ā'ī) with a fatḥa on the yā', by implying "an" (that) after "aw," so that it is interpreted as a verbal noun coordinated with his saying (quwwatan, strength). A parallel of the accusative by implying "an" after "aw" is the words of the poet:

"Had it not been for men of Rizam, honored, and the family of Subay', or [that] your displeasure would make you taste bitterness."

That is: "or [that] your displeasure would be bitterness."

(p-248) It is narrated that when Lut, peace be upon him, was overpowered and they tried to break down the door while he was holding it shut, the messengers said to him: "Step aside from the door," and he stepped aside. The door was flung open, and Jibril, peace be upon him, struck them with his wing, blinding their eyes. They were blinded and turned back on their heels, saying: "Salvation! Salvation! For there are sorcerers with Lut," and they threatened Lut. At that point they said to him: ﴿Indeed, we are the messengers of your Lord﴾.

It is also narrated that Jibril dug through the crevices of the door and cast (dust) into their eyes, and they became blind. It has been said that he took a handful of dust and scattered it in their faces, and it reached the eyes of everyone near and far from that dust, so their eyes were obliterated. They could not find the way, nor could they find their own houses. It has been said that they broke down his door and rushed upon him, and Jibril did to them what he did.

The sentence ﴿they will not reach you﴾ clarifies what precedes it, because when they are the messengers of Allah, they will not be able to reach him, and they have no power to harm him. Then they commanded him to travel by night with his family. The two Harami readers (Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr) read ﴿fa-asri﴾ (with a hamzat al-wasl, i.e., "travel by night", from the root sara) and "an asri" with the alif of sara joined, while the rest of the Seven read ﴿bi-qit'in﴾ (with a hamzat al-qat', i.e., "set out"). His family: his two daughters and a small group of the believers.

﴿with a portion of the night﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: "with a part of the night." Al-Dahhak said: "with the remainder of its last part." Qatadah said: "after the passing of a part of it." Ibn al-A'rabi said: "that is, an hour of the night." It has been said: "with darkness." It has been said: "it is half of it," and it has been said: "it is the midpoint of the night, taken from cutting it into two halves." The poet said:

*"And a wailing woman wails in a portion of the night, over a man by the stony ground of the open land."*

Muhammad ibn Ziyad said: "It is the pre-dawn (al-sahar), because of His saying: ﴿We delivered them at dawn﴾." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is possible that he traveled with his family from the beginning of the night until he passed the uprooted city, and his deliverance occurred at dawn. Thus this verse agrees with His saying: ﴿except the family of Lut; We delivered them at dawn﴾ [al-Qamar: 34]." End of quote.

Ibn al-Anbari said: "The word qit' in the sense of qit'ah (portion) is specific to the night; one does not say, 'I have a qit' of the cloth.'" Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿except your wife﴾ with a raised case (ill-a imra'atuka, as a nominative), while the rest of the Seven read it in the accusative (illa imra'atak). The accusative is explained as an exception from ﴿your family﴾ (bi-ahlika), since before it there is a command, and a command is regarded by them as obligatory. The accusative is necessarily required as an exception from "your family" in the reading of 'Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud), since in his recitation and his codex the phrase ﴿and let none of you look back﴾ is absent. They also permitted it to be accusative as an exception from "anyone" (ahad), even though there is a prohibition before it, and the prohibition is like negation according to the original basis of the exception, as in the reading of Ibn 'Amir: "they did not do it except a few of them" with the accusative, even though there is a negation before it.

The nominative is explained as a substitute (badal) for "anyone," and it is a connected exception. Abu 'Ubayd said: "If the speech were 'and let him not look back' with a raised verb, but it is a prohibition. When you make the woman an exception from 'anyone,' it must be that the woman was permitted to look back, which would give the meaning of the verse..." — meaning the sense would become: "except your wife," since she was not forbidden from looking back.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This objection is sound, and it entails that the exception from 'anyone,' whether you raise the ta' or make it accusative, must be resolved. The answer to it is reported in a statement from al-Mubarrad, that the prohibition was intended only for Lut alone, and that looking back was negated for them. The meaning is: do not let any one of them look back. This is like saying to a man: 'Let none of these people stand up,' while those (the ones referred to) did not hear you. The meaning is: do not let any one of these stand up, and standing up is negated for those referred to."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Regarding her departure with his family there are two reports. It is narrated that he took her out with them and was commanded that none of them should look back except her. When she heard the crash of the punishment, she looked back and said: 'Oh, my people!' and a stone overtook her and killed her. It is also narrated that he was commanded to leave her with her people, and her inclination was toward them, and he did not travel with her."

The difference between the two readings corresponds to the difference between the two reports. End of quote. This is a gross error, for he built the two readings upon the difference of the two reports, namely whether he traveled with her or did not travel with her. This is a contradiction in the reports, and it is impossible that the two readings, which are from the speech of Allah, should be a delusion resulting from contradiction. It has been said regarding the exception from (p-249) "the family" that there is a difficulty in meaning, for it would entail that he did not travel with her, and when she looked back she had certainly traveled with them. This difficulty disappears if he did not travel with her, but when she followed them she looked back. It has been said: "What appears is that the exception in both readings is discontinuous (munqati', istithna' munqati'), not intended to exclude her from those commanded to travel with them, nor from those prohibited from looking back, but rather the report about her was newly begun. The meaning is: 'But your wife, such-and-such will happen to her.'" This meaning is supported by the fact that a verse like this came in Surat al-Hijr, and there is no exception in it at all. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So travel with your family by a portion of the night, and follow their rear, and let none of you look back, and proceed where you are commanded﴾ [al-Hijr: 65]. Thus the concern in that case was only with mentioning those whom Allah saved. The description of his wife's condition came in Surat Hud as a follow-up, not as something intended to be excluded from what preceded. When this meaning is clear, it is known that the two readings came in accordance with what Arabic grammar requires for the discontinuous exception (istithna' munqati'), so in it there is both the accusative and the nominative.

The accusative is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and most speakers use it. The nominative is the dialect of Banu Tamim, and two of the reciters follow it. End of quote.

What he lengthened on this is without verification. If the exclusion of her from those commanded to travel with them was not intended, nor from those forbidden to look back, and it is treated as a discontinuous exception, then the discontinuous exception is one to which the governing verb (al-'amil) did not apply in any way. This type of discontinuous exception requires the accusative by consensus (ijma', agreement) of the Arabs, and in it there is no accusative and nominative according to the two dialects. Rather, that is in the discontinuous exception that the governing verb can apply to. In both types, what follows "illa" is not of the same kind as what precedes it. So the fact that both dialects are permitted in it is evidence that it is something to which the governing verb can apply, and it has been assumed that the exception was not intended to exclude her from those commanded to travel with them, nor from those forbidden to look back. Thus at that point the accusative would have been required without any dispute.

The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿and let none look back﴾ is that it refers to looking with the eyes. A group said: from laftа al-shay'a yalfituhu, when one turns it and twists it; its meaning would then be: "and let none hesitate."

In the book of al-Zahrawi, the meaning is: "and let no one look back at what he has left behind, but let him go out hastening."

The pronoun in ﴿innahu﴾ is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n, the dummy/pronoun of the matter), and ﴿musibuha﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿what has befallen them﴾ is the predicate. According to the doctrine of the Kufans, it is permissible that ﴿musibuha﴾ be the predicate of inna, and ﴿ma asabahum﴾ be the agent of it, since they permit "innahu qa'imun akhwaka." The doctrine of the Basrans is that the pronoun of the matter cannot have a predicate except a sentence whose two parts are explicitly stated, so this construction is not permitted according to them.

Isa ibn 'Umar read ﴿al-subuh﴾ with a dammah on the ba'. It has been said: it is a dialect, so this is not an assimilation (ittiba'), and it is by omitting a noun (hadhf mudaf), meaning: "Indeed, the appointed time of their destruction is the dawn." It is narrated that Lut, peace be upon him, said: "I want it sooner than that," and the angels said to him: ﴿Is not the dawn near?﴾ The dawn was made the appointed time for their destruction, because souls are most at rest in it and comfort is most complete in it.

It is narrated that Lut went out with his two daughters, with no one with him besides them, at the rising of dawn, and Allah folded the earth for him at that time until he was saved and reached Ibrahim, peace be upon them both. The pronoun in ﴿'aliyaha﴾ refers to the cities of the people of Lut. Jibril placed his wing beneath them, then lifted them up to the sky, until the people of heaven heard the barking of dogs and the crowing of roosters, then he overturned them upon them, and they were followed by stones from above. They are the mu'tafikat (overturned cities): seven cities. It has been said: five, which the exegetes counted, but there is a difficulty in determining them, so I have omitted mentioning them. Sadum was in the greatest town. ﴿And We rained upon it﴾ means upon its people. It is narrated that the stones struck those of them who were outside their cities, until they killed them all. It is also narrated that a man was in the Sacred Precinct (haram), and the stone remained suspended in the air until he went out of the Sacred Precinct, and then the stone killed him.

Abu al-'Aliyah and Ibn Zayd said: "Sijjil is the name of the lowest heaven." This is weak, because it is described as ﴿manduad﴾ (layered), and its explanation was mentioned in the lexical discussion. It has been said: it is from asjalahu, when he sent it; it has been said: it is from what Allah wrote that He would punish with it from the sijjil (register), and sajjala li-fulan (he recorded for so-and-so). The meaning of this word is: water and clay. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, al-Suddi, and others. They held that the stones with which they were struck were like baked brick. It has been said: a stone mixed with clay (p-250), that is, stone and clay, and this may refer back to baked brick. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Shadid (hard) among stones means solid." ﴿Musawwamatan 'inda rabbika﴾ (marked): marked with a sign by which it is known that they are not stones of the earth. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

'Ikrimah and Qatadah said: "There was whiteness in them." It has been said: "Written on each stone is the name of the one it was thrown at." This was said by al-Rabi'.

From Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan: whiteness with redness. Also from Ibn 'Abbas: the stone is white with a black spot, and black with a white spot. From 'Ikrimah and Qatadah also: in them are red streaks in the shape of a jiz' (a kind of striped stone). It has been said: they were like the heads of camels, and like the resting places of camels.

It has been said: "the handful of a man." Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: the meaning of ﴿min 'inda rabbika﴾ is: they came from before your Lord. It has been said: "prepared with your Lord," said by Abu Bakr al-Hudhali. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning is: this marking was attached to the stones with Allah, as a notice of the penetration of His power and the severity of His punishment.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿wa-ma hiya﴾ refers to the cities whose upper parts Allah made lower. The meaning is: the very essence of these cities lay between Medina and Syria, over which the Quraysh pass on their journeys, so looking at them and in them is a lesson and a warning. It has been said: it refers to the stones, since it is the nearest thing mentioned. Ibn 'Abbas said: "And their punishment is not far from those who do the deeds they did." The apparent meaning is the general sense of "the wrongdoers." It has been said: the Quraysh are meant by it.

In a hadith: "There will come among my community a sinking (khasf), and a transformation (maskh), and being struck with stones." It has been said: the idolaters of the Arabs. It has been said: the people of Lut, meaning the stones would not miss them. In a hadith: "There will come at the end of my community a people whose men are content with men and whose women with women; so when that happens, expect the punishment of the people of Lut: that Allah sends upon them stones of sijjil." Then he recited: ﴿And it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾.

If the pronoun in His saying "wa-ma hiya" refers to the stones, then it may be meant: "not with a far thing," and it may be meant: "not with a far place," because although they are in the sky, which is a far place, when they fall from it they are the swiftest thing to overtake the one struck, so it is as if they were in a place near to him.

The answer to it is reported in a statement from al-Mubarrad, that the prohibition was intended only for Lut alone, and that looking back was negated for them. The meaning is: do not let any one of them look back. This is like saying to a man: 'Let none of these people stand up,' while those (the ones referred to) did not hear you. The meaning is: do not let any one of these stand up, and standing up is negated for those referred to."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Regarding her departure with his family there are two reports. It is narrated that he took her out with them and was commanded that none of them should look back except her. When she heard the crash of the punishment, she looked back and said: 'Oh, my people!' and a stone overtook her and killed her. It is also narrated that he was commanded to leave her with her people, and her inclination was toward them, and he did not travel with her."

The difference between the two readings corresponds to the difference between the two reports. End of quote. It has been said: it is a dialect, so this is not an assimilation (ittiba'), and it is by omitting a noun (hadhf mudaf), meaning: "Indeed, the appointed time of their destruction is the dawn." Jibril placed his wing beneath them, then lifted them up to the sky, until the people of heaven heard the barking of dogs and the crowing of roosters, then he overturned them upon them, and they were followed by stones from above. They are the mu'tafikat (overturned cities): seven cities. It has been said: five, which the exegetes counted, but there is a difficulty in determining them, so I have omitted mentioning them. Sadum was in the greatest town. ﴿And We rained upon it﴾ means upon its people. It is narrated that the stones struck those of them who were outside their cities, until they killed them all. It is also narrated that a man was in the Sacred Precinct (haram), and the stone remained suspended in the air until he went out of the Sacred Precinct, and then the stone killed him.

Abu al-'Aliyah and Ibn Zayd said: "Sijjil is the name of the lowest heaven." This is weak, because it is described as ﴿manduad﴾ (layered), and its explanation was mentioned in the lexical discussion. It has been said: it is from asjalahu, when he sent it; it has been said: it is from what Allah wrote that He would punish with it from the sijjil (register), and sajjala li-fulan (he recorded for so-and-so). The meaning of this word is: water and clay. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, al-Suddi, and others. They held that the stones with which they were struck were like baked brick. It has been said: a stone mixed with clay (p-250), that is, stone and clay, and this may refer back to baked brick. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Shadid (hard) among stones means solid." ﴿Musawwamatan 'inda rabbika﴾ (marked): marked with a sign by which it is known that they are not stones of the earth. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

'Ikrimah and Qatadah said: "There was whiteness in them." It has been said: "Written on each stone is the name of the one it was thrown at." This was said by al-Rabi'.

From Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan: whiteness with redness. Also from Ibn 'Abbas: the stone is white with a black spot, and black with a white spot. From 'Ikrimah and Qatadah also: in them are red streaks in the shape of a jiz' (a kind of striped stone). It has been said: they were like the heads of camels, and like the resting places of camels.

It has been said: "the handful of a man." Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: the meaning of ﴿min 'inda rabbika﴾ is: they came from before your Lord. It has been said: "prepared with your Lord," said by Abu Bakr al-Hudhali. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning is: this marking was attached to the stones with Allah, as a notice of the penetration of His power and the severity of His punishment.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿wa-ma hiya﴾ refers to the cities whose upper parts Allah made lower. The meaning is: the very essence of these cities lay between Medina and Syria, over which the Quraysh pass on their journeys, so looking at them and in them is a lesson and a warning. It has been said: it refers to the stones, since it is the nearest thing mentioned. Ibn 'Abbas said: "And their punishment is not far from those who do the deeds they did." The apparent meaning is the general sense of "the wrongdoers." It has been said: the Quraysh are meant by it.

In a hadith: "There will come among my community a sinking (khasf), and a transformation (maskh), and being struck with stones." It has been said: the idolaters of the Arabs. It has been said: the people of Lut, meaning the stones would not miss them. In a hadith: "There will come at the end of my community a people whose men are content with men and whose women with women; so when that happens, expect the punishment of the people of Lut: that Allah sends upon them stones of sijjil." Then he recited: ﴿And it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾.

If the pronoun in His saying "wa-ma hiya" refers to the stones, then it may be meant: "not with a far thing," and it may be meant: "not with a far place," because although they are in the sky, which is a far place, when they fall from it they are the swiftest thing to overtake the one struck, so it is as if they were in a place near to him.

(p-248) It is narrated that when Lut, peace be upon him, was overpowered and they tried to break down the door while he was holding it shut, the messengers said to him: "Step aside from the door," and he stepped aside. The door was flung open, and Jibril, peace be upon him, struck them with his wing, blinding their eyes. They were blinded and turned back on their heels, saying: "Salvation! Salvation! It is also narrated that Jibril dug through the crevices of the door and cast (dust) into their eyes, and they became blind. It has been said that he took a handful of dust and scattered it in their faces, and it reached the eyes of everyone near and far from that dust, so their eyes were obliterated. They could not find the way, nor could they find their own houses. It has been said that they broke down his door and rushed upon him, and Jibril did to them what he did.

The sentence ﴿they will not reach you﴾ clarifies what precedes it, because when they are the messengers of Allah, they will not be able to reach him, and they have no power to harm him. Then they commanded him to travel by night with his family. The two Harami readers (Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr) read ﴿fa-asri﴾ (with a hamzat al-wasl, i.e., "travel by night", from the root sara) and "an asri" with the alif of sara joined, while the rest of the Seven read ﴿bi-qit'in﴾ (with a hamzat al-qat', i.e., "set out"). His family: his two daughters and a small group of the believers.

﴿with a portion of the night﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: "with a part of the night." Al-Dahhak said: "with the remainder of its last part." Qatadah said: "after the passing of a part of it." Ibn al-A'rabi said: "that is, an hour of the night." It has been said: "with darkness." It has been said: "it is half of it," and it has been said: "it is the midpoint of the night, taken from cutting it into two halves." The poet said:

*"And a wailing woman wails in a portion of the night, over a man by the stony ground of the open land."*

Muhammad ibn Ziyad said: "It is the pre-dawn (al-sahar), because of His saying: ﴿We delivered them at dawn﴾." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is possible that he traveled with his family from the beginning of the night until he passed the uprooted city, and his deliverance occurred at dawn. Thus this verse agrees with His saying: ﴿except the family of Lut; We delivered them at dawn﴾ [al-Qamar: 34]." End of quote.

Ibn al-Anbari said: "The word qit' in the sense of qit'ah (portion) is specific to the night; one does not say, 'I have a qit' of the cloth.'" Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿except your wife﴾ with a raised case (ill-a imra'atuka, as a nominative), while the rest of the Seven read it in the accusative (illa imra'atak). The accusative is explained as an exception from ﴿your family﴾ (bi-ahlika), since before it there is a command, and a command is regarded by them as obligatory. The accusative is necessarily required as an exception from "your family" in the reading of 'Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud), since in his recitation and his codex the phrase ﴿and let none of you look back﴾ is absent. The nominative is explained as a substitute (badal) for "anyone," and it is a connected exception. When you make the woman an exception from 'anyone,' it must be that the woman was permitted to look back, which would give the meaning of the verse..." — meaning the sense would become: "except your wife," since she was not forbidden from looking back.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verses 84–86:

﴿To Madyan (We sent) their brother Shu'ayb. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Do not diminish the measure and the balance. Indeed I see you in prosperity, and indeed I fear for you the punishment of an all-encompassing day."﴾ ﴿"And O my people, give full measure and balance with justice, and do not deprive people of their things, and do not commit corruption on the earth, causing corruption."﴾ ﴿"What remains with Allah is better for you, if you are believers. And I am not a guardian over you."﴾

[p. 251]

Al-Rahṭ (the group): Ibn 'Attiyya said: the group of a man. It was also said: al-rahṭ and al-rahit are names for what is fewer than ten men, and al-rahṭ, al-'usba and al-nafar apply only to men.

Al-Zamakhshari said: from three to ten. It was also said: up to nine. It is pluralised as arhuṭ, and arhuṭ is pluralised as arahit, so it is a plural of a plural. Al-Rummani said: the root meaning of al-rahṭ is "binding tightly." From it comes al-rahir, meaning intense eating. And al-rahit is the name for the burrow of the jerboa, because it secures itself with it and hides its young in it.

Al-Warid: Ibn al-Sikkit said: it is the coming of a people to water. Al-warid also means the camels that come to water. Thus it is a verbal noun meaning "the coming," and in meaning it is also like the passive participle, as in al-ṭaḥn meaning "the thing ground."

Rafada al-rajul yarfiduhu rafdan wa rifdan: he gave him and helped him. From rafada al-ha'iṭ: he propped up the wall. From al-Asma'i: al-rafd with a fatḥa is the cup, and al-rifd with a kasra is what is in the cup of drink. Al-Layth said: the root of al-rafd is giving and aid, and from it comes the rifada of Quraysh. It is said rafadahu yarfiduhu rifdan and rafdan, with the ra' either kasra or fatḥa. It is said that with the kasra it is the noun and with the fatḥa it is the verbal noun.

Al-Tatbib: al-takhsir (ruin, making someone lose). Tabba: he lost, and tabbahu: he made him lose. Labid said:

> "I have been tested, and every companion of freshness is tested by a stick, and that is al-tatbib."

Al-Zafir and al-Shahiq: The lexicographers among the Kufans and Basrans claimed that al-zafir is like the beginning of a donkey's cry, and al-shahiq is like the end of its bray. Ru'ba said:

> "It rattled in the chest as a neigh and gasped, until it is said he brays, though he has not brayed."

Ibn Faris said: al-shahiq is the opposite of al-zafir, because al-shahiq is the return of breath, and al-zafir is the expulsion of breath from intense running. It is derived from al-zafr, which is carrying on the back because of its heaviness. Al-Shammakh said:

> "Far in its extent of modulation is the first of its sound, a zafir, followed by a rattling shahiq."

Al-Shahiq is a long, extended breath, derived from their saying jabal shahiq, meaning tall. Al-Layth said: al-zafir is when a man fills his chest while in severe distress, and then expels the breath. Al-shahiq is when he expels that breath forcefully. It is said: he has a great zafra (sigh).

Al-Shaqa': hardship of life and its badness. It is said: shaqa yashqa shaqa'an, shiqwatan, shaqawatan. Its opposite is al-sa'āda (happiness), from which: sa'ida yas'adu. Both can be made transitive with the hamza, so it is said: ashqāhu Allah (may Allah make him wretched) and as'adahu Allah (may Allah make him happy). The reading shaqū (Q 11:106) and su'idū (Q 11:108) with a ḍamma on the shin and the sin has been transmitted, which shows that they can be transitive. From it come the phrases mas'ud. It is reported that al-Farra' related that the Hudhayl say sa'idahu Allah meaning as'adahu. Al-Jawhari said: sa'ida with a kasra is sa'id, like salima is salim, and sa'ida is mas'ud.

Abu Nasr 'Abd al-Rahim al-Qushayri said: warada sa'idahu Allah, so he is mas'ud, and as'adahu Allah, so he is mus'ad.

Al-Jadhdh: cutting, with the dotted and undotted letters. Ibn Qutayba said: jadhadhtu and jadadtu, and the dhal form is more common. Al-Nabigha said:

> "She cuts the double-woven Salukī, and kindles with the flint the fire of al-Ḥubāḥib."

[p. 252]

"And to Madyan (We sent) their brother Shu'ayb. He said: O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Do not diminish the measure and the balance. Indeed I see you in prosperity, and indeed I fear for you the punishment of an all-encompassing day." "And O my people, give full measure and balance with justice, and do not deprive people of their things, and do not commit corruption on the earth, causing corruption." "What remains with Allah is better for you, if you are believers. And I am not a guardian over you":

The people of Shu'ayb were idol-worshippers, and he called them to worship Allah alone. By disbelief they deserved punishment. Allah did not punish a community with a punishment of annihilation except for disbelief. If sin was added to that, it was a follower. Ibn 'Abbas said: "in prosperity" means in cheap prices.

The punishment of the all-encompassing day is the arrival of a destructive famine. This interpretation accords with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "No people diminish the measure and the balance except that provision is lifted from them." By his saying "in prosperity" he drew attention to the cause that requires fulfilment, not to the cause of diminishing. Al-Rahṭ (the group): Ibn 'Attiyya said: the group of a man. It was also said: al-rahṭ and al-rahit are names for what is fewer than ten men, and al-rahṭ, al-'usba and al-nafar apply only to men.

Al-Zamakhshari said: from three to ten. It was also said: up to nine. It is pluralised as arhuṭ, and arhuṭ is pluralised as arahit, so it is a plural of a plural. Al-Rummani said: the root meaning of al-rahṭ is "binding tightly." From it comes al-rahir, meaning intense eating. And al-rahit is the name for the burrow of the jerboa, because it secures itself with it and hides its young in it.

Al-Warid: Ibn al-Sikkit said: it is the coming of a people to water. Al-warid also means the camels that come to water. Thus it is a verbal noun meaning "the coming," and in meaning it is also like the passive participle, as in al-ṭaḥn meaning "the thing ground."

It is said that with the kasra it is the noun and with the fatḥa it is the verbal noun.

Al-Tatbib: al-takhsir (ruin, making someone lose). Tabba: he lost, and tabbahu: he made him lose. Labid said:

Al-Zafir and al-Shahiq: The lexicographers among the Kufans and Basrans claimed that al-zafir is like the beginning of a donkey's cry, and al-shahiq is like the end of its bray. Ru'ba said:

> "It rattled in the chest as a neigh and gasped, until it is said he brays, though he has not brayed."

> "Far in its extent of modulation is the first of its sound, a zafir, followed by a rattling shahiq."

Al-Shahiq is a long, extended breath, derived from their saying jabal shahiq, meaning tall. Al-Layth said: al-zafir is when a man fills his chest while in severe distress, and then expels the breath. Al-shahiq is when he expels that breath forcefully. It is said: he has a great zafra (sigh).

Abu Nasr 'Abd al-Rahim al-Qushayri said: warada sa'idahu Allah, so he is mas'ud, and as'adahu Allah, so he is mus'ad.

> "She cuts the double-woven Salukī, and kindles with the flint the fire of al-Ḥubāḥib."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verses 87–90:

(p. 253) ﴿They said, "O Shu'ayb, does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped, or that we do with our wealth as we please? Indeed, you are the forbearing, the rightly guided."﴾ ﴿He said, "O my people, tell me, if I am upon a clear proof from my Lord, and He has provided me with good provision from Him, (then how can I oppose you?) And I do not intend to oppose you in what I forbid you. I intend only reform, as much as I am able. My success is only through Allah. Upon Him I rely, and to Him I turn."﴾ ﴿And O my people, let not my opposition cause you to incur the like of what befell the people of Noah, or the people of Hud, or the people of Salih. And the people of Lot are not far from you.﴾ ﴿And seek forgiveness from your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance. Indeed, my Lord is Merciful, Loving.﴾

When Shu'ayb commanded them to worship Allah and abandon the worship of their idols, and to give full measure in weight and measure, they answered him mockingly and derisively, saying: ﴿does your prayer…﴾ Shu'ayb was known for much prayer, and whenever he prayed they would wink at one another and laugh.

﴿that we abandon what our fathers worshipped﴾ corresponds to his saying: ﴿Worship Allah; you have no god other than Him﴾ [Hud: 84]. ﴿or that we do with our wealth as we please﴾ corresponds to his saying: ﴿And do not diminish the measure and the balance﴾ [Hud: 84]. That the prayer is said to "command" is figurative, just as it "forbids" in His saying: ﴿Indeed, prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing﴾ [al-Ankabut: 45]. Or it may be said that it commands what is good and right, meaning it calls to it and prompts it.

However, they framed their speech in the manner of mockery, making the prayer the one that commands, as a sarcastic mockery of his prayer. The meaning is: "your command to us is to abandon," so the genitive term is omitted, because a person is not commanded to do another's act. The apparent sense is that "prayer" refers to the prayer known in that religious law. Al-Hasan said: "Allah did not send any prophet without making prayer and zakat obligatory upon him." It was also said: "your recitation" is meant; it was said: "your mosques"; it was said: "your supplications." Ibn Wathhab, al-Akhawan, and Hafs read ﴿أصَلاتُكَ﴾ (aṣalātuka) in the singular. The majority read ﴿أوْ أنْ نَفْعَلَ في أمْوالِنا ما نَشاءُ﴾ with nun in both places. Al-Dahhak ibn Qays, Ibn Abi 'Abla, and Zayd ibn 'Ali read with ta' in both places, as second-person address, and it is reported from Abu 'Abd al-Rahman.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and Talha read ﴿نَفْعَلُ﴾ with nun and ﴿ما تَشاءُ﴾ with ta', as second-person address, and it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas. Whoever reads with nun in both places, then His saying ﴿أوْ أنْ نَفْعَلَ﴾ is conjoined to ﴿ما يَعْبُدُ﴾, meaning: "that we abandon what our fathers worshipped and that we do with our wealth as we please." Whoever reads with ta' in both places, or with nun in both places, then it is conjoined to ﴿أنْ نَتْرُكَ﴾, meaning: "your command is to abandon what our fathers worshipped, and to do, with our wealth, what you please," or "and what we do with our wealth, what you please." Here ﴿أوْ﴾ is for variety, meaning: "it commands you once with this, and once with that." It was also said that it has the sense of "and" (waw).

The apparent meaning is that what they used to do with their wealth was the cheating in measure and weight mentioned above. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: it was their clipping of the dinar and the dirham, and passing that off alongside sound coins by way of deception. And from Ibn al-Musayyab: the cutting of dinars and dirhams is among the corruption on earth.

It was also said: the altering of the minting dies, by which the wealth of people is consumed. Whoever reads with ta' in both places, or in ﴿نَشاءُ﴾, the apparent meaning is the giving of full measure in weight and balance. Sufyan al-Thawri said: he used to command them to pay zakat.

As for His saying ﴿إنَّكَ لَأنْتَ الحَلِيمُ الرَّشِيدُ﴾: its apparent sense is that it is a report from them about him, with these two beautiful qualities. It is possible that they meant it literally: that you are indeed characterized by these two qualities; so how did you come to this matter of opposing the religion of our fathers and what they were upon, when one like you, his forbearance and rightness should prevent him from that? Or it is possible that they meant: "you are the forbearing, the rightly guided" according to your own claim, since you command us with what you command. Or it is possible they said that as mockery and derision, as Qatadah said. Or they said that in a manner of contempt for him, as a man says to his companion when he pays no heed to his speech: "I do not know what you are saying." This came in relation to the addressees, as in His saying: ﴿Say, O my people, act according to your position﴾ [Al-An'am: 135], as it came here.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): what is the matter with the two stories of 'Ad and Madyan, that they came with the waw, while the two middle stories came with the fa'? The explanation of the like of ﴿And when Our command came﴾ [Hud: 58] up to His saying ﴿as if they had never prospered therein﴾ [Hud: 68] has preceded. Al-Sulami and Abu Haywa read ﴿kama ba'idat﴾ with a damma on the ʿayn, from al-bu'd (distance), which is the opposite of nearness; the majority (p-258) read it with a kasra. Al-Nahhas said: what is known in the language is ba'uda yab'udu bu'dan and ba'adan when he perished. Al-Mahdawi said: ba'uda is used for good and evil, while ba'ida is used for evil only.

They say, "Do not perish," while they bury me,
and where is the place of perishing except my place?

And "distance to so-and-so" is a supplication against him, and it is only used against a hated one, like your saying: "Destruction to the disbelievers."

The people of the science of eloquence said: no digression (istitrad) occurs in the Qur'an except in this place. Istitrad (digression), they said, is that you praise a thing or disparage it, then at the end of the speech you come with something which is your aim at the beginning. Hassan said:

If you are lying in what you told me,
then you have escaped like al-Harith ibn Hisham's escape.

He left the beloved ones to fight in their defense,
and escaped with the head of a swift horse and its bridle.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 11, verses 96–99**

﴿And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs and a manifest authority﴾ ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs. But they followed the command of Pharaoh, and the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾ ﴿He will precede his people on the Day of Resurrection and bring them to the Fire, and wretched is the watering place to which they are brought﴾ ﴿And they were made to follow a curse in this world and on the Day of Resurrection. Wretched is the gift that is given﴾: The signs are the nine miracles: the staff, the hand, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, and a loss of wealth, lives and crops. Some of them replaced the loss with the overshadowing of the mountain.

It is said that the signs are the Torah. This is not correct, because He said ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾, and the Torah was revealed only after the destruction of Pharaoh and his chiefs. The manifest authority (sultan mubin) is the clear proofs. It is possible that by His saying ﴿and a manifest authority﴾ He means: in them, i.e., in the signs, which indicate the truthfulness of Musa, peace be upon him. It is also possible that He means by them the staff, because it is the most dazzling of those signs, so it was singled out by name, just as Gabriel and Michael were singled out by name after the mention of the angels, as an honour through mention. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿the command of Pharaoh﴾ is his command to them to disbelieve and to deny the miracles of Musa. It is possible that He means: the way and the affair.

﴿And the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾: He negated right guidance from him, and this is a declaration of the ignorance of his followers, since they backed him in his affair. It is a clear misguidance that is hidden from no one who has even a little intellect. That is because he claimed divinity while he was a human like them. They witnessed the signs and the manifest authority in the matter of Musa, peace be upon him, and they knew that with him was guidance and truth. Then they turned away from following him to following one who had no guidance in being followed.

It is possible that ﴿rashid﴾ [Hud: 78] means rashid in the sense of rashid (rightly guided), and that rashid here means murshid (one who guides), i.e., one who guides to good. Pharaoh was a dahri (materialist), denying the Creator and the Return, and he used to say: there is no god for the world, and it is only obligatory for the people of every land to occupy themselves with obeying their ruler. Therefore his command was entirely devoid of right guidance. Rushd (right guidance) is used for everything that is praised and approved, and ghayy (error) is its opposite. It is said: Zayd preceded the people (qadama Zaydun al-qawma yaqdumu qadman wa-quduman), meaning he went before them. The meaning is: he will precede his people, who are drowned, into the Fire. Just as he was a model in misguidance who was followed, so he goes before them into the Fire while they follow him. It is possible that His saying ﴿rashid﴾ means: with a praiseworthy outcome, and that His saying ﴿He will precede his people﴾ is an explanation and clarification of it, i.e., how can the command of one whose outcome is this be rightly guided? He turned from saying "fa-yuridahum" to ﴿fa-awradahum﴾ (and He brought them) because of the certainty of its occurrence without doubt, as if it had already occurred, and because of the terror and warning in that.

Or it may be a past tense in reality, i.e., He brought them into the Fire in this world, meaning its cause, which is disbelief. What makes this interpretation unlikely is the fa' (the "then" of fa-awradahum). The wurud (coming to) in this verse is the wurud of entering in eternity, not the wurud of arriving at something and reaching it, as in His saying ﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾ [al-Qasas: 23]. It is possible that the Fire is what befalls him according to i'mal al-thani (the operation of the second of two competing verbs), because it is in tanazu' (grammatical contention) with yaqdumu, i.e., "to the Fire" and "fa-awradahum." So the second was made to operate, and the object of the first was omitted.

The hamza in fa-awradahum is for ta'diya (making the verb transitive). Warada is transitive to one object, and when the hamza was added it became transitive to two, so it includes "warid" (the one who brings) and "mawrud" (the one brought). The term al-wird is applied to the one who arrives (al-warid), so al-wird is not the mawrud itself. Therefore an ellipsis was needed to match the agent of بِئْسَ (bi'sa, "how wretched"), which is the subject of dispraise. The estimate is: وَبِئْسَ مَكانُ الوِرْدِ المَوْرُودُ (wa-bi'sa makanu al-wirdi al-mawrud), meaning: the Fire. So al-wird is the agent of bi'sa, and the object of dispraise (al-makhsus bi'l-dhamm) is al-mawrud, which is the Fire. The case of al-mawrud is the same as the case of Zayd in your saying: بِئْسَ الرَّجُلُ زَيْدٌ (bi'sa al-rajulu Zaydun, "how wretched the man is, Zayd").

Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu al-Baqa' allowed that al-mawrud could be an adjective of al-wird, i.e., "how wretched is the place of the watering to which they come, the Fire," with the object of dispraise omitted because the meaning is understood, just as it was omitted in His saying ﴿so how wretched is the resting place﴾ [Sad: 56]. This reading is based on the permissibility of describing the agent of نِعْمَ (ni'ma) and بِئْسَ (bi'sa), and there is disagreement about this. Ibn al-Sarraj and al-Farisi held that it is not permitted. Al-Zamakhshari said: "al-wird al-mawrud is the watering to which they came. He likened him to the forerunner who precedes the arriving party to the water, and likened their following him to the arriving party. Then it was said: how wretched is the watering that they come to, which is the Fire, because the watering is only brought for quenching thirst and cooling the livers, and the Fire is its opposite." End of quotation.

His saying "al-wird al-mawrud" (applying wird to mawrud) is majaz (figurative usage), since they transmitted that the word can be a masdar in the sense of wurud (arrival), or in the sense of al-warida min al-ibil (a group of camels coming to water). Its estimate, "bi'sa al-wirdu alladhi yaridunahu al-nar" (how wretched is the watering place that they come to, the Fire), indicates that al-mawrud is an adjective of al-wird, that the object of dispraise is omitted, and therefore he estimated it as "al-nar" (the Fire).

We have mentioned that this is based on the permissibility of describing the agent of bi'sa and ni'ma. It is said that the estimate is: بِئْسَ القَوْمُ المَوْرُودُ بِهِمْ هُمْ (bi'sa al-qawmu al-mawrudu bihim hum, "how wretched are the people brought to it, they"). In this case al-wird refers to the arriving group, al-mawrud is an adjective for them, and the object of dispraise is the omitted pronoun hum. That is then a dispraise of those who arrive, not a dispraise of the place of arrival.

The reference in His saying "fi hadhihi" (in this) is to the world, and it appears explicitly in the story of Hud. His saying ﴿and on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Hud: 60] indicates it, because that is the Hereafter. So yawma (on the day) is conjoined to the position of fi hadhihi, and the meaning is: they were made to follow a curse in this world and on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Kalbi said: ﴿a curse in this﴾ is from the believers or by drowning, and ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾ is from the angels or by the Fire. Mujahid said: for them are two curses. Some people held that the division is that they have a curse in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection they are given with it (yarfidun bihi), so it is one curse first and a wretched giving afterward. End of quotation.

This is not correct, because this interpretation indicates that yawma al-qiyama is an object of بِئْسَ (bi'sa), and بِئْسَ does not inflect (it is a fixed verb of dispraise), so its object does not precede it. If yawma al-qiyama were delayed, it would be valid, as the poet said:

*"And how excellent is the padding of the coat of mail when you are called to the fray and plunge into terror."*

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Bi'sa al-rifdu al-marfud rifduhum," i.e., how wretched is the aid that is aided. The curse in this world is an aid to the punishment and a reinforcement of it, and they were aided with a curse in the Hereafter. It is also said: how wretched is the gift that is given. It appears from his words that al-marfud is an adjective of al-rifd, and the object of dispraise is omitted, its estimate being "rifduhum" (their aid). As for his explanation, i.e., "bi'sa al-'awnu al-mu'an" (how wretched is the helper who is helped), it is the saying of Abu 'Ubayda. The punishment was called rifd in the manner of their saying: تَحِيَّةُ بَيْنِهِمْ ضَرْبٌ وَجِيعُ (tahiyyatu baynihim darbun wajee', "their greeting among them is a painful blow"). Al-Kalbi said: al-rifd is al-rifada (the act of aiding), i.e., how wretched is what they are aided with after drowning: the Fire.

The case of al-mawrud is the same as the case of Zayd in your saying: بِئْسَ الرَّجُلُ زَيْدٌ (bi'sa al-rajulu Zaydun, "how wretched the man is, Zayd").

Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu al-Baqa' allowed that al-mawrud could be an adjective of al-wird, i.e., "how wretched is the place of the watering to which they come, the Fire," with the object of dispraise omitted because the meaning is understood, just as it was omitted in His saying ﴿so how wretched is the resting place﴾ [Sad: 56]. This reading is based on the permissibility of describing the agent of نِعْمَ (ni'ma) and بِئْسَ (bi'sa), and there is disagreement about this. Ibn al-Sarraj and al-Farisi held that it is not permitted. Al-Zamakhshari said: "al-wird al-mawrud is the watering to which they came. He likened him to the forerunner who precedes the arriving party to the water, and likened their following him to the arriving party. Then it was said: how wretched is the watering that they come to, which is the Fire, because the watering is only brought for quenching thirst and cooling the livers, and the Fire is its opposite." End of quotation.

His saying "al-wird al-mawrud" (applying wird to mawrud) is majaz (figurative usage), since they transmitted that the word can be a masdar in the sense of wurud (arrival), or in the sense of al-warida min al-ibil (a group of camels coming to water). Its estimate, "bi'sa al-wirdu alladhi yaridunahu al-nar" (how wretched is the watering place that they come to, the Fire), indicates that al-mawrud is an adjective of al-wird, that the object of dispraise is omitted, and therefore he estimated it as "al-nar" (the Fire).

We have mentioned that this is based on the permissibility of describing the agent of bi'sa and ni'ma. It is said that the estimate is: بِئْسَ القَوْمُ المَوْرُودُ بِهِمْ هُمْ (bi'sa al-qawmu al-mawrudu bihim hum, "how wretched are the people brought to it, they"). In this case al-wird refers to the arriving group, al-mawrud is an adjective for them, and the object of dispraise is the omitted pronoun hum. That is then a dispraise of those who arrive, not a dispraise of the place of arrival.

The reference in His saying "fi hadhihi" (in this) is to the world, and it appears explicitly in the story of Hud. His saying ﴿and on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Hud: 60] indicates it, because that is the Hereafter. So yawma (on the day) is conjoined to the position of fi hadhihi, and the meaning is: they were made to follow a curse in this world and on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Kalbi said: ﴿a curse in this﴾ is from the believers or by drowning, and ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾ is from the angels or by the Fire. Mujahid said: for them are two curses. Some people held that the division is that they have a curse in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection they are given with it (yarfidun bihi), so it is one curse first and a wretched giving afterward. End of quotation.

This is not correct, because this interpretation indicates that yawma al-qiyama is an object of بِئْسَ (bi'sa), and بِئْسَ does not inflect (it is a fixed verb of dispraise), so its object does not precede it. If yawma al-qiyama were delayed, it would be valid, as the poet said:

*"And how excellent is the padding of the coat of mail when you are called to the fray and plunge into terror."*

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Bi'sa al-rifdu al-marfud rifduhum," i.e., how wretched is the aid that is aided. The curse in this world is an aid to the punishment and a reinforcement of it, and they were aided with a curse in the Hereafter. It is also said: how wretched is the gift that is given. It appears from his words that al-marfud is an adjective of al-rifd, and the object of dispraise is omitted, its estimate being "rifduhum" (their aid). As for his explanation, i.e., "bi'sa al-'awnu al-mu'an" (how wretched is the helper who is helped), it is the saying of Abu 'Ubayda. The punishment was called rifd in the manner of their saying: تَحِيَّةُ بَيْنِهِمْ ضَرْبٌ وَجِيعُ (tahiyyatu baynihim darbun wajee', "their greeting among them is a painful blow"). Al-Kalbi said: al-rifd is al-rifada (the act of aiding), i.e., how wretched is what they are aided with after drowning: the Fire.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 11, verses 96–99**

﴿And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs and a manifest authority﴾ ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs. But they followed the command of Pharaoh, and the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾ ﴿He will precede his people on the Day of Resurrection and bring them to the Fire, and wretched is the watering place to which they are brought﴾ ﴿And they were made to follow a curse in this world and on the Day of Resurrection. Wretched is the gift that is given﴾: The signs are the nine miracles: the staff, the hand, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, and a loss of wealth, lives and crops. Some of them replaced the loss with the overshadowing of the mountain.

It is said that the signs are the Torah. This is not correct, because He said ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾, and the Torah was revealed only after the destruction of Pharaoh and his chiefs. The manifest authority (sultan mubin) is the clear proofs. It is possible that by His saying ﴿and a manifest authority﴾ He means: in them, i.e., in the signs, which indicate the truthfulness of Musa, peace be upon him. It is also possible that He means by them the staff, because it is the most dazzling of those signs, so it was singled out by name, just as Gabriel and Michael were singled out by name after the mention of the angels, as an honour through mention. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿the command of Pharaoh﴾ is his command to them to disbelieve and to deny the miracles of Musa. It is possible that He means: the way and the affair.

﴿And the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾: He negated right guidance from him, and this is a declaration of the ignorance of his followers, since they backed him in his affair. It is a clear misguidance that is hidden from no one who has even a little intellect. That is because he claimed divinity while he was a human like them. They witnessed the signs and the manifest authority in the matter of Musa, peace be upon him, and they knew that with him was guidance and truth. Then they turned away from following him to following one who had no guidance in being followed.

It is possible that ﴿rashid﴾ [Hud: 78] means rashid in the sense of rashid (rightly guided), and that rashid here means murshid (one who guides), i.e., one who guides to good. Pharaoh was a dahri (materialist), denying the Creator and the Return, and he used to say: there is no god for the world, and it is only obligatory for the people of every land to occupy themselves with obeying their ruler. Therefore his command was entirely devoid of right guidance. Rushd (right guidance) is used for everything that is praised and approved, and ghayy (error) is its opposite. It is said: Zayd preceded the people (qadama Zaydun al-qawma yaqdumu qadman wa-quduman), meaning he went before them. The meaning is: he will precede his people, who are drowned, into the Fire. Just as he was a model in misguidance who was followed, so he goes before them into the Fire while they follow him. It is possible that His saying ﴿rashid﴾ means: with a praiseworthy outcome, and that His saying ﴿He will precede his people﴾ is an explanation and clarification of it, i.e., how can the command of one whose outcome is this be rightly guided? He turned from saying "fa-yuridahum" to ﴿fa-awradahum﴾ (and He brought them) because of the certainty of its occurrence without doubt, as if it had already occurred, and because of the terror and warning in that.

Or it may be a past tense in reality, i.e., He brought them into the Fire in this world, meaning its cause, which is disbelief. What makes this interpretation unlikely is the fa' (the "then" of fa-awradahum). The wurud (coming to) in this verse is the wurud of entering in eternity, not the wurud of arriving at something and reaching it, as in His saying ﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾ [al-Qasas: 23]. It is possible that the Fire is what befalls him according to i'mal al-thani (the operation of the second of two competing verbs), because it is in tanazu' (grammatical contention) with yaqdumu, i.e., "to the Fire" and "fa-awradahum." So the second was made to operate, and the object of the first was omitted.

The hamza in fa-awradahum is for ta'diya (making the verb transitive). Warada is transitive to one object, and when the hamza was added it became transitive to two, so it includes "warid" (the one who brings) and "mawrud" (the one brought). The term al-wird is applied to the one who arrives (al-warid), so al-wird is not the mawrud itself. ﴿That is from the news of the towns which We relate to you; some of them are standing and some are harvested.﴾ ﴿We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves. Their gods, whom they invoked besides Allah, did not avail them in anything when the command of your Lord came, and they added nothing to them but ruin.﴾: The reference of "that" (dhalika) is to what was mentioned earlier about the prophets and their peoples, and the punishments that befell them. That is, that report is some of the reports of the towns.

It is possible that "the towns" refers to the towns of those destroyed peoples mentioned earlier. It is also possible that "the towns" is general, meaning: this report related to you is the habit of cities when they disbelieved, so the contemporary cities are included. The pronoun in "minha" (of them) refers to "the towns."

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿qa'imun wa-hasidun﴾ (standing and harvested) means "inhabited, like *zaghir* and *dathir*," and this is based on the general interpretation of "the towns." Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj said: "standing of the walls and collapsed," and this is based on the particular interpretation, that these are the towns of those destroyed nations. Al-Zamakhshari said: some of them remain and some have been effaced, like a crop standing on its stalk and one that has been harvested.

This is the meaning of Qatadah's statement. Qatadah said: "standing of trace and effaced," making the harvesting of the crop a metaphor for annihilation. The poet said:

*And people, in the distribution of death among them,*
*are like a crop: of it, some standing and some harvested.*

Al-Dahhak said: (standing) means "not swallowed by the earth," and (harvested) means "swallowed." Ibn Ishaq said: (standing) means "not yet destroyed," and (harvested) means "destroyed." It was also said: standing means its offspring remain, and harvested means its offspring are cut off. This fits the reading that the estimate is: "that is from the reports of the people of the towns." It was also said that this is by omitting a modifier, meaning: "from the reports of the people of the towns," and this is supported by His saying ﴿and We did not wrong them﴾, so the pronoun returns to that omitted noun.

Al-Akhfash said: *hasid* means *mahsud* (harvested). Its plural is *hasda* and *hisad*, like *marda* and *mirad*. The pattern *fa'la* as a plural of *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul* (passive participle, "object") is typically used for rational beings, like *qatil* and *qatla*.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, what is the position (*mahall*, grammatical place) of this clause? I say: it is a fresh resumptive clause with no grammatical position." Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿minha qa'im﴾ is a *mubtada'* (grammatical subject of a nominal sentence) with a *khabar* (predicate), in the position of a *hal* (circumstantial clause) of the *ha'* in *naqussuhu*. And ﴿hasid﴾ is a *mubtada'* whose *khabar* is omitted, meaning "and of them is the harvested."

What he mentioned is figurative usage (*tajawwuz*), meaning: "We relate to you, while the state of the towns is that." The state is more forceful in warning and in striking an example for those present, i.e., We relate to you some of the reports of the towns, and they are in this state, witnessing Allah's act upon them.

﴿And We did not wrong them﴾, i.e., by destroying them. Rather, We placed on them the punishment they deserved, ﴿but they wronged themselves﴾ by placing disbelief in the place of faith and committing what led to their destruction.

It is apparent that His saying ﴿fa-ma aghnat﴾ (so they did not avail) is a negation, i.e., they did not repel any of Allah's might from them, nor were they of any benefit. (*Yad'una*, "they invoke") is a narration of a state, i.e., those they used to invoke, meaning they worshipped them, or they invoked them: al-Lat, al-Uzza, and Hubal. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿lamma﴾ (when) is governed by *aghnat* (availed). This is based on the view that *lamma* is a time adverb, which is contrary to the school of Sibawayh, since his view is that it is a particle (*harf*) of necessity for necessity. ﴿Amru rabbika﴾ (the command of your Lord) [Hud: 76] means His punishment and vengeance.

﴿And they added nothing to them﴾: the verb is treated as if the subject were rational beings, using the *waw* of the plural pronoun that is for rational beings, because they treated those gods as rational beings in their belief that they benefit, and in their worship of them.

*Tatbib* means loss. Ibn Zayd said: evil. Qatadah said: loss and destruction. Mujahid said: causing loss. It was also said: destruction. All of these are close in meaning. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the form of the idols' increasing *tatbib* can be understood as follows: their hope in them, their trust in them, and their toil in worshipping them occupied their souls from considering the law and its outcome, so punishment and loss befell them. As for their punishment for disbelief being increased because of it beyond the mere worship of idols, that is also possible.

(p-261)

﴿And thus is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are wrongdoers. Indeed, His seizure is painful and severe.﴾ ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for those who fear the punishment of the Hereafter. That is a Day on which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day witnessed.﴾ ﴿And We do not delay it except for a term counted.﴾ ﴿On the Day it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission; and among them are the wretched and the happy.﴾ I.e., like that seizing, the seizing of earlier nations by Allah, is the seizing of your Lord.

"The towns" is general for the wrongdoing towns, and wrongdoing includes the wrongdoing of disbelief and other wrongs. Allah may give respite to some disbelievers. As for wrongdoers in general, they are usually hastened to punishment. In a hadith: "Indeed Allah gives respite to the wrongdoer, until when He seizes him, He does not let him go," then he recited: ﴿And thus is the seizing of your Lord when...﴾

Abu Raja' and al-Jahdari recited ﴿wa-kadhalika akhdhu rabbika idha akhadha﴾ (And thus is the seizing of your Lord when He seized), with *akhdhu rabbika* as a verb and subject, and *idha* as an adverb referring to the past, and this is information about the habit of Allah regarding the destruction of earlier nations.

Talhah ibn Musarrif recited: ﴿wa-kadhalika akhadha rabbuka idha akhadha﴾. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this reading has a fully sound meaning, but the reading of the majority conveys warning and its continuity over time, which is the usual pattern of putting the future in the place of the past. ﴿Al-qura﴾ (the towns) is the *maf'ul* (grammatical object) of *akhadha* by the rule of *i'mal* (governing in grammar), since the verbal noun *akhdh* and the verb *akhadha* compete for it, and the second was made to govern it. ﴿Wa-hiya zalimah﴾ (while they are wrongdoers) is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*). ﴿Inna akhdhahu alim shadid﴾: "painful" means painful and difficult for the one seized. The *akhdh* here is the seizing of destruction.

﴿Indeed, in that﴾, i.e., in what Allah related of the reports of the earlier nations and their destruction, ﴿is a sign (la-ayah)﴾, meaning a clear indication, ﴿for those who fear the punishment of the Hereafter﴾. I.e., if they were punished in this world for denying the prophets and associating others with Allah, and this world is the abode of action, then being punished for that in the Hereafter, the abode of recompense, is more fitting. The prophets had reported the uprooting of those who denied them and associated others with Allah, and what they reported occurred exactly as they had said. This indicates that what they reported about resurrection and recompense is true beyond doubt.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿la-ayatan li-man khaf﴾ means a lesson for him, because he looks at what Allah brought upon the criminals in this world, and this is only a model of what is prepared for them in the Hereafter. When he sees its greatness and severity, he takes lesson from the great punishment that is promised, so it becomes admonition, a lesson, and subtle guidance to increase piety and fear of Allah. A similar verse is ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson for one who fears﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 26].

﴿That﴾ is a reference to the Day of Resurrection, indicated by His saying ﴿the punishment of the Hereafter﴾. ﴿Al-nas﴾ (mankind) is a *maf'ul* whose *fa'il* (agent) is not named (*maf'ul lam yusamma fa'iluhu*, passive object), and its raising is ﴿majmu'﴾ (gathered). Ibn 'Atiyyah permitted that ﴿al-nas﴾ be a *mubtada'* and ﴿majmu'﴾ be a fronted *khabar*, but this is far-fetched, because the pronoun in ﴿majmu'﴾ is singular, and by analogy with its grammatical case it would be *majmu'un*. The expression ﴿majmu' lahu al-nas﴾ (for which mankind is gathered) is a phrase for the gathering (*hashr*). ﴿Mashhud﴾ (witnessed) is general: the first and last generations witness it, of humans, jinn, angels, and animals, according to the majority.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, what is the benefit of choosing the *ism maf'ul* (passive participle) over its verb?" I say: it is because the passive participle indicates the stability of the meaning of gathering for that day, and that it must be an appointed set time for people to be gathered to it, and that it is the thing described by it as a necessary attribute. It is also more firmly established as the attribution of gathering to people, and that they cannot escape it, and there is in it a firmness and stability of description that the verb does not have. The meaning of ﴿mashhud﴾ is "witnessed in it." The prepositional phrase was extended, and the verb was connected to the pronoun, treating it as a *maf'ul bihi* (direct object) by poetic extension, as in the verse:

*And a day we witnessed it, Sulaym and 'Amir.*

The meaning is that the creatures witness the standing place, and no one is absent from it. From this comes the saying: "For so-and-so there is a witnessed gathering," and "a present feast" (*ma'hur*). The day was not described as "witnessed" in itself, as in ﴿whoever of you witnesses the month﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], because the purpose is to describe that day with terror and greatness, and to distinguish it from other days. Its being witnessed in itself would not distinguish it, since it is like all other days in being witnessed.

﴿And We do not delay it﴾, i.e., that day. It was also said that it refers to the recompense, as al-Hawfi said. ﴿Except for a term counted﴾, i.e., for a prior decree that has already been executed, with a limited term that it neither precedes nor lags behind.

Al-A'mash recited ﴿wa-ma yu'akhkhiruhu﴾ with a *ya'* (as a pronoun for Allah). The two grammarians (*al-nahwiyan*) and Nafi' recited ﴿ya'ti﴾ with the *ya'* affirmed in connected speech and omitted in pause. Ibn Kathir affirmed it both in connection and in pause. It is firmly attested in the codex of Ubayy. The remaining seven read it without the *ya'*, both connected and in pause. It is absent from the codex of Imam 'Uthman. Al-A'mash also read ﴿ya'tun﴾ (with the plural *nun*), and this is also in the codex of 'Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud). Affirming the *ya'* in both connection and pause is the preferred reading. The reason for omitting it in pause is assimilation to the verse-endings (*fawasil*), and in connected speech it is lightness, as they say "*la adri wa-la ubali*" (I don't know and I don't care).

Al-Zamakhshari said that replacing the *ya'* with a *kasrah* is common in the dialect of Hudhayl. Al-Tabari cited:

*Your palm is a palm that cannot part with a dirham in generosity,*
*and another [palm] gives blood by the sword.*

It is apparent that the *fa'il* (subject) of ﴿ya'ti﴾ is a pronoun referring to what the pronoun in ﴿nu'akhkhiruhu﴾ refers to, namely ﴿dhalika yawmun﴾ (that is a day), and its governing word (*nasib*) is ﴿la tukallamu﴾ (no soul shall speak). The meaning: no soul speaks on the day that day comes except by His permission, and this is from the magnitude of awe and terror on that day. A parallel is ﴿They do not speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits﴾ [al-Naba: 38], and it governs in the same way as ﴿The day the Spirit and the angels stand in rows﴾ [al-Naba: 38]. The meaning of "the day's coming" is the coming of its terrors and hardships, since a day cannot be the time for the coming of another day.

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the *fa'il* of ﴿ya'ti﴾ be a pronoun referring to Allah, as in ﴿Do they await except that Allah should come to them?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210], or ﴿your Lord comes﴾, and ﴿your Lord came﴾. He supported this with the reading ﴿ma yu'akhkhiruhu﴾ with the *ya'*, and with His saying ﴿bi-idhnihi﴾ (by His permission). He also permitted that ﴿yawma ya'ti﴾ be governed by ﴿udhkur﴾ (remember), or by the implied verb "ends" in ﴿illa li-ajalin ma'dud﴾, i.e., the term ends on the day it comes.

Al-Hawfi permitted that ﴿la tukallamu﴾ be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun of the day mentioned earlier in ﴿mashhud﴾, or an adjective, since the noun is indefinite. The estimate is: no soul speaks in it on the day it comes except by His permission.

Al-Zamakhshari said that replacing the *ya'* with a *kasrah* is common in the dialect of Hudhayl. Al-Tabari cited:

*Your palm is a palm that cannot part with a dirham in generosity,*
*and another [palm] gives blood by the sword.*
