Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this reading has a fully sound meaning, but the reading of the majority conveys warning and its continuity over time, which is the usual pattern of putting the future in the place of the past. ﴿Al-qura﴾ (the towns) is the *maf'ul* (grammatical object) of *akhadha* by the rule of *i'mal* (governing in grammar), since the verbal noun *akhdh* and the verb *akhadha* compete for it, and the second was made to govern it. ﴿Wa-hiya zalimah﴾ (while they are wrongdoers) is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*). ﴿Inna akhdhahu alim shadid﴾: "painful" means painful and difficult for the one seized. The *akhdh* here is the seizing of destruction.

﴿Indeed, in that﴾, i.e., in what Allah related of the reports of the earlier nations and their destruction, ﴿is a sign (la-ayah)﴾, meaning a clear indication, ﴿for those who fear the punishment of the Hereafter﴾. I.e., if they were punished in this world for denying the prophets and associating others with Allah, and this world is the abode of action, then being punished for that in the Hereafter, the abode of recompense, is more fitting. The prophets had reported the uprooting of those who denied them and associated others with Allah, and what they reported occurred exactly as they had said. This indicates that what they reported about resurrection and recompense is true beyond doubt.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿la-ayatan li-man khaf﴾ means a lesson for him, because he looks at what Allah brought upon the criminals in this world, and this is only a model of what is prepared for them in the Hereafter. When he sees its greatness and severity, he takes lesson from the great punishment that is promised, so it becomes admonition, a lesson, and subtle guidance to increase piety and fear of Allah. A similar verse is ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson for one who fears﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 26].

﴿That﴾ is a reference to the Day of Resurrection, indicated by His saying ﴿the punishment of the Hereafter﴾. ﴿Al-nas﴾ (mankind) is a *maf'ul* whose *fa'il* (agent) is not named (*maf'ul lam yusamma fa'iluhu*, passive object), and its raising is ﴿majmu'﴾ (gathered). Ibn 'Atiyyah permitted that ﴿al-nas﴾ be a *mubtada'* and ﴿majmu'﴾ be a fronted *khabar*, but this is far-fetched, because the pronoun in ﴿majmu'﴾ is singular, and by analogy with its grammatical case it would be *majmu'un*. The expression ﴿majmu' lahu al-nas﴾ (for which mankind is gathered) is a phrase for the gathering (*hashr*). ﴿Mashhud﴾ (witnessed) is general: the first and last generations witness it, of humans, jinn, angels, and animals, according to the majority.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, what is the benefit of choosing the *ism maf'ul* (passive participle) over its verb?" I say: it is because the passive participle indicates the stability of the meaning of gathering for that day, and that it must be an appointed set time for people to be gathered to it, and that it is the thing described by it as a necessary attribute. It is also more firmly established as the attribution of gathering to people, and that they cannot escape it, and there is in it a firmness and stability of description that the verb does not have. The meaning of ﴿mashhud﴾ is "witnessed in it." The prepositional phrase was extended, and the verb was connected to the pronoun, treating it as a *maf'ul bihi* (direct object) by poetic extension, as in the verse:

*And a day we witnessed it, Sulaym and 'Amir.*

The meaning is that the creatures witness the standing place, and no one is absent from it. From this comes the saying: "For so-and-so there is a witnessed gathering," and "a present feast" (*ma'hur*). The day was not described as "witnessed" in itself, as in ﴿whoever of you witnesses the month﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], because the purpose is to describe that day with terror and greatness, and to distinguish it from other days. Its being witnessed in itself would not distinguish it, since it is like all other days in being witnessed.

﴿And We do not delay it﴾, i.e., that day. It was also said that it refers to the recompense, as al-Hawfi said. ﴿Except for a term counted﴾, i.e., for a prior decree that has already been executed, with a limited term that it neither precedes nor lags behind.

*Your palm is a palm that cannot part with a dirham in generosity,*
*and another [palm] gives blood by the sword.*

The meaning: no soul speaks on the day that day comes except by His permission, and this is from the magnitude of awe and terror on that day. Al-Hawfi permitted that ﴿la tukallamu﴾ be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun of the day mentioned earlier in ﴿mashhud﴾, or an adjective, since the noun is indefinite. The estimate is: no soul speaks in it on the day it comes except by His permission.

It may also be that ﴿la tukallamu nafs﴾ is an adjective of ﴿yawma ya'ti﴾, or that ﴿yawma ya'ti﴾ means the time and the hour, not the day itself. His discussion of the *i'rab* (grammatical analysis) of ﴿la tukallamu﴾ seems to be transmitted from al-Hawfi's words.

It was said: the Day of Resurrection is a long day with many stations. In some of them they argue on their own behalf; in some they refrain from speech and are not permitted to speak; in some they are permitted and speak; and in some their mouths are sealed, their hands speak, and their feet testify. The pronoun in ﴿minhum﴾ (of them) refers to mankind in ﴿majmu' lahu al-nas﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the pronoun refers to the people of the standing place, who are not mentioned, but this is known, and because ﴿la tukallamu nafs﴾ indicates it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿minhum﴾ refers to the whole collective implied by ﴿nafs﴾ (soul), since it is a generic noun intended to mean the whole.

Ibn 'Abbas said: the wretched (*shaqi*) is the one for whom wretchedness was written, and the happy (*sa'id*) is the one for whom happiness was written. It was also said: "the punished and the blessed"; "the deprived and the provided." It was said that the pronoun in ﴿minhum﴾ refers to the community (*ummah*) of Muhammad (ﷺ), as mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

﴿That is from the news of the towns which We relate to you; some of them are standing and some are harvested.﴾ ﴿We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves. Their gods, whom they invoked besides Allah, did not avail them in anything when the command of your Lord came, and they added nothing to them but ruin.﴾: The reference of "that" (dhalika) is to what was mentioned earlier about the prophets and their peoples, and the punishments that befell them. That is, that report is some of the reports of the towns.

It is possible that "the towns" refers to the towns of those destroyed peoples mentioned earlier. It is also possible that "the towns" is general, meaning: this report related to you is the habit of cities when they disbelieved, so the contemporary cities are included. The pronoun in "minha" (of them) refers to "the towns."

Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj said: "standing of the walls and collapsed," and this is based on the particular interpretation, that these are the towns of those destroyed nations. Al-Zamakhshari said: some of them remain and some have been effaced, like a crop standing on its stalk and one that has been harvested.

This is the meaning of Qatadah's statement. Qatadah said: "standing of trace and effaced," making the harvesting of the crop a metaphor for annihilation. The poet said:

*And people, in the distribution of death among them,*
*are like a crop: of it, some standing and some harvested.*

Al-Dahhak said: (standing) means "not swallowed by the earth," and (harvested) means "swallowed." Ibn Ishaq said: (standing) means "not yet destroyed," and (harvested) means "destroyed." It was also said: standing means its offspring remain, and harvested means its offspring are cut off. This fits the reading that the estimate is: "that is from the reports of the people of the towns." It was also said that this is by omitting a modifier, meaning: "from the reports of the people of the towns," and this is supported by His saying ﴿and We did not wrong them﴾, so the pronoun returns to that omitted noun.

Al-Akhfash said: *hasid* means *mahsud* (harvested). Its plural is *hasda* and *hisad*, like *marda* and *mirad*. The pattern *fa'la* as a plural of *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul* (passive participle, "object") is typically used for rational beings, like *qatil* and *qatla*.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, what is the position (*mahall*, grammatical place) of this clause? I say: it is a fresh resumptive clause with no grammatical position." Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿minha qa'im﴾ is a *mubtada'* (grammatical subject of a nominal sentence) with a *khabar* (predicate), in the position of a *hal* (circumstantial clause) of the *ha'* in *naqussuhu*. And ﴿hasid﴾ is a *mubtada'* whose *khabar* is omitted, meaning "and of them is the harvested."

What he mentioned is figurative usage (*tajawwuz*), meaning: "We relate to you, while the state of the towns is that." The state is more forceful in warning and in striking an example for those present, i.e., We relate to you some of the reports of the towns, and they are in this state, witnessing Allah's act upon them.

﴿And We did not wrong them﴾, i.e., by destroying them. Rather, We placed on them the punishment they deserved, ﴿but they wronged themselves﴾ by placing disbelief in the place of faith and committing what led to their destruction.

It is apparent that His saying ﴿fa-ma aghnat﴾ (so they did not avail) is a negation, i.e., they did not repel any of Allah's might from them, nor were they of any benefit. (*Yad'una*, "they invoke") is a narration of a state, i.e., those they used to invoke, meaning they worshipped them, or they invoked them: al-Lat, al-Uzza, and Hubal. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿lamma﴾ (when) is governed by *aghnat* (availed). This is based on the view that *lamma* is a time adverb, which is contrary to the school of Sibawayh, since his view is that it is a particle (*harf*) of necessity for necessity. ﴿Amru rabbika﴾ (the command of your Lord) [Hud: 76] means His punishment and vengeance.

﴿And they added nothing to them﴾: the verb is treated as if the subject were rational beings, using the *waw* of the plural pronoun that is for rational beings, because they treated those gods as rational beings in their belief that they benefit, and in their worship of them.

*Tatbib* means loss. Ibn Zayd said: evil. Qatadah said: loss and destruction. Mujahid said: causing loss. It was also said: destruction. All of these are close in meaning. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the form of the idols' increasing *tatbib* can be understood as follows: their hope in them, their trust in them, and their toil in worshipping them occupied their souls from considering the law and its outcome, so punishment and loss befell them. As for their punishment for disbelief being increased because of it beyond the mere worship of idols, that is also possible.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verses 106–108:

﴿As for those who are wretched, they will be in the Fire, having therein groaning and wailing﴾ ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills. Indeed, your Lord is the Doer of what He intends﴾ ﴿And as for those who are made happy, they will be in the Garden, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills — a gift uninterrupted﴾. Al-Dahhak, Muqatil and al-Farra' said: al-zafir (groaning) is the first braying of the donkey, and al-shahiq (wailing) is its last part. It was also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: al-zafir is in the throat, and al-shahiq is in the chest (p-263), also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: al-zafir is the braying of the donkey, and al-shahiq is the neighing of mules.

The accusative of khalidin (abiding) is as a circumstantial state (hal) that is determined (muqaddarah), and ma is a temporal verbal (masdariyyah zarfiyyah) particle, meaning: the duration of the continuance of the heavens and the earth. The intended meaning of this time-specification is eternity, like the saying of the Arabs: "as long as Thabir remains and as long as a star shines." The Arabs used this for eternity without regard to the perishing of Thabir or the star, or their not perishing.

It has been said: the heavens and earth of the Hereafter are meant, which are everlasting necessarily, as indicated by: ﴿On the day when the earth will be replaced by another earth, and the heavens﴾ [Ibrahim: 48], and His saying: ﴿And they have inherited the earth, to dwell in the Garden wherever we wish﴾ [al-Zumar: 74]. And because the people of the Hereafter necessarily need something to bear them and shade them, either a sky which Allah creates, or the Throne shades them, and everything that shades you is a sky.

And it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: indeed the heavens and the earth in the Hereafter will be returned to the light from which they were taken, so they are everlasting forever in the light of the Throne. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿except as your Lord wills﴾ is an exception from the time indicated by His saying ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾. The meaning: except the time which Allah the Exalted wills, so he will not be in the Fire, nor in the Garden. It is possible that this excepted time is the time in which Allah separates the creatures on the Day of Resurrection, if the exception is from being in the Fire and the Garden, because it is a time in which the wretched and the happy are free from entering the Fire or the Garden.

It has been said: it is an exception from the length of the duration, according to what is narrated that Jahannam will be destroyed and its people will perish, and its gates will clap; so they, on this view, abide until their affair reaches this point, and this is an impossible view. What is narrated and transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud and others is that it will be emptied of the Fire; this refers only to the lowest level, which is specific to the disobedient believers, and which is called Jahannam, and the whole was named by it figuratively. It has been said: illa here means "waw" (and), so the meaning of the verse is: "and what Allah wills" [al-An'am: 128], additionally beyond that.

It has been said: illa in this verse means "siwa" (other than), and the exception is disconnected, as you say: "I have with you two thousand dirhams except the thousand which I had lent you," meaning: other than that thousand. So it is as if He said: "abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure," other than what Allah wills in addition to that. This interpretation is supported by His saying, exalted is He, after this: ﴿a gift uninterrupted﴾, and this is the view of al-Farra'. It has been said: other than what is prepared for them of kinds of punishment which are not known, such as the zamharir.

It has been said: an exception from the duration of the heavens and the earth which passed for them in the worldly life. It has been said: in the barzakh between this world and the Hereafter. It has been said: in the intervals which are between them in entering the Fire, since their entry is only in groups after groups.

It has been said: the exception is from His saying "fa-fi al-nar" (then in the Fire), as if He said: "except what your Lord wills of delaying a people from that." This is a view narrated by Abu Nadrah from Jabir, or from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. Then He informed, alerting to the power of Allah, the Exalted, and said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is the Doer of what He intends﴾. End of quote. Abu Mijlaz said: "except what your Lord wills" — that He pardons him with a punishment whose recompense is abiding in the Fire, so He does not cause him to enter the Fire. It has been said: the meaning of ﴿except as your Lord wills﴾ is "as your Lord wills," as in His saying: ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married of women, except what has already passed﴾ [al-Nisa': 22], i.e., as has already passed. Al-Hasan read shuqqu with a damma on the shin, and the majority with a fatha. Ibn Mas'ud, Talhah ibn Musarrif, Ibn Thabbab, al-A'mash, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read su'idu with a damma on the sin, and the rest of the seven and the majority with a fatha. 'Ali ibn Sulayman used to be amazed at al-Kisa'i's reading "sa'idu," despite his knowledge of Arabic; yet this is not surprising, since it is a reading transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud and those mentioned with him. Al-Kisa'i argued with the saying "mas'ud"; it was said: there is no proof in it, since it is said "makan mas'ud fihi" (a place made happy in it), then "fihi" was elided and it became a name. Al-Mahdawi said: whoever reads "sa'idu" it is taken as referring to "mas'ud," and this is rare and weak, since one does not say "sa'adahu Allah"; rather one says "as'adahu Allah."

Al-Tha'labi said: sa'ida and as'ida have the same meaning, and "'ata'an" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: they were given a gift, in the sense of giving (i'ta'), like His saying: ﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17], i.e., causing to grow. The meaning of ﴿ghayra majdhudh﴾ (not cut off): not severed, rather it extends to endlessness.

(p-265) ﴿So do not be in doubt about what these worship. They worship only as their fathers worshipped before. And We will surely give them their portion in full, without reduction.﴾ ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book, but it was disputed. Had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been decided between them. Indeed, they are in disquieting doubt about it.﴾ ﴿And indeed, to each of them your Lord will fully repay their deeds. Indeed, He is Acquainted with what they do.﴾ [Hud: 111] ﴿So remain upright as you have been commanded, and [so too] those who turned back with you, and do not transgress. Indeed, He is Seeing of what you do.﴾ [Hud: 112] ﴿And do not incline toward those who wronged, lest the Fire touch you, and you will have no protectors other than Allah; then you will not be helped.﴾ [Hud: 113] ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in the first hours of the night. Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds. That is a reminder for those who remember.﴾ [Hud: 114] ﴿And be patient, for indeed Allah does not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost.﴾ [Hud: 115] ﴿Why were there not, among the generations before you, people of virtue who would forbid corruption on earth, except a few of those We saved from among them? But those who wronged followed what they had been given in luxury, and they were criminals.﴾ [Hud: 116]

al-Zulfah (a portion of the night): al-Layth said: it is a part of the beginning of the night, and its plural is al-Zulaf. Tha'lab said: al-Zulaf are the first hours of the night, and its singular is zulfah.

Abu 'Ubayda, al-Akhfash and Ibn Qutayba said: al-Zulaf are the hours of the night and its times, and every hour is a zulfah. al-'Ajjaj said:

"A lean she-camel whom weariness from us folded up, and who shunned the folding of nights, zulfa by zulfa."

"Its sky was the crescent moon until it curved back."

The root of the word is from al-Zulfa, which means nearness. It is said: azlafahu fazdalaf, meaning he brought him near and he drew near; and azlafani meaning he brought me close. al-Taraf: blessing. A child is mutraf: his body is pampered. A mutraf is one whom blessing and ease of living have made wanton. al-Farra' said: atraf means he was made accustomed to al-turfah, which is blessing.

﴿So do not be in doubt about what these worship. They worship only as their fathers worshipped before. And We will surely give them their portion in full, without reduction.﴾ (When He, exalted is He, mentioned the accounts of idol worshippers among the earlier nations, and followed that with the mention of the conditions of the wretched and the blessed, He explained to the Messenger (ﷺ) the conditions of the disbelievers of his people, and that they follow their fathers, just as the nations before them followed their fathers in misguidance.

And "these" (ha'ula'): is a reference to the polytheists of the Arabs by agreement, and that their custom is like the custom of the past nations in blind imitation and in turning away from examining the proofs and arguments. This is a consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ) and a promise of retribution against them, since their situation in this is the situation of the past nations, and you have been told of what happened to the past nations of evil outcome.

The comparison in His words ﴿as they worship﴾ means: their state in polytheism is like the state of their fathers without difference. You have learned what befell their predecessors, so something like it will befall them.

(Wa ma ya'budu): is a resumptive clause that functions as a justification for the prohibition against doubt. The ma in (mimma) and in (kama) may be a verbal particle (masdariyyah, meaning "the verb with its subject forms a verbal noun") or it may mean "that which" (alladhi). The majority of reciters read ﴿لَمُوَفُّوهُمْ﴾ with a shadda, from wafa, and Ibn Muhaysin read it without a shadda, from awfa. The word al-nasib (portion) here: Ibn 'Abbas said: what has been decreed for them of good and of evil.

Abu al-'Aliya said: of provision. Ibn Zayd said: of punishment. al-Zamakhshari also said likewise, saying: as We fulfilled to their fathers their portions. And ﴿غَيْرَ مَنقُوصٍ﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from nasibihim, and in my view it is an emphatic circumstantial clause, because fulfilling (tawfiyah) implies completion.

al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say): how is ﴿غَيْرَ مَنقُوصٍ﴾ put in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (p-266) of the portion that is fulfilled? (I say): it is permissible that it be fulfilled while it is deficient, and fulfilled while it is complete.

Do you not see that you say: I fulfilled to him a half of his right, and a third of his right, and his right complete and deficient? End of quotation. This is a fallacy. When one says: I fulfilled to him a half of his right, the fulfilling occurred in the half, and likewise a third of his right, and the meaning is: I gave him the half or the third complete, I did not reduce anything from it.

As for his saying: and his right complete and deficient, as for complete, it is correct, and it is an emphatic circumstantial clause, because fulfilling implies completion. As for "and deficient," it is not said, because it contradicts fulfilling.

The address in ﴿فَلا تَكُ﴾ [Hud: 17] is directed to whoever has been touched by doubt, not to the Messenger. The meaning, and Allah knows best: Say, O Muhammad, to everyone who doubts: do not be in doubt about what these worship, for Allah did not command them to do that. They only followed their fathers in that, imitating them and turning away from the proofs of reason.

﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book, but it was disputed. Had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been decided between them. Indeed, they are in disquieting doubt about it.﴾ When He made clear the insistence of the disbelievers of Makkah on denying monotheism, the prophethood of the Messenger, and the Qur'an that he brought, He explained that the disbelievers of the earlier nations were upon this same wicked course with their prophets. So this is nothing new from those who lived in the time of the Messenger. He gave as an example for this: the sending down of the Torah to Moses, and they disagreed about it.

The Book here is the Torah. Some accepted it and some rejected it, just as these people disagreed about the Qur'an. The apparent reference of the pronoun in "fihi" is to the Book because of its nearness, and it is permissible that it refers to Moses, peace be upon him.

It follows that disagreement about one of them entails disagreement about the other. It is also permissible that (fi) means (ʿala), i.e. "they disagreed about it," and the Children of Israel were more obstinate toward Moses and more contentious against him.

The explanation of ﴿ولَوْلا كَلِمَةٌ سَبَقَتْ مِن رَبِّكَ لَقُضِيَ بَيْنَهُمْ﴾ has already been given. The apparent reference of the pronoun in "baynahum" is to the people of Moses, peace be upon him, since they are the ones who disagreed about it, or about the Book. It was also said: it refers to those who disagreed about the Messenger among his contemporaries.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: that the wording includes them all is better in my view, and this sentence is also part of the consolation for him.

The apparent meaning is the generality of *kull* (all) and its inclusion of both the believer and the disbeliever. Al-Zamakhshari said: the tanwin is a substitute for the omitted genitive complement, meaning "and indeed all of them," and all of those who differ concerning it. Muqatil said: it refers to the disbelievers of this community.

The two Harams (Ibn Kathir and Nafi') and Abu Bakr read *wa-in kullan* with a light *nun* (*in*, pronounced without emphasis). Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, and Hamza read *lamma* with shadda here, in Ya-Sin, and in al-Tariq. All seven readers agreed on the accusative of *kullan*. Thus four readings are conceived in their recitation:

The first: light *in* and light *lamma*, which is the reading of the two Harams.

The second: shadda on both, which is the reading of Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, and Hafs.

The third: light *in* and shadda on *lamma*, which is the reading of Abu Bakr.

The fourth: shadda on *inna* and light *lama*, which is the reading of al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr.

Ubayy, al-Hasan (according to one transmission from him), and Aban ibn Tha'lab read: *wa-in* with light *in*, *kullun* with *raf'* (nominative), *lamma* with shadda. Al-Zuhri and Sulayman ibn Arqam read: *wa-inna kullan lamma* with shadda on the *mim* and tanwin on it, and they did not address the lightening or the shadda of *inna*.

Abu Hatim said: what is in the codex of Ubayy is *wa-inna min kullin illa layuwaffiyannahum*. al-A'mash read: *wa-inna kullun illa*, which is the variant of Ibn Mas'ud. These are four irregular (shadhdh) readings.

As for the first reading, the operation of *in* when light is like its operation when heavy. This issue is disputed. The Kufans held that lightening *in* cancels its governing power, so that it may not govern. The Basrans held that its governing is permissible but rare, except with a pronoun, and so it is not permissible unless it occurs in poetry. This is the correct view, because it is established in the speech of the Arabs. Sibawayh related that a trustworthy informant told him that he heard some Arabs say: *an 'Umaru al-muntaliqu* (indeed 'Umar is the one who sets out). And because this mass-transmitted (mutawatir) reading is established, the Kufans interpreted it otherwise.

As for *lamma*, al-Farra' said: the *lam* in it is the *lam* that enters the predicate of *inna*, and *ma* is a relative pronoun meaning "those who," as in His words: ﴿so marry what is good for you﴾ [al-Nisa': 3]. The clause consisting of the omitted oath and its answer, which is ﴿He will surely pay them in full﴾, is the relative clause of *lamma*, like His saying: ﴿And indeed among you is he who will surely lag behind﴾ [al-Nisa': 72]. This is a good view. Among the uses of *ma* for one who has reason is the saying: *la siyyama Zaydun* with *raf'*, meaning "not especially the one who is Zayd."

It was also said: *ma* is an indefinite qualifying noun, used for one who has reason, and the oath clause with its answer took the place of the qualifying clause, because the meaning is: "And indeed all of them are created with their deeds fully paid." al-Tabari preferred and chose this view.

Abu 'Ali said: the custom is for the *lam* of initiation to enter the predicate, and the predicate here is the oath, and in it there is a *lam* that enters its answer. When the two *lams* and the oath (which is omitted) came together, and they agreed in the wording and in receiving the oath, they were separated by *ma*, just as they separated between *inna* and the *lam*. End of quotation.

It appears from his words that the *lam* in *lamma* is the *lam* that enters the predicate. al-Hawfi explicitly stated that it is the *lam* of *inna*, except that what is transmitted from Abu 'Ali is that the predicate is ﴿He will surely pay them﴾, and his editing of what we have mentioned is that it is the oath and its answer. It was also said: the *lam* in *lamma* is the preparatory *lam* for the oath, *ma* is extra, and the predicate is the oath clause with its answer. In verification, Abu 'Ali's view returns to this view.

As for the second reading, shadda on *inna* and its governing of *kullan* is clear. As for shadda on *lamma*, al-Mubarrad said: this is a grammatical error (lahn); the Arabs do not say *inna Zaydan lamma kharijun*. This is an audacity on the part of al-Mubarrad, as is his habit.

How can a mass-transmitted reading be a grammatical error? The structure of the verse is not like the example he gave, *inna Zaydan lamma kharijun*, which is an error. But in the verse it is not an error. Had he kept silent and said, as al-Kisa'i said: "I do not know what the reading's justification is," he would have been successful. As for others among the grammarians besides these two, they disagreed about its explanation.

Abu 'Ubayd said: its origin is *lamman* with tanwin, and it has been read so. Then from it was formed the pattern *fa'la*, so it became like *tatra*, tanwin being applied because its alif was made for the purpose of *ilhaq* (assimilation to a pattern), like *arta*, and it was denied the diptote (ṣarf) because its alif was made the feminine alif. It is derived from *lammahu*, meaning "I gathered it." The estimate is: "And indeed all of them together will surely pay them," and *jamiʿan* in it has the meaning of emphasis like *kull*. It is not said that this *lamma* is the tanwinated *lamma* stopped on with the alif, because the alif is a substitute for tanwin, and he treated the original as if pausing, because that happens only in poetry.

What Abu 'Ubayd said is far-fetched, for the pattern *fa'la* from *al-lamm* is not known; and for one who inclines *fa'la* there is a requirement that he incline it, and no one inclined it by consensus; and [it is far-fetched] from its being written with a *ya'*, when it is not written with it. It was said: the shadda-ed *lamma* is the light *lama*, and he doubled it in pausing, like your saying: "I saw *farrahan*," meaning *farahan*, and he treated the connected form as the pause. This is very far-fetched, and it was transmitted from al-Mazini.

Ibn Jinni and others said: *illa* occurs only as an extra element, so it is not far-fetched that *lamma* in its meaning occurs as an extra element. End of quotation.

This is a weak view, built upon a weak view concerning *illa*. al-Mazini said: *in* is the light form made heavy, and it is a negator meaning *ma*, just as *in* is lightened while having the meaning of its heavy form, and *lamma* has the meaning of *illa*. This is false, because the heavying of the negating *in* is not known, and because of the accusative of *kullan*, and the negating *in* does not govern the accusative.

It was said: *lamma* has the meaning of *illa*, as in your saying: "I adjure you by God *lamma* you do it," meaning *illa* you do it. al-Hawfi said this, and Abu 'Ali weakened it, saying: because this *lamma* does not leave the oath. End of quotation.

It is not as he mentioned; it does leave the oath. This view is refuted only because it is not a place where *illa* enters: if you said *in Zaydan illa darabtuhu*, it would not be an Arabic construction. It was said: the origin of *lamma* is *laman ma*, where *man* is the relative pronoun, and what follows *ma* is extra, and the *lam* in *lamma* enters the predicate of *inna*, and the relative clause is the oath clause. When *man* was assimilated into the extra *ma*, three *mim*s came together; the middle one was removed, which is the one replaced from the *nun*, so two identical letters came together, and the *mim* of *man* was assimilated into the *mim* of *ma*, and it became *lamma*. This was said by al-Mahdawi.

al-Farra' said, and a group followed him, including Nasr al-Shirazi: the origin of *lamma* is *lamin ma*, where the preposition *min* entered upon *ma*, as in the saying of the poet:

*And indeed we are of those who strike the ram a blow on its head, that throws out the tongue from the mouth.*

Thus it acted in the way it acted in the preceding view. These two views are very weak, for the deletion of the *nun* of *man* is not known, nor the deletion of the *nun* of *min* except in poetry, when it meets the definite article or its like, unassimilated, as in their saying *milmal*, meaning *min al-mal*.

All these explanations are very weak, and the Qur'an is to be held above them. I had myself found an explanation conforming to the rules of Arabic: this *lamma* is the conditional *lamma*, whose verb is apocopated and omitted for the indication of meaning, just as they omitted it in their saying [p. 268]: *qaribtu al-madinata* (I nearly reached the city), and *lamma* (and not yet), meaning *lamma yadkhulha* (and not yet entered it). Likewise here the estimate is: "And indeed all of them, *lamma* [there is no diminution] from the reward of their deeds." What indicates it is His saying: ﴿Your Lord will surely pay them their deeds﴾; when He informed of the negation of diminishing the reward of their deeds, He confirmed it with an oath, saying: ﴿Your Lord will surely pay them their deeds﴾. I had believed I had preceded others to this sound explanation free of artificiality. I mentioned this to one of those who read with me, and he said: Abu Amr and Ibn al-Hajib have mentioned it. Because I had neglected to examine the words of this man, I did not come upon it. Then I saw in the book *al-Tahrir* the transmission of this explanation from Ibn al-Hajib, who said: this *lamma* is the conditional one, whose verb is omitted for the indication upon it, because it is established that its verb may be omitted, as in their saying: "I went out and *lamma* (I had not) travelled," and *lamma* and the like. This is permissible and eloquent. So the estimate is: *lamma yutrakū* (not yet left), because of the indication upon it from the detailed division of the two groups in His saying: ﴿So among them are the wretched and the happy﴾ [Hud: 105], then he mentioned the wretched and the happy and their recompense, then he clarified that with His saying: ﴿Your Lord will surely pay them their deeds﴾. He said: I know of no explanation more similar to this, though people find it far-fetched because the like of it did not occur in the Qur'an. End of quotation.

As for the third and fourth readings, their explanation is understood from the explanation of the two readings before them.

As for the reading of Ubayy and those mentioned with him, *in* is negating, and *lamma* has the meaning of *illa*. The estimate is: "Nothing is every one of them except that, by God, He will surely pay them." *Kullun* is the subject, and the predicate is the oath clause, and its answer is what comes after *lamma*, like the reading of the one who read ﴿And if all of them are gathered, all together﴾ [Ya-Sin: 32] and ﴿No soul but has over it a guardian﴾ [al-Tariq: 4]. No attention is paid to the words of Abu 'Ubayd and al-Farra' denying that *lamma* can have the meaning of *illa*. Abu 'Ubayd said: we have not found this in the speech of the Arabs, and whoever says this must say: "I saw the people *lamma* your brother," meaning "except your brother," and this does not exist.

al-Farra' said: as for the one who makes *lamma* mean *illa*, it is an explanation we do not know, though the Arabs have said with an oath by God: *lamma qumta 'anna* (only if you rise from us), and *illa qumta 'anna*. But as for the exception, we have not transmitted it in poetry. Do you not see that if that were permissible it would be heard in speech: "The people went *lamma* Zayd"? The mass-transmitted reading in His words: ﴿And if all of them [are gathered]﴾ [Ya-Sin: 32] and ﴿No soul but has over it a guardian﴾ [al-Tariq: 4] is a proof against both of them.

That *lamma* has the meaning of *illa* was transmitted by al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and al-Kisa'i. That the Arabs restricted its occurrence to certain structures does not discredit it, nor does it require its generality in the domain of exception, for many a thing is restricted to one structure and not to what resembles it.

As for the reading of al-Zuhri and Ibn Arqam: *lamman* with tanwin and shadda, *lamma* here is a verbal noun from their saying *lamamtu al-shay'*, meaning "I gathered the thing." Its accusative is explained in two ways. The first: that it is an adjective of *kullan*, described by the verbal noun, and *kull* is estimated as governing an indefinite noun, so that the description by an indefinite noun is valid, as it was described in His saying: ﴿devouring the heritage, all of it, devouring﴾ [al-Fajr: 19]. This is Abu 'Ali's explanation. The second: that it is accusative by His saying: ﴿He will surely pay them﴾, after the manner of their saying: *qiyaman la-aqumanna* (standing, I will surely stand) and *qu'udan la-aq'udanna* (sitting, I will surely sit). The estimate is: "a comprehensive payment of their deeds, He will surely pay them." This is Ibn Jinni's explanation. The predicate of *inna* in these two explanations is the oath clause and its answer.

As for what is in the codex of Ubayy, *in* is negating and *min* is extra. As for the reading of al-A'mash, it is clear, and the meaning is: "all that belongs to them." It was said: this sentence contains emphases by *in*, by *kull*, by the *lam* in the predicate, by the oath, by *ma* when it is extra, by the emphatic *nun*, and by the *lam* before it; and that is an exaggeration in promising the obedient and threatening the disobedient. It is followed by the emphasized sentence: ﴿Indeed He is, of what they do, All-Aware﴾. This attribute implies knowledge of what is hidden. Ibn Harmuz read: *bi-ma ta'malūn* (of what you do), in the second-person address.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verses 112–113:**

﴿So be steadfast as you were commanded, and [so too] those who have turned back with you, and do not transgress. Indeed, He is Seeing of what you do.﴾ Ibn 'Uyayna and a group [of scholars] said: its meaning is, "Be steadfast upon the Qur'an." Al-Dahhak said: "Be steadfast through jihad." Muqatil said: "Persist in monotheism (tawhid)." A group said: "Be steadfast in obeying your Lord's command by calling to Him." Ja'far al-Sadiq said: "Be steadfast in conveying what is from Allah, with sincere resolve." Al-Zamakhshari said: "So be steadfast with a steadfastness like the steadfastness you were commanded, upon the straight path of truth, not deviating from it."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "He was commanded to be steadfast while he was already upon it, and it is a command to continuance and firmness. The address is to the Messenger and his companions who turned back from disbelief, and to the rest of the community. The meaning is 'and you were commanded'; it is an address of honour." End of quote. It has also been said that *istaf'ala* here carries the sense of seeking (*talab*), i.e., "seek to remain upon the religion," just as you say *istaghfir*, meaning "seek forgiveness" [p. 269]. ﴿And those who have turned back﴾ is coordinated (*ma'tuf*) with the concealed pronoun in *fastaqim* (be steadfast), and the separating element (the phrase "with you") served as emphasis, so no separate emphatic pronoun was needed.

﴿And do not transgress﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: "[Do not transgress] in the Qur'an, by making lawful and making unlawful what I have not commanded you." Ibn Zayd said: "Do not disobey your Lord." Muqatil said: "Do not mix tawhid with doubt." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Do not go beyond the limits of Allah." Al-Hasan and al-A'mash read *bima ya'malun* (what they do) with *ya* (the third person, the grammatical "they" form), and it is also reported from 'Isa al-Thaqafi. [The meaning is:] "He is Seeing (basir), watching over their deeds, seeing them and recompensing for them."

﴿And do not incline toward those who wronged, lest the Fire touch you, and you have no protectors apart from Allah, then you will not be helped.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning of *rukun* (inclination) is leaning (*al-mayl*). Al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: "Do not flatter the wrongdoers."

Qatada said: "Do not join them." Sufyan said: "Do not draw close to those who wronged." Abu al-'Aliya said: "Do not approve of their deeds." It was also said: "Do not sit with them." Ja'far al-Sadiq said: "﴿Those who wronged﴾: [this refers to] your own selves, for they are wrongdoing," and this resembles the interpretation of the Batiniyya (an esoteric sect). It was also said: "Do not imitate them."

The majority read *tarkanu* with a *fatha* on the *kaf*, and the past tense is *rakina* with a *kasra*, which is the dialect of Quraysh. Al-Azhari said: this is the most eloquent dialect (al-lugha al-fusha).

It is reported from Abu 'Amr: *tarkanu* with a *kasra* on the *ta'*, according to the dialect of Tamim in the imperfect of *'alima*, apart from the *ya'*. Qatada, Talha and al-Ashhab read, and it is reported from Abu 'Umar: *tarkunu* with a *damma* on the *kaf*, from the past *rakana* with a *fatha*, and this is the dialect of Qays and Tamim. Al-Kisa'i and the people of Najd said: *yarkanu* with a *fatha* on the *kaf* is anomalous (shadhdh), being the imperfect of *rakana* with a *fatha*.

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *wa la tarkanu* in the passive voice, from *arkanahu*, meaning he inclined it. The prohibition encompasses: sinking into their desires, attachment to them, keeping their company, sitting with them, visiting them, flattering them, approving of their deeds, imitating them, adopting their outward appearance, casting the eye toward their splendour, and mentioning them in a manner that exalts them. Consider His saying ﴿wa la tarkanu﴾, for *rukun* is slight inclination. And His saying ﴿ilā alladhīna ẓalamū﴾ means "those in whom wrongdoing was found," and He did not say "the wrongdoers" (*al-ẓalimin*). So said al-Zamakhshari.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Its meaning is calm settling toward a thing and approval of it." Abu al-'Aliya said: "*Rukun* is approval." Ibn Zayd said: "*Rukun* is flattery, and *rukun* occurs in both little and much of this."

The prohibition here, derived from the meaning of *rukun*, is against inclining toward them so as to associate with them, down to the lowest degree, such as refraining from rebuking them while being able to do so. The phrase ﴿those who wronged﴾ here refers to the disbelievers, and this is the explicit view of the exegetes (al-mu'awwilin), though by implication it also includes the people of sins. [End of Abu Hayyan's quotation from Ibn 'Atiyya.] Sufyan al-Thawri said: "In Jahannam there is a valley which none inhabits except the reciters (qurra') who visit the kings." Sufyan was asked about a wrongdoer who had come close to death in a desert, whether he should be given a sip of water. He said, "No." It was said to him, "He will die." He said, "Leave him to die."

In a hadith: "Whoever prays for a wrongdoer to remain [alive] has loved that Allah be disobeyed upon His earth." When a brother of his in religion who was mixing with the sultans wrote to al-Zuhri, he sent him a long letter reproaching him with the utmost severity, which is recorded in the tafsir of al-Zamakhshari.

Ibn Wathhab, 'Alqama, al-A'mash, Ibn Musarrif, and Hamza, as reported from him, read ﴿fa-tamassakumu﴾ with a *kasra* on the *ta'* according to the dialect of Tamim. *Al-Massu* (touching) is a metaphor for befalling. The verb is in the subjunctive as an answer to the prohibition (*jawab al-nahy*), and the clause after it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*). The meaning of *min awliya'* ("protectors") is: helpers who are able to prevent you from His punishment.

﴿Then you will not be helped﴾: Al-Zamakhshari said: "Then He will not help you, because it is required by His wisdom that you be punished, and that He not spare you." [He further said:] "If you ask, what is the meaning of *thumma* (then)? I say: its meaning is remoteness (*al-istib'ad*), because help from Allah is remote given that they have merited punishment and His wisdom has decreed it for them." End of quote. These are the words of the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school).

Zayd ibn 'Ali read *thumma la tunsarū* with the *nun* deleted, the verb being in the subjunctive, coordinated with his saying ﴿fa-tamassakum﴾; and the clause is either a circumstantial clause or a parenthetical insertion between the two coordinated elements.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verses 114–115:

﴿And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day and in the first hours of the night. Indeed, good deeds remove misdeeds. That is a reminder for those who remember.﴾ ﴿And be patient, for indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers.﴾ The occasion of its revelation is what is in Sahih Muslim concerning the man who made advances toward a woman who was not lawful to him, and did with her everything short of intercourse, so this was revealed. It has been said: it was revealed before that, and the Messenger ﷺ applied it to the case of this man. A man said: "Is it for him specifically?" He said: "No, rather it is for the people in general." Consider the commands and prohibitions in these verses: the address in the command is ﴿So remain upright as you have been commanded﴾ [Hud: 112], and ﴿establish the prayer﴾ is in the singular outwardly, although what is commanded is general in meaning. The address in the prohibition, ﴿and do not incline﴾ [Hud: 113], is directed to other than the Messenger ﷺ, addressed to his community. Thus, where the matter concerns acts of goodness, the address is directed to him, and where it concerns prohibition of forbidden things, the address turns away from him to others of his community. This is among the sublime eloquences.

There is a difference of opinion as to whether what is commanded regarding its establishment is the obligatory prayers. Its establishment means its continuance. It has been said: performing it in its completeness. It has been said: performing it at its best times. These are the three opinions concerning the saying of Him, the Exalted: "And establish the prayer."

The phrase ﴿طَرَفَيِ النَّهارِ﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time. The "end" of a thing necessarily belongs to that thing, so what appears is that the two ends are the dawn prayer (Subh) and the afternoon prayer (Asr), because they are the two ends of the day. For this reason consensus has been formed, except for one who deviated, that whoever eats or has intercourse after the break of dawn deliberately, that his day is a day of fast-breaking and he is liable for qada' and expiation (kaffarah); and what comes after the break of dawn is part of the day.

Al-Tabari and al-Mawardi claimed consensus that one of the two ends is the dawn prayer, and the disagreement on this is as we shall mention.

Among those who said: they are the dawn prayer and the afternoon prayer were al-Hasan and Qatadah and al-Dahhak, and they said: the "zulaf" are the sunset prayer (Maghrib) and the night prayer (Isha'), and these are not apparent in this verse according to this view, rather they are in other than it. Mujahid and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: the first end is the dawn prayer, and the second is the noon prayer (Zuhr) and the afternoon prayer, and the "zulaf" are the sunset and night prayers, and the dawn prayer is not included in this verse. Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan also said: they are the dawn prayer and the sunset prayer, and the "zulaf" is the night prayer, and the noon and afternoon prayers are not in the verse. It has been said: they are the noon and afternoon prayers, and the "zulaf" are the sunset and night prayers and the dawn prayer, and it seems this speaker took into account the audible and silent recitation.

Ibn Atiyyah chose the view of Mujahid, but making the noon prayer part of the second end is not clear, since noon is the midpoint of the day, and a midpoint is not called an end except by a distant metaphor. Al-Tabari preferred the view of Ibn Abbas: that the two ends are the dawn prayer and the sunset prayer, and sunset cannot be made an end of the day except metaphorically; it is rather an end of the night.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "ghudwah and ashiyyah." He said: the prayer of ghudwah is the dawn prayer, and the prayer of ashiyyah is the noon and afternoon prayers, because what comes after the decline of the sun is ashiyy (evening), and the prayer of the zulaf is the sunset and night prayers, and he ended.

The application of the term ashiy to what comes after the decline does not necessitate that noon be an end of the day, because the command came for establishing prayer at the two ends of the day, not at the morning and evening.

The majority read ﴿وزُلَفًا﴾ with a fatha on the lam. Talhah, Isa al-Basrah, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu Ja'far read it with a damma, as if it were a singular noun. Ibn Muhaysin and Mujahid read it with a sukun, and it is narrated from them: "wa-zulfa" on the pattern fu'la, as an adjective of a feminine singular, since it carries the meaning of a station (manzilah). As for the other readings of the plurals, it means station after station: zulaf is a plural like zulam, zulf is like busr in busr, and zulut is like busr in busrah; so these are collective nouns, and zulfa is like the single unit zulfah. The apparent reading is that "wa-zulafan min al-layl" is coordinated with "ta-rafay al-nahar," coordinating one end with another end. Al-Zamakhshari said: these readings have been mentioned; it is what is near the end of the day from the night. It has been said: zulafan min al-layl and qurban min al-layl, and by this interpretation it should be coordinated with the prayer, meaning: establish the prayer in the day, and establish zulfa from the night, in the sense of prayers by which one draws near to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in part of the night.

The apparent meaning of "good deeds" is general, including the obligatory prayers, the fast of Ramadan, and similar obligations of Islam. The "misdeeds" are specific, namely the minor sins, and the sound hadith supports this: "So long as major sins are avoided." The majority of the early exegetes among the Companions and Successors went to the view that "good deeds" refers to the five prayers, and Uthman took this view when performing ablution while seated on the benches, and this is Malik's interpretation. Mujahid said: good deeds are a man saying: "Subhan Allah, al-hamdu lillah, la ilaha illa Allah, Allahu akbar, la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah al-Ali al-Azim." All of this should be understood as examples in reckoning, and because the five prayers are the greatest of deeds. The minor sins that are removed are, on condition of repentance from them and not persisting in them, and this is the text of the skilled scholars of the principles of jurisprudence. The meaning of their removal is the expiation of minor sins; minor sins have occurred, and the good deeds have removed what was consequent upon them, not that their very reality is removed, since they have already occurred.

Ibn Muhaysin and Mujahid read it with a sukun, and it is narrated from them: "wa-zulfa" on the pattern fu'la, as an adjective of a feminine singular, since it carries the meaning of a station (manzilah). As for the other readings of the plurals, it means station after station: zulaf is a plural like zulam, zulf is like busr in busr, and zulut is like busr in busrah; so these are collective nouns, and zulfa is like the single unit zulfah. The apparent reading is that "wa-zulafan min al-layl" is coordinated with "ta-rafay al-nahar," coordinating one end with another end. Al-Zamakhshari said: these readings have been mentioned; it is what is near the end of the day from the night. It has been said: zulafan min al-layl and qurban min al-layl, and by this interpretation it should be coordinated with the prayer, meaning: establish the prayer in the day, and establish zulfa from the night, in the sense of prayers by which one draws near to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in part of the night.

The apparent meaning of "good deeds" is general, including the obligatory prayers, the fast of Ramadan, and similar obligations of Islam. The "misdeeds" are specific, namely the minor sins, and the sound hadith supports this: "So long as major sins are avoided." The majority of the early exegetes among the Companions and Successors went to the view that "good deeds" refers to the five prayers, and Uthman took this view when performing ablution while seated on the benches, and this is Malik's interpretation. Mujahid said: good deeds are a man saying: "Subhan Allah, al-hamdu lillah, la ilaha illa Allah, Allahu akbar, la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah al-Ali al-Azim." All of this should be understood as examples in reckoning, and because the five prayers are the greatest of deeds. The minor sins that are removed are, on condition of repentance from them and not persisting in them, and this is the text of the skilled scholars of the principles of jurisprudence. The meaning of their removal is the expiation of minor sins; minor sins have occurred, and the good deeds have removed what was consequent upon them, not that their very reality is removed, since they have already occurred.

The meaning may be that performing good deeds acts as a gentle means of abstaining from evil deeds, not that they are an actual cause, as in His saying: ﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 45]. The apparent reading is that the reference in His saying "that" points to the nearest previous mention, which is His saying: ﴿Establish the prayer﴾, meaning, its establishment at these times. ﴿A reminder﴾, i.e., a cause of admonition and remembrance, ﴿for those who remember﴾, i.e., those who take heed. It has also been said that it refers to the report that good deeds remove evil deeds, so that this reminder contains an incitement to doing good deeds. It has also been said that it refers to what preceded of the command to uprightness and establishing the prayer, and the prohibition of transgression and inclining toward the wrongdoers; this is the view of al-Zamakhshari. Al-Tabari said: it refers to the commands and prohibitions in this surah. It has been said that it refers to the Qur'an. It has also been said that the meaning of "reminder" is repentance. Then God, exalted is He, commanded patience in conveying the message and in the hardships endured for the sake of God, after what preceded of the commands and prohibitions, and alerting to the locus of patience, since nothing of what has been commanded or forbidden is completed except by it. He used a general term, His saying: ﴿the reward of the doers of good﴾ [Hud: 115], so that everyone who did good in all the qualities of goodness that require patience is included in it, and also those that may not require it, such as the disposition of one created noble, who does not strain to do good, since it is ingrained in his nature.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "the doers of good are those who pray," as if he looked to the context of the speech. Muqatil said: "they are the sincere." Abu Sulayman said: "the doers of good in their deeds."

﴿Why were there not, among the generations before you, people of residual virtue who forbade corruption on earth, except a few of those whom We saved from among them? And those who did wrong followed what they had been given in luxury, and they were criminals.﴾ "Why ... not" (lawla) here is for urging (al-tahdid), accompanied by the meaning of lamentation and regret that ought to befall human beings over these nations who were not guided. This is like His saying: ﴿Alas for the servants!﴾ [Ya Sin: 30]. "The generations" are the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, and those previously mentioned. "Residual virtue" (baqiyyah) here means goodness, insight, and resolve in religion. Bounty and generosity were called "baqiyyah" because a man retains of what he gives out the best and most excellent part, so it became a proverb for generosity and excellence. Thus one says: "So-and-so is of the baqiyyah of the people," meaning, of their best. By this is explained the verse of the Hamasah:

*If you sin, then there will come to me your baqiyyah (best)*

From this is the saying: "In corners are hidden things, and among men are remnants." It was said "baqiyyah" because laws, states, and the like have their strength at their beginning, then they keep weakening; so whoever remains steadfast in the time of weakness is "the remnant of the first era."

"Baqiyyah" is the form fa'ilah, an intensive active participle. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that baqiyyah means baqwa, like taqiyyah means taqwa," i.e., "there were not among them those with self-preservation and protection of themselves from God's wrath and punishment." A group read (baqiyyatin) with the yā' lightened, as an active participle from baqiya, like shajiyat, fa-hiya shajiyyah. Abu Ja'far and Shayba read (buqyatin) with a damma on the bā' and a sukun on the qāf, on the pattern fu'lah. It was also read (baqyatin) on the pattern fa'lah, for the single occurrence, from baqahu baqyan when he watched him and awaited him. The meaning: "there were not among them people of vigilance and fear of God's vengeance, as if they were waiting for it to befall them out of their apprehension."

"Corruption" here means disbelief and what accompanies it of sins. In this is an alert to this community and an incitement to it to change the wrong. "Except a few" is a disjunctive exception, i.e., "but a few of those whom We saved from among them did forbid corruption, and they were few in comparison with their groups." It cannot be a connected exception while the exhortation keeps its apparent meaning, because the meaning would be corrupted, leading to the conclusion that the saved did not urge forbidding corruption.

According to Sibawayh, the speech with exhortation is obligatory, while others see it as negated in meaning: that there were not among them people of residual virtue. For this reason al-Zamakhshari said, after he prevented it from being connected: "If you say: in their urging to forbid corruption there is the meaning of negating it of them, so it is as if it were said: 'Of the generations, there were not people of residual virtue except a few,' it would be a connected exception and a sound meaning, and its accusative would be on the original basis of exception, although the more eloquent is that it be construed as a substitute," end of quote.

Zayd ibn 'Ali read (illa qalilun) with a nominative, observing that the exhortation includes negation, so he made it a substitute, as is done with explicit negation. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "so there was not," because in interrogation there is a kind of denial. Al-Akhfash refused the exception to be disjunctive. The apparent reading is that those who did wrong are those who abandoned forbidding corruption.

﴿What they had been given in luxury﴾ means what they enjoyed of love of leadership and wealth and seeking the means of a comfortable life, and they abandoned what contained the soundness of their religion. "And followed" (ittaba'a) is a resumptive statement about the condition of these who did wrong, and informs that, together with their abandoning of forbidding corruption, they were criminals, i.e., people of crimes other than that.

Al-Zamakhshari said: if its meaning is "they followed their desires," it would be coordinated with an implied element, because the meaning is "except a few of those whom We saved from among them, who forbade corruption on earth, while those who did wrong followed their desires," so it is coordinated with "forbade." If its meaning is "they followed the consequence of luxury," they said, it is for the circumstance, as if it were said: "We saved the few, while those who did wrong had followed their consequence." He said: "and they were criminals," is coordinated with "had been given in luxury," i.e., "they followed luxury." And that they were criminals is because the follower of desires is steeped in sins, end of quote. So he made "mā" in His saying: ﴿what they had been given in luxury﴾ a verbal-noun (masdariyyah), and for this he estimated it as "they followed luxury." The apparent reading is that it means "the one," because the pronoun in "fīhi" returns to it. He also allowed that it be coordinated with "they followed," i.e., "they followed their desires and were criminals by that." He said: it is also possible that it be an interjection (i'tiraḍ) and a judgment against them that they are a criminal people, end of quote.

This is not called an interjection in the terminology of grammar, because it is the end of a verse, so it is not between two things where one needs the other.

Ja'far ibn Muhammad, al-'Ala' ibn Sayyaba (thus in the Kitab al-Lawami'), and Abu 'Amr in the transmission of al-Ju'fi read (wa-ut'iba'u) with a silent tā', in the passive voice, with an elided genitive (muḍāf) because it is of what is transitive to two objects, i.e., "the recompense of what they had been given in luxury." Al-Zamakhshari said: it is also possible that the meaning in the well-known reading is that they followed the recompense of their luxury, and this is a strong meaning because the deliverance is mentioned first, as if it were said: "except a few of those whom We saved from among them, and the rest perished." ﴿Your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people were doing right﴾: the interpretation of a similar verse was given in al-An'am, except that here it is "to destroy," and this is more emphatic in negation. Because according to the Kufans, the lam was added in the predicate of kana for emphasis, and according to the Basrans, we direct the negation to the omitted predicate to which the lam is attached. And here "while their people were doing right." Al-Tabari said: "with shirk among them, while they were doing right," i.e., doing right in their deeds and conduct, and justice of some of them toward others. That is, there must be disobedience accompanying their disbelief; this is what al-Tabari transmitted. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is weak; its proponent went toward the idea that God gives respite to states in disbelief but does not give them respite in wrongdoing and oppression. If it were reversed it would be sound, i.e., God would not punish a nation for their wrongdoing in their disobediences while they were doing right in faith.

What Ibn 'Atiyya preferred is that the interpretation be: "with wrongdoing from Him, exalted is He above that." Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿and its people doing right﴾ is to declare His essence free of injustice, and to signal that destroying the righteous is injustice, end of quote.

This contradicts the hadith: "Shall we be destroyed while among us are the righteous? He said: Yes, when wickedness increases," and the verse: ﴿Guard against a trial that will not strike only those among you who have done wrong﴾ [al-Anfal: 25].

[p. 273] ﴿Had your Lord willed, He would have made mankind one community, but they will not cease to differ﴾ ﴿except those whom your Lord has shown mercy. For that He created them, and the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: "I will fill Hell with jinn and mankind together."﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: He means that they are compelled to be people of one religion, which is the religion of Islam, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, this community of yours is one community﴾ (21:92). This is a statement that implies the negation of compulsion, and that He did not force them to agree upon the religion of truth. Rather, He gave them the choice (ikhtiyar), which is the basis of moral responsibility (taklif). So some of them chose the truth and some chose falsehood, and so they differed. ﴿But they will not cease to differ﴾ ﴿except those whom your Lord has shown mercy﴾: except people whom God guided and treated with kindness, so they agreed upon the religion of truth without differing concerning it. End of quotation. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila (I'tizal, the rationalist theological school). Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada said: "one community of believers," so that no disbelief would occur among them, but He, exalted is He, did not will that. Al-Dahhak said: "Had He willed, He would have placed them upon guidance or misguidance." The apparent meaning of His words ﴿but they will not cease to differ﴾ is that it is from the difference which is the opposite of agreement, and that the meaning is: concerning truth and falsehood, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Mujahid said: concerning religions. Al-Hasan said: concerning provisions and conditions, through some of them being made subservient to others. 'Ikrima said: concerning desires. Ibn Bahr said: the intended meaning is that some of them succeed others, so that the later one is a successor to the earlier one. He said: and from this is their saying, "ma ikhtalafa al-jadidan" (the two renewals never alternated), meaning: one of them succeeded the other. ﴿Except those whom He has shown mercy﴾ is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil) from His words ﴿but they will not cease to differ﴾. There is no necessity that it be in the sense of "but" (lakin), which would make it a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), as al-Hawfi held. The pronoun in His words ﴿For that He created them﴾ refers to the verbal noun implied by ﴿differing﴾, as the poet said: "When he forbids the fool, he rushes toward it." So the pronoun refers to the verbal noun implied by the active participle, as if it were said: "For difference He created them." This would involve an elided genitive construction (mudaf mahdhuf), meaning: "For the fruit of difference, namely wretchedness and happiness, He created them." What indicates this elided word is that it is established from the rule of the Shari'a that God created a creation for happiness and a creation for wretchedness, and then facilitated for each what they were created for, and this is explicit in the authentic hadith.

In verification, this lam is the lam of result (lam al-sayrura) in that elided word, or it is the lam of result without that elided word, meaning: He created them so that their affair would end up in difference. This does not conflict with His words ﴿I did not create jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ (51:56), because the meaning of that is the command to worship. Mujahid and Qatada said: "that" is a reference to the mercy included in His words ﴿except those whom your Lord has shown mercy﴾, and the pronoun in "He created them" refers to those who received mercy. Ibn 'Abbas, whom al-Tabari also chose, said: the reference by "that" is to both difference and mercy together. On this view, a singular demonstrative is used to refer to two things, as in His words ﴿neither old nor young, but between that﴾ (2:68), meaning between the old and the virgin. The pronoun in "He created them" refers to both categories: the excepted and the excepting. There is nothing in this sentence to which the pronoun can refer except difference, as al-Hasan and 'Ata' said, or mercy, as Mujahid and Qatada said, or both, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Interpreters have strayed far in assigning anything other than these three. It was reported that it refers to what follows it, and that there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it, meaning: "And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: I will fill Hell with jinn and mankind together, and for that He created them," meaning: for filling Hell with them. This is very far from the constructions of Arabic speech. It was said: it refers to witnessing that Day, the witnessed Day. It was said: it refers to His words ﴿Among them are the wretched and the happy﴾ (11:105). It was said: it refers to the fact that one group will be in Paradise and one group in the Blaze. It was said: it refers to His words ﴿forbidding corruption on earth﴾ (11:116). It was said: it refers to worship. It was said: (p. 274) it refers to Paradise and Hell. It was said: it refers to happiness and wretchedness. Al-Zamakhshari said: "for that" refers to what the speech indicated at the beginning, namely the empowerment and choice from which difference results: He created them so that He would reward the one who chooses the truth for his good choice and punish the one who chooses falsehood for his bad choice. End of quotation. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila. Were it not that these sayings have been recorded in the books of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis), I would have turned away from mentioning them entirely.

﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled﴾: that is, His decree was carried out and His command was realized. The lam in "la-amla'anna" (I will surely fill) is the one introducing an oath, or the clause before it has been given the meaning of an oath, as in His words ﴿And when God took the covenant of the prophets﴾ (3:81), then He said ﴿you shall surely believe in Him﴾ (3:81).

"Al-jinna" and "al-jinn" have one meaning. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the ha' in it is for emphasis (mubalagha), and although "al-jinn" applies to a single being, "al-jinna" is its collective noun.

Thus it is among those cases in which the singular is without ha', and its collective takes ha', according to the statement of some Arabs: "kam'" for the singular and "kam'a" for the collective (both meaning truffle).

What indicates this elided word is that it is established from the rule of the Shari'a that God created a creation for happiness and a creation for wretchedness, and then facilitated for each what they were created for, and this is explicit in the authentic hadith.

In verification, this lam is the lam of result (lam al-sayrura) in that elided word, or it is the lam of result without that elided word, meaning: He created them so that their affair would end up in difference. This does not conflict with His words ﴿I did not create jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ (51:56), because the meaning of that is the command to worship. Mujahid and Qatada said: "that" is a reference to the mercy included in His words ﴿except those whom your Lord has shown mercy﴾, and the pronoun in "He created them" refers to those who received mercy. Ibn 'Abbas, whom al-Tabari also chose, said: the reference by "that" is to both difference and mercy together. On this view, a singular demonstrative is used to refer to two things, as in His words ﴿neither old nor young, but between that﴾ (2:68), meaning between the old and the virgin. The pronoun in "He created them" refers to both categories: the excepted and the excepting. There is nothing in this sentence to which the pronoun can refer except difference, as al-Hasan and 'Ata' said, or mercy, as Mujahid and Qatada said, or both, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Interpreters have strayed far in assigning anything other than these three. It was reported that it refers to what follows it, and that there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it, meaning: "And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: I will fill Hell with jinn and mankind together, and for that He created them," meaning: for filling Hell with them. This is very far from the constructions of Arabic speech. It was said: it refers to witnessing that Day, the witnessed Day. It was said: it refers to His words ﴿Among them are the wretched and the happy﴾ (11:105). It was said: it refers to the fact that one group will be in Paradise and one group in the Blaze. It was said: it refers to His words ﴿forbidding corruption on earth﴾ (11:116). It was said: it refers to worship. It was said: (p. 274) it refers to Paradise and Hell. It was said: it refers to happiness and wretchedness. Al-Zamakhshari said: "for that" refers to what the speech indicated at the beginning, namely the empowerment and choice from which difference results: He created them so that He would reward the one who chooses the truth for his good choice and punish the one who chooses falsehood for his bad choice. End of quotation. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila. Were it not that these sayings have been recorded in the books of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis), I would have turned away from mentioning them entirely.

﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled﴾: that is, His decree was carried out and His command was realized. The lam in "la-amla'anna" (I will surely fill) is the one introducing an oath, or the clause before it has been given the meaning of an oath, as in His words ﴿And when God took the covenant of the prophets﴾ (3:81), then He said ﴿you shall surely believe in Him﴾ (3:81).

"Al-jinna" and "al-jinn" have one meaning. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the ha' in it is for emphasis (mubalagha), and although "al-jinn" applies to a single being, "al-jinna" is its collective noun.

Thus it is among those cases in which the singular is without ha', and its collective takes ha', according to the statement of some Arabs: "kam'" for the singular and "kam'a" for the collective (both meaning truffle).

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 11, verses 120–122:**

﴿And We relate to you of the news of the messengers that by it We strengthen your heart. And there has come to you in this the truth, and an admonition and a reminder for the believers.﴾ The apparent meaning is that *kullan* (كُلًّا, "all of them") is the direct object (maf'ul bih), its governing verb is *naqussu* ("We relate"), and the tanwin (التنوين, nunation) is a substitute (ʿiwad) for an omitted noun. The estimated meaning is: "Every report (nabaʾ) that We relate to you." The phrase *min anbaʾi al-rusul* ("of the news of the messengers") is in the position of a qualifier (sifa) to *kullan*, since *kullan* is, in estimation, an idafa (إضافة, construct phrase) to an indefinite noun. *Ma* (ما) is a relative complement (sila), as it is in the verse ﴿little do you remember﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 3]. It has been said that it may also be a substitute (badal), or the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject, meaning: "it is what We strengthen [your heart with]," in which case *ma* means "that which" (alladhi), or it may be a verbal noun (masdariyya).

They permitted *kullan* to be in the accusative as an absolute object (masdar), with *ma nuthabbitu* ("that by which We strengthen") as the direct object of *naqussu*, as if it were said: "And We relate to you the thing by which We strengthen your heart, every kind of relating."

They also permitted that *kullan* be an indefinite noun meaning "entirely" (jamiʿan), and in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the object *ma*, or of the genitive pronoun in *bihi* (بِهِ), according to the view of those who permit placing the circumstance of a prepositional genitive before it. The estimated meaning is: "And We relate to you of the news of the messengers the things by which We strengthen your heart, entirely," that is, those that strengthen your heart entirely.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: *nuthabbitu* (نُثَبِّتُ) means "We calm" (nusakkinu). al-Dahhak said: "We firm up" (nashuddu). Ibn Jurayj said: "We strengthen" (nuqawwi).

The strengthening of the heart comes through what happened to the prophets, peace be upon them, and to their believing followers, and what they suffered from their deniers of harm. In all of this there is a model for them, since sharing in difficult matters eases what a person suffers of harm. Then, the informing of what befell their deniers of punishments that uprooted them, with various kinds of torment: drowning, wind, earthquake, and sinking into the earth, and other things. This brings tranquility and comfort to the soul, namely that God may strike those who denied the Messenger ﷺ with punishment as it befell the deniers of the messengers. It is also an announcement to him, peace be upon him, of a good outcome for him and his followers, as it happened for the messengers and their followers.

The indication in His saying "in this" (فِي هَذِهِ) refers to the reports of the messengers which God related to him, that is, the true and right report which corresponds to what happened, with no alteration or distortion, as some historians transmit parts of it.

"An admonition" (مَوْعِظَةٌ): that is, a warning and a deterrent for its hearer, and "a reminder for the one who believes," since admonition and reminder benefit only the believer, as in His saying ﴿And remind, for the reminder benefits the believers﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 55], and His saying ﴿He who fears will be reminded﴾ [al-Aʿla: 10] ﴿and the most wretched will avoid it﴾ [al-Aʿla: 11].

Ibn ʿAbbas said: the indication is to the surah and the verses in which there is a reminder of the stories of the nations, and this is the view of the majority (al-Jumhur, الجمهور). The reason for specifying this surah by describing it as "the truth," although the whole Qur'an is truth, is that this implies the meaning of a threat to the disbelievers and an alert to the observer. That is: "There has come to you in this surah the truth which struck the wrongdoing nations." This is like how it is said at times of hardship: "the truth has come," even though the truth comes in other than hardship and in other than one way, and "the truth has come" is not used in that sense.

al-Hasan and Qatada said: the indication is to the life of this world. Qatada said: "the truth" is prophethood. It has been said: it is an indication to the surah together with its counterparts.

﴿And say to those who do not believe: "Act according to your position; indeed we are acting. And wait; indeed we are waiting."﴾ "Act" (اعْمَلُوا) is an imperative form whose meaning is threat and warning, and the address is to the people of Mecca and others.

"According to your position" (عَلى مَكانَتِكم): that is, your direction and your state in which you are. It has been said: "Act to destroy me according to your ability." "And wait for us, the calamities; indeed we are waiting for what resembles the punishments God has recounted, which descended upon your likes, to descend upon you." It may be that this is a command to peaceful disengagement (muwadaʿa, مُوادَعَة), and for this reason it has been said that these two verses are abrogated (mansukhatan, منسوختان, by naskh). It has also been said that they are firm (muhkamatan, مُحْكَمَتانِ, not abrogated), and they are for threat and warning, while the war is ongoing.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 11, verse 123:

﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and to Him the whole matter is returned. So worship Him and rely upon Him. And your Lord is not unaware of what you do.﴾

Nothing of your deeds is hidden from Him, and no created being has any share in knowledge of the unseen. Nafi' and Hafs read (yurja'u) in the passive voice, and (al-amru kulluhu) refers to their affair and your affair, so that He avenges you upon them. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "He knows what is hidden in the heavens and the earth; He attributed the unseen (al-ghayb) to them by way of extension (tawassu'an)." End of quotation. The first clause indicates that His knowledge encompasses all existents, both universal and particular, present and absent; for if His knowledge encompasses what is absent, then it encompasses what is present, since His knowledge, exalted is He, does not vary.

The second clause indicates the all-penetrating power and the will.

The third clause indicates the command to single out with worship, both bodily and of the heart, the One who possesses these attributes; and worship (ibadah) is the first of the ranks by which the servant adorns himself.

The fourth clause indicates the command to place one's trust (tawakkul) in Him, and it is the last of the ranks; for by the light of worship he perceived that all existents are suspended (ma'dhuqah) from Allah, the Exalted, and that He alone is the One who disposes of all of them, with none of His creation sharing with Him in any of them. So he entrusted himself to Him, the Exalted, and renounced all else that is imagined to be a cause in any of them.

The fifth clause includes an alert to recompense, so that He neglects neither the obedience of the obedient nor disregards the state of the rebellious. Al-Sahibani, Hafs, Qatadah, al-A'raj, Shaybah, Abu Ja'far and al-Jahdari read (ta'malun) with the feminine-second-person-address (ta' al-khitab), because before it is (i'malu 'ala makanatikum). The rest of the seven read it with ya' in the third person (al-ghaybah); and differing readings are reported from al-Hasan and 'Isa ibn 'Umar.
